name: avatar
title: Avatar
description: A person or entity's image, falling back to initials when there is none.

props.name: name
props.description: The person or entity's name: both the fallback initials and the accessible name.
props.summary: The person or entity's name. Required — it is both the fallback initials and the accessible name.
use: Always. The name is what makes the fallback possible and the image describable.
dont: Passing an email or a user id. Initials derived from `a.hartley@` are not initials, and the accessible name would be an address.
props.a11y: Used as the image's `alt` when `decorative` is not set. When the image is missing, the initials are shown but the full name is still what is announced — a screen reader should never hear 'AH'.

props.name: src
props.description: Image URL. Omit, or let it fail, to fall back to initials.
props.summary: Image URL. Omit, or let it fail, to fall back to initials.
use: A real photo or logo. The fallback is automatic, so there is no need to branch on whether one exists.

props.name: size
props.description: Diameter, from the control scale so an avatar lines up with the controls beside it.
props.summary: Diameter, from the `size.control.*` scale so an avatar lines up with the controls beside it.
dont: Mixing sizes within one stack of avatars — they read as a set.

props.name: decorative
props.description: Marks the avatar as redundant to a name already on screen.
props.summary: Marks the avatar as redundant to a name already on screen.
use: An avatar immediately beside the person's name in a row — announcing it again is noise.
dont: Anything standing alone. Without adjacent text the avatar is the only thing identifying the person, so hiding it removes that identification entirely.
props.a11y: Renders `aria-hidden` with an empty `alt`. The `name` is still required, because it still produces the initials.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the avatar's wrapper.
use: Placing the component in its surrounding layout — a span, a width, a margin the parent cannot express.
dont: Overriding the size — the three steps are the scale, and a fourth written in a component's CSS is the drift the scale exists to prevent.
Restyling the component's internals through descendant selectors. Those are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer somewhere the contract cannot see.

usage.case: A photo with its name beside it
usage.when: A row in a member list, where the name is already text.
usage.example: Ada Hartley
usage.notes: `decorative` because the name is right there — announcing it twice is noise. Note `name` is still required: it is what produces the initials if the photo fails to load.

usage.when: An avatar in a toolbar or a stack, with no adjacent name.
usage.example: <Avatar name="Ada Hartley" src={user.photo} />
usage.notes: Not decorative: the avatar is the only thing identifying this person, so it carries the name.

usage.when: A user who has not uploaded a photo — which is most of them.
usage.example: <Avatar name="Ada Hartley" />
usage.notes: Initials are shown and the full name is announced. There is nothing to branch on: omitting `src`, and an `src` that 404s, land in the same place.

decisions.decision: No drawn edge on the circle
decisions.why:
It had one, because the fallback sits on theme.bg.muted and vanished against any container using that same tone — unavoidable while the background ladder had four names and three distinct values, and sections had taken theme.bg.muted for want of a usable theme.bg.subtle. With subtle given a tone of its own, a section band and a placeholder circle are different colours and the ring bought nothing; on a small circle it read as a border round a border.

The remaining case, stated because it is real rather than hypothetical: an avatar placed directly on a theme.bg.muted surface still has no visible edge. Sections use theme.bg.subtle now, so that is an unusual placement — but it is the one to remember, and the separation is modest everywhere else too (1.26:1 on a surface).

base.summary: A circular image, falling back to initials on the most recessed surface.

tokens.size: size.control.md, with the sm and lg steps at the other sizes — an avatar lines up with the controls beside it, which is the whole reason it borrows the control scale
tokens.fallback background: theme.bg.muted — the most recessed surface, so initials read as a placeholder rather than a filled badge
tokens.fallback color: theme.fg.secondary — the pairing the muted background documents for text; theme.fg.muted falls to AA-large there
tokens.image fit: cover, so a non-square photo is cropped rather than squashed — a layout fact, not a token
tokens.background: theme.bg.muted — the most recessed step, so initials read as a placeholder rather than a filled badge. No drawn edge: it had one only because a section band and this fill used to be the same colour, which theme.bg.subtle having a tone of its own has fixed

name: badge
title: Badge
description: A small inline label for a status, a count, or a category.

props.name: children
props.description: The badge's text.
props.summary: The badge's text.
dont: A sentence. A badge that wraps is a Notice wearing the wrong component.

props.name: variant
props.description: Which role's tone the badge wears.
props.summary: Which role's tone the badge wears.
use: `neutral` for a count or a category — the default, and right whenever the badge is not reporting health.
`success` / `warning` / `danger` only for actual status, where the colour is telling the reader something the text also says.
dont: Colour as decoration. Five badges in five colours that mean nothing teaches readers to ignore the colour on the one that does.
`danger` for 'important'. It means something is wrong.
props.a11y: Every variant uses its role's subtle background with that role's foreground — never the saturated `bg`, which is a non-text indicator tone. The text carries the meaning; colour only reinforces it, so a badge is never colour-only.

props.name: dot
props.description: Renders a status dot before the text.
props.summary: Renders a status dot before the text.
use: A status badge in a dense table, where the dot is findable at a glance and the text confirms it.
dont: A dot with no text. A bare coloured dot is colour-only information, which is exactly what the variant contract forbids.
props.a11y: Decorative and `aria-hidden` — it repeats what the text already says.

usage.when: The commonest case: a number qualifying something next to it.
usage.example:
<Button>
  Messages
  <Badge>3</Badge>
</Button>
usage.notes: Neutral by default: a count is not a status, and colouring it would imply something about the number.

usage.case: A status in a table row
usage.when: Reporting health, where the colour reinforces text that already says it.
usage.example: <Badge variant="danger" dot>Failed</Badge>
usage.notes: The dot is decorative and aria-hidden. Removing it would lose nothing for a screen reader, which is the test of whether a visual flourish is safe.

usage.when: The text is a sentence explaining something.
usage.example: <Badge variant="warning">Your trial ends in three days, renew to keep your data</Badge>
usage.notes: Don't. That is a Notice: it has room for the sentence, a heading, and somewhere to put the action. A badge that wraps onto two lines has already stopped being a badge.

neutral.summary: The default: a count or a category, saying nothing about health.

tokens.color: theme.fg.secondary — verified on that background at AA
tokens.block-size: size.icon.lg — a badge is glyph-height, not control-height; it sits inside a line of text rather than beside a button
tokens.font-weight: type.control.weight — heavier than the text around it, because a badge has to be found before it is read
tokens.dot size: space.gap.sm — a dot is a mark, not a glyph, so it takes a spacing step rather than the icon scale

accent.summary: A category the brand wants noticed, still not a status.

tokens.color: theme.accent-role.fg — a verified pairing on that tint
tokens.block-size: size.icon.lg — a badge is glyph-height, not control-height; it sits inside a line of text rather than beside a button
tokens.font-weight: type.control.weight — heavier than the text around it, because a badge has to be found before it is read
tokens.dot size: space.gap.sm — a dot is a mark, not a glyph, so it takes a spacing step rather than the icon scale

tokens.color: theme.success-role.fg — never theme.success-role.bg, which is a non-text indicator tone that fails contrast under white

tokens.dot size: space.gap.sm — a dot is a mark, not a glyph, so it takes a spacing step rather than the icon scale

warning.summary: Degraded, expiring, needs attention but not broken.

tokens.color: theme.warning-role.fg — same reason as success: the saturated bg carries no text

name: bottom-nav
title: Bottom Nav
description: Three to five top-level destinations in a bar held to the bottom of a narrow viewport.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: items
props.summary: The destinations, in the order they are read: each `{ label: string; href: string; icon: LucideIcon; current?: boolean; badge?: { count?: number; label: string }; onClick?: (event) => void }`.
use: Three to five top-level sections of the app — the places a reader moves between constantly, from anywhere.
`current: true` on exactly one item, the section the reader is in, including when they are on a page inside it.
`onClick` to route client-side; `href` is still required, so the item is still a link.
dont: Actions. 'Compose' or 'New post' is not a place — it is a FAB, or a Button in the TopNav's actions.
A sixth item, or a 'More' item. Past five, use MobileNav.
A badge as decoration. If the number is not something the reader acts on, leave it out — a badge on every item is the same as a badge on none.
props.a11y: Each item's `label` is its link's accessible name, and the badge's `label` is appended to it. `current` becomes `aria-current="page"`, which is the only cue that is not visual.

props.name: label
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: A different name from any other `<nav>` on the page that is visible at the same time.
dont: The word 'navigation'. The landmark already announces itself as navigation, so 'Main navigation' is read as 'Main navigation navigation'.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-label` on the `<nav>`. The default matches TopNav's, on the expectation that only one of the two is displayed at any width — if both are visible together, name them apart.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the `<nav>`, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Hiding it at the widths where the layout shows a rail or a TopNav instead, with `display: none`.
dont: `position: fixed`. The bar is sticky so it reserves its own space; fixing it puts the page's last screenful under it.
Shrinking the items' block size. The target height is the one thing this component exists to guarantee.

usage.case: An app's four top-level sections on a phone
usage.when: The common case: a handful of places the reader moves between from anywhere in the app, at widths too narrow for a rail.
usage.example:
<BottomNav
  items={[
    { label: "Home", href: "/", icon: Home, current: true },
    { label: "Search", href: "/search", icon: Search },
    { label: "Inbox", href: "/inbox", icon: Inbox, badge: { count: 3, label: "3 unread messages" } },
    { label: "Profile", href: "/me", icon: User },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: Rendered as the last child of the page's column so it sticks to the bottom without covering anything. The badge's `label` is what a screen reader hears; the `3` is only what a sighted reader sees.

usage.case: The same destinations as a TopNav, at a different width
usage.when: A responsive app whose banner carries its navigation on a wide viewport and moves it to the bottom on a narrow one.
usage.example:
<TopNav items={sections} className="app-top-nav" />
<main>{children}</main>
<BottomNav items={sections} className="app-bottom-nav" />
usage.notes: The page's own media query sets `display: none` on whichever is not in use. Both carry the default name `Main`, which is correct only because they are never displayed together — `visibility: hidden` or an off-screen position would leave two landmarks with the same name in the accessibility tree.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: switching panels
usage.when: The bar's buttons swap what is shown in one region of a single page, and the URL does not change.
usage.example: <BottomNav items={[{ label: "Map", href: "#", icon: Map }, { label: "List", href: "#", icon: List }]} />
usage.notes: Don't. `href="#"` is the giveaway: nothing is being navigated to. Choosing which content is shown is Tabs, and two views of the same data is a SegmentedControl.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: seven sections
usage.when: An app with more top-level destinations than fit in a thumb's width.
usage.example: <BottomNav items={sevenSections} />
usage.notes: Don't, and don't add a 'More' item either. That is MobileNav, whose drawer holds a SideNav with as many grouped sections as the app needs.

behavior.summary: A `<nav>` landmark holding a list of links, each with an icon and a visible label, held to the bottom of the viewport. No primitive: links need no keyboard model beyond Tab, which is the point of rendering them as links.

decisions.decision: It is navigation, not tabs — on the web
decisions.why: iOS calls this a tab bar and that name is why `tab-bar` resolves ambiguously here. But on the web each destination is a page with an address: following one changes the URL, the back button undoes it, and it can be opened in a new tab. That is a link, and a row of links is a `<nav>`. `role="tablist"` would promise a panel on the same page and arrow-key movement between tabs, neither of which exists — the same mistake TopNav's contract names for `role="menu"`. If choosing an item reveals a panel rather than loading a page, it is Tabs, which can be drawn at the bottom of the screen and is still a tablist. `tab-bar` stays an alias of both BottomNav and Tabs, so the lookup commands report it as ambiguous and refuse to guess (decision C12, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Three to five items, and no 'More' overflow item
decisions.why: Fewer than three is not a navigation bar — two destinations are a SegmentedControl or a link. More than five shrinks every target below a usable width on a 320px viewport and turns the labels into ellipses. A 'More' item that opens a sheet of the rest hides the overflow behind a destination that is not a destination, and the reader's current page can end up inside it with nothing in the bar marked current. Past five, the app has outgrown this pattern and the answer is MobileNav, which holds a SideNav. The type cannot count an array, so the React component warns in development when the count is outside 3–5 rather than truncating.

decisions.decision: Every item has an icon and a visible label, always
decisions.why: `icon` and `label` are both required, and there is no option to hide labels on the items that are not current — Material's 'shifting' mode. A glyph alone has to be learned, and on touch there is no hover to learn it from; this system has no Tooltip, and SideNav's contract already declined to ship an icon-only rail for exactly that reason. The label is also the link's accessible name, so it cannot be optional without the name becoming an `aria-label` that a sighted reader never sees and a translator might forget.

decisions.decision: The current page is stated per item, as in TopNav and SideNav
decisions.why: Only the caller's router knows whether /inbox/42 counts as being on /inbox. `current` on the item renders `aria-current="page"` and the current treatment; nothing here matches paths. Rows carry an optional `onClick` for client-side routing and still require a real `href`, for the reason TopNav's contract gives: it is what makes the item a link.

decisions.decision: Sticky to the bottom of the page, not fixed
decisions.why: A `position: fixed` bar is lifted out of the flow, so the last screenful of content scrolls under it and every page has to reserve padding equal to a height it does not know — which changes with the safe-area inset. `position: sticky` with `inset-block-end: 0`, rendered as the last child of the page's scrolling column, holds the bar to the bottom of the viewport while the page scrolls and still occupies its own space in the flow, so nothing is ever hidden under it. The cost is a placement rule: it must be the last child of a column that is at least the viewport's height (`min-block-size: 100dvh` — dynamic viewport units, because `vh` is the large viewport and would push the bar below a visible mobile address bar).

decisions.decision: It never hides on scroll
decisions.why: A bar that slides away when the reader scrolls down moves its targets out from under the thumb that was about to use them, and brings them back at an unpredictable moment. It also makes the navigation landmark appear and disappear for a screen-reader user whose virtual cursor never scrolled at all. The vertical space it saves is a few percent of a phone screen.

decisions.decision: It does not decide when it applies
decisions.why: MobileNav's rule, for the same reason: the breakpoint at which a layout swaps a rail or a TopNav for this bar is the layout's decision, and a component that hid itself with its own media query would fight the page's. When both this and a TopNav carry the same destinations at different widths, the hidden one must be `display: none` — not merely off-screen — so the page does not expose two navigation landmarks with the same name. `label` exists so the two can be told apart when both are genuinely visible.

decisions.decision: Safe-area insets are read from `env()`, not from a token
decisions.why: `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` is a measurement of the device — where the home indicator is — not a design decision, so there is no value a token could hold and nothing a theme could change. What IS a decision is the minimum air when the inset is zero, and that is `space.1`, through `max()`. The page owes one thing in return: `<meta name="viewport" content="…, viewport-fit=cover">`, without which every inset reads as zero and the bar sits under the home indicator's gesture area on a notched phone.

decisions.decision: Touch target: size.target.min
decisions.why: The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: A badge carries its own words
decisions.why: A count of 3 next to 'Inbox' tells a sighted reader 'three unread'; a screen reader reading the link would hear 'Inbox 3', which says nothing about what the three are. So an item's `badge` is `{ count?: number; label: string }`, where `label` is the full phrase — '3 unread messages' — appended to the link's accessible name through visually hidden text, and the visible count is `aria-hidden`. With no `count` it renders a dot, which is the same mark with no number to show; `label` is still required, because a dot that means nothing to a screen reader means nothing at all. A count over 99 renders `99+`, and `label` is where the real number goes.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: On the web it renders `<nav aria-label={label}>` holding a `<ul role="list">` of `<li>`, each with an `<a href>` that carries `aria-current="page"` when current. (`role="list"` is explicit because Safari drops list semantics from a list styled `list-style: none`.) On React Native there is no address bar and no link, and the platform convention is the one VoiceOver and TalkBack announce for UITabBar and BottomNavigationView: a `View` with `accessibilityRole="tablist"` holding a `Pressable` per item with `accessibilityRole="tab"` and `accessibilityState={{ selected: current }}`, so it is read 'Inbox, tab, 1 of 4, selected'. That divergence is deliberate — each platform gets the role its readers already know. Web-only: `href`, `onClick` (a DOM `MouseEvent`), and `className`. Native-only, when that package exists: `onPress` on the item in place of `href`, and the safe-area inset read from `useSafeAreaInsets()` rather than `env()`. There is no gesture in this component, so nothing needs a non-gesture equivalent. Rata-drawn, not the OS tab bar (decision N5): `UITabBar` and `BottomNavigationView` belong to a navigator, and `@rata/native` does not couple to one (decision N3), so the bar is a drawn `View` driven by each item's `onPress` and `current`, carrying the tab roles those OS bars announce. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: The bar. Separated from the content by a rule rather than a shadow: it is part of the page's frame, in the same plane as the content it sits under, and theme.elevation.raised documents a border as the way to separate two things in one plane.

tokens.position: sticky, inset-block-end space.0 — see the decision on sticky rather than fixed
tokens.padding-block-end: max(space.1, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) — the home indicator's inset on a notched phone, and a step of air everywhere else
tokens.padding-inline: max(space.0, env(safe-area-inset-left)) and max(space.0, env(safe-area-inset-right)) — a phone in landscape puts the notch on an inline edge
tokens.item layout: one row; every item takes an equal share of the inline size, so the targets do not resize with their labels

item.summary: One destination: an icon over a visible label, the whole column the target.

tokens.icon size: size.icon.lg — a standalone glyph at the scale's largest step, the size at which it renders unscaled
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

current.summary: The page you are on. Marked by a shape as well as a colour, and announced by aria-current — so no single cue carries it alone.

tokens.color: theme.accent-role.fg — verified against theme.bg.surface for text
tokens.indicator behind the icon: theme.accent-role.subtle, radius.pill, padding-inline space.padding.sm — the shape is the cue a reader who cannot tell the two foregrounds apart still gets

badge.summary: A count or a dot on a destination's icon. A count is text, so it takes the accent fill with its own label token; a dot is a non-text indicator and takes the fill alone.

tokens.count color: theme.fg.on-accent — the one label token that belongs on theme.accent-role.bg
tokens.dot size: space.gap.sm — Badge's dot, for the reason Badge gives: a dot is a mark, not a glyph
tokens.separation from the icon: a ring of theme.bg.surface at border.2, so the mark stays legible where it overlaps the glyph

name: breadcrumbs
title: Breadcrumbs
description: The trail from the site's root to the current page.

props.name: items
props.description: The trail in order, root first. The last item is the current page.
props.summary: The trail in order, root first. The last item is the current page and is not a link.
use: Every ancestor of the current page, ending with the page itself.
dont: Omitting the current page. The trail ends at where you are; ending it at the parent leaves the reader unsure whether the last crumb is a link they are already on.
A trail that is not a hierarchy. Breadcrumbs say where this page sits, not how the user got here — history is the back button's job.
Giving the last item an `href`. It is the page you are on, and this component drops it.
props.a11y: Rendered as an ordered list inside a `<nav>`, so the count and the order are announced. The last item gets `aria-current="page"` and renders as text rather than a link.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Changing it only when a page has more than one navigation landmark and they need telling apart.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`. A page with several landmarks needs distinct names or they are indistinguishable in a landmark list.

props.name: separator
props.description: What sits between crumbs.
props.summary: What sits between crumbs.
dont: A character that carries meaning, such as an arrow implying a flow. The separator is punctuation.
props.a11y: Decorative and `aria-hidden`: the list structure already conveys the order, and announcing 'slash' between every crumb is noise.

usage.when: The ordinary case.
usage.example:
<Breadcrumbs
  items={[
    { label: "Home", href: "/" },
    { label: "Reports", href: "/reports" },
    { label: "Q3 revenue" },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: The last item has no `href` — it is the page you are on. It renders as text with `aria-current="page"` rather than a link to itself.

usage.when: A page that also has a primary nav and a pagination nav.
usage.example: <Breadcrumbs label="Breadcrumb" items={trail} />
usage.notes: Distinct `aria-label`s are what make landmarks tellable apart in a screen reader's landmark list. Two navs both called 'Navigation' are worse than one.

base.summary: A trail of links ending in the current page.

tokens.font-size: type.supporting.size — a trail is orientation, not content, so it sits below body size
tokens.link color: theme.accent-role.fg — the token documented for an inline link
tokens.current page color: theme.fg.primary — the end of the trail is where you are, so it reads as text rather than as another link
tokens.separator color: theme.fg.muted — punctuation, quieter than either crumb

name: button
title: Button
description: Primary, secondary, tertiary, and destructive actions in three sizes, with loading and icon-only modes.

props.name: variant
props.summary: Which action tier this button occupies, and therefore how loud it is.
use: `primary` for the single highest-priority action in a view — one per view.
`secondary` for a supporting action shown beside a primary one.
`tertiary` for low-emphasis actions in dense areas, like a row action.
`destructive` for an action that deletes or revokes something.
dont: Two `primary` buttons in one view — the tier is a claim about priority, and two claims cancel out.
`destructive` for merely irreversible actions like Submit; it means data is lost.
props.a11y: Variant is visual only. A destructive action still needs its own confirmation step — colour is not a warning.

props.name: size
props.summary: Control height and inline padding, from the `size.control.*` scale. Text size does not change with it.
use: `md` everywhere by default.
`sm` inside dense rows, toolbars, and table cells.
`lg` for a single prominent call to action on a marketing or empty-state surface.
dont: Shrinking to `sm` to fit a cramped layout — fix the layout budget instead.

Expecting the label to grow with it. All three sizes set the same text size, so `size` buys a bigger target for the same action rather than a louder one — and an icon inside, being sized from that text, does not change either.
Setting height or padding yourself; the size prop is the only supported way to change either.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping the button focusable and announced.
use: An action that is unavailable for a reason the surrounding UI already explains.
dont: Hiding why an action is unavailable — pair it with visible helper text or a tooltip.
Form validation gating, where an inline error explains more than a dead button does.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled`, never the native `disabled` attribute: the control stays in the tab order and discoverable by screen readers, and activation is blocked in the primitive's click guard.

props.name: loading
props.description: Shows a spinner and blocks activation while preserving focus.
props.summary: Shows a spinner and refuses activation while an operation is in flight.
use: Async work started by this button, so the same control reports its own progress.
dont: Page-level or unrelated loading — that belongs to the region that is actually loading.
Swapping the label to 'Loading…' as well; the spinner and `aria-busy` already say it, and a changing label loses the action's name.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-busy` alongside `aria-disabled`, so assistive technology hears both that the control is working and that it will not respond yet.

props.name: iconOnly
props.description: Square icon-only button; pass the icon as children and set aria-label.
props.summary: Square button carrying an icon and no visible text.
use: Dense toolbars and row actions where the icon is unambiguous and repeated.
Icon-only buttons in this system: there is no separate `IconButton` component, and one would be a second way to do what this prop already does.
dont: Any action whose icon is not already conventional — an unlabelled novel icon is unreadable.
Passing text children as well; the square sizing assumes a single glyph.
props.a11y: You MUST pass `aria-label`. Nothing in the component supplies an accessible name when there is no visible text.

usage.when: The most common pairing: one primary button that owns its own progress.
usage.example: <Button loading={saving} onClick={save}>Save changes</Button>
usage.notes: `loading` blocks repeat activation on its own — don't also guard with `disabled`.

usage.when: Deleting something, with the safe action given equal visual weight beside it.
usage.example: <Button variant="destructive" onClick={remove}>Delete project</Button>

usage.when: A dense table row where a labelled button would not fit.
usage.example: <Button variant="tertiary" size="sm" iconOnly aria-label="Remove row">×</Button>
usage.notes: Without `aria-label` this button has no accessible name at all.

behavior.summary: Activation guarding and disabled/busy semantics, independent of React and of any styling.

decisions.decision: `aria-disabled` instead of the native `disabled` attribute
decisions.why: A natively disabled button leaves the tab order and stops being announced, so users navigating by keyboard or screen reader cannot discover that the action exists. Activation is blocked in the click guard instead.

decisions.decision: `loading` implies inert
decisions.why: One flag covers both halves of what callers actually want — show progress, and refuse a second click — so the two cannot be set inconsistently.

primary.summary: The single highest-priority action in a view.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

secondary.summary: A supporting action shown next to a primary one. Its label is accent-toned rather than neutral, so the outlined button still reads as an action and not as a disabled box — the border alone carries very little at this fill.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes

destructive.summary: An action that deletes or revokes something.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes

name: button-group
title: Button Group
description: A named set of related buttons, spaced or attached into one bar, horizontal or vertical.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the group. Required unless `labelledBy` names an existing element.
props.summary: Accessible name for the group — what these buttons have in common.
use: Always, unless `labelledBy` points at a visible heading that already says it.
Naming the group by its subject rather than its shape: "Row actions", not "Button group".
dont: Restating the buttons' own labels — "Save and Cancel" tells a screen reader what it is about to read anyway.
Leaving it off because the group looks obvious on screen; an unnamed group adds a level to navigate and says nothing about what is inside it.
props.a11y: Becomes the group's `aria-label`. Every group MUST have a name from this or from `labelledBy` — the component cannot supply one, because only the caller knows what the buttons have in common.

props.name: labelledBy
props.description: Id of an element that already names this group — a heading above it, typically.
props.summary: Id of an element that already names this group, used instead of a written label.
use: A visible heading sits directly above the group and says the same thing a label would.
dont: Pointing at an element that is conditionally rendered — a dangling `aria-labelledby` leaves the group unnamed with no visible sign of it.
props.a11y: Wins over `label` when both are passed, because it points at text the user can see: when the visible heading changes, the name changes with it.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Which way the buttons stack.
use: `vertical` in a narrow rail or a menu-like column where a row would wrap.
dont: `vertical` as a substitute for a menu — a list of navigation choices is a menu, not a stack of buttons.
Switching orientation per breakpoint by swapping the prop mid-interaction; pick one per layout and let the group wrap if it must.
props.a11y: Presentational only. It sets a data attribute for styling and deliberately does not set `aria-orientation`, which would promise arrow-key navigation this group does not implement.

props.name: attached
props.description: Joins the buttons into one continuous bar, with only the outer corners rounded.
props.summary: Joins the buttons into one continuous bar, with shared borders and only the outer corners rounded.
use: Actions that are variations of one thing and are read as a unit — a pager's Previous/Next, a split of one action into its two directions.
dont: Actions of different weight. Attaching a primary to a destructive makes them look like one control with two halves, which is exactly the moment a mis-click costs the most.
Expressing a choice. Attached buttons that hold a selected state are a `toggle-button-group`, and it says so to assistive technology; this one does not.
props.a11y: Visual only — nothing about the attached form changes what is announced. The buttons stay separately focusable either way.

usage.case: Two actions at the end of a form
usage.when: The default case: a primary action and its escape hatch, spaced rather than joined.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Form actions">
  <Button variant="secondary">Cancel</Button>
  <Button>Save changes</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Spaced, not attached — these are two different decisions, and joining them makes them read as one control.

usage.when: Two halves of the same action, which is what `attached` is for.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Pagination" attached>
  <Button variant="secondary" iconOnly aria-label="Previous page">‹</Button>
  <Button variant="secondary" iconOnly aria-label="Next page">›</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: `iconOnly` still requires its own `aria-label` on each button — the group's name says what the pair is, not what each half does.

usage.case: Named by a heading that is already on screen
usage.when: The group sits under a heading that says exactly what the label would have said.
usage.example: Export
usage.notes: Prefer this to a written `label` whenever the heading exists: one string, visible, and it cannot drift from what the group actually contains.

usage.when: A narrow column where a horizontal row would wrap into an unreadable grid.
usage.example:
<ButtonGroup label="Layer actions" orientation="vertical">
  <Button variant="tertiary">Bring forward</Button>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Send backward</Button>
</ButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Still tab-navigated, not arrow-navigated. If the column is long enough that tabbing through it is tedious, it wants to be a menu.

behavior.summary: The group's accessible name and its grouping role — the two things the buttons inside cannot own between them. No selection state and no value: a button group runs actions, it does not hold an answer.

decisions.decision: `role="group"` with a required accessible name, not `role="toolbar"`
decisions.why: A toolbar is a single tab stop with arrow-key navigation between its controls. That is right for a dense, persistent bar of many actions and wrong for the common case here — two or three buttons in a card footer — where collapsing them into one tab stop makes them harder to reach, not easier. Groups that genuinely want toolbar semantics should say so explicitly rather than getting them by accident from a layout wrapper.

decisions.decision: Each button keeps its own tab stop
decisions.why: Follows from the role decision above. It also keeps the group composable: a `Button` inside a group behaves exactly like a `Button` outside one, so nothing about focus or activation has to be re-learned.

decisions.decision: Orientation is a data attribute, not `aria-orientation`
decisions.why: Orientation here changes how the group stacks and nothing else. `aria-orientation` announces a navigation direction, which would promise arrow-key movement this group deliberately does not implement.

decisions.decision: No per-item position data — corner joining is `:first-child`/`:last-child` in CSS
decisions.why: The DOM already knows which button is first and last. Emitting `data-position` would be a second copy of that fact, and a copy that goes stale the moment a button is conditionally rendered.

decisions.decision: Not a selection control
decisions.why: A group whose items hold a pressed state is `toggle-button-group`: it needs a value, a selection mode, and roving focus, none of which belong in a container for plain actions. Keeping them separate is what stops this component growing a `value` prop that only makes sense half the time.

spaced.summary: The default: buttons that belong together but read as separate controls.

tokens.item border-radius: radius.element — each button keeps the corners it sets for itself

attached.summary: Buttons joined into one continuous bar.

tokens.outer corner border-radius: radius.element, as logical corners so the bar flips in RTL
tokens.collapsed shared border: negative margin of border.1, so adjacent borders read as one
tokens.focused item stacking: raised above its neighbours so the focus ring is not clipped — a stacking fix, not a token

name: card
title: Card
description: A bordered surface holding one self-contained item among several — a widget, a gallery entry, a settings group.

props.name: children
props.description: The card's content.
props.summary: The card's content.
use: One self-contained item: a heading and its body, a metric and its caption, a group of related settings.
dont: Another Card. A card inside a card is a section wearing two borders — use a Divider or a heading inside the one card.
A dense list of records. That is a Table, and a table inside a card is a table that has lost its edge-to-edge alignment for no reason.

A `variant="standalone"` Link in the card's heading. The standalone variant composes `.rata-state-layer`, which already owns the link's `::after` and makes the link `position: relative` — the stretched hit area would be trapped inside the link, its clicks swallowed, and a second hover tint stacked on the card's. Use the inline Link, the default.
props.a11y: Read in document order. If the card is a `section`, its first heading should name it through `aria-labelledby`. An inline Link inside the card's heading is stretched over the whole card, so put the card's one destination there and nowhere else.

props.name: as
props.description: Which element the card is, because that depends on what is in it.
props.summary: Which element the card is, because that depends on what is in it.
use: `li` for every card in a gallery or a grid of peers, inside a `<ul>` the page renders.
`article` for an entry that would make sense lifted out of the page on its own — a post, a result.
`section` for a titled group of settings, named by its heading.
dont: `section` without a heading. An unnamed section is not exposed as a region, so the element claims structure it does not deliver.
`li` outside a list. The browser accepts it and the accessibility tree does not.
props.a11y: Each option is chosen for the role its element already carries, so this prop adds no ARIA. Web only: on React Native the card is a `View` and this prop is ignored.

props.name: variant
props.description: How the card's edge is drawn: a border, or the resting-card shadow.
props.summary: How the card's edge is drawn: a border, or the resting-card shadow.
use: `outlined` for cards that are peers in one plane — a gallery, a dashboard, a settings page. Almost always.
`raised` for a card that sits above its surroundings: one featured card on a plain section, or cards over an image or a tinted band.
dont: `raised` on every card in a grid. A field of shadows says everything is lifted, which is the same as saying nothing is.
`raised` to show that a card is clickable. A stretched heading link already gives the card hover, press and focus feedback; a shadow is not an affordance.
props.a11y: Visual only. Neither variant changes the element, its role or its name.

props.name: media
props.description: An image or preview shown flush with the card's top edge, above the content.
props.summary: An image or preview shown flush with the card's top edge, above the content.
use: A thumbnail in a gallery card, a chart preview in a dashboard widget.
dont: An icon. An icon sits in the content beside the text it belongs to; this slot is for a picture that fills the card's width.
Decorative imagery carrying meaning. If the picture says something the text does not, it needs alt text that says it.
props.a11y: The caller's image owns its own alternative text. A purely decorative preview takes `alt=""` so the card is not read twice.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for placement in a grid — not for restyling the card.
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement in a grid — not for restyling the card.
use: Spanning grid columns, or aligning the card inside the page's layout.
dont: Changing its surface, border or padding. A card that differs per page is a different component wearing this one's name — propose a variant instead.

usage.when: Several things of the same kind, each read on its own and chosen between — templates, projects, themes.
usage.example: {templates.map((t) => ( }> {t.name} {t.summary} ))}
usage.notes: `as="li"` inside the page's own `<ul>`, so a screen reader announces how many templates there are. The grid's gap lives on `.template-grid`, not on the cards. The preview is `alt=""` because the heading already names it.

usage.case: A whole card that goes somewhere
usage.when: A gallery where each card opens its own page, and pressing anywhere on the card should open it.
usage.example: {projects.map((p) => ( }> {p.name} {p.summary} ))}
usage.notes: No `href` or `onClick` on the Card: the inline Link in the heading is the control — not `variant="standalone"`, whose state layer would trap the stretched hit area inside the link, and the card stretches its hit area over the whole card and shows its hover and focus. The link's name is the project's name, not every word in the card, and each card is one tab stop. A secondary action — a Menu button, say — placed after the heading sits above the stretched area, so pressing it does not also open the project.

usage.when: A settings page whose groups are understood, and often saved, separately.
usage.example:
<Card as="section" aria-labelledby="billing-heading">
  <Heading level={2} id="billing-heading">Billing</Heading>
  <TextField label="Billing email" />
</Card>
usage.notes: A `section` card is named by its heading, or it is not exposed as a region at all — which is why `section` is not the default.

usage.when: A list of invoices, each with a number, a date, an amount and a status.
usage.notes: Don't. Those are rows compared by column — is this amount larger, is that one overdue — and putting each in its own card destroys the column. That is a Table. Equally, a single card holding a whole page's content is a `<section>` with a border; drop the card.

behavior.summary: A box with a surface, an edge and padding, rendered as whichever element its content actually is. No primitive: it owns no keyboard interaction and no state — when a whole card is clickable, the link in its heading is the control, not the card. Card exists so that the one container this system has been telling people not to hand-roll — `<div className="card">` — has a governed version, and so that the choice between a card, a table and a plain section is written down once.

decisions.decision: Card, Table or a plain `<section>` — the test is how the content is read
decisions.why: Rows that are scanned and compared column by column are a Table: putting each record in its own card destroys the column, which is the thing the reader came to compare. Several self-contained items that are each read on their own — dashboard widgets, a gallery, groups of settings that are saved or understood separately — are Cards: the outline says "this is one thing" and the gap between them says "and these are separate". Everything else, which is most of a page, is a plain `<section>` with a heading and no box at all. A single card alone on a page is almost always a section wearing a border, and a card inside a card is always one: if the inner thing needs separating, a Divider or a heading does it without a second outline.

decisions.decision: Outlined by default; `raised` is the one alternative
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C1, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). `theme.border.default` is documented for separating two elements in the same plane, and a grid of cards IS one plane — nothing in it is above anything else — so a shadow on every card in a dashboard turns the page into a field of competing lifts. That is why `outlined` is the default. `raised` uses `theme.elevation.raised`, which is documented for resting cards, for the case where a card genuinely sits above its surroundings: one featured card on a plain section, or cards over an image or a tinted band. Two variants and no more: a third elevation on a resting surface would compete with the overlay and modal shadows that mean something.

decisions.decision: `as` chooses the element, and the default claims nothing
decisions.why: What a card IS depends on what is in it. A card in a gallery is a list item, because a gallery is a list and a screen reader announcing "list, 12 items" is the most useful thing it can say. A self-contained entry that would make sense lifted out of the page is an `article`. A titled group of settings is a `section`. A component that defaulted to `article` would be wrong for every settings group, so the default is `div` — a box with no semantic claim — and the caller states the claim when there is one.

decisions.decision: Whole-card click is a stretched heading link; Card takes no `href` or `onClick`
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C2, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). A whole card wrapped in an `<a>` makes every word inside it the link's accessible name, so a reader tabbing through a gallery hears each card read out in full, and any button inside the card becomes interactive content nested in a link, which is invalid. A card with a `<div onClick>` is unreachable by keyboard. So the card is never the control: a real Link inside the card's heading is, and its hit area is stretched over the card with a pseudo-element — the construction ListItem uses for a row. The accessible name stays the heading's text, the card is one tab stop, and secondary actions sit above the stretched area so pressing them does not also follow the link. Card styles a heading link this way when it finds one; it needs no prop to do it, and a card with no link in its heading is not clickable at all.

decisions.decision: No `title` prop and no heading of its own
decisions.why: Many cards have no title — a gallery thumbnail, a metric widget whose number is its content. The ones that do need a heading at the right outline level, which only the caller knows; Panel solves that with `headingLevel` because a landmark must be named, but a card is not a landmark. A `Heading` inside the card, at whatever level the page needs, gets the outline right without this component guessing.

decisions.decision: It carries no margin and no width
decisions.why: The same bargain Heading and Panel make. Cards live in a grid or a stack, and the gap between them is the grid's — a card that shipped its own margin would double up with the grid's gap and be overridden everywhere. Width is the grid's too: there are no breakpoint tokens, because where a card stops fitting is the page's knowledge.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: the element `as` names — `div` by default, or `article`, `section` or `li` — with no role added, because each of those elements already carries the right one. A `section` card should be named by its heading through `aria-labelledby`, or it is not exposed as a region at all. React Native: a `View` with no `accessibilityRole`, because RN has no article, section or listitem role that platforms announce; the list semantics of a gallery belong to the `FlatList` that renders the cards, not to each card. `as` is web-only and is ignored on native. `media` works on both; on native the clip comes from `overflow: "hidden"` with the same radius token. No OS control (decision N5): the card is Rata-drawn on both platforms, from the same recipe. On native, `raised` is the platform shadow (`elevation` on Android) taken from the same token. The stretched link is web-only — a nested `Text` link cannot be stretched — so on native the heading's Link is the target, and a list of whole-row targets is ListItem's job. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: Gate 2: every state's token mapping is approved
decisions.why: Approved state by state — C1 outlined rest, C2 raised (border kept), C3 full-bleed media, C4 linked hover/press via the state layer, C5 linked focus drawn around the card, C6 secondary actions above the stretched link. The focus ring is moved to the card, never removed: it is suppressed on the link only where the card's :has() rule can draw it instead (gate 2, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: A linked card's heading uses the inline Link
decisions.why: Decided at gate 3 (decision C7, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). C4 stretches the heading link's hit area with its `::after`. A standalone Link composes `.rata-state-layer`, whose `::after` is already the link's hover tint and whose `position: relative` makes the link the containing block: the stretched area would be trapped inside the link instead of covering the card, the layer's `pointer-events: none` would swallow its clicks, and the link's own tint would stack on the card's. The inline Link has no state layer and no position of its own, so nothing collides — and its underline is drawn on the heading text, while the card draws the hover, press and focus.

base.summary: The outlined card, at rest (C1).

tokens.margin: space.0 — the grid or stack the cards sit in owns the gap between them, via space.grid.gap (C1)

tokens.border: border.default solid theme.border.default — kept, so a raised card is the same size as an outlined one and its edge does not depend on a shadow alone, which is faint on a dark canvas (C2)

tokens.margin-inline and margin-block-start: the negative of space.padding.md — the media cancels the card's padding rather than the card dropping it (C3)
tokens.corner clip: radius.container on the card, overflow clipped, so the media needs no radius of its own (C3)

linked.summary: A whole-card link through a stretched heading link (C4–C6).

tokens.card position: relative, so the link's stretched pseudo-element is bounded by the card (C4)
tokens.stretched hit area: a ::after on the heading's link — the inline Link variant (C7) — inset space.0 on every side of the card. The card's own ::after belongs to the state layer — the two pseudo-elements sit on different elements, so they never collide (C4)
tokens.hover / press: compose the .rata-state-layer class on the card, driven by :has() on the link's :hover and :active (C4)
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, drawn around the card while the link matches :focus-visible; the link's own outline is suppressed only inside a card that draws it, so a browser without :has() keeps the link's ring (C5)
tokens.secondary actions: position: relative and later in source order than the heading, so they paint above the stretched area without a z-index and stay separately clickable and focusable (C6)

example:
<Card as="section" aria-labelledby="pg-card-billing">
        <Heading level={4} id="pg-card-billing">
          Billing
        </Heading>
        <TextField label="Billing email" />
      </Card>

name: checkbox
title: Checkbox
description: A single on/off choice, with an indeterminate state for a parent summarising its children.

props.name: label
props.description: The checkbox's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The checkbox's label. Always required — `labelHidden` can take it off screen, but nothing removes it.
use: Always. A checkbox with no label is a control nobody can describe.
dont: Using the surrounding sentence as the label and leaving this empty — the binding is what makes the text a hit target and an accessible name.
Passing an empty string. An empty label is an unnamed control; hide it with `labelHidden` instead.
props.a11y: Rendered as a real `<label for>` bound to the input, so clicking the text toggles the box. Still a real label when hidden — only its pixels go away.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A checkbox in a table row or header cell, where the column already names what is being toggled and repeating it per row would be noise.
A dense control panel where the box sits directly under a heading that names it.
dont: Hiding it to save space in a form. In a form the label is the last thing to cut; if space is short the layout budget is wrong.
Hiding it on a standalone checkbox. With no adjacent text naming it, the label is the only thing saying what agreeing to this means.
Hiding it and then relying on a neighbouring cell's position to explain the box — position is not a name, and it is the first thing lost when a layout reflows.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so the accessible name is unchanged — it is clipped, not removed. Not `display: none`, which would take the name with it. The required marker goes off screen with it; `aria-required` still carries that.

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the box is checked. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the box is checked. Makes the component controlled.
use: Whenever the value lives outside the component, which is most of the time.
dont: Passing it without `onCheckedChange`; the box would render its state and then refuse to change it.
props.a11y: Drives the native checked state, which is what assistive technology reports.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled checkbox. Conflicts with `checked`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled checkbox.
use: Genuinely local state nothing else reads.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Called with the state the box should move to, not the one it is leaving.
props.summary: Called with the state the box should move to, not the one it is leaving.
dont: Reading `event.target.checked` instead of the argument — they agree, but the argument is the one this component promises.

props.name: indeterminate
props.description: A parent summarising children that disagree. Outranks `checked`.
props.summary: Shows the box as neither checked nor unchecked: a parent summarising children that disagree.
use: A 'select all' box above a list where only some rows are selected.
dont: Expressing 'unknown' or 'not yet answered'. It means partially checked, and a screen reader announces it as `mixed`.
Combining it with a `checked` that is also true and expecting both to show — indeterminate wins visually and in what is announced, which is why they are not one prop.
props.a11y: Announced as `aria-checked="mixed"`. Set as a DOM property by this component, because HTML has no such attribute.

props.name: description
props.description: Helper text under the label.
props.summary: Helper text under the label.
dont: Error text. A checkbox that is invalid belongs in a field wrapper that owns the message.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
use: Linking an external label, or a scroll-to-error that needs the id to survive a re-render.
dont: Reusing one id across two checkboxes — the derived description id would collide too.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks activation while keeping the box focusable and announced.
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping the box focusable and announced.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` and refuses activation. Never the native `disabled` attribute, which would remove it from the tab order.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the checkbox as required.
props.summary: Marks the checkbox as required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-required`. The visible marker is the label's job.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the checkbox's wrapper.
use: Placing the component in its surrounding layout — a span, a width, a margin the parent cannot express.
dont: Restyling the box. Its size, border and fill are the approved mapping.
Restyling the component's internals through descendant selectors. Those are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer somewhere the contract cannot see.

usage.when: The commonest case: one box, one label, its own state.
usage.example:
<Checkbox
  label="Email me product updates"
  checked={subscribed}
  onCheckedChange={setSubscribed}
/>

usage.when: Some rows selected, so the parent is neither checked nor unchecked.
usage.example:
<Checkbox
  label="Select all"
  checked={all}
  indeterminate={some && !all}
  onCheckedChange={toggleAll}
/>
usage.notes: `indeterminate` is what a screen reader hears as `mixed`. It is deliberately separate from `checked`, because it answers a different question: not this box's value, but whether the children below agree.

usage.when: A choice that cannot be made yet, whose current state still matters.
usage.example: <Checkbox label="Ship to billing address" checked disabled />
usage.notes: aria-disabled and a refused activation, never the native `disabled` attribute — the box stays focusable so a keyboard user can find it and read its state.

usage.case: A column of boxes under a heading that names them
usage.when: A table or a settings grid where the column header already says what is being toggled.
usage.example: <Checkbox label="Notify by email" labelHidden checked={row.email} onCheckedChange={…} />
usage.notes: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, not the name: the `<label for>` is still rendered and still bound, so each box is announced as "Notify by email" exactly as it would be with the label visible. The hit target shrinks to the box itself, which is the cost of this choice — it is why the visible label is the default.

behavior.summary: Checked state, the indeterminate third appearance, and the activation guard. Built on a native input[type=checkbox] so keyboard, form participation and the checked semantics come from the platform rather than being re-implemented.

decisions.decision: A native input, not a div with role="checkbox"
decisions.why: Space to toggle, participation in a form's data, and the checked state itself are all free from the platform and all easy to get subtly wrong by hand. The visual is drawn by a sibling element; the input stays in the DOM and keeps the semantics.

decisions.decision: `indeterminate` is a separate prop, not a third value of `checked`
decisions.why: It answers a different question. `checked` is this control's own value; `indeterminate` says the control is standing in for a set of children that disagree. A tri-state `checked` would force every caller to handle a value that only a parent checkbox can ever have, and would make the common two-state case read as incomplete.

decisions.decision: Indeterminate is set as a DOM property, never an attribute
decisions.why: There is no `indeterminate` content attribute in HTML — only an IDL property — so it cannot be expressed in JSX and has to be assigned to the element. The wrapper owns that, which is the whole reason this component cannot be a bare styled input.

decisions.decision: Activation is guarded, not disabled
decisions.why: This system's disabled controls stay focusable and announced. `readOnly` is the input analogue used by text-field, but it has no effect on a checkbox, so the guard here is a refused activation plus aria-disabled — the same shape as the button primitive.

decisions.decision: The label is required and is a real `<label for>`
decisions.why: A checkbox's hit target should include its text, and a bound label gives that for free. It also means the accessible name cannot drift from what is on screen.

base.summary: A single on/off choice, with a third appearance for a parent summarising its children.

tokens.box size: size.icon.md — the box is sized to the glyph it holds, so it takes the icon scale rather than the control one; the control heights are row heights and would dwarf the box itself
tokens.row height: no reserved row height. An earlier version set it to size.control.md for a bigger hit target, but with the box aligned to the first line that reserved 12px of dead space under every row and inflated the list's pitch to 40px. At the resulting 28px pitch the target conforms through WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception: 24px circles centred on adjacent targets do not intersect. The label is bound, so the target is the full width of the text as well
tokens.control height: one line tall, from calc(type.control.size.md x type.control.line-height.md) = 20px. The line-height token is a unitless ratio, so it is not a length on its own — used alone the browser drops the declaration
tokens.border: border.default solid theme.border.strong — the same boundary tone text-field uses, tone-walked to the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's edge
tokens.gap between box and label: space.gap.sm — the inline role, because this pairing is horizontal
tokens.gap between label and description: none — the label and the description each carry line-height leading, which already reads as 7px of separation. A gap on top of that made 11px and read as two unrelated lines
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — never a hand-written hover rule
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — the offset is kept here, unlike text-field: a 20px box has no room for a flush ring to read as separate from its own border
tokens.border-radius: radius.inner — a nested square, which is what radius.inner names
tokens.checked mark: theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on that fill, and it inverts with the accent in the dark scheme
tokens.indeterminate mark: theme.fg.on-accent on theme.accent-role.bg, drawn as a bar rather than a tick. The fill matches checked because the state is 'partly checked', not a third colour

example: <Checkbox label="Ship to billing address" checked disabled />

name: chip
title: Chip
description: A value the reader has added — a recipient, a selected filter, a tag on a record — shown with a control to remove it.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: children
props.summary: The value, as text.
use: A recipient's name or address, a filter's value, a tag.
dont: Markup. The text is reused in the remove button's name and the `title`, so it is a string rather than a ReactNode.
props.a11y: Read as plain text, and appended to the remove button's default name.

props.name: onRemove
props.summary: Called when the reader removes the value — by pressing the button, or by Backspace or Delete while it has focus.
use: Removing the value from the caller's state, and moving focus in the same handler: to the next chip's remove button, or to the field the chips belong to.
dont: Leaving focus where it was. The focused element is about to be removed, and focus falls to `<body>`.
Asking for confirmation. Removing a chip is undone by adding the value back; a dialog for that is friction with no safety in it.
props.a11y: The caller owns where focus goes next — see the decision on focus after removal.

props.name: removeLabel
props.summary: The remove button's full accessible name.
use: A translated phrase, in whatever word order the language needs: `removeLabel={t("remove", { name })}`.
dont: A bare 'Remove' or '×'. It must name the value, or every chip's button sounds the same.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`, and on native the label of the `delete` accessibility action.

props.name: icon
props.summary: A glyph before the text that says what kind of value it is.
use: A mail glyph on an address that is not a known contact, beside chips that are.
dont: The same glyph on every chip in a set. If it does not distinguish anything it is noise.
props.a11y: Decorative — `aria-hidden`. If the kind of value matters, say it in the text.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks removal while keeping the button focusable and announced.
use: A value the reader cannot remove right now — a required recipient, a filter locked by a permission.
dont: A value that can never be removed. That is a Badge.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` on the remove button, not the `disabled` attribute, so it stays in the tab order and is announced as unavailable.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rare. A set of chips gets its gap from the list that holds them.
dont: A status colour to mark an invalid value. Invalid input is a Field's message, and a red chip with no words says only 'something is wrong'.

usage.when: A set of values the reader built up and may trim.
usage.example:
{recipients.map((person, i) => (
  • removeRecipient(i)}>{person.name}
    • ))}
usage.notes: Each button is named 'Remove <name>'. `removeRecipient` must move focus to the next chip's button, or to the To field when the last chip goes — the component cannot, because it does not know what comes after it.

usage.case: The active filters above a result list
usage.when: Filters chosen elsewhere — in a Sheet of options — shown as a summary the reader can clear one by one.
usage.example: <Chip onRemove={() => clearFilter("colour")} removeLabel="Clear colour filter: Blue">Blue</Chip>
usage.notes: This is the removable summary of a filter, not the filter control. The control that sets it — a row of toggles — is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"`.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: a filter toggle
usage.when: A row of options above a list, each turning a filter on or off in place.
usage.example: <Chip onRemove={() => {}}>Unread</Chip>
usage.notes: Don't. A filter that toggles in place is pressed or not pressed, and that is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"` and `attached={false}`, which announces `aria-pressed`. An empty `onRemove` is the giveaway — there is nothing to remove.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: a status label
usage.when: A label on a record that says what state it is in.
usage.example: <Chip onRemove={noop}>Paid</Chip>
usage.notes: Don't. Nobody removes 'Paid' from an invoice by pressing an ×. That is a Badge, with `variant="success"`.

behavior.summary: A `<span>` holding the value's text and a `<button type="button">` that removes it. No primitive: the only behaviour is one button, and Button's activation already owns it.

decisions.decision: One component, and it is the input chip — the other four chips are already here
decisions.why: 'Chip' names five things that share a pill shape and differ in semantics, which is this system's test for splitting. A filter chip is a pressed toggle — a row of them is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"` and `attached={false}`, announced with `aria-pressed`. A choice chip is one answer from a few — SegmentedControl, or ToggleButtonGroup in single mode, announced as a radio group. A static tag is a label nobody acts on — Badge. An assist or suggestion chip is an action — a small secondary Button. The one thing left is a value the reader added and can take away, which is text plus a removal command, and no existing component is that. Shipping a `Chip` with a `kind` prop over all five would put a radiogroup, a toggle, a label, a button and a removable value behind one name, and the prop would be choosing the ARIA pattern — exactly the mistake Tabs and SegmentedControl were split to avoid.

decisions.decision: `onRemove` is required
decisions.why: A chip that cannot be removed is a Badge. Making the handler optional would make this a second way to draw a static label, and the two would drift; requiring it means reaching for this component is itself the statement that the value is removable.

decisions.decision: The chip is not focusable — its remove button is
decisions.why: There is one thing to do with a chip, so there is one tab stop: the button. A focusable chip around a focusable button would be two stops for one action, and a focusable chip with no button would need a keyboard command nobody could discover. The button's name is the full phrase, so focusing it says both what the value is and what will happen.

decisions.decision: The remove button is named after the value
decisions.why: Five buttons called 'Remove' tell a screen-reader user nothing about which recipient each one removes. The default name is 'Remove' followed by the chip's text — 'Remove Ada Lovelace' — and `removeLabel` replaces the whole phrase, rather than a prefix, so a translation can put the words in its own order.

decisions.decision: Backspace and Delete on the focused remove button also remove
decisions.why: Enter and Space activate it because it is a button. Backspace and Delete are what a reader expects to remove a selected value in every token field they have used, and on native platforms 'delete' is the standard accessibility action for exactly this. Accepting them costs nothing and removes a moment of 'how do I get rid of this'.

decisions.decision: Focus after removal is the caller's, until a multi-value field exists
decisions.why: Removing the chip removes the focused button, and a browser whose focused element disappears sends focus to `<body>` — a keyboard user is thrown to the top of the page. This component cannot fix that alone: only something that holds all the chips knows that the next one, or the input they were typed into, is where focus should go. So the obligation is stated on `onRemove`: move focus before or as you remove. The real fix is a multi-value field — a text input with its chips, roving focus between them, and Backspace in an empty input removing the last one — which this system does not have and which needs its own gate 1.

decisions.decision: Long values truncate, and the full value stays reachable
decisions.why: An email address can be wider than a phone. The text truncates with an ellipsis at the container's width, which is the one place truncation is acceptable: the full value is still the remove button's name and the chip's `title`, so a screen reader and a long-press both have it. Text's contract declined line clamping in general precisely because truncated text needs that second path, and here it already exists.

decisions.decision: Touch target: size.target.min
decisions.why: The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: On the web it renders `<span>` with the text and `<button type="button" aria-label="Remove …">` holding an `aria-hidden` glyph, with `aria-disabled` on the button when disabled. A set of chips is the caller's `<ul role="list">` with one per `<li>`, so the count is announced. On React Native it renders a `View` with `accessible`, `accessibilityLabel` set to the value, and `accessibilityActions={[{ name: "delete", label: removeLabel }]}` handled by `onAccessibilityAction` — one focus stop with the platform's own delete action, which is the native idiom and the reason the web needs a separate button and native does not. The visible remove `Pressable` is then `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` / `accessibilityElementsHidden`, so it is a touch target and not a second stop. `className` is web-only; no prop is native-only. There is no gesture: removal is always a press. Rata-drawn (decision N5): neither platform's OS controls include an input chip, so it is drawn from the same recipe; the delete action is the OS accessibility action. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: An outlined value, drawn with the secondary role so it reads as something the reader can act on rather than as a status. That is the visible difference from a neutral Badge, which is a filled label that nobody removes.

tokens.padding-inline-end: space.1 — the remove control sits in the end padding's place
tokens.border-radius: radius.element — documented as the radius for chips
tokens.max-inline-size: 100% of its container, with the text truncated by an ellipsis — the full value stays the remove control's name and the chip's title

remove.summary: The one interactive part. Visibly small, with a hit area stretched to the chip's full block size and past its end.

tokens.hit area: size.target.min in both dimensions, centred on the visible remove circle with a pseudo-element; the circle itself stays small so the chip stays a chip
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

name: combobox
title: Combobox
description: A text input that filters a popup list of options, for choices too many to scan or too rich for a native select.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: The control's name. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: A short noun phrase naming what is being chosen: "Assignee", not "Search for an assignee".
dont: Leaving it off because the placeholder says it. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke, which is exactly when a reader is mid-search.
props.a11y: Bound to the input by Field, so it is the combobox's accessible name. The popup listbox is labelled by the same element, so the list and the field are announced as one thing.

props.name: options
props.summary: The choices, as `{ value, label, description?, disabled? }`, in the order they are read.
use: Every option when the list is local; the current page of results when the server filters (with `filter="none"`).
`description` for the second line a native `<option>` cannot hold — an email under a name, a region under a city.
dont: A ReactNode `label`. The label is what the input shows once chosen and what typing is matched against, so it has to be text — the second line is `description`.
A short list a reader can scan without typing. That is `Select`, and it gets the phone's own picker for free.
props.a11y: Each becomes a `role="option"` in a `role="listbox"`. A disabled option stays in the list, reachable by arrow keys and announced as unavailable, and cannot be chosen.

props.name: value
props.summary: Controls the chosen option's `value` from outside. `null` means nothing is chosen.
use: A form library, or a field whose options depend on another field's answer.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the state.

props.name: defaultValue
props.summary: The starting choice when the component owns the state.
use: A genuine default the reader usually wants.
dont: A value missing from `options`. With local options the input would have no label to show; with server options, pass the chosen option in the first page.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Fires with the chosen option's value when a choice is committed — Enter, a click, or clearing the text.
use: Reading the answer, which is the option's `value`, never the text in the box.
dont: Expecting it on every keystroke. Typing changes the text, not the value — that is `onInputChange`.

props.name: onInputChange
props.summary: Fires with the text in the box on every edit.
use: Fetching the next page of options when the server does the filtering — debounce it on your side, the component does not.
dont: Treating the text as the answer. Unless `allowCustomValue` is set, text that matches no option is discarded on blur.

props.name: filter
props.summary: How typed text narrows `options` locally.
use: `none` when `options` is already the server's answer to the current text — filtering it again would hide results the server matched on fields the reader cannot see.
`starts-with` for codes and identifiers, where a match in the middle is noise.
dont: `none` with a local list. Nothing narrows, and the reader is typing into a field that ignores them.
props.a11y: Whatever the mode, the result count is announced politely after each change, because a list changing under an `aria-activedescendant` is otherwise silent in most screen readers.

props.name: allowCustomValue
props.summary: Accepts text that matches no option as the answer.
use: Suggestions over an open answer: a tag that may not exist yet, a city the list does not know.
dont: A choice that must be one of the options. Leave it off and unmatched text reverts to the last chosen label on blur.
A search box that proposes completions and then runs a query. That is still `Search` until something needs completions; then it is this, with this prop on.
props.a11y: With it on, the value reported is the text itself, so `onValueChange` receives a string that may not be any option's value — the caller has to expect that.

props.name: loading
props.summary: Options are being fetched. The popup shows a spinner row and the field is busy.
use: Between an `onInputChange` that went to the network and its answer.
dont: Leaving it on while the previous results are still useful. Show them; the spinner row sits after them.
props.a11y: Sets `aria-busy` on the listbox. The count announcement waits for it to clear, so a reader does not hear "0 results" for a search that has not answered yet.

props.name: emptyMessage
props.summary: What the popup says when nothing matches.
use: Translating it, or saying what to try: "No people match — check the spelling or invite them."
