dont: An empty string. An open popup with nothing in it reads as broken, and the reader gets no answer at all.
props.a11y: Rendered as a plain row outside the listbox's options, so it is announced by the count region rather than being arrowed onto as if it were a choice.

props.name: placeholder
props.summary: A hint shown while the box is empty.
use: Naming the act: "Type a name".
dont: Using it as the label, for the reason `label` gives.

props.name: name
props.summary: Form field name. The submitted value is the chosen option's `value`, not the text in the box.
use: A native form post, where the server needs the id rather than the display label.
dont: Reading the visible input in a form handler. It holds the label; the value lives in the hidden input this name is on.
props.a11y: Carried by a hidden input, which is not in the tab order and is not announced.

props.name: size
props.summary: Control height and inline padding. Text size does not change with it.
use: Matching whatever the control sits beside — a combobox and a button in one row should be the same height.
dont: `sm` to fit more on the page. It is the same text at a smaller target.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: the label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.summary: Stable id for the combobox, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the field it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message, popup — is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged.

props.name: description
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: A constraint the reader needs before they answer.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative.
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks choosing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
use: A choice that depends on an answer nobody has given yet.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. The hidden input still submits — if the value must not reach the server, do not render the field.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly` on the input, from Field. The popup never opens, so arrow keys and the toggle do nothing, and the field stays in the tab order.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides.
dont: Restyling the popup. It is positioned against the input's own box and inherits its width.

usage.case: Choosing one of many from a local list
usage.when: The list is too long to scan and every option is known up front.
usage.example:
<Combobox
  label="Time zone"
  placeholder="Type a city"
  options={timeZones}
  name="tz"
  required
/>
usage.notes: Filtering is `contains` by default, so "york" finds New York. The form posts the option's `value` — the zone id — not the label in the box.

usage.case: Options fetched as the reader types
usage.when: The server owns the matching, typically a people or product search.
usage.example:
<Combobox
  label="Assignee"
  options={people}
  filter="none"
  loading={pending}
  onInputChange={fetchPeople}
  onValueChange={setAssignee}
/>
usage.notes: `filter="none"` is the important part: the server may have matched on an email the reader cannot see, and filtering its answer again would hide it. Debounce `fetchPeople` yourself.

usage.when: The list helps, but the answer does not have to be on it.
usage.example:
<Combobox
  label="Tag"
  options={existingTags}
  allowCustomValue
  onValueChange={addTag}
/>
usage.notes: `onValueChange` now receives text that may match no option. Without `allowCustomValue`, that text would be discarded on blur.

usage.when: Five environments, plain labels, nothing to type.
usage.example:
<Combobox
  label="Environment"
  options={[
    { value: "dev", label: "Development" },
    { value: "prod", label: "Production" },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: Don't. A reader can see all of these at once, and `Select` gives them the platform's own picker, which on a phone is better than any popup this component can draw.

behavior.summary: An APG combobox: a text input that keeps focus while `aria-activedescendant` walks a popup listbox, composed with Field for its label, helper text and validation. The answer is an option's value; the text is only how the reader finds it.

decisions.decision: This is not Select, and the line between them is the native picker
decisions.why: `Select` is a native `<select>`: the phone's own wheel or sheet, the platform's typeahead, correct accessibility by construction — and options that are strings and nothing else. Reach for Select when the reader can scan the list, which in practice means it fits on a screen and its options are plain text. Reach for Combobox when the reader has to type to find the answer: the list is long, the options come from a server, or each one needs a second line. Combobox costs a popup, a focus model and an announcement policy that Select gets free, so it is the wrong default — it is the component a list grows into, not the one it starts as. The alias `combo` points here, not at Select: someone who says "combo box" means a field they can type into, which a native `<select>` is not (decision C7, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: It follows the WAI-ARIA APG combobox pattern with a listbox popup, list autocomplete, manual selection
decisions.why: The input keeps DOM focus the whole time and `aria-activedescendant` points at the highlighted option. Arrow keys move the highlight; only Enter or a click commits it. Automatic selection — where arrowing onto an option makes it the value — means a reader browsing the list with a screen reader changes the answer as they listen, which is a value change nobody asked for. APG's list-autocomplete variant with manual selection is the one that keeps browsing and choosing separate.

decisions.decision: The value and the text are two things, and the text gives way
decisions.why: The input shows text; the answer is an option's `value`. Typing changes only the text. On blur, text that matches no option reverts to the chosen option's label (or empties, if nothing is chosen) unless `allowCustomValue` is set — otherwise a form would submit a stale value under a label the reader overwrote, which looks right and is wrong. Clearing the text entirely is a deliberate act and does clear the value.

decisions.decision: It opens on typing, ArrowDown and the toggle — never on focus
decisions.why: Opening on focus ambushes a keyboard user tabbing through a form: every combobox they pass throws a popup over the fields below it. The toggle button at the end of the field is `tabindex="-1"`, as APG specifies, because the keyboard already has ArrowDown and Alt+ArrowDown; it exists for pointer and touch.

decisions.decision: Escape is consumed only when there is something for it to do
decisions.why: First press closes an open popup; with the popup closed, a press clears the text if there is any. With neither, the key bubbles — the same rule `Search` follows, and for the same reason: a field that always swallows Escape stops every Dialog, Sheet and Menu it sits inside from closing.

decisions.decision: The popup reuses Popover's positioning and dismissal, not Menu's, and Popover ships first
decisions.why: Popover is the component that owns an anchored, non-modal surface: the top layer, CSS anchor positioning with a per-instance anchor name — an anchor name written once in a stylesheet makes every instance position against the last trigger on the page — and the dismissal rules of Escape, a press elsewhere and focus leaving. Combobox takes both from it rather than from Menu, because Menu's mechanism is bound to a list of actions that receives focus. The one difference is focus: Popover moves focus in, a combobox never does, so the popup is `popover="manual"` and Popover's dismissal rules are run by the shared primitive with the input counted as inside the surface. Popover is still a spec, so the combobox cannot be built until it ships; that order is the decision, not an accident of scheduling (decision C6, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: The result count is announced politely, after filtering settles
decisions.why: A listbox changing under `aria-activedescendant` is silent in most screen readers, so a reader typing has no idea whether their text matched anything. A polite status region says "7 results" or the `emptyMessage`. It waits for `loading` to clear, because announcing zero results for a query still in flight is a false answer.

decisions.decision: No multiple selection
decisions.why: Choosing several values needs chips in the field, a removal model for each chip and a different announcement for each add and remove. That is a tags input — a separate entry with its own contract — not a boolean here that changes what `value` means.

decisions.decision: Option labels are text, with one ReactNode slot for a second line
decisions.why: The label is what the box shows once chosen and what typing matches against, so a ReactNode label would need a second, hidden text version anyway. `description` is the slot for everything Select cannot show — and it is announced after the label as part of the option's name, so it should be short.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: The system rule. The popup cannot open, the field stays in the tab order, and — the consequence `text-field` already documents — the hidden input still submits its value.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getComboboxProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet, so `behavior.primitive` is left unset. The proposal is a pure function over `{ open, inputText, highlightedIndex, value, options, filter }` returning the input, toggle, listbox and option prop bags plus the next state for each key — the same shape as `getMenuProps`, minus roving focus, plus `aria-activedescendant`. It is the thing approved at this gate.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: an `<input role="combobox">` with `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `aria-autocomplete="list"` and `aria-activedescendant`, a `<ul role="listbox">` of `<li role="option" aria-selected>` in a manual popover, and a hidden input carrying `name`. Touch works the same as pointer; on a narrow viewport the popup still anchors below the field, sized to stay above the on-screen keyboard. React Native: a `TextInput` with `accessibilityRole="combobox"` and `accessibilityState={{ expanded }}`, with results in a `FlatList` of `Pressable` rows carrying `accessibilityState={{ selected, disabled }}`. There is no `aria-activedescendant` on native — the screen reader moves into the list itself — so the highlight model and the count region are web-only behaviour, and native announces the count with `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility`. On a phone the results render in a full-screen `Modal` with the input pinned at the top, because an anchored list below a field is under the keyboard. `name` is web-only: there is no form post on native. `size` is web-only; native rows take the platform's minimum touch height. Rata-drawn (decision N5): neither platform has an OS combobox, so the field is the platform `TextInput` and the results list is drawn by Rata from the same recipe. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

name: date-picker
title: Date Picker
description: A labelled field for one calendar date: typed in the page's locale, or chosen from a calendar grid.

dont: "Date". Every date picker is a date; the label says which one.

props.summary: The starting date when the component owns the state.

props.name: onValueChange

props.summary: The earliest choosable date, as ISO.

props.name: max
props.summary: The latest choosable date, as ISO.

props.name: isDateUnavailable

props.name: calendarLabel

use: Translating it.
dont: An empty string. The button is icon-only.

props.name: placeholder

use: Matching whatever the control sits beside.

usage.case: A date in the near future
usage.when: Booking, scheduling — the calendar is the likely path.
usage.example:
<DatePicker
  label="Check-in"
  min={today}
  isDateUnavailable={(d) => booked.has(d)}
  name="checkin"
  required
/>
usage.notes: `today` and every entry in `booked` are ISO strings, like the value. Unavailable days stay focusable in the grid and are announced as such.

usage.case: A date far in the past
usage.when: A date of birth, an issue date read off a document.
usage.example:
<DatePicker
  label="Date of birth"
  max={today}
  description="As it appears on your passport."
/>
usage.notes: The reader will type this. The placeholder shows the locale's format, which is the same one the parser accepts; nobody should be paging back four hundred months.

usage.case: A typed date that is not allowed
usage.when: Typed entry reached a day the calendar would have refused.
usage.example:
<DatePicker
  label="Delivery"
  value={date}
  onValueChange={setDate}
  status="invalid"
  message="We do not deliver on Sundays. Choose another day."
/>
usage.notes: Typing can always reach any date, so availability has to be reported in the message as well as enforced in the grid — and on native it is reported only here.

usage.when: A stay with a check-in and a check-out.
usage.example:
<DatePicker label="Check-in" />
<DatePicker label="Check-out" />
usage.notes: Workable, but it is not a range: the second calendar cannot show the stay, and each end validates alone. A range is DateRangePicker, which is a spec with no code behind it yet (decision C10) — say so rather than wiring two of these together and calling it one.

behavior.summary: A text input that parses a locale-formatted date, beside a button opening the APG Date Picker Dialog — a modal with a keyboard-navigable grid of days. Composed with Field. The value is an ISO calendar date, which is the only representation of a date with no time zone in it.

decisions.decision: The value is an ISO calendar date string, never a `Date`
decisions.why: A `Date` is an instant: midnight on 1 November in Colombo is still 31 October in New York, so a birthday stored as a `Date` moves by a day when a server, a browser and a time zone disagree — the commonest date-picker bug there is. "2026-11-01" has no time and no zone, sorts as text, round-trips through JSON and forms unchanged, and is what `<input type="date">` itself uses as its value.

decisions.decision: Typing is the primary path; the calendar is help
decisions.why: Someone entering a date of birth, or a date they are reading off a document, types it faster than they can page back forty years. So the field is a text input that parses the page locale's numeric format — the same format the placeholder shows — and the calendar button sits beside it. Parsing happens on blur and Enter, not per keystroke, for the reason Number Field gives.

decisions.decision: Not `<input type="date">` on the web
decisions.why: The native control cannot mark individual days unavailable, cannot be styled to match the system, displays in the browser's locale rather than the page's, and differs enough between engines that one contract cannot describe it: its segmented editing is announced differently by every screen reader, and on desktop Safari it existed for only a few years before this was written. The price of not using it is that this component carries a whole calendar, and that price is named here rather than discovered.

decisions.decision: The calendar is the APG Date Picker Dialog with a grid
decisions.why: The button opens a modal dialog (the native `<dialog>` with `showModal()`, as Dialog does) containing month navigation and a `role="grid"` of days. One day is the tab stop — roving tabindex, starting on the chosen date or today — and arrows move a day, Up and Down a week, Home and End to the row's ends, PageUp and PageDown a month, Shift with them a year. Enter or Space chooses and closes; Escape closes without changing anything. Focus returns to the calendar button either way, because that is where the reader was.

decisions.decision: Anchored on wide screens, a bottom sheet on narrow ones
decisions.why: Both are the same modal dialog. Above a breakpoint it is positioned against the field with anchor positioning; below it, it sits at the bottom edge at full width with larger day cells, because a popup anchored under a field on a phone is either off-screen or under the keyboard, and 32px day targets are too small for a thumb. The keyboard model and the markup do not change, only the placement.

decisions.decision: Unavailable days are focusable and announced
decisions.why: The system's `aria-disabled` rule applied to a day: arrow keys land on it, it is read as unavailable, and choosing it is refused. Skipping unavailable days would make the grid's geometry lie — Down would no longer mean "same weekday, next week".

decisions.decision: No ranges and no times in this component
decisions.why: A range needs two values, a preview between them, and an announcement for each end — that is DateRangePicker, which has its own contract (decision C10, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). A time is a different value type (`"14:30"`) with its own input. Both are built on the same calendar-grid primitive, which is why that is proposed separately below.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: The system rule, and the text field's consequence with it: the value still submits.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitives: `getDatePickerProps` and `getCalendarGridProps`
decisions.why: Neither exists yet. The grid is split out because the date-range picker and any future inline calendar need the same date arithmetic, keyboard model and `aria-disabled` handling without the input. Both work on ISO strings only; locale formatting goes through `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, and the week start through `Intl.Locale`'s week info with a Monday fallback where the engine does not expose it.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a text input inside a Field, a calendar `<button>` with a click guard, a hidden input carrying `name`, and a modal `<dialog>` holding a `<table role="grid">` whose day cells are buttons with `aria-selected`, `aria-current="date"` on today, and `aria-disabled` on unavailable days. Touch, pointer and keyboard share it; only placement changes with width. React Native: no typed entry and no drawn calendar — the field is a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="button"`, the label as its name and the formatted date as `accessibilityValue={{ text }}`, opening the OS picker (UIDatePicker on iOS, the Material date dialog on Android). That is the right picker on a phone and it is accessible by construction, but it costs three things: it is not in core, so it is a community-package dependency; it cannot be styled; and Android's picker supports `min` and `max` but not individual unavailable days, so on native `isDateUnavailable` is enforced after the choice, as an `invalid` status with a message, rather than in the picker. `firstDayOfWeek` is honoured on Android only. `isDateUnavailable` as an in-grid affordance, `placeholder`, `name` and `size` are web-only. The OS control on native, not a Rata-drawn calendar (decision N5): the system picker is the one a phone's readers already know, and it is accessible by construction; the web keeps the Rata-drawn calendar for the reasons above. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

usage.example:

usage.when: A filter over past data.

<DateRangePicker
  label="Period"
  startLabel="From"
  endLabel="To"
  max={today}
  value={range}
  onValueChange={setRange}
/>
usage.notes: Readers will often type these. `range` arrives with one end `null` while the other is being filled.

usage.when: Typed entry produced a range that runs backwards.

<DateRangePicker
  label="Stay"
  value={range}
  onValueChange={setRange}

  message="Check-out must be after check-in."
/>
usage.notes: The component passes typed values through rather than swapping them, so the caller says what is wrong.

usage.when: One date, such as a delivery day.
usage.example: <DateRangePicker label="Delivery" />
usage.notes: A single date is DatePicker. A range picker with equal ends is a valid value, but asking for two inputs to get one date is the wrong question.

behavior.summary: Two text inputs — start and end — inside one Field, beside one button opening the same modal calendar dialog DatePicker uses, where the first day chosen is the start and the second the end. Its own contract rather than a mode of DatePicker (decision C10, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md), built on the same calendar-grid primitive. The value is a pair of ISO calendar dates.

decisions.decision: Its own component, not a `range` prop on DatePicker
decisions.why: A range changes the value's type, adds a second input with its own name, a preview between the ends, a rule about what an end before the start means, and an announcement for each end. A boolean on DatePicker would change what `value` is depending on another prop — the shape this system refuses everywhere else. The two share the calendar-grid primitive instead, so the date arithmetic, keyboard model and `aria-disabled` handling exist once (decision C10, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: The value is `{ start, end }`, each an ISO calendar date or `null`
decisions.why: DatePicker's reason for ISO strings applies twice over: a stay stored as two `Date`s can lose a night when a server and a browser disagree about the zone. Each end can be `null` on its own, because a reader fills one end before the other and a form needs to see that state to say what is missing. A one-day range — start equal to end — is valid.

decisions.decision: Two inputs, each labelled, typing first
decisions.why: Someone reading dates off a booking types them faster than they can page a calendar. So each end is its own text input with its own visible label (`startLabel`, `endLabel`), parsing the page locale's numeric format on blur and Enter as DatePicker does, and the group is labelled by `label`. One input holding "1/11/2026 – 7/11/2026" would need a parser for the separator and announce as one value nobody can edit half of.

decisions.decision: In the calendar, the first choice is the start and the second the end
decisions.why: Choosing a day with no start, or with both ends set, starts a new range and clears the end; the next choice sets the end and closes the dialog. Choosing a day before the start makes that day the new start rather than an end — reordering behind the reader's back would put the cursor's meaning in the wrong place. After the start is chosen, moving focus or the pointer previews the range up to that day, and the dialog's live hint says "Choose end date".

decisions.decision: Typed ends are passed through, never silently reordered
decisions.why: An end typed before the start is reported as typed: `onValueChange` fires with both values, and the caller's validation reports it through `status` and `message` — the same path a typed unavailable date takes in DatePicker. Swapping them would change a value the reader can see they did not enter.

decisions.decision: A range cannot span an unavailable day
decisions.why: Once a start is chosen, every day after the next unavailable one is unavailable as an end, because a booking across a booked night is not a booking. Those days stay focusable and are announced as unavailable, so the grid's geometry does not lie — DatePicker's rule, unchanged.

decisions.decision: Each day's name says where it sits in the range
decisions.why: Fill and tint are invisible to a screen reader, so the start, the end and the days between append "start date", "end date" and "in range" to their accessible name, and the chosen ends use `aria-selected`. The days between are not `aria-selected`: they were not chosen, and announcing six selected days for one choice of two ends misstates what the reader did.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: The system rule, on both inputs and the calendar button. And the text field's consequence with it: both values still submit.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getDateRangePickerProps`, over the shared `getCalendarGridProps`
decisions.why: Neither exists yet. The range primitive adds what the grid lacks — which end the next choice sets, the preview span, the unavailable-span rule and the range-position names — and delegates date arithmetic, the keyboard model and locale handling to the grid DatePicker proposes. Both work on ISO strings only.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `role="group"` labelled by `label`, holding two text inputs with their own labels, a calendar `<button>` with a click guard, two hidden inputs carrying `startName` and `endName`, and a modal `<dialog>` holding a `<table role="grid">` whose day cells are buttons with `aria-selected` on the ends, `aria-current="date"` on today and `aria-disabled` on unavailable days. Touch, pointer and keyboard share it; only placement changes with width. React Native: the two ends are `Pressable` fields with `accessibilityRole="button"` and the formatted date as `accessibilityValue={{ text }}`, opening one calendar through the core `Modal` as a sheet. Rata-drawn, not the OS control (decision N5): iOS's date picker has no range mode and Android's range picker belongs to the Material library rather than the OS, so native draws the calendar from the same grid primitive and recipe as the web — which is also why the grid is a primitive. Typed entry, `placeholder`, `startName`, `endName` and `size` are web-only. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: Two date inputs in one box, matching the date picker's step for step, with a separator between them and the calendar button's well at the end. Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming.

tokens.font-variant: tabular-nums, so a typed date does not shift as digits change
tokens.block-size: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / size.control.lg at the other sizes
tokens.padding-inline-start: space.control.padding-inline.md — and the sm / lg steps
tokens.padding-inline-end: space.control.padding-inline.md plus size.control.sm, for the calendar button
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset — the text field's departure
tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2 as an inset shadow, idle only
tokens.separator colour: theme.fg.secondary — an en dash, aria-hidden; the two inputs' own labels carry the meaning

trigger.summary: The one calendar button at the field's end, opening the calendar on whichever end is empty — the start if both are. A tab stop with the system ring, as in DatePicker, because it opens a dialog the keyboard has no other way to reach.

tokens.inline-size / block-size: size.control.sm, inset space.0-5 from the end edge
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

calendar.summary: The dialog surface on wide screens, DatePicker's unchanged. One month at a time — two side by side would need a second grid and a second focus model, and a range across a month boundary is reached with PageDown.

tokens.month navigation buttons: size.control.sm square, radius.inner, compose the .rata-state-layer class, theme.focus-ring on :focus-visible

calendar-narrow.summary: The same dialog below the breakpoint, at the bottom edge. Sheet-level radius and modal elevation, because here it does take over the screen.

tokens.border-radius: radius.page on the top corners only

day.summary: One day, DatePicker's, plus the three range states. The ends are the filled accent; the days between are a continuous tint, so the stay reads as one band.

tokens.outside the month: theme.fg.muted — shown so the rows are whole weeks, and still choosable
tokens.today: theme.accent-role.fg at type.control.weight — marked by tone and weight rather than a ring, since a ring is the selection and validation stroke
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible — kept on the ends, where offset 0 on a filled accent would vanish
tokens.unavailable: state.disabled-opacity and a line-through, so the state is not carried by dimming alone
tokens.start / end colour: theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on that fill
tokens.in-range colour: theme.fg.primary — verified at AA-text on theme.accent-role.subtle
tokens.in-range border-radius: radius.none, so consecutive days join into one band; the start and end keep radius.pill on their outer side
tokens.preview (start chosen, end not yet): theme.accent-role.ring at border.default as an inset stroke from the start to the focused or hovered day — a selection stroke, distinct from the focus ring

name: dialog
title: Dialog
description: Modal dialog with focus trapping, scroll locking, and dismiss behavior.

props.name: title
props.summary: The dialog's name. Required.
use: A noun phrase naming what this is about: “Delete project”, not “Are you sure?”
dont: A question. The title is the name, and “Are you sure?” names nothing — put the question in the body.
Leaving it out. It is required, and the type will not let you.
props.a11y: Rendered as an `<h2>` and wired with `aria-labelledby`, so the dialog announces with this name when it opens. A real heading, because a modal is its own outline — everything behind it is inert.

props.name: children
props.description: The dialog's content.
props.summary: The dialog's content.
use: What the reader needs in order to answer the title. It scrolls on its own if it is tall.
dont: Another dialog. Two modals deep, the reader has lost track of what the first one asked.
props.a11y: Scrolls in its own region so the title stays put and the footer actions stay reachable — a dialog taller than the viewport otherwise puts its buttons off-screen.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the dialog is showing. Always controlled — `showModal()` has no prop.
props.summary: Whether the dialog is showing. Always controlled.
use: Always. There is no uncontrolled mode, because `showModal()` is a method rather than an attribute and the component has to drive it.
dont: Expecting the dialog to close itself. Every dismissal arrives through `onClose`; setting this to false is what actually closes it.
props.a11y: Drives `showModal()` and `close()`. Nothing else makes the dialog modal — see the behaviour note.

props.name: onClose
props.description: Called when the dialog asks to close. Set `open` to false in it.
props.summary: Called when the dialog asks to close, with why.
use: Setting `open` to false.
Branching on the reason: `escape`, `close-button` or `backdrop` — a form might confirm on a backdrop click but not on the close button.
dont: Ignoring it. Nothing closes the dialog on its own, so an empty handler makes a dialog nobody can leave.
props.a11y: Focus returns to whatever opened the dialog automatically, because the platform restores it — you do not need to do it yourself.

props.name: description
props.description: A line under the title, wired as the dialog's description.
props.summary: A line under the title, wired as the dialog's description.
use: A consequence worth hearing with the name: “Everything in it goes too.”
dont: The whole body. It is announced along with the title, so a paragraph here is read before the reader has asked for it.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-describedby`. Omitted, there is no dangling reference — a describedby pointing at nothing is silently dropped by some screen readers and read as empty by others.

props.name: footer
props.description: The actions. Reads after the body it acts on.
props.summary: The actions.
use: One or two buttons, the primary one last.
The only way out when `dismissible` is false.
dont: Putting the close control here. That is what `dismissible` renders, placed and named for you.
props.a11y: Rendered after the body in DOM order, so the actions are reached after the content they act on.

props.name: size
props.summary: How wide it is allowed to get.
use: `sm` for a confirm — one question and two buttons.
`md` for a short form. The default.
`lg` for content that genuinely needs the room, such as a table.
dont: `lg` for a confirmation. A wide dialog with one sentence in it reads as a mistake, and the buttons end up a long way from the text.
props.a11y: Width only. Every size shrinks to fit a narrow viewport rather than overflowing it.

props.name: dismissible
props.summary: Whether the reader can close it themselves.
use: `true` — the default — for everything except the case below.
`false` for a blocking error where dismissing would lose work, or a decision that genuinely must be made now.
dont: A dialog with no footer action. Escape and the close button are the reader's escape hatches; removing both without giving them another traps them, which is the one thing this prop can do wrong.
`false` to stop people skipping something. A dialog that cannot be dismissed is a dialog people close by leaving the page.
props.a11y: `false` removes the close button and prevents the `cancel` event, so Escape does nothing. The footer then MUST contain a labelled way out.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the close button.
props.summary: Accessible name for the close button.
use: Translating it, or naming what is being closed when the context needs it.
dont: An empty string. The button is icon-only, so this is the only name it has.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`. Without it the control announces as an unnamed button, a 4.1.2 failure.

props.name: role
props.summary: ARIA's kind of dialog.
use: `alertdialog` when the dialog's whole content is a message needing a response — a destructive confirmation, a blocking error.
`dialog`, the default, for anything with work in it: a form, a panel, a picker.
dont: `alertdialog` for a form. It is announced more insistently and its description is read with its name, which is wrong for something the reader has to fill in and right for something they have to answer.
Reaching for it to make a dialog feel important. The role describes what the dialog is, not how much it matters.
props.a11y: A native `<dialog>` is already `role="dialog"`; this only ever narrows it to `alertdialog`, which the element cannot be on its own. Under `alertdialog` a screen reader reads `description` along with `title` rather than waiting to be asked, which is why the destructive confirmation below sets both.

props.name: initialFocus
props.summary: What to focus when it opens. Defaults to the platform's choice.
use: A destructive confirm, pointed at Cancel — so the dangerous button is not one Enter away.
A form, pointed at the first field.
dont: React's `autoFocus` instead. It does not work here: React calls `.focus()` during commit rather than emitting the attribute, so `showModal()` runs afterwards and applies its own default, undoing it.
props.a11y: Applied after `showModal()`, which is the only order that works. Left out, focus lands on the first focusable thing inside — usually the close button.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the dialog, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rarely. `size` is the intended way to change its shape.
dont: Overriding the backdrop or the position. Both come from `dialog.css`, and a competing rule is how a modal ends up unreachable on one page.

usage.when: The commonest modal: one question, two ways out, and the dangerous one must not be the easy one.
usage.notes: `initialFocus` on Cancel is the point: without it focus lands on the first focusable thing, and a reader who opens this and presses Enter should not have deleted anything. `sm` keeps the buttons near the sentence. `alertdialog` is the role for this: the dialog's whole content is a question the reader has to answer, so the description is read along with the name instead of waiting to be asked.

usage.case: A blocking error, where dismissing would lose work
usage.when: Rare, and the only kind of dialog that should refuse to close.
usage.example:
<Dialog
  open={disconnected}
  onClose={() => {}}
  dismissible={false}
  title="Connection lost"
  footer={<Button onClick={reconnect}>Reconnect</Button>}
>
  Your changes are saved locally and will sync when you reconnect.
</Dialog>
usage.notes: The footer action is not optional here — with no close button and Escape blocked, it is the only way out, and a dialog like this without one traps the reader.

usage.case: Don't: a dialog opened from inside a dialog
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example:
{/* Don't: by the time the second one is open, the reader has lost
    track of what the first one asked. */}
<Dialog open={editing} onClose={close} title="Edit project">
  <Button onClick={() => setConfirming(true)}>Delete project</Button>
  <Dialog open={confirming} onClose={closeConfirm} title="Delete project">
    This cannot be undone.
  </Dialog>
</Dialog>
usage.notes: Don't. Close the first, then ask — or ask inline in the dialog already open. The scroll lock and the focus trap both cope with stacking, so nothing breaks; it is the reader who loses the thread.

behavior.summary: A native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`. The browser supplies a real focus trap, `inert` on everything behind it, the top layer, `::backdrop`, Escape-to-close and focus returned to whatever opened it. A hand-written focus trap is the most bug-prone component in any design system, and the platform's is correct by construction — including for the cases hand-rolled ones miss, such as a screen reader's own navigation and the browser's find-in-page.

decisions.decision: `showModal()`, never the `open` attribute
decisions.why: Rendering `<dialog open>` shows the dialog NON-modally: no focus trap, no backdrop, and a live page behind it. There is no attribute for the modal state, only the method, which is why `open` is applied in an effect. Getting this wrong is the easiest way to ship a "modal" that is not one, and it looks correct on screen.

decisions.decision: `title` is required rather than optional
decisions.why: A modal with no accessible name is announced as "dialog" and nothing else. There is no sensible default and no case where omitting it is right, so the type refuses it instead of the contract asking nicely.

decisions.decision: The title is a real `<h2>`, unlike Notice's
decisions.why: A modal is genuinely its own context — everything behind it is inert — so the outline inside it starts fresh and the title is the top of it. A notice sits inside the page's existing outline and cannot know what level it is at, which is why that one is a styled paragraph.

decisions.decision: Escape is always prevented, then reported
decisions.why: The platform would close the dialog itself, leaving `open` still saying it is showing. Preventing the default and reporting through `onClose` keeps React the single source of truth for whether it is open.

decisions.decision: Initial focus is a ref, because React's `autoFocus` cannot work here
decisions.why: React implements `autoFocus` by calling `.focus()` during commit rather than by emitting the HTML attribute, so `showModal()` — which runs afterwards, in an effect — never sees an `[autofocus]` element and applies its own default, undoing it. `initialFocus` is applied after `showModal()` and therefore wins.

decisions.decision: The scroll lock counts holders rather than saving and restoring
decisions.why: Save-and-restore is wrong the moment two dialogs overlap: the second captures `hidden` as the value to put back, so closing it leaves the page locked with nothing open. A counter has no stale state — the property is set while anything holds the lock and removed when the last holder lets go.

decisions.decision: The modal motion band was wrong, and the tempo behind it was too slow
decisions.why: `motion.modal.duration` resolved to `motion.duration.slow`, which this system's own motion contract documents as “Continuous animation” — the spinner band. That was the category error; it is `medium-max` now, the slowest step of the entrance/exit band, which is where the expander's config names “(dialog, drawer)”. Fixing the band alone still left 545ms, because the medium band itself was too slow: Astryx's 175/410/975 tempo meant a menu took 410ms to appear. The seed came down to 130/210/700, so a dialog now enters in 280ms and a menu in 210ms. The bands kept their meanings and no role had to be remapped to one it does not belong to.

decisions.decision: The page's scroll is locked with the scrollbar's width held open
decisions.why: Hiding the overflow takes the scrollbar away and the page reflows into the space it occupied, so everything shifts sideways as the dialog opens and jumps back as it closes — more noticeable than the scrolling being prevented. The width is measured at lock time rather than tokenised, because it is whatever the browser and the reader's settings make it, and it is zero for overlay scrollbars.

decisions.decision: A native close is reported rather than ignored
decisions.why: `<form method="dialog">` is the documented HTML way to close a dialog, and the platform can close one for its own reasons too. Neither goes through `onClose`, and the effect that drives the dialog is keyed on `open`, so it never re-runs to notice — `open` went on claiming the dialog was showing, and the scroll lock stayed on the body with nothing open, leaving the page unable to scroll at all. The native `close` event now reports `external`, and only while React still believes the dialog is open, so the component's own `close()` is not mistaken for someone else's.

decisions.decision: The modal machinery moved out of this component when Sheet arrived
decisions.why: showModal, the counted scroll lock, the Escape interception, the backdrop click and the report of a close nobody asked for are now `useModalDialog`, shared with Sheet. Every one of them exists because of a specific bug, several of them silent, and a second hand-written copy would have drifted on exactly those. Nothing about this component's behaviour changed — the same 27 tests pass against it.

base.summary: A modal surface that takes over the screen.

tokens.enter transition: motion.modal.duration with motion.easing.enter, fading and rising
tokens.exit pointer-events: none while closing — the top layer is held for the exit, so the backdrop would go on catching clicks after the reader closed it

backdrop.summary: The wash over the inert page behind it. Its own token, added for this component: nothing else in the system dims the page, and a non-modal overlay must not. It transitions `overlay` alongside the dialog, which is what keeps the scrim on screen for the length of the exit rather than dropping it the instant the dialog starts closing.

size.summary: Three widths, derived from the control scale rather than stated: a dialog is measured in controls, and inventing a size.dialog.* family for three numbers would be a scale with one consumer. Flagged as a known gap if a fourth width ever appears.

tokens.sm max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 10, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller
tokens.md max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 14, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller
tokens.lg max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 20, or the viewport less its inset — whichever is smaller

footer.summary: The actions, reading after the body they act on.

dismiss.summary: The close control. Same construction as Notice's: currentColor on a transparent background, so it cannot clash with the surface it sits on.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the dialog's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible
tokens.block alignment: centred on the title's first line, from type.heading.size and type.heading.line-height

example:
<Dialog
        open={open}
        onClose={() => setOpen(false)}
        title={title}
        description={description}
        size={size}
        dismissible={dismissible}
        initialFocus={cancelRef}
        footer={
          <>
            <Button ref={cancelRef} variant="secondary" onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>
              Cancel
            </Button>
            <Button variant={destructive ? "destructive" : "primary"} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}>
              {destructive ? "Delete" : "Save"}
            </Button>
          </>
        }
      >
        This cannot be undone.
      </Dialog>

name: disclosure
title: Disclosure
description: A button that shows and hides a panel of content, expanded in place.

props.name: title
props.description: The trigger's label — what the button says it will reveal.
props.summary: The trigger's label — what the button says it will reveal.
use: A short phrase naming the content, not the action: "Shipping address", not "Show shipping address". The button already announces that it expands.
dont: A sentence. The trigger is a control at control size, and a label that wraps has stopped being one.
Anything interactive. A button inside a button does not nest, and the browser will not render what you wrote.
props.a11y: Becomes the trigger's accessible name, and — through `aria-labelledby` — the panel's as well, so the revealed region is never anonymous. With `headingLevel` set it is also the heading's text.

props.name: children
props.description: The content the trigger reveals.
props.summary: The content the trigger reveals.
use: Anything: prose, a form, a table. The panel is a plain region and imposes no structure on it.
dont: Content that must keep state while closed. The panel's content unmounts rather than hiding, so a half-filled form inside it is gone on reopen — lift that state above the disclosure.
props.a11y: Everything inside stays in the tab order exactly where it is. That is the promise a disclosure makes and a menu does not.

props.name: headingLevel
props.description: Wraps the trigger in a heading at this level, so a stack of these is navigable by heading.
props.summary: Wraps the trigger in a heading at this level, turning a stack of these into an accordion someone can navigate by heading.
use: On every section of a set that divides a page — the level below whatever heading the set sits under.
Left off for a single disclosure inside a form or a paragraph, which heads nothing.
dont: Picking it for size. The trigger is a control and takes the control type scale at every level; this only changes what the outline says.
props.a11y: The APG's accordion pattern is a heading containing a button, and that pairing is what lets a reader jump between sections instead of tabbing through them. A skipped level breaks that navigation, which is why there is no default — only the caller knows the depth.

props.name: open
props.description: Controls the panel from outside, for when something other than the trigger decides.
props.summary: Controls the panel from outside, for when something other than the trigger decides.
use: Opening the section that holds a failed field after a form is submitted.
Persisting which sections a reader had open across a navigation.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`. One of them owns the state; passing both means the uncontrolled value is silently ignored from the first render.
props.a11y: Drives `aria-expanded` on the trigger. Because the panel unmounts when closed, this prop is also what decides whether its content exists at all.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: The starting state when the component owns it.
props.summary: The starting state when the component owns it.
use: Opening the one section that is the point of the page, leaving the rest closed.
Opening the section containing the current item, the way `SideNav` expands the group holding the current page — a reader inside a collapsed group cannot see where they are.
dont: Opening everything. A set that starts fully open is a page with headings in it, and the disclosures are only costing the reader a click to get back to.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description: Fires when the trigger is pressed or Escape closes the panel.
props.summary: Fires when the trigger is pressed or Escape closes the panel.
use: Storing which sections a reader keeps open.
Loading the section's content the first time it opens.
dont: Treating it as a click handler. Escape calls it too, and so does any future way of closing the panel.
props.a11y: The component returns focus to the trigger when Escape closes the panel, before this fires — a caller does not have to restore it and should not fight it.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Marks the disclosure unavailable without removing it from the page.
props.summary: Marks the disclosure unavailable without removing it from the page.
use: A section that has nothing in it yet, where hiding it entirely would make the page change shape.
dont: Hiding content the reader is not allowed to see. Disabled is a statement about the control, not a security boundary, and the panel's absence is not enforcement.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled`, never the native attribute: the trigger stays focusable and discoverable, and the primitive blocks the activation. Styled with state.disabled-opacity.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The margin the page wants around it, or the rule between it and the next one, neither of which this component owns.
dont: Rebuilding the trigger's hover. Compose `.rata-state-layer`, which it already carries.

usage.case: One optional section in a form
usage.when: Settings most people never change, kept off the page until asked for.
usage.example:
<Disclosure title="Advanced options">
  <TextField label="Retry limit" />
</Disclosure>
usage.notes: No `headingLevel`: this heads nothing and nobody navigates to it. The fields inside stay in the tab order where they are, which is the promise that makes a disclosure the right pattern here rather than a menu.

usage.when: Several disclosures in a row, each a part of one document.
usage.example:
<Disclosure title="Shipping address" headingLevel={3} defaultOpen>
  <Text>Where the order goes.</Text>
</Disclosure>
usage.notes: `headingLevel` is what makes the set navigable by heading instead of only by tabbing. Level 3 because the section it sits in is headed by an h2 — the same outline rule `Heading` enforces.

usage.case: Opened from outside by something that went wrong
usage.when: A submit failed and the offending field is inside a collapsed section.
usage.example:
<Disclosure title="Billing" open={hasBillingError} onOpenChange={setBillingOpen}>
  <TextField label="Card number" status="invalid" message="Check this number." />
</Disclosure>
usage.notes: Controlled, because the trigger is no longer the only thing that decides. A reader must never be shown an error message about a field they cannot see.

usage.when: The panel holds commands rather than content — Rename, Duplicate, Delete.
usage.example:
<Disclosure title="Actions">
  <Button variant="tertiary">Rename</Button>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Delete</Button>
</Disclosure>
usage.notes: Don't. That is `Menu`: a list of commands promises arrow-key navigation and one tab stop, and a disclosure gives neither — so every command lands in the page's tab order. The two are different ARIA patterns for different things, which is exactly why the primitive is separate from `getMenuProps`.

behavior.summary: A trigger that shows and hides a panel, built on `getDisclosureProps` — the primitive three navigation components already use. Open state is controlled or uncontrolled; Escape closes it from either half and hands focus back to the trigger.

decisions.decision: This is a disclosure and not a menu, and the difference is the whole reason the primitive exists separately
decisions.why: A menu promises a keyboard model — one tab stop, arrow keys, typeahead — that assistive technology announces and users then expect. A disclosure promises nothing beyond "this button reveals that", and everything inside the panel stays in the tab order where it was. Reaching for `role="menu"` on a panel of links or form fields is among the commonest mistakes in this area, and `getDisclosureProps` documents it at length. This component is the standalone consumer of that argument.

decisions.decision: Closed empties the panel rather than removing it
decisions.why: Two promises pull against each other here and the split keeps both. The content is unmounted, for the reason `SideNav` first gave: hidden content is still reachable by find-in-page, so a panel claiming to be collapsed could be scrolled to and read, and a chart inside a closed section would go on measuring a hidden box. But the panel ELEMENT stays, empty and `hidden`, because `getDisclosureProps` points `aria-controls` at it whether open or shut — a reference that appears and disappears is one assistive technology has to re-read to discover, and a dangling IDREF is simply ignored, which made that reference inert exactly half the time. An empty hidden shell is reachable by no find-in-page and resolves for every reader. The cost is unchanged: state inside the panel resets, which is the caller's to manage and is stated in `children`'s entry.

decisions.decision: It does not animate open in this version
decisions.why: Transitioning to `height: auto` needs either a measured pixel height or a `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr` wrapper, and both put a second element around the caller's content purely to move it. Unmounting when closed forecloses the transition anyway — there is nothing in the DOM to animate from. The chevron rotates, which is the part that reports the state change, and the panel appears. Animating the panel is its own pass with its own decision about the wrapper.

decisions.decision: `headingLevel` is optional and there is no default
decisions.why: The APG's disclosure pattern is a bare button, and that is right for one "Show advanced options" in a form. The APG's accordion pattern wraps each trigger in a heading, and that is what makes a stack of sections navigable by heading. Those are the same component in two situations, so the wrapper is a prop rather than a second component — and it has no default for the reason `Heading`'s `level` has none: only the caller knows the depth, and a component that guessed would produce a page of `h3`s.

decisions.decision: It owns no box, no background and no rule between sections
decisions.why: A lone disclosure sits in running content, where a border and a padded box would be an uninvited card. The rules that divide a stack of sections are a property of the stack — they need to know which section is first and last — and inventing them here would mean every standalone use has to override them. Same reasoning as `Heading` carrying no margin.

decisions.decision: An accordion — a set where opening one closes the others — is a different entry, and this is not it
decisions.why: That behavior needs an owner above the individual sections: something holding which one is open, the way `RadioGroup` holds the selected radio and `ToggleButtonGroup` holds its selection mode. A `single`/`multiple` prop on the unit could not express it, because a unit cannot close its siblings. `accordion` resolves here for now because one collapsible section is what most people asking for one actually want; when the coordinating entry ships, the alias moves to it.

decisions.decision: `disabled` is `aria-disabled`, and the primitive blocks the activation
decisions.why: This system's rule for every interactive primitive: a disabled control stays focusable and screen-reader-discoverable, and `getDisclosureProps` already guards the click and emits `aria-disabled` rather than the native attribute. Nothing new is decided here — it is named so the contract does not read as though the question were open.

decisions.decision: Escape closes it from the trigger as well as from inside the panel
decisions.why: A disclosure does not move focus when it opens, so after the trigger is pressed focus is still on the trigger. An Escape handler bound only to the panel would therefore never fire in the commonest case: open it, press Escape, nothing happens. The primitive puts the same handler on both halves for exactly this, and leaves the key alone while closed so a surrounding Dialog still receives it.

base.summary: Nothing. The component owns no box, no background and no rule — a lone disclosure sits in running content, and the divider between stacked sections belongs to the set rather than to the unit.

tokens.box: none — see the decision on why the rules between sections are not this component's

trigger.summary: A control, sized and padded from the control scale so it lines up with the buttons around it. Full-bleed in its inline axis: the whole row is the target, which is what makes a wide section header feel pressable rather than only its text.

tokens.min-block-size: size.control.md as a FLOOR rather than a fixed height — a section title long enough to wrap must be allowed to, the same call `SideNav` made for its rows. A fixed block-size would clip the second line.
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

chevron.summary: The only thing that moves. It rotates between the two states at the interactive duration, which is the pair reserved for a control answering a press.

tokens.colour: currentColor — it repeats what aria-expanded already says, so it can never disagree with the trigger it sits in

panel.summary: The revealed content. Indented to the trigger's own inline padding so the two read as one block, and given room above it rather than below — what follows the disclosure is the page's spacing problem, not this component's.

tokens.padding-inline: space.control.padding-inline.sm — matching the trigger, so the label and the content it reveals share an edge
tokens.colour: inherited — the panel holds whatever the caller puts in it and tints none of it
tokens.when closed: display: none via [hidden] — stated rather than left to the UA stylesheet, because a `display` added to this rule later would silently outrank it and start painting an empty box

example:
<Disclosure title="Advanced options">
          <TextField label="Retry limit" description="How many times to try again." />
        </Disclosure>

name: divider
title: Divider
description: A rule marking a change of topic within a page, or a separation between groups in a toolbar.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Which way the rule runs.
props.summary: Which way the rule runs.
use: `vertical` between groups of controls in a horizontal row, such as a toolbar.
dont: `vertical` between two columns of a page layout. That is the layout's border, not a separator.
props.a11y: `horizontal` renders an `<hr>`; `vertical` renders `role="separator"` with `aria-orientation="vertical"`.

props.name: decorative
props.description: Hides the rule from assistive tech when it marks no real change of topic.
props.summary: Hides the rule from assistive tech when it marks no real change of topic.
use: A line the design wants where the content does not change subject — around an "or" between two sign-in options.
dont: Every divider, by habit. A real topic break should be heard as one.
props.a11y: Adds `aria-hidden="true"`. Web only: on React Native the rule is always hidden.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for placement.
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement.
use: The space the page wants either side, which this component deliberately does not own.
dont: A thicker or coloured rule. A heavier boundary is `theme.border.strong` on the component that owns it, not a restyled divider.

usage.case: A change of topic in running content
usage.when: Two parts of a page about different things, where a heading alone would be too quiet.
usage.example:
<Text>Your plan renews on 1 March.</Text>
<Divider />
<Heading level={2}>Danger zone</Heading>
usage.notes: Semantic, so it is announced as a separator. The space either side comes from the parent's stack gap, not from the divider.

usage.when: A row of controls in two or more groups.
usage.notes: Vertical renders `role="separator"` with `aria-orientation`, which is what the toolbar pattern expects between groups.

usage.when: A rule between every row of a list.
usage.notes: Don't. A screen reader hears "separator" between every row, and the list cannot drop the last one cleanly. The list owns its row borders — a Table, or the list's own CSS with `theme.border.default`.

behavior.summary: An `<hr>` when horizontal, a `role="separator"` element when vertical, or an `aria-hidden` rule when `decorative`. No primitive: a non-focusable separator has no interaction to own.

decisions.decision: Most lines in a UI are not Dividers
decisions.why: The rule between table rows is the table's, the rule between menu groups is `MenuSeparator`, the rule between a stack of Disclosures belongs to the stack, and the outline of a Card is the card's. Each of those is a border owned by the component that knows where it goes. A Divider is for the one case none of them cover: a change of topic in running content, or a group boundary in a row of controls. If you are placing a Divider between every item of a list, the list should own the border.

decisions.decision: Semantic by default, `decorative` to opt out
decisions.why: An `<hr>` is a thematic break, announced as a separator, and it tells a screen-reader user what a sighted reader sees: the topic changed here. When the line is only visual — the gap would have done, but the design wants a line — `decorative` hides it so a reader does not hear "separator" between two things that are not separate. Defaulting the other way would make every semantic break silent unless the caller remembered.

decisions.decision: Vertical is a `role="separator"`, not an `<hr>`
decisions.why: An `<hr>` is horizontal by definition, and styling one vertical leaves it announcing the wrong orientation. A vertical divider between toolbar groups is a `div` with `role="separator"` and `aria-orientation="vertical"`, which is what the ARIA toolbar pattern expects.

decisions.decision: No label in the middle
decisions.why: "— or —" between two sign-in options is a sentence, not a rule, and rendering text inside a separator makes a screen reader either skip the text or read the separator as content. Write the word as text between two decorative dividers if the design needs it. A labelled divider is not part of this gate.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: `<hr>` horizontally; `<div role="separator" aria-orientation="vertical">` vertically; with `decorative`, the same element with `aria-hidden="true"` (and `role="none"` on the `<hr>`). React Native has no separator role: a hairline `View` that is always hidden from assistive tech with `importantForAccessibility="no"` and `accessibilityElementsHidden`, whatever `decorative` says — the topic change is carried by the heading that follows it, which is the only structure native screen readers navigate by. `decorative` therefore has an effect on web only. Rata-drawn (decision N5): there is no OS separator control. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: One hairline in the divider colour `theme.border.default` documents. No margin: the stack it sits in owns the space either side.

tokens.margin: space.0 — the parent's gap places it, as with Heading
tokens.inline-size: the full width of its container

vertical.summary: The same hairline on the other axis, stretching to the height of the row it divides.

tokens.block-size: stretched to the row by the parent's alignment

name: empty-state
title: Empty state
description: What a collection shows when it has nothing in it: why it is empty, and the one thing to do about it.

props.name: title
props.description: What is empty, said plainly.
props.summary: What is empty, said plainly.
use: First use: "No invoices yet".
No results: "No tokens match ‘brand-teal’" — restate the query, so the reader can see what they typed.
dont: "Nothing here" or "Oops". Say what is missing.
Reporting a failure. "Couldn't load" is a Notice.
props.a11y: Read first, and announced on its own when `live` is set.

props.name: description
props.description: One or two sentences on why it is empty or what the action will do.
props.summary: One or two sentences on why it is empty or what the action will do.
use: What the first item will be for, or which filter is excluding everything.
dont: Repeating the title in more words.

props.name: action
props.description: The one way out: a Button or a Link.
props.summary: The one way out: a Button or a Link.
use: Create the first item; clear the search or filters.
dont: Two buttons. Put secondary help in the description as a link.
props.a11y: A real control, reached by Tab in reading order after the text.

props.name: icon
props.description: A glyph marking the area as intentionally empty. Omit for none.
props.summary: A glyph marking the area as intentionally empty. Omit for none.
use: An icon for the kind of thing that is missing — a file for documents, a search glyph for no results.
dont: An illustration or image. This slot is an icon at the icon scale's largest step.
props.a11y: Always `aria-hidden`; the title carries the meaning.

props.name: live
props.description: Whether the empty state is announced when it appears.
props.summary: Whether the empty state is announced when it appears.
use: `polite` for no-results after a search or filter the reader just changed.
dont: `polite` on an empty state present at page load. It interrupts the page being read.
`assertive`, almost ever. Being empty is not urgent.
props.a11y: The same contract as Notice's `live`: a live region announces changes, so this matters only when the empty state arrives after the page did.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for placement.
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement.
use: Positioning it in the space the content would fill.
dont: Boxing it in a card. It replaces content; it is not a widget.

usage.when: A collection the reader has not created anything in yet.
usage.example:
<EmptyState
  icon={FileText}
  title="No invoices yet"
  description="Invoices you send will appear here, newest first."
  action={<Button>Create invoice</Button>}
/>
usage.notes: Silent, because it is there when the page loads. One action, the one that ends the empty state.

usage.when: A filter or search the reader just changed matched nothing.
usage.example:
<EmptyState
  live="polite"
  icon={SearchX}
  title={`No tokens match ‘${query}’`}
  action={<Button variant="secondary" onClick={clearSearch}>Clear search</Button>}
/>
usage.notes: `live="polite"` because the reader's focus is in the search field and the list changed somewhere else. The title restates the query, so a typo is visible.

usage.when: The request for the list failed.
usage.example: <EmptyState title="No invoices" />
usage.notes: Don't. Telling the reader they have no invoices when the request failed is the worst message on the page. That is a Notice with `variant="danger"` and a retry action.

behavior.summary: A `div` with a title, an optional description and an optional action, rendered where the empty collection would be. Silent by default; `live` announces it when it appears because of something the reader did, as Notice's `live` does. No primitive: no interaction to own and no state to hold.

decisions.decision: Empty is not an error
decisions.why: "No invoices yet" and "Couldn't load invoices" look alike and mean opposite things — one is a correct answer, the other is a failure the reader may need to retry or report. A failure is a Notice with the danger variant, in the same place. Keeping them apart stops a failed request from quietly telling the reader they have no data.

decisions.decision: Two kinds of empty, and the copy differs, not the component
decisions.why: First use — nothing has been created yet — wants an invitation and the action that creates the first item. No results — a search or filter matched nothing — wants the query restated and a way to clear it. Both are the same layout with different words; a `kind` prop would be a switch that changes nothing visible. The usage cases below are where the difference is written down.

decisions.decision: The title is a styled paragraph, not a heading
decisions.why: The empty state sits inside a section that already has a heading — the list's own — and cannot know its level, which is the problem Notice solves the same way. A heading here would add an outline entry for content that does not exist. The section's own heading, still visible above it, is what names the area.

decisions.decision: `live` is a prop, silent by default
decisions.why: Notice's reasoning, applied unchanged. An empty state present when the page loads is read in place, and announcing it would interrupt the page being read. One that appears because the reader typed a search that matched nothing must be announced, because their attention is on the search field and the list changed somewhere else. That depends on how the empty state arrived, not on what it says, so the caller states it.

decisions.decision: One action, at most
decisions.why: An empty state exists to get the reader out of it. One action — Create the first one, Clear filters — is the way out; two is a choice the reader did not come here to make. Secondary help belongs in the description as a link.

decisions.decision: An icon, never an illustration
decisions.why: Illustrations are brand, they carry no token, and they push the action below the fold on a phone. A `size.icon.lg` glyph in `theme.fg.muted` marks the area as intentionally empty without competing with the text. It is `aria-hidden`: the title says what it means.

decisions.decision: Line length: size.measure.compact
decisions.why: The description is bounded at size.measure.compact, 45ch — short enough to read as one thought, centred under its heading, and in ch so it follows the text. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `div`; with `live`, it carries `role="status"` (polite) or `role="alert"` (assertive), as Notice does. The icon is `aria-hidden`. React Native: a `View`; the title is plain `Text`, not `accessibilityRole="header"`, for the outline reason above. `live` maps to `accessibilityLiveRegion` on Android and to `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility` with the title on iOS. All props work on both. Rata-drawn (decision N5): React Native exposes no OS empty-state view, so it is drawn from the same recipe as the web. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: Centred text in the space the content would have filled, with no box: an empty state replaces content, so it sits on the content's surface rather than on a card of its own.

name: fab
title: FAB
description: The one primary action of a screen, floating over its content at the bottom inline-end corner.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: What the action does, as a verb phrase — shown beside the icon, or used as the accessible name when hidden.
use: A short imperative: 'Compose', 'New invoice', 'Add photo'.
dont: A noun alone ('Invoice'), which says what the screen is about rather than what the button does.
props.a11y: The accessible name in both states. Visible text when shown; `aria-label` when `labelHidden` is set.

props.name: icon
props.summary: The glyph, which is always shown.
use: A glyph that means the action on its own — a plus for create, a pencil for compose.
dont: A brand mark or an illustration. Above `size.icon.lg` a graphic is no longer an icon, and the FAB's size is fixed.
props.a11y: Decorative: `aria-hidden`, because `label` is the name.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Shows the icon alone, as a circle, with `label` as the accessible name.
use: An action so conventional on its screen that the glyph explains it — the plus on a list of notes.
dont: Saving space on a screen where the action is not obvious. The label is what explains a floating control, and a circle with a glyph in it saves one word's width.
props.a11y: The name does not change; only whether it is visible.

props.name: placement
props.summary: Which bottom corner it floats at — inline-end, or centred.
use: `center` when the screen's content is symmetrical and the action belongs to all of it, such as a camera's shutter.
dont: `center` above a BottomNav. It lands over the middle destination's label and reads as a sixth item.
props.a11y: Visual only; reading order follows the DOM, not the corner.

props.name: loading
props.summary: Shows a Spinner in place of the icon and blocks activation, while staying focusable.
use: The action's request is in flight and a second press would send it twice.
dont: As a page-loading indicator. The FAB is busy only with its own action.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled="true"` and `aria-busy="true"`, as on Button. The label stays, so the name does not change while it is pending.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping it focusable and announced.
use: The action exists on this screen but cannot run yet, and the reader should be able to find out it exists.
dont: Permanently. A FAB that can never be pressed on a screen should not be rendered there — a disabled control floating over everything is the most prominent thing on the screen, and it does nothing.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled`, not the `disabled` attribute, so it stays in the tab order and screen readers announce it as unavailable rather than skipping it.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement adjustments — not for restyling it.
use: Hiding it at widths where the action lives in a toolbar instead.
dont: A hand-written `bottom` offset. The placement is computed from the safe area and the BottomNav; a fixed number is wrong on the next device.

usage.case: Creating the thing a list is a list of
usage.when: A screen that is mostly one collection, where adding to it is the reason the screen exists.
usage.example: <Fab label="New note" icon={Plus} onClick={createNote} />
usage.notes: Rendered at the start of `<main>`, before the list, so a keyboard reaches it first. The list reserves `padding-block-end` so its last row is not left under the FAB.

usage.case: A conventional glyph with the label hidden
usage.when: The action is the one every reader of this screen expects, and the glyph is its well-known mark.
usage.example: <Fab label="Compose" icon={Pencil} labelHidden onClick={compose} />
usage.notes: `label` is still required: it becomes the `aria-label`. Hiding it is the exception, not the default, because nothing near a floating control explains it.

usage.case: Several creation actions behind one FAB
usage.when: A screen where the primary action is 'add', and there are two or three kinds of thing to add.
usage.example:
<Menu label="Add" trigger={<Fab label="Add" icon={Plus} />}>
  <MenuItem onSelect={addPhoto}>Photo</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem onSelect={addNote}>Note</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: This is the speed dial, and it is Menu's job: focus moves into the list, Escape returns to the FAB, arrow keys move between items.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: two floating actions
usage.when: A screen with a primary action and a secondary one, both wanting to float.
usage.example:
<Fab label="Save" icon={Check} />
<Fab label="Discard" icon={X} />
usage.notes: Don't. Two FABs is no primary action. Discard is not something to keep under the thumb at all — it belongs in a footer or a Menu, as a Button or a destructive MenuItem.

behavior.summary: A `<button type="button">` fixed to a corner of the viewport, with Button's activation, loading and disabled behaviour. No primitive of its own: it composes `getButtonProps`, because activation is identical and a second implementation of it is a second place for the aria-disabled guard to go wrong.

decisions.decision: It is a component, not a Button with a className
decisions.why: This system's test for a new component is a difference in semantics, and a FAB has none: it is announced as a button and activated as one. What it adds is a placement that every consumer would otherwise hand-write — fixed to a corner, offset by the safe-area inset, lifted clear of a BottomNav — and that is exactly the kind of value that ends up as `bottom: 72px` in a stylesheet and wrong on the next phone. It composes Button's primitive rather than restating it, so the only new thing is the geometry.

decisions.decision: One per screen, and always the primary fill — so there is no `variant`
decisions.why: A FAB says 'this is what this screen is for'. Two of them say nothing, and a secondary-styled one is a primary action that has been told to look unimportant while still floating over everything. The fill is Button's primary pair because it is the primary action; a destructive action never floats, because the one control that is always under the thumb is the last one that should delete something.

decisions.decision: `label` is required and shown by default
decisions.why: A floating glyph is the least explained control on a screen: it is detached from any content that could give it context. So the label is visible unless `labelHidden` is set, the same default and the same prop name as Switch. When it is hidden it becomes the `aria-label`, and it is still required, because an icon-only button with no name is announced as 'button' — this is Button's `iconOnly` obligation, enforced by the type instead of the contract.

decisions.decision: It does not shrink or hide on scroll
