decisions.why: Collapsing a labelled FAB to its icon on scroll, or sliding it off-screen, is common and has the problem BottomNav's contract names: it moves a target out from under a thumb that was about to use it. It also changes the accessible name's visibility mid-gesture. The vertical space it saves is one control's worth in one corner.

decisions.decision: Reading order follows the DOM, so where it is rendered matters more than where it floats
decisions.why: Fixed positioning moves the paint and not the tab order. Rendered after a long list, the FAB is reached by keyboard only after every row in it; rendered at the start of `<main>`, it is reached first, which matches its importance. The contract cannot choose this for the caller, so it says it: render it before the content it acts on.

decisions.decision: It covers content, and the page reserves space for that
decisions.why: A fixed control sits over whatever scrolls beneath it, so the last row of a list ends behind it. BottomNav avoids this by being sticky; a FAB cannot, because it floats in a corner rather than spanning an edge. The page's scrolling content needs `padding-block-end` of at least the FAB's block size plus its offset — the recipe states both in tokens, so the reservation is a sum of the same tokens rather than a measured number.

decisions.decision: A speed dial is a Menu, not a mode of this
decisions.why: A FAB that fans out into three smaller actions is a trigger and a transient list of actions, which is precisely Menu — focus moves into it, Escape returns to the trigger, the arrow keys move between items. `<Menu trigger={<Fab … />}>` gets all of that from a component that already owns it; a `speedDial` prop here would be a second, unreviewed menu.

decisions.decision: `loading` and `disabled` behave exactly as they do on Button
decisions.why: Both are aria-disabled: the FAB stays focusable and discoverable and activation is blocked in the primitive. `loading` shows a Spinner in place of the icon and keeps the label, so the FAB does not change size while an action is pending. They are mutually exclusive for Button's reason — a control cannot be both busy and unavailable.

decisions.decision: Touch target: size.target.min
decisions.why: The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Elevation: theme.elevation.floating
decisions.why: A FAB is persistent and floats over moving content, which is neither raised (a resting card), overlay (a transient surface anchored to a trigger) nor modal. theme.elevation.floating is that role. It points at the same primitive as overlay today, and is a separate role so a theme can strengthen one without the other. A menu opened from the FAB still uses overlay. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: On the web it renders `<button type="button">`, position fixed, with `aria-label={label}` only when `labelHidden` is set — otherwise the visible text is the name, and the icon is `aria-hidden`. While `loading` it carries `aria-disabled="true"` and `aria-busy="true"`. On React Native it renders a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="button"`, `accessibilityLabel={label}`, and `accessibilityState={{ disabled, busy: loading }}`, absolutely positioned inside the screen and offset by `useSafeAreaInsets()`. Web-only: `className`, and the BottomNav clearance, which is a CSS `:has()` rule — a native screen knows its tab bar's height from the navigator and offsets by that instead. No prop is native-only. There is no gesture. Rata-drawn (decision N5): iOS has no floating action button and Android's is a Material library component rather than an OS control, so it is a drawn `Pressable` from the same recipe on both. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A primary button in shape and colour, held to a corner of the viewport. The fill and its label token are Button's primary pair unchanged, because this is the screen's primary action and nothing about floating changes that.

tokens.color: theme.fg.on-accent — the one label token that belongs on theme.accent-role.bg
tokens.inline-size, label hidden: equal to the block-size, so the hidden-label FAB is a circle
tokens.border-radius: radius.pill — one radius that makes the hidden-label FAB a circle and the labelled one a pill, so the two are visibly the same control
tokens.hover / press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible — never offset 0, because this is a filled accent control

placement.summary: Where it floats. Measured from the viewport's safe area rather than its edge, and lifted clear of a BottomNav when one is on the page.

tokens.placement center: inset-inline-start 50% with a translate of half its own inline size, in place of inset-inline-end
tokens.clearance above a BottomNav: when `:root:has(.rata-bottom-nav)`, inset-block-end adds the bar's own block size — computed from the same tokens BottomNav's recipe uses, so nothing is measured at runtime
tokens.z-index: above page content and below the top layer — a Dialog, Sheet or Menu opened from it must cover it, and they do, because the top layer is above every z-index

name: field
title: Field
description: The label, helper text, message and validation state around a form control.

props.name: label
props.description: The control's name. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The control's name.
use: A short noun phrase: "Billing email", not "Enter your billing email".
dont: Leaving it out for a field whose purpose looks obvious. There is no unlabelled option — `labelHidden` is how a visually bare field is built.
props.a11y: Bound to the control with `for`/`id` by the primitive, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

props.name: children
props.description: Renders the control, given the id and ARIA it must carry.
props.summary: Renders the control, given the id and ARIA it must carry.
use: Spreading the argument onto the control and nothing else: `{(control) => <select {...control} />}`.
Wrapping a control this system does not own yet, which is the case Field exists for outside its own components.
dont: Dropping the argument. A control rendered without it has no id, no accessible name and no description chain — and it will look correct, which is what makes it worth saying.
props.a11y: The argument carries `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Every one of them is derived, so none can drift from the label and message beside it.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A field whose meaning is already carried by its surroundings — a search box under a heading that names it.
dont: Using it and then relying on `placeholder` to carry the name. The placeholder disappears on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound. Nothing about the accessible name changes — only the pixels.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the control. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an external error summary linking to the field it describes.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message — is derived from this, so a duplicate silently crosses two fields' wiring.

props.name: status
props.description: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and the control's ring.
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the control's ring.
use: `validating` for an in-flight check, such as a uniqueness lookup.
`invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong and the colour says it twice; only the message says what.
props.a11y: `invalid` sets `aria-invalid` and pulls the message into `aria-describedby`; `validating` sets `aria-busy`. While `idle` the message stays on the page but leaves the description chain, so a stale message is not announced.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text under the control.
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: A constraint the reader needs before they type: a format, a limit, where the value ends up.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.description: Status-dependent message under the control: the error, confirmation, or in-flight note.
props.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative: "Check this number."
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It vanishes from the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert: it is already in `aria-describedby`, and an assertive region would announce it a second time when focus lands.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the field required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission. On a form where nearly everything is required, mark the optional ones instead.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. This renders one, and the second would be read out.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control. The rendered asterisk is `aria-hidden`, because announcing it too would say the requirement twice.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
props.summary: Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
use: A field whose value is decided elsewhere and should still be readable.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits — if the value must not reach the server, do not render the field.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute, so the field stays in the tab order and the accessibility tree.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides, which this component deliberately does not own.
dont: Restyling the label or message. Those come from the type scale, and a hand-written size drifts the moment the seed moves.

usage.case: A control this system does not wrap yet
usage.when: The case Field exists for: a native control with no component of its own.
usage.example:
<Field label="Country" description="Where the order ships.">
  {(control) => (
    <select {...control}>
      <option>Sri Lanka</option>
    </select>
  )}
</Field>
usage.notes: The argument is spread onto the control and nowhere else. Everything the reader hears — the name, the helper text, the requirement — is wired from it.

usage.when: Reporting what went wrong, where the reader can act on it.
usage.example:
<Field label="Card number" status="invalid" message="Check this number." required>
  {(control) => <input {...control} inputMode="numeric" />}
</Field>
usage.notes: The ring, the colour and the message say it three ways, and only the message says what to do. `status` also decides that the message joins the description chain — while idle it stays on the page and leaves the chain, so a stale error is not announced.

usage.case: A third-party control given the system's treatment
usage.when: A date picker or combobox from another library, which should still look and announce like every other field.
usage.example:
<Field label="Departure" description="Any date after today.">
  {(control) => <ThirdPartyDatePicker {...control} />}
</Field>
usage.notes: Field styles nothing inside the control, which is what makes this work — it owns the label, the helper text and the state, and leaves the box alone.

usage.when: The control already has a wrapper of its own.
usage.example:
<Field label="Email">
  {(control) => <TextField label="Email" {...control} />}
</Field>
usage.notes: Don't. `TextField` is built on Field and renders its own label, so this produces two labels and two ids for one input. `<TextField label="Email" />` is the whole thing — reach for Field only where no wrapper exists.

behavior.summary: Owns everything around a form control — the label, the required marker, the helper text, the message, and the `data-status` the control's own CSS selects on. Built on `getFieldProps`, which derives every id from the field's own and is the same primitive `TextField` has always used.

decisions.decision: The control arrives as a function, not as children
decisions.why: Field has to hand the control its `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Of the three ways to do that, cloning `children` breaks the moment someone wraps their input in a fragment or a div; a context the control opts into makes a control rendered OUTSIDE a Field silently unlabelled, which is the failure this component exists to prevent. A function makes the wiring visible at the call site, works for a control from another library, and cannot be forgotten — there is nothing to render without it.

decisions.decision: It does not style the control's box
decisions.why: Height, inline padding, border and focus ring stay with each control, because they genuinely differ: a textarea grows with its content, a select reserves a well for its chevron, a checkbox is square and small. Field owning them would mean every control overriding them. What Field owns is what is identical across all of them — which is everything outside the box.

decisions.decision: `status` lives here rather than on the control
decisions.why: It drives `data-status` on the root, and each control's stylesheet selects on that for its own ring. One state, read by many controls, set in one place — and it is also what decides whether the message joins the description chain, which is an accessibility fact about the group rather than about the input.

decisions.decision: `TextField` keeps its flat API and is rebuilt on this, not replaced by it
decisions.why: `<TextField label="Email" />` stays one element with one prop — a component whose commonest use got more verbose to serve an abstraction would be a bad trade. Field is what TextField is made of. Callers reach for Field directly for the controls that have no wrapper yet and for third-party ones; everything else keeps the shorthand.

decisions.decision: The primitive is renamed `getFieldProps`, with the old name kept as an alias
decisions.why: It was called `getTextFieldProps`, and nothing in it has ever been about text: it returns `root`, `label`, `input`, `description` and `message` bags containing ids and ARIA, and a `<select>` or `<textarea>` could consume it unchanged today. A Select built on something called `getTextFieldProps` would be the lookup surface lying about itself. `getTextFieldProps` and `TextFieldStatus` continue to be exported as aliases so nothing outside this repo breaks.

decisions.decision: `disabled` is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute
decisions.why: This system's rule, and for an input `readOnly` is the analogue of the button's click guard: it blocks editing while keeping the control in the tab order and the accessibility tree. Note the consequence, which is the same one `TextField`'s contract already carries — a readOnly field still submits its value.

decisions.decision: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, never the label
decisions.why: The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so nothing about the accessible name changes. The alternative people reach for — dropping the label and letting `placeholder` stand in — loses the name on the first keystroke, which is when the reader most needs it.

base.summary: A column. The gap is the only measurement here, and it is deliberately tighter than it looks it should be.

tokens.gap: space.stack.2xs — not space.stack.xs: the label and the helper text each carry their own line-height leading, so the perceived gap is already larger than the number, and the next step up reads as separation rather than as grouping

label.summary: The control's name, at the label role of the type scale.

required-marker.summary: The asterisk. Required-ness is information, not a fault, so it is not the danger tone.

description.summary: Persistent helper text, and always ahead of the message in the description order so a constraint is heard before a failure.

message.summary: The status-dependent line. Neutral until the status says otherwise, so a field that has not been judged does not look judged.

tokens.when invalid: theme.danger-role.fg — the role's text colour on the page background, never its saturated bg, which is a non-text indicator tone

disabled.summary: Dimmed as a whole rather than removed, because the control underneath stays focusable and readable.

tokens.opacity: state.disabled-opacity, on the root so the label and helper text dim with the control

name: file-upload
title: File Upload
description: Choose files with a button or drop them in, see what was chosen, and remove what was not meant.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: What the files are for. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: The document being asked for: "Proof of address", "Attachments".
dont: "Upload". That is the act, and the button already says it.
props.a11y: Labels the group: the choose button, the drop zone and the file list are announced as belonging to it.

props.name: accept
props.summary: Which files are allowed, as MIME types and extensions: "image/*,.pdf".
use: MIME types first — they are the part that works on every platform, including native.
dont: Treating it as enforcement. The OS dialog's filter is a hint the reader can override, and drag and drop ignores it entirely; the component re-checks every file and reports the misses through `onReject`.
props.a11y: Restated in the description chain in words — "PDF or image" — because a reader who cannot see a file dialog's filter never learns it.

props.name: multiple
props.summary: Accepts more than one file.
use: Attachments, a photo set.
dont: Leaving it on for a single document. The button then says "Choose files" and a reader may send two when the form wanted one.

props.name: maxFiles
props.summary: The most files the list may hold. Only meaningful with `multiple`.
use: A real limit on the receiving side.
dont: Setting it without saying it in `description`. A rejection is a worse place to learn a limit than the field's own helper text.

props.name: maxSize
props.summary: The largest file allowed, in bytes.
use: The server's real limit, so a reader learns it before a long upload fails.
dont: Stating it only here. Put it in `description` in human units — "Up to 10 MB".

props.name: value
props.summary: Controls the chosen files from outside. Each is `{ name, size, type }` plus the platform's handle — `file` on web, `uri` on native — and, optionally, `progress` (0–100) and `error`, which the caller's uploader sets and the row displays.
use: A form library, or restoring a selection after a validation round-trip.
Passing each file back with `progress` while it uploads, and `error` if it fails — the rows show both.
dont: Expecting it to hold uploaded files. It holds chosen ones; uploading is the caller's.
Expecting the component to set `progress` or `error`. It only displays them; uploading is the app's.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Fires with the whole accepted list whenever a file is added or removed.
use: Starting an upload per file, or enabling a submit button.
dont: Assuming it fires for rejected files. They never enter the list — that is `onReject`.

props.name: onReject
props.summary: Fires with the files that were refused and why: `{ file, reason: "type" | "size" | "count" }`.
use: Setting `status="invalid"` and a `message` that names the file and the rule it broke.
dont: Ignoring it. Without it a dropped file that was refused simply does not appear, and the reader has no idea why.
props.a11y: The component announces nothing about rejections itself; the message you set from this is what joins the description chain, which keeps one announcement policy for every field.

props.name: dropzone
props.summary: Draws a drop target around the button, for dragging files in from the desktop.
use: Turning it off in a compact row — a reply box's attachment control — where a large target would dominate.
dont: Removing the button in its favour. The drop zone is an addition; the button is the control.
props.a11y: The zone has no role and no tab stop. Dragging is not available to keyboard, switch or most screen-reader users, so it is never the only way in — WCAG 2.5.7.

props.name: buttonLabel
props.summary: The choose button's text.
use: Naming the kind of file: "Choose photos".
dont: "Browse". It describes the OS dialog, which is not what the reader wants to do.

props.name: name
props.summary: Form field name. A native form post submits exactly the listed files.
use: A plain `multipart/form-data` form.
props.a11y: Carried by the native file input, which is visually hidden and out of the tab order — the button stands in for it.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: the label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.summary: Stable id for the file field, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the field it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message, popup — is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged.

props.name: description
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: The limits, in words, before the reader picks: "PDF or JPEG, up to 10 MB."
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative.
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks choosing, dropping and removing while keeping the controls focusable and announced.
use: While uploads are in flight, if the form cannot accept changes to the set.
dont: Assuming the chosen files are withheld. They are still in the input and still submit — the text field's consequence, applied to files.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` on the choose button and every remove button, each with a click guard; drops are ignored.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure the form decides.

usage.when: A form that needs exactly one file of a known kind.
usage.example:
<FileUpload
  label="Proof of address"
  description="PDF or photo, up to 10 MB."
  accept="application/pdf,image/*"
  maxSize={10_000_000}
  name="proof"
  required
/>
usage.notes: The limits are said in `description` as well as enforced by `accept` and `maxSize`. A reader should learn a rule before they break it.

usage.when: Something was dropped or picked that the field cannot take.
usage.example:
<FileUpload
  label="Photos"
  multiple
  accept="image/*"
  onReject={(r) => setError(`${r[0].file.name} is not an image.`)}
  status={error ? "invalid" : "idle"}
  message={error}
/>
usage.notes: Refused files never enter the list, so without `onReject` they vanish silently. Name the file and the rule in the message.

usage.when: The app uploads each file as it is chosen and wants the rows to show how far each one got.
usage.example:
<FileUpload
  label="Attachments"
  multiple
  value={files}
  onValueChange={startUploads}
/>
usage.notes: `startUploads` uploads the new files and updates `files`, setting `progress` (0–100) on each while it runs and `error` on any that fail. The component draws both and uploads nothing (decision C11).

usage.when: A reply box or a chat composer, where a drop zone would dwarf the field it serves.
usage.example:
<FileUpload
  label="Attachments"
  labelHidden
  multiple
  dropzone={false}
  buttonLabel="Attach files"
/>
usage.notes: The button alone is the full control. The drop zone only ever added a pointer shortcut.

usage.when: Choosing an avatar, where the reader wants to see and crop the image.
usage.example: <FileUpload label="Profile photo" accept="image/*" />
usage.notes: This will take the file, but shows its name, not the picture, and offers no crop. An avatar editor is a different component with previews and their alt-text and memory decisions; it does not exist yet.

behavior.summary: A visually hidden native file input opened by a Button, an optional drop zone around it, and a list of the chosen files with a remove control each — composed with Field. It validates and holds a selection; it does not upload.

decisions.decision: A native `<input type="file">` is the control; a Button opens it
decisions.why: The native input owns things nothing else can: the OS file dialog, the camera option on phones, and form submission. Its own rendering cannot be styled and its text cannot be translated, so it is visually hidden and out of the tab order, and the system's Button calls it. A `<label>` styled as a button is the other common approach and is worse: a label is not focusable, so the keyboard cannot reach it.

decisions.decision: The drop zone is an enhancement, never the way in
decisions.why: Drag and drop is a pointer-only gesture, and phones have no files to drag. So the zone has no role and no tab stop, its "or drag files here" text is shown only under `(pointer: fine)`, and the button inside it is always present — the alternative to dragging that WCAG 2.5.7 asks for.

decisions.decision: The component re-validates everything it is given
decisions.why: `accept` filters the OS dialog only as a suggestion, and drag and drop bypasses it entirely, so a `.exe` dropped onto an image field arrives like any other file. Every file is checked against `accept`, `maxSize` and `maxFiles` before it enters the list, and refusals go to `onReject` with a reason. The caller writes the message, because Field's `message` is the one place a field reports a failure.

decisions.decision: The list and the submission cannot disagree
decisions.why: A file input's selection replaces itself on every pick, and it cannot be edited — removing one file from it is not possible through its API. So the component keeps the list, and writes it back into the input through a `DataTransfer` after every change. A native form post therefore submits exactly the files the reader can see, including after a removal.

decisions.decision: Removing a file moves focus somewhere that exists
decisions.why: The remove button the reader pressed is gone, and focus on a removed node falls to the body — back to the top of the page for a keyboard user. Focus moves to the next file's remove button, or the previous one at the end, or the choose button when the list empties. A polite status region says "report.pdf removed" and "2 files added".

decisions.decision: It chooses files; it does not upload them
decisions.why: Uploading is a network policy — chunking, retries, auth, progress, cancellation — that belongs to the caller, and baking one in would make this component wrong for every backend but one. The app does the uploading; this component chooses, validates and lists. What the list does take from the caller is each file's state: see the next decision (decision C11, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Rows show per-file `progress` and `error` that the caller supplies on the file items
decisions.why: A `PickedFile` may carry `progress` (0–100) and `error` (a string), and a row renders what it is given: a bar while `progress` is set, the error line under the name when `error` is. The caller's uploader writes them back into `value`, so showing progress means using the component controlled. The component never sets either itself and never infers success from 100 — completion is whatever the caller says it is. The bar in a row is a `role="progressbar"` named by the file name, and it is not announced on every change; the component's polite region announces when a file's `error` appears, and the error text joins the remove button's `aria-describedby` so it is heard with the file it belongs to. This keeps the network out of the component while the rows can still say what happened to each file (decision C11, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: No image previews in this version
decisions.why: A preview means an object URL per file and revoking each one when the file leaves the list, or a memory leak per photo; and a thumbnail needs alt text the reader did not write. It is a separate pass, not a boolean here.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` with a click guard, not the native attribute
decisions.why: The system rule, applied to the choose and remove buttons. And the text field's consequence, applied to files: whatever is already chosen still submits.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getFileUploadProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet. The proposal validates candidate files against the constraints, returns the accepted list and the rejections, computes where focus goes after a removal, and produces the announcement strings — all pure. The `DataTransfer` write-back and the drag events are the React wrapper's, since both are DOM acts.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a visually hidden `<input type="file">` carrying `name`, `accept` and `multiple`; the system Button; a drop zone `<div>` with no role; and the file list as a `<ul>` with one remove button per row, all inside a `role="group"` labelled by `label`. React Native has no file input. The native component is a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="button"` opening the OS document picker — which is not in core, so it is a community-package dependency every native consumer installs, and photos from the library are a second picker with its own permission prompt. That costs three things: `dropzone` is web-only; `accept` extensions such as `.pdf` are web-only, because native pickers filter by type (MIME on Android, translated to UTIs on iOS), which is why `accept` should lead with MIME types; and `name` is web-only, since there is no form post. `PickedFile` is the same shape on both — `{ name, size, type }` — with `file: File` on web and `uri` on native, so validation code is shared. The OS control, not a Rata-drawn one (decision N5): choosing goes through the OS document picker on native and the OS file dialog on web, because no drawn control can reach the file system; the button and the file list around it are Rata-drawn from the same recipe. On native a row's bar is a `View` with `accessibilityRole="progressbar"` and `accessibilityValue={{ min: 0, max: 100, now: progress }}`. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

dropzone.summary: The target around the button. A dashed edge says "put something here" without looking like a field that needs typing into.

tokens.border: border.2 dashed theme.border.strong — strong, so the edge meets the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control boundary
tokens.invalid border-color: theme.danger-role.fg — the text field's error edge, so a field that refused a file looks like any other invalid field

list.summary: The chosen files, one row each. Bordered rows rather than a table: there are two facts per file and one action.

tokens.row progress track background: theme.bg.muted — Progress's status track (decision C8), because this bar reports and cannot be adjusted
tokens.row progress fill background: theme.accent-role.bg — Progress's fill, with its pairing gap
tokens.row progress block-size: space.1 — Progress's placeholder, until the shared track-thickness token (decision C8)
tokens.row error colour: theme.danger-role.fg — the role's text colour on the row's theme.bg.surface, never its saturated bg
tokens.row error border-color: theme.danger-role.fg — the field's error edge, on the failed row only

remove.summary: The per-row remove control. Same construction as Search's clear and Dialog's dismiss: currentColor on a transparent background.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

name: heading
title: Heading
description: A heading whose outline level and visual size are stated separately.

props.name: level
props.description: Where this heading sits in the document outline.
props.summary: Where this heading sits in the document outline.
use: The level below whatever heading contains this one — a heading inside a section headed `h2` takes `3`.
dont: Picking it for size. That is `role`, and the two exist separately so this one can stay correct.
props.a11y: Becomes the element: `level={3}` renders an `<h3>`. A skipped level breaks heading navigation, which is how many readers move through a page — and only the caller knows the depth, which is why there is no default.

props.name: role
props.description: How large it looks, independent of its level.
props.summary: How large it looks, independent of its level.
use: A display role on a page title: `level={1} role="display-3"`.
A smaller role than the level suggests, when a deep heading should not shout: `level={3} role="heading-5"`.
dont: Using it to fix an outline. If the heading looks wrong at its correct level, this prop is the fix; if the level is wrong, change the level.
props.a11y: Purely visual. It changes no element and no announcement, which is the point: the outline stays whatever `level` says.

props.name: children
props.description: The heading text.
props.summary: The heading text.
use: A short noun phrase naming what follows.
dont: Anything interactive. A heading is a signpost, not a control.
props.a11y: Becomes the heading's accessible name, so it is what a reader hears when navigating by heading.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The margin the page wants around it, which this component deliberately does not own.
dont: Overriding the size. That is what `role` is for, and a hand-written size drifts from the scale the moment the seed changes.

usage.case: A page title that outranks its own size
usage.when: The commonest reason both props exist: one `h1` per page, set at a display step so it reads as the title.
usage.example: <Heading level={1} role="display-3">Design tokens</Heading>
usage.notes: The level is what a screen-reader user navigates by; the role is only how large it looks. Writing `level={3}` to get this size would leave the page with no `h1` at all.

usage.case: A section heading at its natural size
usage.when: Inside a page already headed `h1`, where nothing about the section asks to be louder.
usage.example: <Heading level={2}>Contrast pairings</Heading>
usage.notes: No `role`: `heading-2` is the default for `level={2}`, and the common case should not have to say so twice.

usage.case: A deep heading that should not shout
usage.when: A sub-subsection whose correct level would otherwise draw more attention than it deserves.
usage.example: <Heading level={4} role="heading-5">Known gaps</Heading>
usage.notes: The outline stays correct and only the size moves — which is the direction this prop is for. If the heading feels wrong at its correct level, change the role; if the level itself is wrong, change the level.

usage.when: The text is an uppercase eyebrow over a group, not an entry in the outline.
usage.example: <Heading level={6}>Foundations</Heading>
usage.notes: Don't. Nothing navigates to it and it heads no section, so it does not belong in the outline — that is `<Text role="label">`. A heading level spent on decoration is a level a real heading can no longer use.

behavior.summary: An `h1` through `h6`, with its visual size stated independently of its level. No primitive: there is no keyboard interaction to own and no state to hold.

decisions.decision: `level` and `role` are two props, and that is the whole reason this component exists
decisions.why: A heading's level is an outline decision — it is how a screen-reader user navigates a page, and skipping one breaks that. Its size is a visual decision about emphasis on the page. They are answers to different questions and they disagree constantly: a page's first subsection often wants to be visually large and is still an `h2`, and a small `h4`-sized label deep in a form may be the `h3` of its section. Every typography component that offers only `size`, or only `level`, forces the caller to pick which of the two to get wrong.

decisions.decision: `role` defaults to the matching heading step, and that is a convenience rather than a coupling
decisions.why: `level={2}` with no role renders `heading-2`, because that is right most of the time and asking for both every time would make the common case worse. The point is that the default is overridable in one prop — the coupling is a starting position, not a constraint.

decisions.decision: `level` is required and has no default
decisions.why: There is no level that is right by default. A component that defaulted to `h2` would produce a page of `h2`s, which is exactly the flat outline this playground was already guilty of — every page title was an `h2` and no page had an `h1`. The type refuses it instead of the contract asking nicely, the same way Dialog's `title` is required.

decisions.decision: The unnumbered `type.heading` role is not offered
decisions.why: It resolves to the same size as `heading-3`, so offering both would be two names for one step and a caller would have to guess whether they differ. The numbered ladder is the one that maps onto levels.

decisions.decision: It carries no margin
decisions.why: Only the page knows what a heading sits between — a title above a dense table wants different air from one above prose. A component that shipped its own margin would be overridden everywhere, and an overridden default is worse than none because it looks like a decision.

decisions.decision: Tracking comes with the display roles and not with the heading roles
decisions.why: The type family carries `tracking.display-1/2/3` precisely because large type set at normal tracking reads loose, and it carries no tracking step for the heading roles because they do not need one. Taking the role whole means taking its tracking when it has one — the roles are generated from the seed in proportion to each other, and cherry-picking across them is what breaks that.

base.summary: One type role, taken whole. Nothing else — a heading has no box of its own.

tokens.font-size: the size of the chosen role — type.display-1.size through type.heading-6.size
tokens.font-weight: that same role's weight, which is 400 for the display roles and 600 for the heading roles
tokens.letter-spacing: type.tracking.display-1 / display-2 / display-3 for the display roles, and normal for the heading roles — large type set at normal tracking reads loose, which is why the scale carries a tracking step per display role
tokens.color: currentColor — a heading takes the colour of the text around it, and the surface it sits on decides that
tokens.margin: space.0 — every margin is the page's, since only the page knows what the heading sits between

name: icon
title: Icon
description: A Lucide glyph sized from the size.icon.* scale, inheriting its colour from the text around it.

props.name: icon
props.description: The Lucide component to render, passed as a value so the set stays tree-shakeable.
props.summary: The Lucide component to render, passed as a value rather than a name.
use: Any icon imported from `@rata/icons` — the curated set — or from `lucide-react` directly when the set is missing one.
Passing the component itself (`icon={Trash2}`), which is what keeps the icon set tree-shakeable: a string name would force every icon into the bundle.
dont: Rendering the Lucide component directly instead of through `Icon`. It would take Lucide's default 24px rather than a step from the scale, and it would not get the a11y switch below.
An emoji or a text glyph as a stand-in. Those inherit font metrics rather than the icon scale, so they will not line up with real icons beside them.
props.a11y: Rendered `aria-hidden` unless `label` is set — see `label`.

props.name: size
props.description: Which step of the `size.icon.*` scale to draw at. Defaults to following the surrounding text.
props.summary: Which step of the `size.icon.*` scale the glyph is drawn at. Defaults to following the surrounding text.
use: Leave it alone for anything with text near it — the default `text` step is 1.15em, so the glyph tracks whatever font-size it lands in and needs no decision per control.
`xs` / `sm` / `md` / `lg` only for a standalone glyph with no text to inherit from: a status dot in a table cell, or an icon-only control whose name is an `aria-label` rather than visible text.
`lg` when the glyph should render unscaled — 24px is Lucide's native artboard.
dont: Picking a fixed step to match a control's size. A control's `size` changes its box, not its text, so an icon inside it should not change either — and a fixed step stops matching the moment the surrounding text does change.
Mixing steps within one row of icons — they read as a set, so they measure as a set.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name, for an icon that carries meaning nothing else conveys.
props.summary: Accessible name, for an icon that carries meaning nothing else conveys.
use: An icon that is the only thing communicating something — a status glyph in a table cell with no adjacent text.
dont: An icon inside a `Button` with `iconOnly`. That button already carries the `aria-label` the contract requires, so labelling the icon too announces the same thing twice.
An icon sitting beside a visible text label. The text is the name; the icon is decoration and must stay hidden from assistive technology.
props.a11y: Present, the glyph becomes `role="img"` with this as its name. Absent, it is `aria-hidden` — the same switch `Spinner` uses for the same reason, and the reason the decorative case needs no thought to get right.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the glyph, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: A layout concern the parent cannot express, such as a margin token when the icon is not already inside a flex row with a gap.
dont: Overriding the size. The four steps are the scale; a fifth size written in a component's CSS is the drift `size.icon.*` exists to prevent — add a step to the scale instead.
Setting a colour. The glyph strokes with `currentColor` so it always matches the text it sits in; colouring it separately is how an icon ends up contradicting its own label.

usage.when: The most common pairing, and the one where the a11y split matters most.
usage.example:
<Button iconOnly aria-label="Delete row">
  <Icon icon={Trash2} />
</Button>
usage.notes: No `label` on the icon: the button owns the accessible name, so the glyph stays `aria-hidden`. `size` is left at `md`, which is what a 32px control wants.

usage.when: An action whose icon reinforces a word rather than replacing it.
usage.example:
<Button>
  <Icon icon={Download} />
  Export CSV
</Button>
usage.notes: No `size`: the default `text` step is 1.15em, so the glyph is sized from the button's own label and stays matched to it. The icon is decorative here, so it takes no `label` either.

usage.when: A status glyph in a dense row, with no adjacent text to name it.
usage.example: <Icon icon={CircleAlert} size="xs" label="Needs review" />
usage.notes: This is the only case that takes a `label`. Without one the row would announce nothing at all where a sighted user sees a warning.

base.summary: A glyph sized from the text around it, taking its colour from that text too.

tokens.width: size.icon.text — 1.15em, so it follows the inherited font-size. size.icon.xs / .sm / .md / .lg for a standalone glyph.
tokens.height: same step as width; the scale is one number and the glyph is square
tokens.stroke: currentColor — the icon inherits the colour of the text it sits in, so it needs no colour token of its own and cannot contradict its label
tokens.flex-shrink: 0 — a glyph beside text must not be squeezed by it, which is a layout fact rather than a token

name: link
title: Link
description: A navigation to another page or place, styled either inside running text or standing on its own.

props.name: href
props.description: Where the link goes.
props.summary: Where the link goes.
use: A real URL, even inside a single-page app — the router intercepts `onClick`, and the address stays usable for new tabs and copying.
dont: `#` or `javascript:` to make a clickable thing. That is a Button.
props.a11y: A link without an `href` is not a link to the accessibility tree, which is why this is required.

props.name: children
props.description: The link text — the name of where it goes.
props.summary: The link text — the name of where it goes.
use: Text that makes sense out of context: "View invoice INV-204".
dont: "Click here" or "Learn more" alone. Screen-reader users list a page's links, and a list of ten "Learn more"s is useless — name the destination, or extend the name with visually-hidden text.
props.a11y: Becomes the link's accessible name.

props.name: variant
props.description: Whether the link sits inside running text or on its own.
props.summary: Whether the link sits inside running text or on its own.
use: `inline` inside a sentence.
`standalone` for "View all" under a list, "Back to invoices" above a page, or a link in a row of actions.
dont: `standalone` inside a sentence. Without its underline it is distinguished from the text by colour alone.
props.a11y: `inline` is always underlined, which is the non-colour cue WCAG 1.4.1 requires inside text.

props.name: newTab
props.description: Opens the link in a new tab, and says so.
props.summary: Opens the link in a new tab, and says so.
use: A link out of a task the reader must not lose — help docs opened from the middle of a form.
dont: Every external link, by habit. Opening a new tab takes Back away; the reader can choose a new tab themselves.
props.a11y: Adds a glyph and visually-hidden "(opens in new tab)", plus `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. Web only.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement.
use: Spacing a standalone link in its row.
dont: Removing the underline from an inline link, or recolouring it. Both undo the reason it is recognisable.

usage.when: A reference to another page, inside a sentence.
usage.example:
<Text>
  Contrast is verified per brand — see the <Link href="/docs/contrast">contrast report</Link>.
</Text>
usage.notes: `inline` is the default and is always underlined, so it is distinguishable without its colour.

usage.case: A standalone link with a client-side router
usage.when: "View all" under a preview list in a single-page app.
usage.example:
<Link
  variant="standalone"
  href="/invoices"
  onClick={(event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    navigate("/invoices");
  }}
>
  View all invoices
</Link>
usage.notes: `href` stays real, so middle-click and copy-link still work; the router only intercepts the plain click. The text names the destination rather than saying "View all" alone.

usage.when: Text that should trigger an action, such as "Resend code".
usage.example: <Link href="#" onClick={resend}>Resend code</Link>
usage.notes: Don't. Nothing is navigated to, so it is a button: `<Button variant="tertiary" onClick={resend}>Resend code</Button>`, activated by Space as well as Enter and announced as what it is.

behavior.summary: An `<a href>`, always. No primitive: the platform already owns a link's keyboard behaviour, and a router integrates by intercepting `onClick` while `href` stays real — the bargain TopNav and SideNav already make.

decisions.decision: A Link goes somewhere; a Button does something
decisions.why: The reader's expectations differ: a link can be opened in a new tab, copied and bookmarked, and is activated by Enter only; a button performs an action, is activated by Enter or Space, and has no address. Styling one as the other breaks those expectations for keyboard and screen-reader users while looking fine to everyone else. So `href` is required, there is no `onClick`-only Link, and an action styled as text is a tertiary Button.

decisions.decision: Inline links are always underlined, and get no hover change
decisions.why: WCAG 1.4.1: a link in a paragraph must be distinguishable by more than colour, and an underline that appears only on hover fails before the pointer arrives. With the underline always on, a hover change would be a hand-written `:hover` rule, which this system does not write. The state layer is the hover feedback everywhere else, but on inline text it would paint a box behind a phrase that wraps across lines — so inline links have none, and the cursor is enough. Standalone links have a box, so they compose the state layer like any other control.

decisions.decision: No `disabled`
decisions.why: A link with nowhere to go is not a disabled link, it is text. `aria-disabled` on an `<a>` without `href` is a pattern Pagination uses for its Previous and Next, where the row needs its shape; a free-standing link in that state is a puzzle for the reader. Render text, or render the link.

decisions.decision: `newTab` exists so the warning cannot be forgotten
decisions.why: WCAG 3.2.5 asks that a change of context be predictable, and a link that silently opens a new tab breaks Back for the reader who did not expect it. `newTab` sets `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"` together, and adds a glyph plus visually-hidden "(opens in new tab)" so it is announced. Passing `target="_blank"` by hand gets none of that, which is the reason this is a prop rather than an attribute the caller remembers.

decisions.decision: No visited colour
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C4, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). In an application most links are repeated navigation — the same invoices, the same settings — so a visited state would recolour half of every page and tell the reader nothing. A link is recognised by its underline, not its colour, so a visited colour would add no cue the reader needs. And it would be one more foreground to verify for contrast against every surface, in both schemes and every brand, while browsers deliberately limit what `:visited` can style for privacy. There is no visited token, none is to be proposed, and `:visited` gets no rule.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: an `<a href>`; `newTab` adds `target` and `rel`, a glyph and a visually-hidden suffix; a router intercepts `onClick` and calls `preventDefault`. React Native has no anchor: the link is a nested `Text` with `accessibilityRole="link"` and `onPress`, so it flows inside a paragraph, and `href` is opened with `Linking.openURL` unless the caller's `onPress` handles it for in-app navigation. `newTab` is web-only. `variant` works on both; the native state-layer equivalent is the `Pressable` pressed style, and the inline underline is `textDecorationLine: "underline"`. The OS's own text and link handling, not a Rata-drawn control (decision N5): the platform `Text` carries the link and `Linking` opens it; Rata supplies only the colour and underline. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: Gate 2: every state's token mapping is approved
decisions.why: Approved state by state — L1 inline rest, L2 inline hover/press (no change), L3 inline focus, L4 the new-tab glyph, L5 standalone rest, L6 standalone hover/press (state layer), L7 standalone focus. Mapping it surfaced one gap: the link colour was verified on only three surfaces, while links also land in table rows, wells and Notices. theme.accent-role.fg was measured on theme.bg.subtle, theme.bg.muted and the three status subtle backgrounds — 4.89:1 or better in both schemes — and all five are now documented pairings that themes:check re-verifies for every brand (gate 2, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

inline.summary: A link inside a sentence. Always underlined, because colour alone does not distinguish it from the text around it.

tokens.rest · color: theme.accent-role.fg — verified AA-text on theme.bg.canvas, theme.bg.surface, theme.bg.subtle, theme.bg.muted, theme.accent-role.subtle and the success/warning/danger subtle backgrounds (L1)
tokens.hover / press: no change — the underline is already the affordance, and a colour shift mid-sentence reads as flicker; cursor: pointer only (L2)
tokens.focus · outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible (L3)
tokens.focus · wrapping: box-decoration-break: clone, so a link broken across lines gets a ring on each line (L3)

standalone.summary: A link on its own line or in a row of actions — 'View all', 'Back to invoices'. Not underlined, so it gets a box for the state layer.

tokens.focus: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible — the same ring as inline (L7)

new-tab.summary: The glyph that says a link opens a new tab, sized from the text so it never outgrows the line.

tokens.announcement: the glyph is aria-hidden; '(opens in new tab)' is visually hidden text inside the link (L4)

name: list
title: List
description: A vertical stack of rows — contacts, settings, messages, files — each a ListItem, divided and edge-to-edge.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: children
props.summary: The rows: ListItem elements, in reading order.
use: ListItems, and nothing else at the top level.
dont: A heading or a paragraph between rows. A `<ul>` may contain only `<li>`; a section break is two Lists with a Heading between them.
props.a11y: Each ListItem is an `<li>`, so the list's item count is the number of rows a reader hears announced.

props.name: label
props.summary: Accessible name for the list, when no visible heading names it.
use: A list with no heading above it whose purpose is not obvious from its rows.
dont: Repeating a visible heading. Point at it with `labelledBy` instead, so the two cannot drift.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-label` on the `<ul>`.

props.name: labelledBy
props.summary: Id of a visible element — usually the Heading above the list — that names it.
use: Every list with a heading directly above it.
dont: An id that is not on the page. A dangling reference names the list nothing, silently.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-labelledby` on the `<ul>`.

props.name: dividers
props.summary: Whether a rule is drawn between rows.
use: `false` for a short list of tall rows — each with an avatar and two lines — whose height already separates them.
dont: `false` on dense one-line rows. Without the rule they read as one paragraph.

props.name: appearance
props.summary: Edge-to-edge on the page's own surface, or grouped on a rounded surface inside the gutter.
use: `inset` for a settings screen, where each list is a group of related options under a heading.
dont: `inset` for a long feed or a search result. The container says 'this is a small fixed group', and a feed is neither.
props.a11y: Visual only.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the `<ul>`, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The margin the page wants around the list.
dont: Row padding or divider colour. Those are ListItem's, and a list that restyles its rows from outside is two places deciding one thing.

usage.when: A handful of related options on a mobile settings screen, under a heading.
usage.example:
<Heading level={2} id="notifications">Notifications</Heading>
<List labelledBy="notifications" appearance="inset">
  <ListItem trailing={<Switch label="Email" labelHidden checked={email} onCheckedChange={setEmail} />}>Email</ListItem>
  <ListItem href="/settings/quiet-hours" description="10 pm – 7 am">Quiet hours</ListItem>
</List>
usage.notes: The heading names the list through `labelledBy`, so it is read 'Notifications, list, 2 items'. The first row holds a control and is not itself clickable; the second is a link. Both are normal rows in one list.

usage.case: A feed of things, each opening its own page
usage.when: Messages, files, orders — a long column where each row leads somewhere.
usage.example:
<List label="Recent orders">
  {orders.map((order) => (
    <ListItem key={order.id} href={`/orders/${order.id}`} description={order.summary}>
      {order.title}
    </ListItem>
  ))}
</List>
usage.notes: `plain` and divided, edge-to-edge. Each row is one link, so Tab moves from order to order and a screen reader's links list reads the titles alone.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: picking one
usage.when: The rows are the options of a question, and the reader chooses one of them.
usage.example:
<List label="Shipping speed">
  <ListItem onClick={() => setSpeed("standard")}>Standard</ListItem>
  <ListItem onClick={() => setSpeed("express")}>Express</ListItem>
</List>
usage.notes: Don't. Nothing here says which one is chosen or that only one can be. That is a RadioGroup, which announces the choice, holds the answer, and submits it with the form.

behavior.summary: A `<ul role="list">` of ListItems. No primitive and no keyboard model of its own: each interactive row is a link or a button in the normal tab order, which is what a list of rows is everywhere except inside a widget.

decisions.decision: It is a list, not a listbox, not a menu, not a nav
decisions.why: Four patterns look like a column of rows and announce four different things. A listbox is a single form control with a selection, one tab stop and arrow keys — choosing a row from a set is RadioGroup, or Select, or a checkbox per row, not this. A menu is a transient list of commands behind a trigger — that is Menu. A list of destinations that is the site's navigation is SideNav. This is the remaining case, and the commonest one in an app: a stack of independent things, each of which may open its own page or carry its own control, read in order with Tab moving from row to row.

decisions.decision: Dividers are on by default, and the rows draw them
decisions.why: Dense rows without a rule between them read as one block of text; CLAUDE.md's frame table already calls for lists that are 'edge-to-edge, divided'. Each row draws its own top rule except the first, so a list with conditional rows never shows a doubled or orphaned divider, and `dividers={false}` turns them off for a list whose rows are already separated by their own height.

decisions.decision: `appearance="inset"` is the only container variant, and it is not a Card
decisions.why: The grouped settings look — rows on a rounded surface inside the gutter — is common enough on mobile that every consumer would otherwise hand-roll it, and it is a property of the list rather than a wrapper around it. It is deliberately not a general-purpose Card: it holds rows and nothing else, and CLAUDE.md's rule against a hand-rolled `<div className="card">` still stands for everything that is not a list.

decisions.decision: Children, not an items array
decisions.why: Unlike Tabs, there is no id wiring between parts to get wrong: a row stands alone, and its text, slots and control vary from row to row in ways a data shape would have to anticipate. Children keep ListItem's props as the one place a row is described, the same split Menu and MenuItem make.

decisions.decision: Selection is out of scope
decisions.why: A list where rows can be checked for a bulk action is a list of rows each carrying a Checkbox in `leading`, which composes from what exists. A list where exactly one row is the answer is a RadioGroup. A multi-select mode here would need `aria-multiselectable` and a listbox's keyboard model, which would turn this into the widget the first decision says it is not.

decisions.decision: No virtualization in this version
decisions.why: Rendering only the visible rows changes what is in the DOM, which changes what find-in-page, a screen reader's list count and Tab can reach. Those are solvable — `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` on each row — but they are a behaviour of their own and they belong in a primitive that has been through gate 1, not in a styling component.

decisions.decision: Pull-to-refresh is not part of List, and is not a component
decisions.why: It was proposed as a component and declined. On the web the browser already owns the gesture on the document scroller — Chrome on Android and Safari on iOS both reload the page on an overscroll — so a custom one has to disable that with `overscroll-behavior-y: contain` and replace a behaviour readers already know. It has no surface of its own beyond a Spinner, it binds to a scroll container rather than rendering anything, and on React Native it is not a component either: it is `RefreshControl`, passed to a `ScrollView` or `FlatList`'s `refreshControl` prop. Its non-gesture equivalent — a Refresh Button, or refreshing on focus — has to exist regardless, and that equivalent is what ships today. If installed PWAs (which lose the browser's gesture in standalone mode) make the gesture worth having, it is a `refreshing` / `onRefresh` pair on this component, mirroring FlatList's, backed by a new pointer-state primitive proposed through gate 1.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: On the web it renders `<ul role="list">`, named by `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` when given one. The explicit role is load-bearing: Safari removes list semantics from a list styled `list-style: none`, which is every list here, and without it VoiceOver stops announcing 'list, 12 items'. On React Native it renders a `View` with `accessibilityRole="list"` for short static lists. A long native list should be a `FlatList` — virtualization is not optional at a few hundred rows on a phone — so the native package is expected to take `data` and `renderItem` where the web takes `children`; that divergence is an open question for the native package's own gate 1. `className` is web-only. Swipe actions live on ListItem, and this component has no gesture of its own. Rata-drawn rows inside the core list views (decision N5): `View` or `FlatList` supplies the scrolling and the list semantics, and no OS table or list styling (UITableView, RecyclerView) is used. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: The list draws almost nothing itself. The rows own their padding, their dividers and their states; the list owns only the surface they sit on and the space they cannot clip into.

tokens.background: inherited — the list takes the surface it is placed on, which is what lets it sit edge-to-edge in a page or inside a Sheet
tokens.padding-inline: space.0 — rows fill the width, for the reason SideNav's rows do: the whole row is the target
tokens.padding-block: focus.ring-width plus focus.ring-offset — just enough that the first and last rows' focus rings are not clipped when the list is a scroll container, the device Tabs uses for the same problem
tokens.list-style: none, with role="list" restored — see the web and native decision

inset.summary: The grouped look: the list as a rounded surface inside the page's gutter, as in a settings screen.

tokens.overflow: clip, so the first and last rows' state layers take the container's corners — with the padding-block above, so the rings still fit inside

name: list-item
title: List Item
description: One row in a List: a line of text, an optional second line, slots at either end, and optionally a link, a button, or secondary actions.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: children
props.summary: The row's text — what the row is.
use: A short label: a name, a title, a setting.
dont: Two lines run together. The second line is `description`, so it can be styled and announced as secondary.
props.a11y: The accessible name of the row's link or button, and the only thing in it.

props.name: description
props.summary: A second, secondary line under the text.
use: The value of a setting ('10 pm – 7 am'), a message preview, a file's size and date.
dont: The row's only meaningful text. If the description is what tells rows apart, it is the text.
props.a11y: Joined by `aria-describedby`: read on focus, kept out of the name.

props.name: leading
props.summary: A visual at the start of the row — an Icon or an Avatar.
use: An Avatar for a person, an Icon for a kind of thing.
A Checkbox, for a list whose rows can be selected for a bulk action — on a row that is not itself a link or button.
dont: An image that carries information the text does not. The slot is decorative by default, and a meaning that only exists in it is lost to anyone not looking.
props.a11y: Should be decorative — an Icon with no `label`, an Avatar with `decorative` — because the row's text already names it.

props.name: trailing
props.summary: Metadata or one control at the end of the row.
use: A Badge, a count, a timestamp.
One Switch on a settings row that is not itself a link.
dont: A control on a row with `href` or `onClick` — two targets on one line. Put commands in `actions` instead.
Several buttons. That is `actions`, which collapses them into one trigger.
props.a11y: Read after the row's text, in DOM order. A control placed here needs its own accessible name; a Switch's `label` can repeat the row's text with `labelHidden`.

props.name: href
props.summary: Makes the row a link to this address.
use: A row that opens the thing it describes.
dont: `href="#"` to make a row clickable. A row that performs an action rather than going somewhere takes `onClick` alone and becomes a button.
props.a11y: Renders an `<a>`, so the row is in the links list and announced as a link.

props.name: onClick
props.summary: Makes the row a button, or — with `href` — intercepts the link for client-side routing.
use: A row that opens a Sheet or a Dialog in place.
With `href`, a router's navigate call.
dont: Selecting the row as an answer. That is RadioGroup.
props.a11y: Alone, renders a `<button type="button">`, activated by Enter and Space. With `href`, it stays a link.

props.name: actions
props.summary: Secondary commands on this row — `{ label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; destructive?: boolean; onSelect: () => void }` each — shown in a Menu behind a trailing button.
use: Archive, rename, share, delete — what a mobile app would put behind a swipe.
dont: The row's primary action. That is the row itself, via `href` or `onClick`.
One action that every row has and every reader uses. A command that common belongs on the row's own page or in a toolbar, not one tap deep in every row.
props.a11y: The trigger is named '`actionsLabel`, <row text>'. Each action becomes a MenuItem, and `destructive` becomes MenuItem's `destructive`.

props.name: actionsLabel
props.summary: The visible-to-assistive-technology name of the actions trigger, before the row's own text.
use: A translated string.
dont: Repeating the row's text in it. The row's text is already appended.
props.a11y: One part of the trigger's `aria-labelledby`; the row's text is the other.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks the row's activation and its actions, while keeping both focusable and announced.
use: A row that exists but cannot be opened right now — a file still uploading.
dont: A static row. A row with no `href`, `onClick` or `actions` has nothing to disable.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled`, not the `disabled` attribute, on the link or button and the actions trigger.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the `<li>`, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rare. The row's spacing and states are the component's.
dont: Removing the divider on one row. That is List's `dividers`, and a list where some rows are divided reads as two lists.

usage.case: A row that opens a page
usage.when: The commonest row: a thing in a collection, which the reader taps to see in full.
usage.example:
<ListItem
  href="/people/ada"
  leading={<Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" decorative />}
  description="Last seen 2 hours ago"
>
  Ada Lovelace
</ListItem>
usage.notes: The Avatar is decorative because the text names the person. The link's name is 'Ada Lovelace'; the last-seen line is its description.

usage.when: A message or file row where archive and delete are a mobile app's swipe actions.
usage.example:
<ListItem
  href={`/mail/${message.id}`}
  description={message.preview}
  actions={[
    { label: "Archive", icon: Archive, onSelect: () => archive(message.id) },
    { label: "Delete", icon: Trash2, destructive: true, onSelect: () => remove(message.id) },
  ]}
>
  {message.subject}
</ListItem>
usage.notes: The actions render as a Menu behind a trailing button named 'More actions, <subject>'. That is the path for keyboard, switch access and screen readers today, and it stays the path when a swipe gesture is added over the same array.

usage.when: A settings row whose control is the whole point, and the row itself goes nowhere.
usage.example:
<ListItem trailing={<Switch label="Dark mode" labelHidden checked={dark} onCheckedChange={setDark} />}>
  Dark mode
</ListItem>
usage.notes: No `href` or `onClick`, so the row is static and the Switch is its only target. The Switch's `label` repeats the row's text because it is the switch's own name.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: a row that is two targets
usage.when: A row that opens a page and also carries a toggle.
usage.example:
<ListItem href="/settings/wifi" trailing={<Switch label="Wi-Fi" labelHidden checked={wifi} onCheckedChange={setWifi} />}>
  Wi-Fi
</ListItem>
usage.notes: Don't. The stretched link lies under the switch, and a thumb aiming at either has nothing to tell it which it will hit. Make the row static with the Switch, and put a separate 'Wi-Fi networks' row with the `href` below it.

behavior.summary: An `<li>` holding the row's content, and — when interactive — one real `<a>` or `<button>` stretched over it. Secondary actions are data, rendered as a Menu behind a trailing button. No primitive: a row in the normal tab order has no keyboard model to own.

decisions.decision: A row is a link, a button, or neither — decided by `href` and `onClick`
decisions.why: `href` makes the row an `<a>`; `onClick` alone makes it a `<button type="button">`; both makes it a link with the click intercepted, the bargain TopNav and SideNav make for client-side routing. Neither makes it static content. The element is never the `<li>` itself with `role="button"` bolted on — a list item that pretends to be a button loses its list position, and a real element gets keyboard activation, middle-click and the links list for free.

decisions.decision: The whole row is the target, through one stretched element
decisions.why: The link or button wraps only the text, and a pseudo-element stretches its hit area over the row. Wrapping the entire row in an `<a>` instead would put the description, the trailing badge and any control inside the link — so the accessible name becomes everything in the row read together, and a Switch inside a link is an interactive element nested in another, which is invalid and unpredictable. Stretching keeps the name to the row's text and leaves room beside it for a control that is not part of the link.

decisions.decision: The description is a description, not part of the name
decisions.why: The row's text is the accessible name; `description` is joined by `aria-describedby`. A screen reader's links list then reads 'Quiet hours' rather than 'Quiet hours 10 pm – 7 am', and twenty rows remain distinguishable by name alone. The description is still read when the row is focused, so nothing is lost.

decisions.decision: `trailing` is for one thing, and an interactive row cannot hold a control there
decisions.why: A trailing slot holds metadata — a Badge, a timestamp — or one control, such as a Switch on a settings row. A row that is both a link and holds a Switch has two targets on one line with nothing to tell a thumb which it will hit, and the stretched link would sit under the switch. The type cannot see what is inside a ReactNode, so this is a contract rule: a row with `href` or `onClick` takes metadata in `trailing` and nothing interactive. Its secondary commands go in `actions`, which is built to sit beside a stretched link.

decisions.decision: Secondary actions are data, and they are always reachable without a gesture
decisions.why: Swipe actions were proposed as their own component and declined; this prop is what replaced them. `actions` takes `{ label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; destructive?: boolean; onSelect: () => void }[]` and renders them, always, as a Menu behind a trailing icon-only Button — the keyboard, switch-access and screen-reader path, and the pointer path on a desktop. A swipe that reveals the same actions is a future enhancement over this same array, which is the point of it being data: a gesture can then never hold an action the menu does not, and the non-gesture equivalent is not a fallback someone has to remember to add — it is the default rendering.

decisions.decision: No swipe gesture in this version
decisions.why: Sheet's contract declined drag-to-dismiss for reasons that apply here unchanged: a horizontal swipe is a pointer state machine with a distance and velocity threshold, it competes with the browser's own back-swipe on iOS Safari and with horizontal scrolling in the row's container, and it must be reversible before release. That is a primitive — a pure reducer over pointer positions, no DOM — proposed through gate 1 on its own, not a styling detail riding along with the row. When it ships, a full swipe must never complete a destructive action without an undo.

decisions.decision: The actions button is named after its row
decisions.why: Twenty rows each with a button called 'More actions' produce a screen-reader button list of twenty identical entries. The trigger is named by `aria-labelledby` pointing at both its own `actionsLabel` text and the row's text, so it reads 'More actions, Invoice 42' — the row tells the reader which one it is without the caller writing twenty strings.

decisions.decision: Disabled blocks the row and its actions, and keeps both reachable
decisions.why: `disabled` puts `aria-disabled` on the row's link or button and on the actions trigger, and the click guard blocks both; neither leaves the tab order, so a reader can still find out the row exists and why it cannot be used. A row disabled while its actions still work is a row whose most important command is unavailable and whose secondary ones are not, which is a state worth not being able to express.

decisions.decision: Touch target: size.target.min
decisions.why: The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Open: the focus ring at a list's inline edges
decisions.why: An edge-to-edge row's ring sits outside the row, by `focus.ring-offset`, which is outside the list's inline edges. List pads its block edges so the first and last rings survive a scroll container, but padding the inline edges would inset every row from the page's edge and undo 'edge-to-edge'. Either the rule is that an edge-to-edge list is never an overflow-clipping container, or a row's ring is drawn inset (a negative offset of `focus.ring-width` plus `focus.ring-offset`) — which keeps the gap and the width this system requires but moves the ring inside the target. That choice belongs at gate 2.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: On the web it renders `<li>`, with an `<a href>` or `<button type="button">` over the text when interactive, `aria-describedby` to the description, and `aria-disabled` when disabled. The actions trigger is an icon-only Button with `aria-haspopup="menu"` opening a Menu. On React Native it renders a `View` (or a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="link"` or `"button"` when interactive), `accessibilityHint` from the description, and `accessibilityState={{ disabled }}`. `actions` become the row's `accessibilityActions`, with `onAccessibilityAction` dispatching to each `onSelect` — so VoiceOver's actions rotor and TalkBack's actions menu reach them from the row itself — and the visible trailing button remains for touch. A future swipe reveals the same array on both platforms. Web-only: `href`, `onClick` (a DOM `MouseEvent`) and `className`; the native package takes `onPress` in their place. No prop is native-only. Rata-drawn (decision N5): the row is a drawn `View` or `Pressable` from the same recipe, not an OS table cell. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: One row. Leading slot, text, trailing slot, in that order along the inline axis; the text column takes the slack.

tokens.padding-inline: space.padding.md — and max(space.padding.md, env(safe-area-inset-left / right)) when the list is edge-to-edge, so a phone in landscape does not put the text under the notch

divider.summary: A rule above every row but the first, drawn by the row so a conditional row never leaves a doubled or orphaned line.

tokens.inset: starts at the text column when the row has a leading slot, so the rule does not cut between an avatar and its own text
