interactive.summary: A row with `href` or `onClick`. The link or button is stretched over the whole row, so the whole row is the target.

tokens.hover / press: compose the .rata-state-layer class on the row
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible — drawn around the row, which is the target the reader is about to activate
tokens.disclosure chevron: size.icon.sm, theme.fg.muted — decorative, and shown only for href rows, since it promises a new page

actions.summary: The trailing control that opens a row's secondary actions. Above the stretched link in the stacking order, so pressing it does not also follow the row.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

name: menu
title: Menu
description: A transient list of actions anchored to a trigger.

props.name: trigger
props.summary: The control that opens the menu.
use: A `Button`. It is cloned to receive the trigger ARIA, a ref and the handlers.
dont: A `div` or a span. The trigger must be a real button or it is not reachable by keyboard, and none of the ARIA below means anything on a non-interactive element.
Passing `onClick` on it and expecting to be called. The menu owns that handler; put your own work in `onOpenChange`.
props.a11y: Receives `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Its own text names the menu, which is why `label` is only for a trigger that has none.

props.name: children
props.description: `MenuItem` and `MenuSeparator` children, in the order they are read.
props.summary: `MenuItem` and `MenuSeparator`, in the order they are read.
use: Two to about seven actions. Longer than that and the reader is scanning, not choosing.
dont: Anything focusable that is not a `MenuItem`. The arrow keys walk the rows the menu knows about, and a stray button would be a tab stop the pattern does not account for.
A form. A menu is a list of actions; something to fill in belongs in a dialog.
props.a11y: Each row registers itself, so navigation follows DOM order rather than mount order — which is what the reader sees.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the menu is showing. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the menu is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Opening the menu from somewhere else, or keeping it open across a re-render you drive.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`. One of them owns the state.

Opening more than one at a time. The list is a `popover="auto"`, and the platform allows exactly one of those open at once — showing a second closes the first, and the menu reports that through `onOpenChange` rather than silently disagreeing with your state.
props.a11y: Controlled means the menu will not open unless you change this — the trigger still reports the request through `onOpenChange`, and `aria-expanded` follows whatever you set.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled menu. Conflicts with `open`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled menu.
use: Almost never. A menu that is open before the reader asked for it covers the thing they were looking at.
dont: Using it as a way to show the menu on load. That is what a `Notice` or an inline panel is for.
props.a11y: Focus is NOT moved into the menu, and that is deliberate: focus follows the reader's own action, and taking it on page load would be hostile. The first row is still the tab stop, so Tab reaches it and the arrow keys work from there. The same is true of setting `open` programmatically.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.summary: Called when the menu should open or close.
use: Controlled mode, to set `open`.
Uncontrolled mode, to react — closing a toolbar, or logging.
dont: Doing work that belongs in a row's `onSelect`. This fires for every close, including Escape and clicking away.

props.name: label
props.description: Names the list itself, for a trigger whose own name describes the button.
props.summary: Names the list itself, for a trigger whose own name describes the button.
use: An icon-only trigger, where the button is named "Row actions" and the list needs naming separately.
dont: A trigger with visible text. The text already names the menu, and a second name would win over the one the reader can see.
props.a11y: Becomes the menu's `aria-label` and suppresses the `aria-labelledby` pointing at the trigger — never both, because two names on one node is a 4.1.2 problem rather than a fallback.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the list, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Constraining the width when the actions are unusually long.
dont: Positioning it. Placement comes from anchor positioning in `menu.css`; a competing `position` here is how a menu ends up in the wrong place on one page only.

usage.when: The commonest case: a handful of things you can do to one item.
usage.example:
<Menu trigger={<Button variant="secondary">Actions</Button>}>
  <MenuItem onSelect={duplicate}>Duplicate</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem onSelect={download}>Download</MenuItem>
  <MenuSeparator />
  <MenuItem destructive onSelect={remove}>Delete</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: The separator groups the destructive action away from the safe ones, so it is harder to hit by accident. `destructive` colours it; the separator is what actually puts distance between them.

usage.case: An icon-only trigger, which needs the list named separately
usage.when: A dense table where a labelled button would not fit.
usage.example:
<Menu
  label="Row actions"
  trigger={<Button iconOnly aria-label="Row actions" variant="tertiary"><Icon icon={Ellipsis} /></Button>}
>
  <MenuItem onSelect={edit}>Edit</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem destructive onSelect={remove}>Delete</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: Both names are needed and they are not redundant: the button's `aria-label` names the control you press, and `label` names the list that appears. Without the second, the menu is announced with the button's name, which describes the wrong thing.

usage.case: Don't: a menu standing in for a choice that should be a form control
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example:
{/* Don't: this is a select wearing a menu's clothes. */}
<Menu trigger={<Button>Sort: {sort}</Button>}>
  <MenuItem selected={sort === "name"} onSelect={() => setSort("name")}>Name</MenuItem>
  <MenuItem selected={sort === "date"} onSelect={() => setSort("date")}>Date</MenuItem>
</Menu>
usage.notes: Don't. A menu is a list of actions; a choice with a current answer is a `RadioGroup`, or a select once this system has one. `selected` exists for the narrow case where a menu genuinely reflects state — a view switcher — not as licence to build a picker out of actions.

behavior.summary: A trigger and a list in the top layer. The list carries the `popover` attribute, so it escapes every overflow and stacking context without a portal and gets light-dismiss from the platform; CSS anchor positioning places it against the trigger and flips it near a viewport edge. No measurement code and no dependency — which matters more here than usual, because this registry is a copy-paste channel and a dependency becomes an install step for every consumer.

decisions.decision: Focus always returns to the trigger on Escape and after a selection
decisions.why: It is what makes the menu usable by keyboard at all: close it and the reader has to be somewhere, and the only place that makes sense is where they were. The primitive reports the close and the wrapper does the focusing, since moving focus is a DOM act. Light-dismiss is the exception — the reader clicked something else, and taking focus back would undo their own action.

decisions.decision: Selection closes the menu before `onSelect` runs
decisions.why: So focus is already back on the trigger by the time the handler does anything. A handler that navigates, or opens a dialog, would otherwise be fighting a menu that is still tearing down, and the dialog would steal focus from a control that is about to vanish.

decisions.decision: A disabled row is reachable and announced
decisions.why: The `aria-disabled` rule this whole system follows: arrow keys reach it, a screen reader reads it, and activation is refused. Most menus skip disabled rows entirely, which makes the list a different length depending on whether you are looking or listening.

decisions.decision: Tab closes the menu without trapping focus
decisions.why: Someone tabbing through a page expects to keep going. Trapping focus is what a dialog does, because a dialog is modal and a menu is not.

decisions.decision: Typeahead cycles on a single character rather than buffering a prefix
decisions.why: A buffer has to be cleared after a pause, which needs a timer, which needs state — and the primitive is a pure function with neither. Repeating a key walks the matching rows, which is what typeahead is actually used for. Typing `de` to reach Delete past Duplicate is the part that is missing, and it is documented rather than faked. It also ignores a keypress with Ctrl, Meta or Alt held: `event.key` for Ctrl+D is just "d", so without that check a browser shortcut was indistinguishable from someone typing, and typeahead both hijacked the key and preventDefault'd it.

decisions.decision: The list's open state is driven imperatively, not by popovertarget
decisions.why: `popovertarget` would let the platform toggle the popover without telling React, and `open` would drift out of step with what is painted. The trigger's click goes through the primitive instead, and the popover's own `toggle` event is what keeps state honest when the platform closes it.

decisions.decision: The anchor name is generated per instance, not written in the stylesheet
decisions.why: `anchor-name` is a global ident, and the spec resolves a duplicated one to the LAST acceptable anchor in tree order. A single name in the CSS therefore made every menu on a page position itself against whichever trigger came last, which is invisible until a second menu exists. CSS cannot mint a unique ident, so the component passes one in as a custom property — on both the trigger and the list, because a sibling inherits nothing. It is sanitised: React 18's `useId` produces `:r0:` and a colon is not valid in an ident.

base.summary: A transient list of actions anchored to a trigger.

tokens.min-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied — the list should not be narrower than a control

separator.summary: A rule between groups of actions.

example:
<Menu
            label="Account"
            trigger={
              <Button iconOnly aria-label="Account" variant="tertiary">
                <Icon icon={User} />
              </Button>
            }
          >
            <MenuItem icon={Settings} onSelect={() => {}}>Settings</MenuItem>
            <MenuItem onSelect={() => {}}>Sign out</MenuItem>
          </Menu>

name: menu-item
title: MenuItem
description: One action in a Menu, plus the separator that groups them.

props.name: children
props.description: The action's label.
props.summary: The action's label.
use: A verb. "Duplicate", not "Duplication" — a row is a thing you do.
dont: A sentence. If the action needs explaining, the menu is the wrong container.
Only an icon. A glyph with no text is unreadable to anyone who does not already know the icon, and there is no `aria-label` here to rescue it.
props.a11y: The row's accessible name, and — when it is a plain string — the text typeahead matches on.

props.name: value
props.summary: Identifies this row. Defaults to the children when they are a plain string.
use: A row whose children are not a plain string, where there is no text to borrow.
Keeping the identity stable when the label is translated.
dont: Restating the label. Passing the same string the children already are is the duplication the default exists to avoid.
props.a11y: Not announced. It is how the menu tracks which row holds focus, so it has to be unique within one menu.

props.name: onSelect
props.summary: Called when the row is activated.
use: The action itself. The menu has already closed and focus is already back on the trigger by the time this runs.
dont: Closing the menu yourself. It is closed before this is called, and closing again would fight the state.
props.a11y: Runs after focus has returned to the trigger, which is what makes it safe to navigate or open a dialog here.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Unavailable, but still focusable and announced — activation is guarded.
props.summary: Unavailable, but still focusable and announced.
use: An action that exists but cannot run right now — and where the reader benefits from knowing it exists.
dont: Hiding a capability the reader does not have at all. A row they can never use is noise; leave it out.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` with a guarded activation, never the native attribute. Arrow keys reach it and a screen reader reads it, so the list is the same length whether you look or listen.

props.name: destructive
props.description: Marks an action that removes something.
props.summary: Marks an action that removes something.
use: Delete, revoke, discard — something that cannot be undone by doing it again.
dont: "Important". It means something is destroyed, and spending it on emphasis teaches readers to ignore it.
Relying on the colour alone. Put a separator above it so it is harder to hit by accident, and confirm the destruction elsewhere if it matters.
props.a11y: Colour only — nothing about the row is announced differently, because the label is what has to say what it does. "Delete" already does.

props.name: selected
props.summary: Marks the row that is the current answer. Its presence changes the row's role.
use: The narrow case where a menu genuinely reflects state, such as a view switcher.
On EVERY row of the set — `selected={sort === "name"}` on each — not only the chosen one.
dont: Building a picker out of a menu. A choice with a current answer is a `RadioGroup` — see the counter-example in the Menu contract.
Passing it on one row only. The others stay plain `menuitem`s, so the set is not announced as a set and the reader cannot tell how many options there were.
props.a11y: Stating it at all — true or false — makes the row a `menuitemradio` rather than a `menuitem`, because that is the role ARIA lets carry a checked state. `aria-checked` on a plain `menuitem` is invalid and a screen reader may ignore it, which would leave the chosen row marked by colour alone.

props.name: icon
props.summary: A glyph before the label.
use: A set of rows where every one has an icon, so the column reads as a column.
dont: Icons on some rows and not others. The labels then start at two different places and the list is harder to scan than with none at all.
props.a11y: `aria-hidden`, like every decorative glyph here — the label carries the meaning.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the row, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rarely. The row's appearance is the menu's, and a row that looks different reads as a different kind of thing.
dont: Colouring it. `destructive` is the one colour variation a row has, and it is a semantic one.

usage.when: Rows whose actions have recognisable glyphs, all of them.
usage.example: <MenuItem icon={Download} onSelect={download}>Download</MenuItem>
usage.notes: The icon is aria-hidden and the label is the name, so nothing is announced twice.

usage.case: A destructive row, kept away from the safe ones
usage.when: The menu contains something that cannot be undone.
usage.example:
<MenuSeparator />
<MenuItem destructive icon={Trash2} onSelect={remove}>Delete</MenuItem>
usage.notes: The separator is doing the safety work; the colour only confirms it. A destructive row directly under a benign one is one misclick away.

usage.case: A row that exists but cannot run yet
usage.when: The action is real, and the reader benefits from knowing it is there.
usage.example: <MenuItem disabled onSelect={publish}>Publish</MenuItem>
usage.notes: Reachable by arrow keys and announced as unavailable. If the reader could never use it at all, leave it out instead — a permanently dead row is noise.

behavior.summary: A real `<button>` carrying `role="menuitem"`, reading its ARIA, its tabindex and its click handling from the `Menu` above it through context. It throws when rendered outside one rather than degrading: alone it has no list to navigate and no trigger to return focus to, so it would look like a button and behave like nothing.

decisions.decision: Context, not cloneElement
decisions.why: The row writes its ARIA and click handling after spreading `rest`, deliberately, so a caller cannot clobber the accessibility contract with a prop. That same ordering means a cloned prop could not reach those attributes either — so the menu has to be something the row reads, not something done to it. The same reasoning as ToggleButton.

decisions.decision: `value` defaults to the children when they are a plain string
decisions.why: The menu identifies rows by value and typeahead matches on their text, and for almost every row both are just the label. Requiring it stated twice would make the common case noisier than the rare one. A row with non-string children has no text to borrow, so it must say what it is.

decisions.decision: A checkable row is a different role, not a menuitem with an extra attribute
decisions.why: ARIA does not support `aria-checked` on `menuitem` — only on `menuitemradio` and `menuitemcheckbox`. Setting it anyway is invalid and a screen reader is free to drop it, which would leave the selected row distinguished by colour alone: the exact failure the rest of this system's contracts are written to prevent. So `selected` changes the role, and the primitive owns that decision.

base.summary: One action. Its own focus ring, because the roving tabindex means an item — not the menu — is what focus lands on.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

destructive.summary: An action that removes something. Uses the danger role's foreground on the menu's own surface — a pairing the token contracts verify for text at any size — rather than a tinted row, which would read as a status.

selected.summary: A menu standing in for a choice already made, where one row is the current answer.

name: mobile-nav
title: MobileNav
description: A navigation drawer behind a trigger, for viewports too narrow for a rail.

props.name: sections
props.description: The destinations, grouped — the same shape SideNav takes.
props.summary: The destinations, grouped — the same shape SideNav takes.
use: The same array you give the rail, so the two cannot disagree about what the product contains.
dont: A different set from the rail's. Two navigations that list different things is worse than either alone.
props.a11y: Rendered by `SideNav` inside the drawer, so the group naming, the nested disclosures and the current-page marking are the rail's, not a second implementation of them.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark inside the drawer.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark inside the drawer.
use: Naming it for what it contains, as the other navs are named.
dont: Leaving the default when the page's TopNav is also called Main.
props.a11y: Passed to the `SideNav`. The dialog itself is named by `title`.

props.name: title
props.description: The drawer's own name, shown at its top.
props.summary: The drawer's own name, shown at its top.
use: A product name, or what this navigation covers.
dont: Leaving it out. A modal with no accessible name is announced as "dialog" and nothing else.
props.a11y: Wired with `aria-labelledby` on the dialog, and rendered as a paragraph rather than a heading — the drawer sits in the page's outline and cannot know what level it is at, the same reasoning Notice's title follows.

props.name: triggerLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the control that opens the drawer.
props.summary: Accessible name for the control that opens the drawer.
use: Translating it, or naming what is being opened when a page has more than one drawer.
dont: An empty string. The trigger is icon-only, so this is the only name it has.
props.a11y: Becomes the trigger's `aria-label`, alongside `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the drawer is showing. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the drawer is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Closing it from your router when a navigation completes, if you do not want the built-in behaviour.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled drawer. Conflicts with `open`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled drawer.
use: Almost never. A drawer open on arrival covers the page someone came to read.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.summary: Called when the drawer should open or close.
use: Controlled mode, to set `open`.
Reacting — closing a search, or logging.
dont: Using it to close the drawer on navigation. It already does that.

props.name: closeLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the drawer's close control.
props.summary: Accessible name for the drawer's close control.
use: Translating it.
dont: An empty string — the control is icon-only.

props.name: footer
props.description: Content pinned below the destinations — an account link, a sign-out.
props.summary: Content pinned below the destinations — an account link, a sign-out.
use: The things a top nav would put in its actions slot, which has nowhere else to go at this width.
dont: Destinations. Those belong in `sections`, inside the nav landmark where they can be found.
props.a11y: Outside the `SideNav`'s landmark, because none of it is navigation.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the trigger's wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The media query that decides at what width this appears at all.
dont: Styling the drawer through it. The drawer is in the top layer and is not a descendant of this.

usage.case: A drawer beside a rail, sharing one set of destinations
usage.when: The commonest case: the same navigation, presented two ways.
usage.notes: One array, two presentations. Two navigations listing different things is worse than either alone, which is why the same value goes to both rather than each being given its own.

usage.case: A drawer with account actions under the destinations
usage.when: At this width there is no top bar to put them in.
usage.example:
<MobileNav
  title="Ratā"
  sections={sections}
  footer={
    <>
      <Button variant="secondary">Settings</Button>
      <Button variant="tertiary">Sign out</Button>
    </>
  }
/>
usage.notes: `footer` sits outside the nav landmark, because none of it is navigation — the same split TopNav makes between `items` and `actions`.

usage.case: Don't: a non-modal drawer over a live page
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example: {/* Don't: this is what NOT using MobileNav looks like. */}
usage.notes: Don't. A drawer covering the page is modal whether or not it is called one: without `showModal()` the content behind stays in the tab order, a screen reader walks straight into a page nobody can see, and the page scrolls under the drawer. Those three are what this component exists to get from the platform rather than approximate.

behavior.summary: A trigger and a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, holding a `SideNav`. The browser supplies the focus trap, `inert` on the page behind, the backdrop, Escape, and focus returned to the trigger — the same reasoning Dialog follows, and the same reason not to hand-roll any of it.

decisions.decision: It is modal, and a real <dialog>
decisions.why: A drawer covering the page is modal whether or not it is called one: the content behind it must not be reachable by Tab, by a screen reader's own navigation, or by scrolling. `showModal()` supplies all three, plus the focus trap that is the most bug-prone thing anyone writes by hand. A non-modal panel would leave a reader tabbing into a page they cannot see.

decisions.decision: It renders a SideNav rather than reimplementing one
decisions.why: The drawer's content is a rail — sections, nested groups, current-page marking, the lot. Rebuilding that markup here would be a second copy to keep in step, and the two would drift on exactly the details that matter: which element carries the group name, and how the current page is announced.

decisions.decision: Picking a destination closes it
decisions.why: A drawer that stays open over the page you just navigated to is the commonest complaint about this pattern, and under client-side routing nothing else closes it — the document never unloads. Handled here rather than left to every caller, because every caller wants it.

decisions.decision: It does not decide when it applies
decisions.why: There are no breakpoint tokens in this system, deliberately: where a rail stops fitting depends on the rail's width and the page around it, which is the page's knowledge. So this hides itself at no width — the caller's own media query does that, the same way SideNav takes its width from the page.

decisions.decision: The scroll lock is shared with Dialog, not its own
decisions.why: Two components each counting their own holders would fight: with a Dialog and a drawer both open, whichever closed first would unlock the page while the other still covered it. One counter in one module, which is why that helper moved out of Dialog when this was built.

trigger.summary: The control that opens the drawer. Same construction as the other icon-only controls here: transparent, taking its colour from the text.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

drawer.summary: The panel itself: full height, against the inline-start edge, at a width that leaves the page visible behind the scrim so it still reads as a layer over it.

tokens.max-inline-size: size.control.lg multiplied by 8, or the viewport less one large control

backdrop.summary: The wash over the inert page behind it — the same token and the same reasoning as Dialog's.

header.summary: The drawer's name and its close control.

name: notice
title: Notice
description: An inline banner carrying an informational, success, warning, or error message.

props.name: children
props.description: The message.
props.summary: The message.
use: One or two sentences saying what happened and, when there is one, what to do about it.
dont: A bare status word. "Error" tells the reader nothing they cannot already see from the colour.
A paragraph. A notice is read in passing; anything longer belongs on the page itself.
props.a11y: The text carries the meaning. The icon beside it is aria-hidden, so this is the only thing announced besides `title`.

props.name: variant
props.description: Which kind of message this is.
props.summary: Which kind of message this is.
use: `info` for context the reader did not ask for but benefits from — the default.
`success` to confirm something completed.
`warning` for something that will go wrong if it is left alone.
`danger` for something that has already gone wrong.
dont: `danger` for "important". It means something is broken, and spending it on emphasis is how readers learn to ignore it.
`warning` where the reader has nothing to do. A warning with no action is just noise in a louder colour.
props.a11y: Colour alone never carries the severity: each variant also gets its own icon, and the text states the problem. `info` is tinted neutral rather than with the brand accent, so it cannot impersonate an error in a red or orange brand.

props.name: live
props.description: Whether assistive technology is told about this notice when it appears.
props.summary: Whether assistive technology is told about this notice when it appears.
use: `off` for a notice that is part of the page when it loads — the default, and correct more often than it looks.
`polite` for a notice that appears in response to something the user did and can wait for a pause: a save confirmation.
`assertive` only when the user must stop: their work failed to save, or a deadline just passed.
dont: `assertive` as the default for `danger`. It interrupts whatever is being read mid-sentence, and most errors can wait one clause.
Any live setting on a notice that is present at page load. There is no change to announce, so it is read out of context or silently dropped.
More than one assertive region on a screen. They interrupt each other and the user hears fragments.
props.a11y: `polite` renders `role="status"`, `assertive` renders `role="alert"`, and `off` renders no role at all. A live region must already be in the document before its content arrives, so `{error && <Notice live="assertive">…}` is unreliable — the persistent wrapper has to be yours. See the usage case below.

props.name: title
props.description: A short first line above the message.
props.summary: A short first line above the message.
use: A notice long enough that the reader needs to know whether it concerns them before reading it.
dont: Repeating the variant. "Error" over an error notice adds a line and no information.
A title on a one-line notice. The line is already the title.
props.a11y: Renders as a styled paragraph, not an `<h2>`. A notice cannot know the heading level it sits under, and announcing a wrong one breaks heading navigation for the whole page.

props.name: icon
props.description: Overrides the icon the variant chooses, or removes it.
props.summary: Overrides the icon the variant chooses, or removes it.
use: A glyph more specific than the severity when the notice is about one recognisable thing — a clock for an expiry, a lock for a permission.
`false` only where a parent already shows the severity and a second glyph is noise.
dont: `false` to save space. The icon is the non-colour cue for the variant; removing it leaves colour carrying the severity alone.
An icon that contradicts the variant. It is aria-hidden, so a screen reader cannot correct the impression it gives a sighted reader.
props.a11y: Always `aria-hidden`, whichever glyph it is: it repeats the severity the text and the variant already carry.

props.name: actions
props.description: Buttons or links for what to do about the message.
props.summary: Buttons or links for what to do about the message.
use: One action, occasionally two: "Retry", or "Retry" and "Download the log".
`Button` with `variant="secondary"` or a plain link — a notice is not the page's primary call to action.
dont: A third action. At that point the notice is a form and belongs in a dialog.
The dismiss control. That is `onDismiss`, which places and names it for you.
props.a11y: Rendered after the message in DOM order, so it is reached after the text explaining it. Each action needs its own accessible name — "Retry" is fine; an icon-only button here needs `aria-label` like anywhere else.

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Called when the reader closes the notice. Its presence is what renders the close button.
props.summary: Called when the reader closes the notice. Its presence is what renders the close button.
use: A notice the reader can finish with: a confirmation, or a tip.
Removing the notice from your own state in the handler — `Notice` does not hide itself, because it cannot know what should fill the space.
dont: A notice reporting a condition that is still true. Dismissing an unsaved-changes warning does not save the changes, and offering the button implies it might.
Relying on it to unmount anything. The handler is yours; nothing happens to the notice unless you make it happen.
props.a11y: Dismissing destroys the element that had focus, so focus falls to `<body>` and the reader loses their place. `Notice` cannot know where focus belongs next — move it in your handler, usually to whatever the notice was about.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the close button.
props.summary: Accessible name for the close button.
use: Translating it, or naming what is being dismissed when several notices are on screen at once: "Dismiss the payment warning".
dont: An empty string. The button is icon-only, so this is the only name it has.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`. Without it the control announces as an unnamed button, which is a 4.1.2 failure.

usage.case: A page-level message that is there when the page loads
usage.when: The commonest case, and the one where `live` should stay off.
usage.example:
<Notice variant="warning">
  This project is read-only while the migration runs.
</Notice>
usage.notes: No `live`: there is no change to announce. A screen reader reaches this in document order like any other content, which is the behaviour you want for something that was always on the page.

usage.case: An error that appears after an action, announced correctly
usage.when: The user pressed Save and it failed. Their attention is on the button, not on the banner.
usage.notes: `polite` on the wrapper rather than `live` on the Notice, because the region has to pre-exist its content. Use `live` on the Notice when the notice itself is always mounted and only its text changes.

usage.case: A dismissible confirmation, with focus handled
usage.when: Something succeeded and the reader can be done with the message.
usage.notes: The handler does two things, neither of which happens on its own: `Notice` does not own its visibility, and it cannot guess where the reader's place was. Reach for `live` on the notice itself only when the notice stays mounted and only its children change — a status line that updates in place, not a banner that appears.

behavior.summary: A plain div. There is no primitive: nothing here owns keyboard interaction, roving focus or an activation to guard, and the one stateful thing — whether the notice is still on screen — belongs to the caller, who is the only one who knows what replaces it.

decisions.decision: When it announces is a prop, not a consequence of the variant
decisions.why: A live region announces *changes*. A notice already on the page at load is therefore either read out of context during load or not at all, while one that appears because the user pressed something must be read, since their attention is on the button. That distinction is about when the notice arrived, not what it says: a validation summary rendered at load and an error that appears after a failed save are the same variant with opposite requirements. Deriving it from `variant` would get one of them wrong every time, so `live` is explicit and silent by default.

decisions.decision: The icon is on by default
decisions.why: Colour is the only thing separating the four variants, so the icon is the 1.4.1 redundancy rather than decoration — which is also why it is aria-hidden: it repeats the severity the text already carries, and a glyph that could disagree with its message is worse than no glyph.

decisions.decision: `info` is tinted neutral, not with the brand accent
decisions.why: There is no info role in the token set, and the obvious substitute — accent-role.subtle — moves with the brand. In rust (#C22D05) or ember an informational notice would be tinted red and read as an error, which is a worse failure than looking plain. bg.muted with fg.primary is the same pairing Badge's neutral uses and is safe in all seven brands.

decisions.decision: `title` is a styled paragraph, never a heading element
decisions.why: A notice cannot know what heading level it sits under, and a wrong level breaks the document outline for anyone navigating by headings — a quieter failure than an unstyled title, and a harder one to notice.

base.summary: The shared frame. Only the tinted subtle backgrounds carry text; the saturated role fills are not used here at all — they are non-text indicator tones, and text on them is a recorded contrast gap.

info.summary: Tinted neutral rather than with the brand accent: there is no info role, and accent-role.subtle moves with the brand, so in a red or orange theme an info notice would read as an error.

success.summary: The role's subtle tint with its own foreground.

warning.summary: The role's subtle tint with its own foreground.

danger.summary: The role's subtle tint with its own foreground.

dismiss.summary: The close button, when `onDismiss` is passed. It takes currentColor so the glyph always matches the variant's foreground and cannot clash with the tint it sits on — which is also why it is not a Button: a tertiary Button would bring its own colour into a tinted surface.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the variant's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible
tokens.background: transparent — the variant's tint shows through

example: <Notice variant="warning">This project is read-only while the migration runs.</Notice>

name: number-field
title: Number Field
description: A labelled input for a numeric quantity, with keyboard and button stepping, locale-aware formatting, and bounds.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: The quantity's name. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: A noun phrase with the unit when `formatOptions` does not show one: "Seats", "Weight (kg)".
dont: Leaving the unit to the placeholder. It disappears on the first digit.
props.a11y: Bound to the input by Field, so it is the spinbutton's accessible name.

props.name: value
props.summary: Controls the value from outside. `null` is empty, which is different from zero.
use: A form library, or a quantity another control also writes to.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the state.
`0` to mean unanswered. Zero is an answer; empty is `null`.

props.name: defaultValue
props.summary: The starting value when the component owns the state.
use: A genuine default — one seat, one unit.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Fires with the parsed number when the value changes: a step, or text that parses on blur or Enter.
use: Reading a number without parsing a string, which is the whole point of the component.
dont: Expecting it on every keystroke. Partial text like "1." or "-" is not a number yet, so the value changes when the text resolves to one.

props.name: min
props.summary: The lowest allowed value. Typed values below it are clamped on blur.
use: A real floor: zero items, one seat.
dont: Leaving it unset on a quantity that cannot be negative. The decrement button would walk straight past zero.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-valuemin`. Decrement at the floor is refused and the button is `aria-disabled`, not removed.

props.name: max
props.summary: The highest allowed value. Typed values above it are clamped on blur.
use: A real ceiling, such as stock on hand.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-valuemax`.

props.name: step
props.summary: How far ArrowUp, ArrowDown and the buttons move. PageUp and PageDown move ten steps.
use: `0.01` for currency, `0.5` for half-units.
dont: Expecting it to restrict typing. A typed value off the grid is kept — rounding someone's exact entry is a value change they did not make. Validate it with `status` if the grid is a rule.

props.name: formatOptions
props.summary: How the value is displayed when the field is not being edited — currency, percent, units, fraction digits.
use: `{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }` for money, so the reader sees "€12.50" and edits "12.50".
dont: Formatting the value yourself into `value`. It is a number; the format is this prop's job, at the page's locale.
props.a11y: The formatted text is `aria-valuetext`, so "12.50 euros" is what is announced rather than "12.5".

props.name: stepButtons
props.summary: Renders the decrement and increment buttons at either end.
use: Small adjustments a reader makes by touch — quantities in a cart, guests on a booking.
dont: A value nobody adjusts by one — a postcode, a phone number, a card number. Those are not numbers; they are a `TextField` with `inputMode="numeric"`.
props.a11y: The buttons are `tabindex="-1"`, as APG's spinbutton pattern specifies: the keyboard already has the arrow keys, and two extra tab stops per field would triple a form's length.

props.name: incrementLabel
props.summary: Accessible name for the increment button.
use: Translating it.
dont: An empty string. The button is icon-only, so this is the only name it has for a voice-control or touch screen-reader user.

props.name: decrementLabel
props.summary: Accessible name for the decrement button.
use: Translating it.
dont: An empty string, for the same reason.

props.name: placeholder
props.summary: A hint shown while the field is empty.
use: An example in the expected format: "0.00".
dont: The unit or the label. Both vanish on the first keystroke.

props.name: name
props.summary: Form field name. Submits the unformatted number as a plain decimal string.
use: A native form post, where the server should receive "1234.5" and not "1.234,50 €".
props.a11y: Carried by a hidden input; the visible one holds the formatted text.

props.name: size
props.summary: Control height and inline padding. Text size does not change with it.
use: Matching whatever the control sits beside.
dont: `sm` in a touch-first layout. The step buttons shrink with the box, and they are the main way a phone user changes the value.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: the label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.summary: Stable id for the number field, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the field it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message, popup — is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged.

props.name: description
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: A constraint the reader needs before they answer.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative.
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks editing and stepping while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
use: A quantity fixed by an earlier choice that should still be readable.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits — the text field's consequence, unchanged.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly` from Field. Arrow keys and both buttons are refused; the buttons are `aria-disabled` too.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: A narrow measure. A quantity rarely needs a full-width field, and a short box hints at a short answer.

usage.when: A small whole number adjusted by touch more often than typed.
usage.example: <NumberField label="Quantity" defaultValue={1} min={1} max={stock} />
usage.notes: `min={1}` makes the decrement button refuse at one rather than reaching zero, which in a cart would mean removal — a different action that deserves its own button.

usage.when: A decimal amount displayed in a currency.
usage.example:
<NumberField
  label="Budget"
  formatOptions={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }}
  step={0.01}
  stepButtons={false}
  name="budget"
/>
usage.notes: The reader sees "€1,250.00" at rest and edits "1250.00"; the form posts "1250". Step buttons are off because nobody adds a budget one cent at a time.

usage.when: A number that parses but breaks a rule the field cannot enforce by clamping.
usage.example:
<NumberField
  label="Team size"
  min={1}
  status="invalid"
  message="Teams on this plan have at most 10 people."
/>
usage.notes: The rule lives in the message, not in a silent clamp. `max={10}` would have quietly changed 12 to 10 on blur — use it for a hard limit, not for a plan limit the reader might want to upgrade past.

usage.when: Digits that are an identifier rather than an amount.
usage.example: <NumberField label="Postcode" />
usage.notes: Don't. A postcode can start with zero, is never incremented, and grouping separators would corrupt it. It is `<TextField label="Postcode" inputMode="numeric" />`.

behavior.summary: An APG spinbutton built on a text input, so the value is parsed rather than trusted to `type="number"`. Composed with Field for label, helper text and validation; formatting and parsing follow the page's locale.

decisions.decision: It is `<input type="text" inputmode="decimal" role="spinbutton">`, not `type="number"`
decisions.why: The native number input fails readers in ways that are hard to see in a demo: the scroll wheel changes the value of a focused field while the page scrolls past it; it accepts `e`, so "1e5" is valid; its `value` is an empty string both for an empty field and for "1.2.3", so a caller cannot tell blank from broken; it does not accept a decimal comma in most locales; and its spin buttons are too small to touch and cannot be styled. A text input with `inputmode` keeps the right on-screen keyboard and gives the primitive the raw text to parse. The APG Spinbutton pattern supplies the ARIA: `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`, `aria-valuetext`.

decisions.decision: Parse on blur and Enter, not on every keystroke
decisions.why: "-", "1." and "0.0" are all on the way to a valid number. Reformatting or clamping while someone types moves the caret and rewrites their input under them. So typing changes the text only; the value, the clamp to `min`/`max` and the formatting all happen when the reader commits.

decisions.decision: Locale comes from the page, not from a prop
decisions.why: Formatting and parsing use the nearest `lang` attribute, so "1.234,5" parses in German and "1,234.5" in English. A per-field `locale` prop would let one form disagree with itself about what a comma means, which is worse than either answer.

decisions.decision: A typed value off the step grid is kept
decisions.why: `step` is how far a key press moves, not a rule about what can be entered. Rounding 12.37 to 12.4 because step is 0.1 is a value change the reader did not make and may not notice. If the grid is a business rule, it is validation, and Field's `status` and `message` say so where the reader can see it.

decisions.decision: The step buttons are pointer and touch targets, not tab stops
decisions.why: APG puts them at `tabindex="-1"`, and this follows it: keyboard users have the arrow keys and PageUp/PageDown. Pressing and holding a button repeats after a delay, the way a native spinner does. The buttons sit at either end — decrement first, increment last — rather than stacked at the end, because two stacked half-height buttons are a 14px target each.

decisions.decision: Not every number is a NumberField
decisions.why: A postcode, a card number, an account number and a phone number are strings of digits. They have leading zeros, they are never incremented, and formatting them with grouping separators corrupts them. They are a `TextField` with `inputMode="numeric"`; this component is for quantities.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: The system rule, and the text field's consequence with it: the value still submits.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getNumberFieldProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet. The proposal owns parse, clamp, step and format as pure functions over the raw text and the options, and returns the input and button prop bags — including the press-and-hold repeat schedule as data, so the timer lives in the React wrapper rather than in the primitive.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: the text input above with `role="spinbutton"` inside a Field, two `<button tabindex="-1">` with `aria-label`, and a hidden input carrying `name`. React Native: a `TextInput` with `keyboardType="decimal-pad"` — or `numbers-and-punctuation` when `min` is below zero, because the iOS decimal pad has no minus key — flanked by two `Pressable` buttons with `accessibilityRole="button"` and the two labels. iOS cannot make one element both editable text and adjustable, so on native the input keeps its text role and the stepping lives on the buttons; `accessibilityValue={{ min, max, now, text }}` is set on the input so the range is still announced. `name` and `size` are web-only. Rata-drawn around the OS text input (decision N5): the `TextInput` is the platform's own and the step buttons are drawn from the recipe — not `UIStepper`, which has no text entry and no Android counterpart. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: The text field's box, step for step, with a button well at each end. Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming.

tokens.font-variant: tabular-nums, so digits do not shift as the value changes
tokens.text-align: end — numbers compare by their last digit, so a column of them aligns on the right
tokens.block-size: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / size.control.lg at the other sizes
tokens.padding-inline: space.control.padding-inline.md plus size.control.sm at each end when stepButtons is on — the well each button sits in
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset — the text field's departure, so every text box in a form focuses alike
tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2 as an inset shadow, idle only

step-button.summary: Decrement and increment, inside the box at either end. Transparent on the field's surface, like Search's clear control.

tokens.inline-size / block-size: size.control.sm, inset space.0-5 from the box edge
tokens.at the limit: state.disabled-opacity with aria-disabled — the button stays, so the layout does not shift when the value reaches min or max

name: pagination
title: Pagination
description: Links to the pages of a long, ordered result set, with previous, next and the current page marked.

props.name: page
props.description: The current page, counting from 1.
props.summary: The current page, counting from 1.
use: Read from the URL, so the page and the address bar cannot disagree.
dont: Counting from 0. Readers count pages from 1, and so does every label this renders.
props.a11y: The matching item is marked `aria-current="page"`.

props.name: pageCount
props.description: How many pages there are.
props.summary: How many pages there are.
use: The real total, from the result count.
dont: An estimate. A feed with no known end is a "Load more" Button, not pagination.
props.a11y: With a count of 1 nothing is rendered — a landmark with nowhere to go is noise.

props.name: href
props.description: Builds the URL for a page. Web only.
props.summary: Builds the URL for a page. Web only.
use: Every web use — a function of the page number that keeps the address's other query parameters intact.
dont: Omitting it on the web and relying on `onPageChange`. A page of results nobody can link to is a page they lose.
props.a11y: Makes each item a real link: middle-click, copy-link and Back all work.

props.name: onPageChange
props.description: Called when the reader picks a page. Intercepts the link for a client-side router.
props.summary: Called when the reader picks a page. Intercepts the link for a client-side router; required on React Native.
use: Calling the router's navigate and `event.preventDefault()`, so the link stays a link but the page does not reload.
dont: Keeping the page in component state only. Put it in the URL, or Back will not undo it.
props.a11y: Move focus to the top of the new results — usually their heading — after the page changes, or a keyboard user is left on a pagination row for content they cannot see.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Naming what is paged when a page has more than one: "Invoice pages".
dont: Including the word "navigation". The landmark already says it.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for placement.
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement.
use: Aligning the row in the page's layout.
dont: Restyling the items. A page link that differs per page reads as a different control.

usage.when: A long, ordered result set with a known count, under the Table it pages.
usage.example:
<Table caption="Invoices" columns={columns} rows={invoices} getRowKey={(i) => i.id} />
<Pagination
  label="Invoice pages"
  page={page}
  pageCount={Math.ceil(total / perPage)}
  href={(p) => `/invoices?page=${p}`}
/>
usage.notes: The page lives in the URL, so Back and bookmarks work. No `onPageChange`: a full page load is fine here, and the reader lands at the top.

usage.when: A single-page app that should not reload, but whose pages should still be linkable.
usage.example:
<Pagination
  page={page}
  pageCount={pageCount}
  href={(p) => `?page=${p}`}
  onPageChange={(p, event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    navigate(`?page=${p}`);
    resultsHeadingRef.current?.focus();
  }}
/>
usage.notes: `href` stays, so the links are still links. Focus moves to the results heading, because otherwise a keyboard user is left on the pagination row after the content above it changed.

usage.when: An activity feed with no known end.
usage.example: <Pagination page={page} pageCount={999} href={(p) => `?page=${p}`} />
usage.notes: Don't. An invented count lies about where the end is. That is a "Load more" Button below the list.

behavior.summary: A `<nav>` landmark holding a list of links: Previous, a window of page numbers with ellipses, Next. Every page is a real `href`, and a client-side router intercepts through `onPageChange` — the same bargain TopNav and SideNav make with `onClick`. Proposed primitive: `getPaginationItems` in `packages/primitives/src/pagination.ts`, a pure function from `page` and `pageCount` to the list of items; it is a proposal, not yet a commitment.

decisions.decision: Links with real URLs, not buttons with state
decisions.why: A page of results the reader cannot bookmark, share or return to with Back is a page they lose. Every item is an `<a href>` built by `href(page)`, so middle-click, copy-link and the Back button all work, and a router that wants to stay client-side intercepts through `onPageChange` without the link stopping being a link. The precedent is TopNav and SideNav, which keep `href` real and let the caller intercept.

decisions.decision: The window is fixed: first, last, the current page and one either side
decisions.why: "1 … 4 5 6 … 20" is the shape every reader already knows, and it is at most seven items wide whatever `pageCount` is, so the row cannot overflow a phone. A `siblingCount` prop would let every page pick its own width and gain nothing. The ellipsis is `aria-hidden` punctuation, and is not a control; jumping to a page in the gap is what the neighbouring numbers are for.

decisions.decision: Previous and Next stay on the first and last pages, `aria-disabled`
decisions.why: The rule this system follows everywhere: an unavailable control is still announced. Removing Previous on page 1 makes the row a different length depending on where you are, and a screen-reader user hears a list of six on one page and seven on the next. The unavailable link has no `href`, carries `aria-disabled="true"`, and stays in the tab order with `tabindex="0"`.

decisions.decision: Not for infinite or unknown-length lists
decisions.why: Pagination needs `pageCount`. A feed with no known end is a "Load more" Button below the list, which keeps the reader's place and needs no component of its own. Cursor-based APIs that only know whether there is a next page get Previous and Next as two Buttons or Links, not a Pagination with an invented count.

decisions.decision: The landmark is named, and the numbers say what they are
decisions.why: A page with Breadcrumbs, a TopNav and a Pagination has three navigation landmarks, and three that are all called "navigation" are unusable. `label` names this one. Each number link is named "Page 4" rather than "4", and the current one is marked `aria-current="page"`, so a screen reader announces "Page 4, current page".

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: `<nav aria-label>` around a `<ul>` of `<a>` elements, `aria-current="page"` on the current one, `aria-disabled` on an unavailable Previous or Next. React Native has no URLs to link to, so `href` is web-only and `onPageChange` is what drives navigation; it is required there. Each item is a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="button"` — on native, changing a page is an action rather than a link — with `accessibilityLabel` "Page 4" and `accessibilityState` carrying `selected` for the current page and `disabled` for an unavailable Previous or Next. The row wraps in a `View` with `accessibilityLabel` set from `label`. Rata-drawn (decision N5): there is no OS page-selector control, so each item is a drawn `Pressable`. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A row of control-sized targets. Built from the same parts as a SideNav row — size, type, state layer, current tint — so a page link reads as navigation and not as a button.

tokens.numerals: tabular figures, so the row does not shift width as the current page moves
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

current.summary: The page you are on: the same tinted row SideNav uses, plus `aria-current`. The role's subtle step with `theme.fg.primary` on it is a verified text pairing; the saturated fill is not used.

unavailable.summary: Previous on the first page and Next on the last: still present and announced, not removed, so the row keeps its shape.

ellipsis.summary: The gap in the run of page numbers. Punctuation, not a control.

name: panel
title: Panel
description: A titled region beside the content it describes, with its own scroll and an optional close.

props.name: title
props.summary: The panel's name. Required.
use: A noun phrase naming what the panel is about — the token path, the selected row's name.
dont: A verb phrase. This names a region, it does not describe an action.
props.a11y: Rendered as a heading at `headingLevel` and wired to the `<aside>` with `aria-labelledby`, so the landmark is announced by name. An unnamed complementary landmark is listed as "complementary" and nothing else, which is worse than useless when a page has two.

props.name: children
props.description: The panel's content.
props.summary: The panel's content.
use: Whatever the panel is about — the detail, the contract, the form.
dont: The page's primary content. If it is the main thing on the page it is not complementary, and this is the wrong container.
props.a11y: Scrolls in its own region so the title and the close control stay reachable.

props.name: headingLevel
props.description: Where the title sits in the page's outline.
props.summary: Where the title sits in the page's outline.
use: The level below whatever heading the panel's section sits under — a panel inside a section headed `<h2>` takes `3`.
dont: Picking it for type size. The size comes from the recipe; this is the outline only.
props.a11y: A skipped level breaks heading navigation, which is how many readers move through a page. Only the caller knows the depth, which is why there is no sensible default beyond the commonest case.

props.name: edge
props.description: Which side of the content it is attached to.
props.summary: Which side of the content the panel is attached to.
use: `inline-end` for a detail or inspector panel, which is where a reader expects one — and the same side Sheet's `inline-end` drawer comes from, so the two are interchangeable as the viewport changes.
`inline-start` for a filter or tree column.
dont: Using it to move the panel. It states which edge the panel meets so the border and the corners land on the right side; where the panel sits is the page's layout.
props.a11y: Presentational only — it changes no roles and no announcement. Logical, not physical: `inline-start` is the left in a left-to-right document and the right in a right-to-left one.

props.name: onClose
props.summary: Called when the reader closes the panel. Omitting it makes the panel persistent.
use: A panel opened by a selection — clicking a swatch, a row, a node — which the reader can put away again.
dont: Passing a no-op to get the button. No handler means no button, and that is the intended way to say the panel does not close.
props.a11y: No reason argument, unlike Dialog's: the close button is the only way this closes. Escape does not, and there is no backdrop to click.

props.name: closeLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the close button.
props.summary: Accessible name for the close button.
use: Naming what closes when several panels can be open at once: "Close token documentation".
dont: Passing it without `onClose`. There is no button to name.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`. The control is icon-only, so without a name it announces as "button".

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the panel, for placement and measure — not for restyling it.
use: Setting the width and how it sits in the page's grid or flex row, which the component deliberately leaves open.
dont: Changing its surface or border. Those come from the recipe, and a panel that differs per page reads as two different products.

usage.case: An inspector beside the thing it documents
usage.when: The reader needs to compare the detail against the grid, list or canvas it came from. This is the case the component exists for.
usage.example: {selected !== null && ( setSelected(null)} closeLabel="Close token documentation" > )}
usage.notes: The width belongs to `.page-with-rail`, not to the Panel — there is no `size` prop, because where a panel stops fitting depends on the page around it. `closeLabel` is spelled out because "Close" alone is ambiguous on a page that can also close other things.

usage.when: The panel is part of the page rather than a response to a selection, so there is nothing to close.
usage.example:
<Panel title="Properties" headingLevel={3}>
  <PropertyList node={node} />
</Panel>
usage.notes: No `onClose`, so no close button is rendered — that is how a persistent panel is said, rather than by passing a no-op handler to a control the reader can press. `headingLevel={3}` because this page's sections are already `h2`, and a skipped level breaks the heading navigation many readers use to move around.

usage.case: A filter column on the inline-start side
usage.when: The panel sits before the content it refines rather than after it, which is where a filter column belongs.
usage.example:
<Panel title="Filters" edge="inline-start" onClose={() => setFiltering(false)}>
  <CheckboxGroup label="Status" items={statuses} />
</Panel>
usage.notes: `edge="inline-start"` moves the border to the side facing the content — it does not move the panel, which is the page's layout. Logical, so in a right-to-left document this is the right-hand column and the border still faces the content.

usage.case: The same content as a Sheet, chosen by width
usage.when: One piece of detail, beside the content when there is room and over it when there is not.
usage.example:
wide ? (
  <Panel title={record.name} onClose={close}>
    <RecordDetail record={record} />
  </Panel>
) : (
  <Sheet open onClose={close} edge="block-end" title={record.name}>
    <RecordDetail record={record} />
  </Sheet>
)
usage.notes: `wide` is the page's own media query, not a prop on either component: this system has no breakpoint tokens, because where a rail stops fitting is the page's knowledge. Note that the two are not interchangeable in behaviour — the Sheet traps focus and makes the page inert, and the Panel does neither.

behavior.summary: A `<aside>` complementary landmark named by its own heading, in normal flow. Not a dialog, not in the top layer, and not dismissed by Escape. The page reflows around it and everything beside it stays usable — which is the only reason to choose it over a Sheet.

decisions.decision: It is in the layout, and that is the whole distinction from Sheet
decisions.why: Reading a token's contract while still seeing the swatch grid is the point of this pattern: the comparison IS the task. A Sheet covers the page and makes everything behind it inert, so the same content in a sheet would answer a different question. Two components rather than one with a `modal` boolean, because the two render through completely different mechanisms — normal flow against the top layer — and a boolean that swaps the rendering model is two components wearing one name.

decisions.decision: Escape does not close it
decisions.why: Escape dismisses the top layer, and a reader who presses it expects whatever is covering the page to go away. This is not covering anything, nothing has trapped focus, and the reader may well be typing in the page beside it. A panel that vanished on Escape would also take the reader's place in the page with it, since there is nowhere for focus to return to.

decisions.decision: Focus is not moved, trapped, or restored
decisions.why: All three are modal behaviours. Opening a panel adds a region to the page; it does not take the reader anywhere, so moving their focus would be a surprise, and trapping it would strand them in a region they can see past. Tab reaches it in document order like anything else.

decisions.decision: The page owns the measure, not the component
decisions.why: The same bargain SideNav makes. Where a panel stops fitting depends on the panel's content and the page around it, which is the page's knowledge — and this system has no breakpoint tokens for exactly that reason. Found the hard way: the playground's own inspector hardcoded `width: 340px`, a bare pixel value in a repo whose first rule is that there are none.

decisions.decision: The heading level is the caller's, because only they know it
decisions.why: A complementary landmark should be headed, and the heading names the landmark through `aria-labelledby`. But a panel sits inside the page's existing outline and cannot know its depth — the same problem Notice has, which Notice solves by not being a heading at all. A panel cannot take that way out because it needs the name, so the level is stated instead of guessed. Dialog can hardcode `<h2>` only because everything behind a modal is inert and its outline genuinely starts fresh.

decisions.decision: Closing is optional, and its absence means persistent
decisions.why: A panel that is always there — a properties rail, a filter column — has nothing to close, and rendering a close button that the caller has to ignore invites them to wire it to nothing. Omitting `onClose` omits the control.

decisions.decision: The body scrolls, the head does not
decisions.why: Same construction as Dialog's. A panel is tall and narrow by nature, so the title is the first thing to scroll away and the close control goes with it — leaving the reader inside a region with no name in view and no way out of it.

decisions.decision: Gate 2 is where `edge` appeared
decisions.why: The token mapping called for a border on "the edge it sits against" and the API approved at gate 1 gave the component no way to know which edge that was. A caller could have set it through `className`, but a border is styling rather than placement and that prop's contract says so. Recording it because the gated order is the reason this was caught on paper instead of in CSS: writing the recipe state by state is what asks the question.

base.summary: A bordered surface inside the layout. No elevation and no scrim: it is not floating above anything, and a shadow would claim it is.

tokens.border-radius: radius.none — it is flush against the content on one side and the viewport on the other three, and a radius on a flush edge shows as a gap rather than a corner
tokens.border on the edge it meets the content: theme.border.default at border.default, on the inline-start edge for edge="inline-end" and the inline-end edge for edge="inline-start"

head.summary: The title and the close control, which stay put while the body scrolls.

dismiss.summary: The close control. Same construction as Dialog's and Notice's, so a close button is the same control everywhere.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the panel's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset

example:
setClosed(true)} closeLabel={`Close ${typeof title === "string" ? title : "panel"}`} >

Raw hue ramps, 50 → 950, generated from the theme’s seed. The body scrolls on its own so this heading and the close control stay in view.

name: pin-input
title: Pin Input
description: A fixed-length code entered into one input drawn as boxes — one-time codes and PINs.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: What the code is. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: Where the code came from, when that is the useful part: "Code from your authenticator app".
dont: Leaving it off because the boxes look self-explanatory. A screen reader hears one text field and nothing else.
props.a11y: Bound to the single input by Field, so it is the accessible name. The boxes are `aria-hidden` and add nothing to it.

props.name: length
props.summary: How many characters the code has. Draws that many boxes and caps the input.
use: The exact length the server sends — usually 6 for a one-time code, 4 to 8 for a PIN.
dont: A variable-length code. The boxes promise a length; if it varies, use a `TextField` with `autoComplete="one-time-code"`.
props.a11y: Becomes the input's `maxLength`, and is stated in the description chain as "6 characters" so a reader who cannot see the boxes knows how many to type.

props.name: value
props.summary: Controls the code from outside.
use: Clearing the field after a failed attempt.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the state.

props.name: defaultValue
props.summary: The starting text when the component owns the state.
use: Almost never. A pre-filled one-time code is a code someone else already read.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Fires with the whole code on every change.
use: Tracking a partial code, to enable a submit button only when it is complete.

props.name: onComplete
props.summary: Fires once when the code reaches `length` characters.
use: Starting verification — the commonest reason for this component's existence is to save the reader a tap.
dont: Navigating away inside it before the server answers. A mistyped code then becomes a page change the reader cannot undo; verify, and keep them on the field until it passes.

props.name: characters
props.summary: Which characters are accepted, and which on-screen keyboard appears.
use: `alphanumeric` for codes like recovery keys that mix letters and digits.
dont: Assuming lowercase. Alphanumeric codes are uppercased as typed, since case-sensitive one-time codes are a usability bug on the issuing side.
props.a11y: Characters outside the set are dropped rather than rejected with an error, and a paste is filtered the same way — so a pasted "123-456" becomes "123456".

props.name: purpose
props.summary: Whether this is a code the reader was sent or a secret they know.
use: `one-time-code` for SMS and email codes — the browser and the OS offer to fill it from the message.
`pin` for a secret the reader remembers, which masks every box and turns autofill off.
dont: `one-time-code` for a PIN. It would show the secret on screen and invite the OS to suggest a code from the last SMS.
props.a11y: `pin` renders the input as `type="password"`, so a screen reader says "bullet" rather than reading the digits aloud.

props.name: name
props.summary: Form field name. Submits the code as one string.
use: A native form post.

props.name: size
props.summary: Box size. There is no `sm`: a code box smaller than a control is a target smaller than a fingertip.
use: `md` inside a dense dialog where six large boxes do not fit.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: the label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.summary: Stable id for the code input, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the field it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message, popup — is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged.

props.name: description
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: A constraint the reader needs before they answer.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.summary: The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative.
dont: Putting the permanent constraint here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.summary: Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Fields that genuinely block submission.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks typing while keeping the input focusable, readable and announced.
use: While a verification request is in flight, alongside `status="validating"`.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits — the text field's consequence, unchanged.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly` from Field.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — placement, not a restyle.
use: Centring the boxes in a verification screen.

usage.case: A code sent by SMS or email
usage.when: Verifying a phone number or a sign-in.
usage.example:
<PinInput
  label="Verification code"
  description="We sent it to the number ending 0142."
  length={6}
  onComplete={verify}
/>
usage.notes: `purpose` defaults to `one-time-code`, which is what lets iOS, Android and the browser offer to fill it from the message — one tap instead of six.

usage.when: The server rejected the code the reader entered.
usage.example:
<PinInput
  label="Verification code"
  length={6}
  value={code}
  onValueChange={setCode}
  status="invalid"
  message="That code did not match. Check the latest message and try again."
/>
usage.notes: Clear `code` when setting the error, and keep focus on the field. The ring is on every box, because the code is wrong as a whole.

usage.when: Confirming a payment or unlocking a vault with a memorised secret.
usage.example: <PinInput label="PIN" length={4} purpose="pin" />
usage.notes: `pin` masks, uses a password input and turns autofill off. The visible-and-fillable defaults are right for a code someone was sent and wrong for a secret.

usage.when: A recovery key of 24 characters in groups.
usage.example: <PinInput label="Recovery key" length={24} characters="alphanumeric" />
usage.notes: Don't. Twenty-four boxes do not fit a phone and nobody types a key that long one box at a time. It is a `TextField` the reader pastes into.

behavior.summary: A single labelled text input, capped at `length`, rendered as a row of boxes it lies over. Composed with Field for the label, helper text and validation. Autofill, paste and Backspace are the platform's, because there is only one input.

decisions.decision: One input, with the boxes drawn — never one input per box
decisions.why: Six inputs is how most code fields are built and it breaks four things at once: SMS and email autofill (`autocomplete="one-time-code"`) fills one input, not six; paste lands in the first box only unless every box intercepts it; a screen reader announces six unlabelled edit fields; and Backspace across boxes has to be reimplemented and is usually wrong at the boundaries. One input gets all four from the platform. The boxes are an `aria-hidden` rendering of its value, with the caret position drawn as the active box.

decisions.decision: No APG pattern applies, so it is a text input and says so
decisions.why: There is no WAI-ARIA pattern for a segmented code, and inventing a composite role would announce something no reader has learned. It is a labelled `textbox` with `maxLength`, `inputmode` and `autocomplete` — which is what it is.

decisions.decision: `purpose` rather than a `mask` boolean
decisions.why: Masking is a consequence of what the code is, and so are autofill and the input type. A one-time code is something the reader is copying from elsewhere: it should be visible and fillable. A PIN is a secret: it should be masked and never suggested. A `mask` boolean would let someone build a visible PIN or a masked one-time code, and both are wrong.

decisions.decision: `onComplete` does not submit the form
decisions.why: Auto-advancing when the last character lands is the reason the component exists, so the hook is there.
