Submitting a form on the reader's behalf is a different act: it fires on a paste that was the wrong code, and it is unrecoverable if the next screen is a navigation. The caller starts verification; the reader stays on the field until it passes, and a failure clears the value and keeps focus.

decisions.decision: Length is stated, not only drawn
decisions.why: The boxes tell a sighted reader how long the code is. A screen-reader user hears none of them, so the count joins the description chain from the primitive — "6 characters" — ahead of any helper text.

decisions.decision: Disabled is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: The system rule, and the text field's consequence with it: the value still submits.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getPinInputProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet. The proposal filters input to the character set, uppercases alphanumeric codes, caps at `length`, reports completion once per fill, and derives each drawn box's state — filled, active, empty — from the value and the selection, so the boxes cannot disagree with the input.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: one `<input>` with `inputmode="numeric"` (or `text` for alphanumeric), `autocomplete="one-time-code"` or `off`, `type="password"` for `pin`, `maxLength`, inside a Field; the boxes are `aria-hidden` and the input lies over them, transparent, so taps anywhere land in it. React Native: one `TextInput` with `keyboardType="number-pad"`, `textContentType="oneTimeCode"` on iOS and `autoComplete="sms-otp"` on Android — the two platforms' SMS autofill hooks — and `secureTextEntry` for `pin`; the boxes are `View`s with `accessibilityElementsHidden` and `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"`, so only the input is announced. `name` is web-only. Rata-drawn around the OS text input (decision N5): the single `TextInput` is the platform's, so SMS autofill, paste and deletion are too; the boxes are drawn from the recipe. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A row of boxes, each the text field's box in miniature. Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming.

tokens.box inline-size: size.control.md at md, size.control.lg at lg — a control step used as a width, the way Dialog measures itself in controls
tokens.box block-size: size.control.lg at md, calc(size.control.lg plus space.2) at lg
tokens.character font-family: font.family.mono — every character the same width, so a 1 and an 8 sit centred alike
tokens.masked character: a dot of space.2 in theme.fg.primary with radius.pill — a spacing step for a mark rather than a glyph, the reasoning Switch's thumb follows
tokens.active box: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset, on the box at the caret while the input is focused — the text field's focus departure, so this reads as a text box
tokens.caret: border.2 in theme.fg.primary, centred in the active empty box, blinking at motion.duration.slow and steady under prefers-reduced-motion
tokens.invalid ring: theme.danger-role.ring on every box — the code is wrong as a whole, not one digit of it

name: popover
title: Popover
description: A non-modal, titled surface anchored to a trigger, holding a small piece of interactive content the reader opened on purpose.

props.name: trigger
props.summary: The control that opens and closes the popover.
use: A `Button` — including an icon-only help button, which is how a toggletip is built.
dont: A non-interactive element. The trigger must be a real button, or the popover is unreachable by keyboard.
Putting your own `onClick` on it and expecting to be called. The popover owns that handler; use `onOpenChange`.
props.a11y: Receives `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Its own text or `aria-label` names the trigger; `title` names the popover.

props.name: title
props.description: The popover's name, shown at its top. A styled label, not a heading.
props.summary: The popover's name, shown at its top.
use: A noun phrase naming what is inside: "Date range", "Share link".
dont: Repeating the trigger's label word for word when that label is a verb ("Share"). Name the thing, not the action.
props.a11y: Names the `role="dialog"` through `aria-labelledby`. Rendered as a styled paragraph, never a heading — the page's outline is still live behind a non-modal popover.

props.name: children
props.description: The content: short text, a link, a few fields.
props.summary: The content: short text, a link, a few fields.
use: A filter with two or three controls, a help text with a "Learn more" link, a copyable link.
dont: A list of actions. That is a Menu, with arrow-key navigation this component does not have.
A long form or a decision that blocks the task. That is a Dialog — modal, with a footer.
props.a11y: Reached by Tab in document order from wherever focus lands on open. Not trapped.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the popover is showing. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the popover is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Opening it from somewhere other than the trigger, or closing it after a submit inside it.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultOpen`. One of them owns the state.
props.a11y: `aria-expanded` on the trigger follows it.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled popover. Conflicts with `open`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled popover.
use: Almost never. A popover open before the reader asked covers what they came to see.
dont: Using it to show a message on load. That is a Notice.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.description: Called whenever it asks to open or close — trigger, Escape, light-dismiss or Tab out.
props.summary: Called whenever the popover asks to open or close — trigger, Escape, light-dismiss or Tab out.
use: Keeping `open` in step, or saving a filter's draft when it closes.
dont: Refusing to close it. A non-modal surface that will not dismiss is a modal without the semantics.

props.name: placement
props.description: Which side of the trigger it prefers. Anchor positioning flips it near an edge.
props.summary: Which side of the trigger the popover prefers.
use: `block-start` for a trigger near the bottom of the viewport.
dont: Using it to keep the popover on screen. Anchor positioning flips it near an edge already.
props.a11y: Visual only, and logical rather than physical. Web only: on React Native the popover is a sheet from the block-end edge.

props.name: initialFocus
props.description: Focused on open, when the first focusable element is the wrong place to start.
props.summary: The element to focus on open, when the first focusable one is the wrong place to start.
use: The input in a popover whose first focusable element is a link in its help text.
dont: Pointing it outside the popover. Focus would leave, and leaving closes it.
props.a11y: A ref rather than `autoFocus`, for the reason Dialog's contract gives: React's `autoFocus` runs on mount, before the popover is shown and focusable.

usage.case: A toggletip: help that has to work on touch
usage.when: A short explanation beside a field, with a link to more — which a Tooltip cannot hold and would not show on a phone.
usage.example:
<Popover
  title="Billing email"
  trigger={
    <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="About billing email">
      <Icon icon={CircleHelp} />
    </Button>
  }
>
  <Text>Invoices and receipts go here, not to your login email.</Text>
  <Link href="/docs/billing">Learn more</Link>
</Popover>
usage.notes: Opened by a tap, a click, Enter or Space alike. The link is reachable because focus moves into the popover on open. The trigger's `aria-label` names the button; `title` names the popover.

usage.when: Two or three controls that refine a list beside them, applied when the popover closes.
usage.example:
<Popover
  title="Status"
  trigger={<Button variant="secondary">Status</Button>}
  open={filtering}
  onOpenChange={setFiltering}
  initialFocus={firstOptionRef}
>
  <RadioGroup label="Status" value={status} onValueChange={setStatus}>
    <Radio ref={firstOptionRef} value="open" label="Open" />
    <Radio value="closed" label="Closed" />
  </RadioGroup>
</Popover>
usage.notes: Not a Dialog: the list beside it stays live and visible, which is the point of filtering. Not a Menu: these are fields, not actions.

usage.when: Rename, Duplicate and Delete for a row.
usage.example:
<Popover title="Actions" trigger={<Button variant="tertiary">More</Button>}>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Rename</Button>
  <Button variant="tertiary">Duplicate</Button>
</Popover>
usage.notes: Don't. A list of actions is a Menu — arrow keys, typeahead, focus returned after a choice, `role="menu"`. A popover of buttons is a menu with none of that.

behavior.summary: A non-modal `role="dialog"` carrying `popover="auto"`, positioned against its trigger with CSS anchor positioning — the same top-layer and anchoring machinery as Menu, including the per-instance anchor name. It moves focus in when opened, does not trap it, and returns it to the trigger on Escape. Proposed primitive: `getPopoverProps` in `packages/primitives/src/popover.ts`, sharing Menu's open/close reporting; it is a proposal, not yet a commitment.

decisions.decision: Popover, Menu, Dialog and Tooltip are four components because they are four contracts
decisions.why: A Menu is a list of actions with arrow-key navigation and `role="menu"` — putting a text field in one breaks both. A Dialog is modal: the page goes inert and focus is trapped, which is right for a decision that blocks the task and wrong for a filter you glance at. A Tooltip is never focusable and holds nothing interactive. A Popover is the remaining case: a small, non-modal surface the reader opens on purpose, which may contain anything a short form can — a date range, a colour picker, a share link with a copy button, a help text with a "Learn more" link. Each of these differs in focus behaviour, keyboard contract and ARIA role; one component with modes would be four components wearing one name.

decisions.decision: Focus moves in on open, is not trapped, and returns to the trigger on Escape
decisions.why: The reader opened it to use it, so focus goes to the first focusable element, or to `initialFocus` when the first one is the wrong place to start. It is not trapped because the popover is not modal — the page behind it is still live, and Tab past the last control leaves the popover and closes it, the same way Tab leaves a Menu. Escape returns focus to the trigger, because that is where the reader was. Light-dismiss by clicking elsewhere is the exception, as in Menu: the reader chose a new place, and taking focus back would undo it.

decisions.decision: `title` is required, and is a styled label rather than a heading
decisions.why: A `role="dialog"` must be named, and a visible title naming it through `aria-labelledby` is the name sighted readers get too. It is not a heading element because a popover is not modal: the page's outline is still live behind it, and the popover cannot know what level it sits under — the reason Notice gives. Dialog can use `<h2>` only because everything behind a modal is inert.

decisions.decision: It is the touch answer for anything a Tooltip cannot do
decisions.why: A tooltip does not appear on touch, by design. A popover opens on a tap, a click, Enter or Space — the same activation on every input — so supplementary help that must be reachable on a phone, sometimes called a toggletip, is a Popover with a help-icon trigger.

decisions.decision: No close button by default, and no scrim
decisions.why: Escape, clicking elsewhere and tabbing out all close it, and the trigger toggles it — four ways out, all expected for a non-modal overlay. A close button is content the caller can add when the popover holds a form with an explicit Done. A scrim would claim the page is inert, which `theme.scrim`'s contract reserves for modals.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `role="dialog"` element, not `aria-modal`, with the `popover="auto"` attribute and `aria-labelledby` pointing at its title; the trigger receives `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` (deliberately not `aria-haspopup="dialog"`, which screen readers announce inconsistently). React Native has no anchored overlay and no top layer, and a small anchored surface is the wrong shape for a phone anyway. On native it renders through the core `Modal` as a sheet from the block-end edge, with `accessibilityViewIsModal` on iOS and the title as `accessibilityRole="header"` — modal on native because the platform offers no non-modal floating surface that screen readers handle. `placement` is web-only. Rata-drawn content inside the OS's own modal presentation (decision N5): the core `Modal` supplies the presentation and its screen-reader behaviour, and Rata draws the sheet; no platform popover or action sheet is used. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: Gate 2: every state's token mapping is approved
decisions.why: Approved state by state — P1 surface (Menu's), P2 title, P3 size and position in the top layer, P4 enter motion, P5 instant close, P6 focus. The exit transition the gate-1 recipe described is dropped: an exit transition on a top-layer element has to hold display with allow-discrete while non-animatable properties revert at once, which is the bug Dialog already shipped and fixed, and Menu closes instantly for the same reason (gate 2, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

base.summary: The popover surface — the same surface as Menu (P1, P3–P5).

tokens.max-inline-size: text bounded by size.measure.compact; never wider than the viewport less space.padding.lg (P3)
tokens.gap from the trigger: space.gap.xs, anchor-positioned with flip-block / flip-inline fallbacks (P3)
tokens.stacking: the browser's top layer via the Popover API — no z-index (P3)
tokens.enter: motion.overlay.duration with motion.easing.enter: fade in and rise by space.1, only under prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference (P4)
tokens.exit: none — closes instantly, as Menu does (P5)

title.summary: The required title, a styled label rather than a heading (P2).

focus.summary: Where the focus ring is drawn (P6).

tokens.popover: no ring of its own — focus moves to the first focusable control inside, or initialFocus (P6)
tokens.controls inside: each draws its own theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible (P6)
tokens.trigger: keeps its own ring and carries aria-expanded (P6)

example:
<Popover
        title="Billing email"
        trigger={
          <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="About billing email">
            <Icon icon={Info} />
          </Button>
        }
      >
        <Text>Invoices and receipts go here, not to your login email.</Text>
        <Link href="#billing">Learn more</Link>
      </Popover>

name: progress
title: Progress
description: A labelled bar showing how much of a task with a known end is done.

props.name: label
props.description: What is in progress, shown above the bar.
props.summary: What is in progress, shown above the bar.
use: A noun phrase naming the task: "Uploading tokens.json", "Import".
dont: "Loading…" on its own. Say what is loading.
props.a11y: The bar's accessible name, wired with `aria-labelledby`.

props.name: value
props.description: How much is done, from 0 to `max`.
props.summary: How much is done, from 0 to `max`.
use: The real count of done units — bytes, files, steps.
dont: A value that is not real. A bar that eases toward 90% to look busy is a spinner pretending to know something; use Spinner.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-valuenow`. Clamped to the range, so an overshoot does not announce 104 percent.

props.name: max
props.description: The value that means done.
props.summary: The value that means done.
use: The total of whatever `value` counts — `max={7}` for seven files.
dont: Converting to a percentage yourself. Pass the real total and let `valueText` say it in the reader's units.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-valuemax`.

props.name: valueText
props.description: The value in the reader's own units, shown beside the label and announced instead of a percentage.
props.summary: The value in the reader's own units, shown beside the label and announced instead of a percentage.
use: "3 of 7 files", "12 MB of 40 MB".
dont: Repeating the label. This is the amount, not the task.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-valuetext`. Without it, screen readers announce a percentage computed from `value` and `max`.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for placement and width.
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement and width.
use: Setting the bar's width in the page's layout.
dont: Recolouring the fill. Status colours on a progress bar read as a verdict on the task; report the outcome in a message instead.

usage.when: A task with a countable end, which the reader is waiting on.
usage.example: <Progress label="Uploading assets" value={done} max={files.length} valueText={`${done} of ${files.length} files`} />
usage.notes: `max` is the real total and `valueText` says it in files rather than percent. Completion is announced by the caller — a Toast saying "7 files uploaded" — because the bar itself is not a live region.

usage.when: A request whose duration nobody knows.
usage.example: <Progress label="Loading" value={fakeProgress} />
usage.notes: Don't. A value that is not real is a spinner pretending to know something — use `<Spinner label="Loading invoices" />`. Equally, storage used out of a quota is a meter, not progress.

behavior.summary: A `role="progressbar"` element with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax` and `aria-valuetext`, named by its visible label. Determinate only. No primitive: it holds no state and takes no input.

decisions.decision: Determinate only; an unknown end is Spinner's job
decisions.why: An indeterminate bar and a spinner answer the same question — "something is happening, I don't know how long" — and two components for one answer means callers pick between them by taste. Progress exists for the other question: how far along is it. Keeping `value` required makes the bar mean something every time it is on screen; a bar that sometimes shows progress and sometimes only motion teaches readers to ignore it.

decisions.decision: Progress is not a meter
decisions.why: Disk usage, a password's strength, a quota: those are measurements on a scale, not a task heading toward done, and ARIA gives them a different role (`meter`) for that reason. A progress bar reading "80% of storage" tells a screen reader that something is 80% finished. A meter is a separate component, and not part of this gate.

decisions.decision: A `div` with `role="progressbar"`, not the native `<progress>` element
decisions.why: `<progress>` is styled through vendor pseudo-elements that differ between engines and cannot carry a transition on the fill, and it has no `aria-valuetext` equivalent of its own. The ARIA role is fully supported, and it lets `valueText` say "3 of 7 files" instead of "43 percent".

decisions.decision: The label is required and visible
decisions.why: A bar with no label is a decoration: the reader sees motion and cannot tell what is moving. The visible label is also the accessible name, through `aria-labelledby`, so sighted and screen-reader users are told the same thing.

decisions.decision: It does not announce every change
decisions.why: A progress bar updating every 200ms as a live region would read a number every time the screen reader paused. The role is enough for a reader who navigates to it to hear the current value. What does need announcing is completion — and that is the caller's message, usually a Toast or a Notice, because only the caller knows what "done" means.

decisions.decision: The track is `theme.bg.muted`, not Slider's `theme.border.strong`
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C8, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). Slider and Progress look alike and are split by role. A slider's empty track is part of a control — it shows how far the value can still go — so it takes the boundary tone tuned to the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control. A progress bar takes no input, and its empty track carries no information on its own: what the reader needs is the fill against it, which the pairing decision below covers. So the track is the recessed well `theme.bg.muted` is documented for, and a progress bar beside a slider does not read as something to drag.

decisions.decision: Track thickness: size.track
decisions.why: The bar is size.track, 4px, the same token Slider's track uses — one thickness for every linear value bar, so a progress bar and a slider side by side read as the same family. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: The fill on its track is a verified pairing
decisions.why: theme.accent-role.bg on theme.bg.muted is now a documented AA-nontext pairing in system.json, measured at 4.89:1 (light) and 7.75:1 (dark) against the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a graphical object, and re-verified against every brand theme by themes:check. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `div` with `role="progressbar"`, `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin="0"`, `aria-valuemax`, `aria-valuetext` when `valueText` is passed, and `aria-labelledby` pointing at the visible label. In forced-colors mode the fill takes the system `Highlight` colour so it stays visible. React Native: a `View` with `accessibilityRole="progressbar"` and `accessibilityValue={{ min: 0, max, now: value, text: valueText }}`, labelled by `accessibilityLabel`. All props work on both; the fill transition is skipped on native when the OS reduce-motion setting is on. Rata-drawn, not the OS progress control (decision N5): React Native core no longer ships one on either platform, and a drawn `View` takes the same tokens as the web bar. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A label above a track, with the filled part in the accent fill. The track is the recessed well `theme.bg.muted` is documented for, because a progress bar reports status and is not a control.

tokens.track background: theme.bg.muted — status, not interactive, so not Slider's theme.border.strong; see the track decision
tokens.fill background: theme.accent-role.bg — a verified AA-nontext pairing on theme.bg.muted (4.89:1 light, 7.75:1 dark)
tokens.fill transition: motion.duration.medium with motion.easing.standard, on inline-size; none under prefers-reduced-motion

example:
<Progress
        label="Uploading assets"
        value={3}
        max={7}
        valueText="3 of 7 files"
        className="pg-wide-specimen"
      />

name: radio
title: Radio
description: One option inside a radio group. Not usable on its own.

props.name: value
props.description: This option's value. What the group reports when it is chosen.
props.summary: This option's value. What the group reports when it is chosen.
dont: Reusing a value across two radios in one group — the group would consider both chosen.

props.name: label
props.description: The option's label.
props.summary: The option's label.
props.a11y: A real `<label for>`, so the text is part of the hit target.

props.name: description
props.description: Helper text under the label.
props.summary: Helper text under the label, for an option whose consequence is not obvious.
dont: Restating the label in more words.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks this one option while leaving it focusable and readable.
props.summary: Blocks this one option while leaving it focusable and readable.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled`. Arrow keys still land on it; it just does not become the answer.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the option's wrapper.
use: Placing the component in its surrounding layout — a span, a width, a margin the parent cannot express.
dont: Setting a width to align options — that is the group's layout decision, not the item's.
Restyling the component's internals through descendant selectors. Those are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer somewhere the contract cannot see.

usage.when: The only correct use — and the reason any example of a Radio necessarily shows a group.
usage.example:
<RadioGroup label="Support plan" value={plan} onValueChange={setPlan}>
  <Radio value="standard" label="Standard" />
  <Radio value="priority" label="Priority" description="One business day response" />
  <Radio value="dedicated" label="Dedicated" disabled />
</RadioGroup>
usage.notes: Everything that makes this a radio comes from the group: the shared name, the exclusivity, and the arrow-key reachability. That is why no example can show a Radio truly on its own — rendered outside a group it throws rather than degrading. Keep the group to one option when the subject is the option itself, and name it with `labelledBy` pointing at an off-screen element: `label` would render a heading above a single row, and leaving it unnamed is the mistake that prop's contract warns about.

behavior.summary: An option rendered by its group, with no primitive of its own. It holds no state: getRadioGroupProps decides whether this one is checked, whether it is the tab stop, and what happens when it is activated. That is the point — a radio that owned any of those could disagree with its siblings.

decisions.decision: A Radio outside a RadioGroup is a mistake, not a fallback
decisions.why: Alone it has no name to share, no siblings to be exclusive with, and no way to be reached by arrow keys — everything that makes it a radio lives in the group. Rendering one standalone would produce a control that looks right and behaves like nothing.

decisions.decision: `value` is required and is the item's whole identity
decisions.why: It is what the group compares against, what arrow keys walk, and what a form submits. Without it the group has no way to refer to this option.

base.summary: One option in a radio group. Circular, so its shape says 'one of these' before the label is read.

tokens.box size: size.icon.md — the box is sized to the glyph it holds, so it takes the icon scale rather than the control one; the control heights are row heights and would dwarf the box itself
tokens.row height: no reserved row height. An earlier version set it to size.control.md for a bigger hit target, but with the box aligned to the first line that reserved 12px of dead space under every row and inflated the list's pitch to 40px. At the resulting 28px pitch the target conforms through WCAG 2.5.8's spacing exception: 24px circles centred on adjacent targets do not intersect. The label is bound, so the target is the full width of the text as well
tokens.control height: one line tall, from calc(type.control.size.md x type.control.line-height.md) = 20px. The line-height token is a unitless ratio, so it is not a length on its own — used alone the browser drops the declaration
tokens.border: border.default solid theme.border.strong — the same boundary tone text-field uses, tone-walked to the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's edge
tokens.gap between box and label: space.gap.sm — the inline role, because this pairing is horizontal
tokens.gap between label and description: none — the label and the description each carry line-height leading, which already reads as 7px of separation. A gap on top of that made 11px and read as two unrelated lines
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — never a hand-written hover rule
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — the offset is kept here, unlike text-field: a 20px box has no room for a flush ring to read as separate from its own border
tokens.border-radius: radius.pill — a circle, which is the one thing that tells a radio from a checkbox before either is read
tokens.checked mark: theme.fg.on-accent as a centred dot; a radio is filled, not ticked

name: radio-group
title: Radio Group
description: A set of radios holding one answer, with the group owning the name, the value and the focus model.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the group — the question these radios answer.
props.summary: Accessible name for the group — the question these radios answer.
use: Always, unless `labelledBy` points at a visible heading that already asks it.
dont: Leaving both this and `labelledBy` unset; an unnamed radiogroup announces its options with no idea what they are options for.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-label` on the group.

props.name: labelledBy
props.description: Id of a visible element that already names this group.
props.summary: Id of a visible element that already names this group.

props.name: value
props.description: The chosen value, or null for nothing chosen yet.
props.summary: The chosen value, or null for nothing chosen yet.
dont: Passing it without `onValueChange` — the group would render a choice and refuse to change it.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Starting choice for an uncontrolled group. Conflicts with `value`.
props.summary: Starting choice for an uncontrolled group.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the value the group should move to.
props.summary: Called with the value the group should move to.
dont: Assuming it only fires on click; arrow keys select as they move, which is the pattern working correctly.

props.name: name
props.description: Shared form field name. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Form field name shared by every radio. Defaults to a generated one.
use: A real form post, where the name is the key the server reads.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Which way the options stack, and which arrows move between them.
use: `vertical` for a list of options, which is the default and the readable shape for anything with more than two.
props.a11y: Announced as `aria-orientation`. Both axes' arrow keys still move, so a user who reaches for Down in a horizontal group does not hit a dead end.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks the whole question while keeping every option focusable.
props.summary: Blocks the whole question while keeping every option focusable and readable.
dont: Disabling one option; that belongs on the radio itself.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` on each option, never the native `disabled` attribute.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the group as requiring an answer.
props.summary: Marks the group as requiring an answer.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-required` on the group.

usage.when: The default: a short list of mutually exclusive options.
usage.example:
<RadioGroup label="Billing period" value={period} onValueChange={setPeriod}>
  <Radio value="monthly" label="Monthly" />
  <Radio value="annual" label="Annual" description="Two months free" />
</RadioGroup>
usage.notes: One tab stop for the whole group; arrows move between options and select as they go. That is the radio pattern, and it is why a radio group is not just several checkboxes.

usage.case: An option that cannot be chosen yet
usage.when: One option unavailable while the rest remain answerable.
usage.example:
<RadioGroup label="Shipping" value={ship} onValueChange={setShip}>
  <Radio value="standard" label="Standard" />
  <Radio value="overnight" label="Overnight" disabled description="Not available to this address" />
</RadioGroup>
usage.notes: The disabled option still takes focus, so a keyboard user discovers it exists and reads why. Arrow keys land on it without selecting it.

usage.when: The options are a filter that should be clearable, or a view switch.
usage.example:
<RadioGroup label="Status" value={status} onValueChange={setStatus}>
  <Radio value="open" label="Open" />
</RadioGroup>
usage.notes: Don't. A radio group cannot go back to nothing once answered — that is the platform's behaviour and users rely on it. A clearable set of options is toggle-button-group with `deselectable`; a view switch is a tab list, which this system does not have yet.

behavior.summary: The radiogroup pattern: one tab stop, arrow keys that move and select, and a single value owned here rather than by any item. Native inputs carry the semantics; this decides which one is checked and which one is the tab stop.

decisions.decision: The group owns the value, not the items
decisions.why: A radio's whole meaning is 'one of these'. Leaving the value on the item would let two claim to be checked, which is a state the control is supposed to make impossible.

decisions.decision: Native input[type=radio] sharing one `name`
decisions.why: Grouping, arrow-key behaviour and form submission all come from the platform when the name is shared. Re-implementing them on divs is how a radio group ends up not announcing how many options it has.

decisions.decision: Roving tabindex is derived from the value
decisions.why: The checked radio is the tab stop; a group with nothing chosen is entered at its first enabled option. Deriving it means focus and value cannot disagree, because there is no second piece of state.

decisions.decision: Arrow keys select as they move, and a disabled option only takes focus
decisions.why: Selecting on arrow is the radio pattern. This system's disabled controls stay focusable and announced, so a disabled radio must still be reachable — it just must not become the answer.

decisions.decision: No deselect
decisions.why: Unlike toggle-button-group, a radio group has no way back to nothing once answered. That is the platform's behaviour and users rely on it; a clearable set of options is a different control, and this system has toggle-button-group for it.

vertical.summary: The default: a readable column of options.

horizontal.summary: A row, for two or three short options that fit on one line.

tokens.gap between options: space.gap.lg — wider than the vertical step, so two options on one line do not read as one phrase

example:
<RadioGroup label="Shipping" defaultValue="standard">
        <Radio value="standard" label="Standard" />
        <Radio
          value="overnight"
          label="Overnight"
          disabled
          description="Not available to this address"
        />
      </RadioGroup>

name: search
title: Search
description: A search field with a clear control, an in-flight state, and an optional landmark.

props.name: label
props.description: The field's accessible name. Required.
props.summary: The field's accessible name. Required.
use: Always. "Search" is fine when there is one; name what is being searched when there are several: "Search invoices".
dont: Relying on the placeholder instead. A placeholder is not a name — it disappears the moment someone types, and some screen readers never read it at all.
The word "search" twice, once here and once in the placeholder. It is one control.
props.a11y: Bound with `for`/`id` like any label. Hidden by default — see `labelHidden` — but always present, because `role="searchbox"` with no name is a 4.1.2 failure.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Whether the label is off screen. Defaults to true, unlike every other field here.
props.summary: Whether the label is off screen. Defaults to true, unlike every other field here.
use: The default. A magnifier and a placeholder are a search field's conventional shorthand, and a visible "Search" label above a search box reads as a mistake.
`false` in a form of labelled fields, where one unlabelled box would be the odd one out.
dont: Assuming hidden means absent. The label element is rendered and bound either way; this only clips it.
props.a11y: Clipped with the `visually-hidden` utility, not `display: none`, so the accessible name is unchanged.

props.name: value
props.description: The query. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: The query. Makes the component controlled.
use: Reading the query from your own state — a URL parameter, or a filter shared with the rest of the page.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the value.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Starting query for an uncontrolled field. Conflicts with `value`.
props.summary: Starting query for an uncontrolled field.
use: A search box that restores the last query without the page owning it.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called on every keystroke, and when the field is cleared.
props.summary: Called on every keystroke, and when the field is cleared.
use: Filtering as you type, over data already on the client.
dont: Firing a network request from it directly. Debounce, or use `onSearch` — a request per keystroke is how a search box becomes the slowest thing on the page.

props.name: onSearch
props.description: Called when the reader commits the query, by pressing Enter.
props.summary: Called when the reader commits the query, by pressing Enter.
use: A search that costs something: a request, or a navigation.
dont: Relying on it inside a `<form>` you also submit. Enter does both, and the work happens twice.
props.a11y: There is no submit button by design: `role="searchbox"` and Enter are the expected interaction, and a button beside the field is the caller's to add if the flow needs one.

props.name: loading
props.description: A query is in flight. The leading glyph becomes a spinner.
props.summary: A query is in flight. The leading glyph becomes a spinner.
use: An `onSearch` that went to the network and has not come back.
dont: Leaving it on while typing. It is for a committed query, and a spinner that flickers on every keystroke reads as breakage.
props.a11y: Sets `aria-busy` on the field. It does NOT announce the result — that is a live region of yours reporting how many things were found, because the count is the thing the reader needs and this component cannot know it.

props.name: landmark
props.description: Wraps the field in a search landmark.
props.summary: Wraps the field in a search landmark.
use: THE search for the site or the app — the one someone navigating by landmark expects to find.
dont: A filter over a list on one page. That is not the site's search, and a second search landmark makes the real one ambiguous.
More than one per page.
props.a11y: Renders `role="search"`. Deliberately unnamed: a single landmark of a kind needs no name, and the guidance for the case that would need one is to not make it a landmark at all.

props.name: placeholder
props.summary: Hint text inside the empty field.
use: Naming the scope when the label is hidden: "Search 1,240 invoices".
dont: Using it as the label. It vanishes on the first keystroke, leaving the field unnamed on screen.

props.name: size
props.summary: Which control height it matches.
use: `md` by default; `sm` in a dense toolbar; `lg` for a page's primary search.
dont: Expecting the text to grow with it. Size changes the box, not the type — the same bargain Button and TextField make, which is what lets the three sit in one row.

props.name: clearLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the clear control.
props.summary: Accessible name for the clear control.
use: Translating it, or naming what is being cleared when a page has more than one field.
dont: An empty string. The control is icon-only, so this is the only name it has.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks the field while keeping it focusable and readable.
props.summary: Blocks the field while keeping it focusable and readable.
use: A search that cannot run yet — the index is still building.
dont: Disabling it to mean "empty". An empty search box is a usable one.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` with `readOnly`, never the native attribute, so the field stays focusable and announced — the same contract `text-field` follows.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
use: Pointing something else at the field — a `<label>` you render yourself, or an external `aria-controls`.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. The label binding and the clear control's naming both hang off it.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Sizing it within a layout: a search that should fill its toolbar.
dont: Changing the focus treatment. It matches TextField on purpose, and a search that focuses differently from the field beside it reads as a different kind of control.

usage.case: The site's search, in a header
usage.when: The commonest case, and the only one that should be a landmark.
usage.example:
<Search
  landmark
  label="Search"
  placeholder="Search invoices"
  onSearch={(query) => navigate(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`)}
/>
usage.notes: `label` is present and hidden, which is the default — the magnifier and the placeholder carry it on screen while the name is still there for anyone listening. `onSearch` rather than `onValueChange`, because this one navigates and should happen once.

usage.case: Filtering a list as you type
usage.when: The data is already on the client, so every keystroke can be answered for free.
usage.example:
<Search
  label="Filter rows"
  size="sm"
  value={query}
  onValueChange={setQuery}
/>
usage.notes: No `landmark`: this is a control over one list, not the site's search, and a second search landmark makes the real one ambiguous. No `onSearch` either — there is nothing to commit when the answer is already on screen.

usage.case: A committed query that went to the network
usage.when: The search costs something, so the reader needs to know it is happening.
usage.example:
<> {/* The count is what the reader needs, and Search cannot know it. */}

{pending ? "" : `${results.length} found`}
usage.notes: `loading` sets `aria-busy` and swaps the glyph for a spinner, which covers the sighted case. The live region is what covers the other one, and it belongs to the caller because only the caller knows what was found.

usage.case: Don't: a placeholder standing in for the label
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.example:
{/* Don't: the name disappears on the first keystroke. */}
<Search label="" placeholder="Search" />
usage.notes: Don't. A placeholder is not a name: it is gone as soon as someone types, several screen readers never read it, and `role="searchbox"` with no name is a 4.1.2 failure. `label` is required precisely so this cannot be written by accident — the empty string above is the only way to get close, and it is still wrong.

behavior.summary: A native `input[type="search"]`, which the platform maps to `role="searchbox"`. Its own construction rather than a `text-field` variant: a search has no validation states, is conventionally unlabelled on screen, carries a clear control, and answers Escape — none of which a text field does, and a `type` prop on TextField would have brought all four along as dead weight.

decisions.decision: Not a variant of TextField
decisions.why: They share a look and nothing else. A text field is a value being collected — it validates, it carries helper text, it is labelled on screen. A search is a question being asked: it has no invalid state, its label is normally hidden, and its Escape and clear behaviours exist nowhere else. Sharing the CSS is the right amount of sharing.

decisions.decision: Escape clears the field only when there is something to clear
decisions.why: Clearing on Escape is the convention, and implementing it unconditionally breaks every overlay a search sits inside: the field would swallow the key and a Dialog or Menu would stop closing. Empty, the key is left alone and bubbles to whatever should handle it. This is the whole reason the behaviour is in a primitive rather than an onKeyDown at the call site.

decisions.decision: The clear control is absent rather than disabled when the field is empty
decisions.why: There is nothing to clear, so there is nothing to announce or tab to. A disabled-but-present button would be a permanent stop in the tab order of every empty search box in the product.

decisions.decision: The platform's own clear button is suppressed
decisions.why: WebKit and Blink draw `::-webkit-search-cancel-button` for `type="search"`. Left alone there would be two clear controls, one of them unstyled, unlabelled and invisible to the component's own state.

decisions.decision: Suggestions are deliberately out of scope
decisions.why: A search field that proposes completions is a combobox — `aria-expanded`, a popup listbox, `aria-activedescendant` and its own focus model. That is a different ARIA pattern, not a prop on this one, and building it in here would make the plain case carry machinery it never uses. It belongs as its own registry entry when something needs it.

base.summary: The field itself, matching text-field step for step so the two line up in a row — including its focus treatment, which is that component's documented departure from the system ring.

tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across sizes, as size changes the box not the text
tokens.hover: inset band of theme.bg.muted at border.2
tokens.focus: outline theme.fg.primary at focus.ring-width, offset space.0, border darkened to match

size.summary: Height and inline padding only, matching button and text-field step for step.

glyph.summary: The leading magnifier, and the spinner that replaces it in flight. Decorative: the label names the field.

clear.summary: The trailing clear control, present only when there is a query. Same construction as Notice's and Dialog's dismiss: currentColor on a transparent background.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

example:
<Search
            label="Search the system"
            placeholder="Search…"
            size="sm"
            value={search}
            onValueChange={setSearch}
          />

name: segmented-control
title: SegmentedControl
description: One answer out of a few, shown all at once in a single enclosed bar.

props.name: options
props.description: The options, in the order they are read.
props.summary: The answers, in the order they are read.
use: Two to about five short answers — a word each, ideally.
dont: More than five, or long labels. The bar stops being scannable and a `RadioGroup` or a select reads better.
Anything that navigates. These are answers, not destinations.
Options that can all be off at once. This control always has an answer; that is a `ToggleButtonGroup` with `deselectable`.
props.a11y: Each becomes a `radio` inside the `radiogroup`, with `aria-checked` on the chosen one. One tab stop for the group; the arrow keys move and select within it.

props.name: value
props.description: The current answer. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: The current answer. Makes the component controlled.
use: Driving it from state the rest of the page reads — a filter, a view mode.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Starting answer for an uncontrolled control. Defaults to the first option.
props.summary: Starting answer. Defaults to the first option.
use: Opening on something other than the first answer.
dont: A value that is not one of the options — nothing would be selected, which this control has no state for.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Called when the answer changes.
use: Controlled mode, to set `value`.
Refetching for the new answer.
dont: Expecting it on every click. Re-picking the current answer is not a change and reports nothing, so a refetch here does not fire twice for one answer.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element.
props.summary: Accessible name for the group.
use: Naming the question the options answer: "Billing period", not "Options".
dont: Leaving it out. A radiogroup with no name is announced as a bare group, and the options alone do not say what is being asked.
props.a11y: Becomes the group's `aria-label`. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element.

props.name: labelledBy
props.summary: Names the group from an element the reader can see.
use: Pointing at the visible question above the bar, so the name changes with it.
dont: Passing it alongside `label` and expecting both. This one wins.
props.a11y: Wins over `label`, because it points at text on screen.

props.name: size
props.summary: Which control height it matches.
use: `md` by default; `sm` in a toolbar beside other small controls.
dont: Expecting the text to grow with it — size changes the box, as everywhere else here.

props.name: fullWidth
props.description: Fills its container instead of hugging its options.
props.summary: Fills its container instead of hugging its options.
use: A narrow column, or a mobile layout where the bar should span the width.
dont: A wide page. Three short answers stretched across it read as three buttons, which is the impression the enclosed bar exists to avoid.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the group, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Spacing it from what surrounds it.
dont: Making it look like Tabs. They are different patterns, and the appearance is the only cue a sighted reader gets.

usage.case: A view mode, chosen from three
usage.when: The commonest case: a short fixed set where showing them all is the point.
usage.example:
<SegmentedControl
  label="Range"
  value={range}
  onValueChange={setRange}
  options={[
    { value: "week", label: "Week" },
    { value: "month", label: "Month" },
    { value: "quarter", label: "Quarter" },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: `label` names the question, not the control — "Range", so a screen reader says "Range, Month, selected" rather than leaving the options unexplained. There is no cleared state to handle, which is the reason this exists rather than a `ToggleButtonGroup`.

usage.when: A sidebar or a phone layout, where hugging the options leaves the bar adrift.
usage.example:
<SegmentedControl
  label="Sort"
  fullWidth
  size="sm"
  options={[
    { value: "newest", label: "Newest" },
    { value: "oldest", label: "Oldest" },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: `fullWidth` is for narrow containers specifically. Across a wide page the same bar reads as two stretched buttons, which is the impression the enclosed shape exists to avoid.

usage.case: Don't: using it to switch which content is shown
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. Swapping content below it is what `Tabs` is: each tab names its panel and each panel names its tab, so a screen reader can move between them as regions. Written this way the relationship is invisible — a radiogroup says a form is being filled in, and the content that changed says nothing about why. `Tabs` with `variant="segmented"` looks identical and is announced correctly.

behavior.summary: A `radiogroup` of `radio` options with one tab stop and arrow keys that select as they move. The radio pattern, because a segmented control is a question being answered and its value is submitted with the rest of a form.

decisions.decision: Which of three — and this is the question to settle first
decisions.why:
Three components in this system can look like one enclosed bar of options, which is why each one's contract says the same thing.

SegmentedControl is a question with a short fixed set of answers, where showing them all is the point: single, always filled, cannot be cleared.

ToggleButtonGroup is the SAME ARIA pattern with a wider API — multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants. Reach for it when you need any of those, because this component deliberately cannot express them.

Tabs is a different pattern: tabs reveal a region, each naming a panel and each panel naming its tab. If what is being chosen is which content is shown rather than what gets submitted, it is Tabs — which can be drawn to look exactly like this, and is still announced as a tablist.

decisions.decision: It is narrower than ToggleButtonGroup on purpose, not by omission
decisions.why: A segmented control has one shape: single selection, always filled, never empty. Every option the toggle group carries is one this cannot honour, so the narrow contract is the feature — an API that cannot express a cleared segmented control cannot produce one by accident. The cost is real and worth stating: this is a second implementation of a pattern the toggle group already covers, and the two can drift. These contracts are the mitigation, which is why both name the other.

decisions.decision: Re-picking the current answer is not a change
decisions.why: There is no deselected state to fall into, so a click on the chosen option reports nothing rather than firing a change with the same value. A handler that refetches on every change would otherwise do so every time someone clicked where they already were.

decisions.decision: No aria-orientation, and both axes' arrow keys work
decisions.why: The bar is horizontal by construction, so announcing an orientation would promise that only one pair of arrows moves. Accepting both leaves a reader who tries the wrong pair unstuck, and claims nothing.

decisions.decision: Equal-width options
decisions.why: Sized to content, the selected option's weight change would reflow its neighbours under the reader's cursor every time the answer moved.

decisions.decision: The track is theme.bg.muted, and the background ladder gained a fourth step to allow it
decisions.why:
theme.bg.muted is documented as the most recessed background — "an inset well, a track" — which is this exactly. It nonetheless collided with the playground's own example stage, which was also using it, and the control vanished into the card demonstrating it.

The stage was the one in the wrong place: a stage is "a quiet section band inside a surface", which is theme.bg.subtle's job. But bg.subtle was tone 95 in light — identical to bg.canvas — and tone 10 in dark, identical to bg.surface, so four named steps resolved to three distinct values and the stage had taken muted because subtle could not do anything. bg.subtle has tones 97 and 15 of its own now, added to the palette's stops for this, so a section band and an inset well are finally different colours and neither needs a border to be seen.

base.summary: The well: a recessed track the chosen option is raised out of, which is what makes the bar read as one control with a part selected rather than as buttons that happen to touch. That is the difference from toggle-button-group, which draws the same pattern as attached bordered buttons.

tokens.track background: theme.bg.muted — exactly what that step is documented for: the most recessed background, an inset well or a track. No border: a track sitting a real step below what it is on does not need an edge drawn round it.
tokens.sizing: hugs its options; fullWidth fills the container

option.summary: One answer. Equal widths, so the bar does not reflow as the answer moves.

tokens.block-size sm / md: size.control.sm / size.control.md, each less space.1 for the track's padding
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

option-selected.summary: The answer, raised out of the track. Marked twice over: the surface is the visual cue and aria-checked is the announced one.

example:
<SegmentedControl
          label="Sort"
          fullWidth
          size="sm"
          options={[
            { value: "newest", label: "Newest" },
            { value: "oldest", label: "Oldest" },
          ]}
        />

name: select
title: Select
description: A labelled control for choosing one option from a list.

props.name: label
props.description: The control's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The control's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: A short noun phrase naming what is being chosen: "Country", not "Choose a country".
dont: Leaving it off because the placeholder says it. The placeholder is gone the moment someone answers.
props.a11y: Bound to the control by Field, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

props.name: options
props.description: The choices, in the order they are read.
props.summary: The choices, in the order they are read.
use: A flat array for a short list; groups once the list is long enough that a reader has to hunt.
The order a reader expects — alphabetical for places, frequency for everything else.
dont: A label that is anything but a string. An `<option>` holds text, so a ReactNode would be flattened or would crash.
One option. A control with a single choice is not a choice; state the value as text.
props.a11y: A disabled option stays in the list and is announced as unavailable rather than removed, so the list a reader hears does not change shape under them.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: Shown while nothing is chosen, as an option that cannot be chosen.
props.summary: Shown while nothing is chosen, as an option that cannot be chosen.
use: Naming the act rather than repeating the label: "Select a country" under a label that already says Country.
dont: Using it as the label. It disappears on the first answer, and a control whose name vanishes when used has no name.
Leaving it off on a `required` control with no `defaultValue`. The first option would then be pre-chosen, and a reader who wanted it cannot tell their answer from the control's assumption.
props.a11y: Rendered disabled and empty, so it is announced but cannot be selected — and `required` validation treats it as unanswered rather than as a value.

props.name: value
props.description: Controls the chosen option from outside.
props.summary: Controls the chosen option from outside.
use: A form library, or one field whose choices depend on another's answer.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the state.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The starting choice when the component owns the state.
props.summary: The starting choice when the component owns the state.
use: A genuine default the reader would usually want, which is different from the first option happening to be selected.
dont: Pairing it with `placeholder`. The placeholder would never be seen, which makes it a lie in the markup.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Fires with the chosen value when it changes.
props.summary: Fires with the chosen value when it changes.
use: Reading the answer without unpacking an event, which is what every other choice component in this system does.
dont: Expecting it on first render. It fires on change, so an initial value is the caller's to know.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height and inline padding. Text size does not change with it.
props.summary: Control height and inline padding. Text size does not change with it.
use: Matching whatever the control sits beside — a select and a button in one row should be the same height.
dont: `sm` to fit more on the page. It is the same text at a smaller target, which costs a reader more than the space is worth.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the control. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the control it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.description: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and the ring.
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text under the control.
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: What the choice affects, when that is not obvious from the options themselves.
dont: Listing the options again in prose.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.description: Status-dependent message under the control.
props.summary: Status-dependent message under the control.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative.
dont: Putting a permanent note here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the control required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.summary: Marks the control required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: With a `placeholder`, so there is an unanswered state for the requirement to be about.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Marks the whole control unavailable.
props.summary: Marks the whole control unavailable while keeping it focusable and announced.
use: A choice that depends on an answer nobody has given yet.
dont: Disabling it to show a fixed value. A control nobody can change is text — render the text.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` from Field. Note that unlike a text input, a select has no `readOnly` to fall back on, so the native attribute IS used here to block the change — the contract's one departure from the system rule, because the alternative is a control that looks unavailable and is not.

props.name: className
props.description: Class for the wrapper. The control itself is styled by the system.
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides.
dont: Restyling the chevron or the options. The first is positioned against the control's own padding, and the second the platform draws.

usage.case: One choice from a short list
usage.when: The commonest case, with nothing chosen until the reader chooses.
usage.example:
<Select
  label="Environment"
  placeholder="Select an environment"
  options={[
    { value: "dev", label: "Development" },
    { value: "prod", label: "Production" },
  ]}
  required
/>
usage.notes: `placeholder` with `required` is the pairing that makes an unanswered state possible. Without it the first option is pre-chosen and a reader cannot tell their answer from the control's assumption.

usage.case: A list long enough to need grouping
usage.when: Enough options that a reader has to hunt rather than scan.
usage.example:
<Select
  label="Region"
  placeholder="Select a region"
  options={[
    { label: "Asia", options: [{ value: "lk", label: "Sri Lanka" }] },
    { label: "Europe", options: [{ value: "pt", label: "Portugal" }] },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: A group in place of an option is the whole API. Nothing about a group is styleable, for the same reason nothing about an option is.

usage.when: Reporting an answer the form cannot accept.
usage.example:
<Select
  label="Environment"
  status="invalid"
  message="Pick an environment you have access to."
  options={[{ value: "prod", label: "Production" }]}
/>
usage.notes: The ring and the message are Field's, identical to a text field's — which is the point of both being built on it.

usage.when: The options need icons, two lines, or colour.
usage.example:
<Select
  label="Assignee"
  options={[{ value: "ada", label: "Ada Hartley — Engineering" }]}
/>
usage.notes: Don't fake it with punctuation. An `<option>` is text the operating system draws, so a design that needs more than a string has outgrown this component — that is the listbox version, which is a separate entry with its own primitive, and it does not exist yet. Say so rather than shipping a string that pretends.

behavior.summary: A native `<select>` inside a `Field`. No primitive of its own: `getFieldProps` supplies every id and ARIA attribute, and the platform supplies the rest.

decisions.decision: It is a native `<select>`, not a listbox built out of divs
decisions.why: What the platform gives away here is enormous and expensive to rebuild: the picker a phone shows instead of a dropdown, the full keyboard model including typeahead, the behaviour when the list is longer than the viewport, and an accessibility implementation that is correct by construction rather than by our testing. A built listbox needs a primitive owning roving focus, `aria-activedescendant`, typeahead and popover placement, and it is worse on a phone no matter how well it is written. The cost of choosing native is real and is stated in the next decision — it is not that nobody noticed.

decisions.decision: Options cannot be styled, and that is the price
decisions.why: A `<option>` renders as the operating system draws it. No icon, no second line, no badge, no colour. So this component cannot express an option that is anything more than a string — and when a design needs that, the answer is not to force it here but to build the listbox version, which will be a separate entry with its own primitive and its own contract. Naming the limit is what stops someone discovering it three screens into a build.

decisions.decision: An option's `label` is a string, where every other option type in this system takes a ReactNode
decisions.why: `TabItem`, `SegmentedControlOption` and the rest take a ReactNode because they render into elements this system controls. An `<option>` holds text and nothing else, so a ReactNode here would either be silently flattened or crash on a fragment. The type says what the element can actually hold, which is the only honest thing it can say.

decisions.decision: No `multiple`
decisions.why: The native multi-select is a scrolling box that requires modifier-clicking to use and that readers routinely fail to operate or even recognise as multi-choice. Choosing several things is a different interaction with a different contract — a checkbox group for a short list, a dedicated component for a long one — and a boolean here would quietly turn a well-understood control into a badly-understood one.

decisions.decision: `placeholder` renders a disabled empty option rather than a real choice
decisions.why: A select always has a value, so an unanswered one has to show something. Making that something selectable would let a reader deliberately choose "Select a country", which then has to be validated against as though it were a mistake they made rather than one the control invited. Disabled and empty means it can be shown and cannot be chosen — and with `required`, the browser's own validation already treats it as unanswered.

decisions.decision: The chevron is drawn by this system, over a control with `appearance: none`
decisions.why: The platform's arrow cannot be themed, sized or recoloured, so a select next to this system's other controls looked like it came from somewhere else. Drawing our own means reserving the space for it in the control's end padding — reserved whether or not a value is chosen, so picking one does not reflow the text under the reader's eye. The glyph takes `pointer-events: none`, so the whole control including the chevron stays one click target.

decisions.decision: `size` exists here where `Textarea` has none
decisions.why: A select is a single-line control and lines up in a row with buttons and text fields, so it takes the same control scale they do. A textarea's height is a line count and has nothing to line up with, which is why that component has `rows` instead. The prop is on the component whose measurement it actually describes.

decisions.decision: Options may be grouped, because the platform does it for free
decisions.why: `<optgroup>` costs three lines here and is the difference between a usable list of forty and an unusable one. Passing a group in place of an option is the whole API — nothing about a group is styleable either, for the reason above.

base.summary: The box, matching `.rata-text-field-input` step for step so a select and a text field in one row are indistinguishable in everything but their content. Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming.

tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, the same constant the button family and the text field use
tokens.block-size: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / size.control.lg at the other sizes
tokens.padding-inline-start: space.control.padding-inline.md — and the sm / lg steps at the other sizes

chevron-well.summary: Room reserved at the end edge for the chevron, which is drawn rather than inherited: the platform's own arrow cannot be themed, so the control sets appearance to none and this system supplies the glyph.

tokens.padding-inline-end: space.control.padding-inline.md plus size.icon.text plus space.gap.sm — reserved whether or not a value is chosen, so nothing reflows when one is
tokens.chevron colour: theme.fg.secondary — it is an affordance rather than content, so it sits below the value it points at

placeholder.summary: The unchosen state. Muted rather than primary, so a control nobody has answered looks unanswered.

states.summary: Selected from the primitive's data-status on the Field root, exactly as the text field's are. The rings are inset strokes, never the focus ring, so a control can be focused and invalid at once.

tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2 as an inset shadow, idle only — the validation rings occupy the same 2px and box-shadow does not accumulate
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset — the same deliberate departure the text field documents, so every control in a form focuses alike
tokens.disabled cursor: not-allowed — the dimming itself is Field's, on the root

example:
<Select
          label="Environment"
          status="invalid"
          message="Pick an environment you have access to."
          defaultValue="prod"
          options={[
            { value: "dev", label: "Development" },
            { value: "prod", label: "Production" },
          ]}
        />

name: sheet
title: Sheet
description: A modal surface anchored to an edge of the viewport — a bottom sheet or a side drawer.

props.name: title
props.summary: The sheet's name. Required.
use: A noun phrase naming what this is about: "Filters", "Token documentation".
dont: Omitting it and relying on the content. A modal with no accessible name announces as "dialog" and nothing else.
props.a11y: Rendered as an `<h2>` and wired with `aria-labelledby`, so the sheet is named the moment it opens.

props.name: children
props.description: The sheet's content.
props.summary: The sheet's content.
use: The detail, the form, the list of options.
dont: Another sheet's trigger, if you can avoid it. Stacked modals are legal and the scroll lock counts holders for that reason, but a reader two layers deep has lost the page.
props.a11y: Scrolls in its own region so the title stays put and the close control stays reachable.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the sheet is showing. Always controlled — `showModal()` has no prop.
props.summary: Whether the sheet is showing. Always controlled.
use: State the caller owns, so opening and closing are things that happen in their code rather than inside this one.
dont: Leaving it stale after `onClose`. The sheet reports; the caller decides.
props.a11y: Drives `showModal()` and `close()`. Nothing else makes the sheet modal — rendering the `open` attribute instead shows it non-modally, with no focus trap and a live page behind it.

props.name: onClose
props.description: Called when the sheet asks to close. Set `open` to false in it.
props.summary: Called when the sheet asks to close, with why.
use: Setting `open` to false.
dont: Ignoring the reason when a backdrop click should be treated differently from the close button — an unsaved form is the usual case.
props.a11y: Focus returns to whatever opened the sheet automatically, because the platform does it.

props.name: edge
props.description: Which edge it is held against. `block-end` is the bottom sheet.
props.summary: Which edge the sheet is anchored to and slides in from.
use: `block-end` for a bottom sheet — options and detail on a narrow viewport, where the bottom is where a thumb is.
`inline-end` for a detail drawer on a wide viewport, where it is the same side a Panel would sit on — so the same content can move between the two as the viewport changes.
dont: `block-start` for anything a reader dismisses often. The top edge is where the browser's own chrome is, and the reach is worst there.
props.a11y: Logical edges, not physical: `inline-start` is the left in a left-to-right document and the right in a right-to-left one, so a drawer follows the reading direction without the caller doing anything.

props.name: size
props.description: How far it comes in, measured on the axis it slides along.
props.summary: How far the sheet comes in, measured on the axis it slides along.
use: `sm` for a short list of actions; `lg` for a form or a document.
dont: Expecting it to control the other axis. `size` is the axis the sheet slides along; the other one spans its edge, capped and centred for a block-edge sheet on a wide viewport.
props.a11y: Every size gives way to a small viewport rather than overflowing it, and never covers the edge it slid from. A bottom sheet is also capped across its width on a wide viewport, which is a line-length decision rather than a size one — it is not affected by this prop.

props.name: description
props.description: A line under the title, wired as the sheet's description.
props.summary: A line under the title, wired as the sheet's description.
use: One sentence of consequence or scope that the title cannot carry.
dont: Content. This is announced with the name, so length here is length before the reader reaches anything.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-describedby`. Omitted, there is no dangling reference.

props.name: footer
props.description: The actions. Reads after the body they act on.
props.summary: The actions.
use: An Apply and a Cancel for a filter sheet.
dont: Navigation. A sheet is a place to do one thing and leave.
props.a11y: Rendered after the body in DOM order, so the actions are reached after the content they act on.

props.name: dismissible
props.summary: Whether the reader can close it themselves.
use: `false` only while something must finish — a migration step, a required choice with no default.
dont: `false` to keep attention. A sheet the reader cannot leave is a trap, and they will reload the page instead.
props.a11y: `false` removes the close button and prevents the `cancel` event, so Escape and a backdrop click do nothing. Provide another way out in the footer or it is a dead end.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.description: Accessible name for the close button.
props.summary: Accessible name for the close button.
use: Naming what closes when the word alone is ambiguous: "Close filters".
dont: Passing it with `dismissible={false}`. There is no button to name.
props.a11y: Becomes the button's `aria-label`. The control is icon-only, so without a name it announces as "button".

props.name: initialFocus
props.summary: What to focus when it opens. Defaults to the platform's choice.
use: The safe action in a destructive sheet, so the dangerous one is not one Enter away.
dont: Pointing it at something that is not rendered yet. It is applied once, after `showModal()`.
props.a11y: Applied after `showModal()`, which is the only order that works — React's `autoFocus` runs during commit and the platform's own default overrides it.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the sheet, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Nothing yet. It exists for the same reason Dialog's does, and the same caution applies.
dont: Changing its geometry or colours. Those come from `edge`, `size` and the recipe.

usage.case: A bottom sheet of filters on a narrow viewport
usage.when: The commonest bottom sheet: a set of choices too big for the bar they belong to, applied and dismissed in one go.
usage.notes: `block-end` is the default, so the edge is not stated. The footer holds both ways out, which is what makes Cancel reachable without hunting for the close button at the top of a sheet the reader's thumb is at the bottom of.

usage.case: A detail drawer from the inline edge
usage.when: The same content a Panel would hold, but over the page rather than beside it — because at this width there is no room to put it beside.
usage.example:
<Sheet
  open={selected !== null}
  onClose={() => setSelected(null)}
  edge="inline-end"
  size="lg"
  title={selected?.name ?? ""}
>
  <RecordDetail record={selected} />
</Sheet>
usage.notes: `inline-end` is logical, so this arrives from the right in a left-to-right document and from the left in a right-to-left one. If the page DOES have room beside the content, this is the wrong component — reach for Panel, which leaves the page usable.

usage.case: A required choice with no way to dismiss it
usage.when: Rare, and worth resisting. A required choice with no sensible default is the only case that justifies it.
usage.notes: `dismissible={false}` removes the close button and blocks Escape and the backdrop, so the footer MUST contain a way out — here Continue is it. Without one the sheet is a dead end and the reader will reload the page instead.

behavior.summary: A native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, held against one edge of the viewport. The browser supplies the focus trap, `inert` on the page behind, the top layer, `::backdrop`, Escape, and focus returned to whatever opened it — the same reasoning Dialog and MobileNav follow, and the same reason not to hand-roll any of it.

decisions.decision: It is modal, and there is no option for it not to be
decisions.why: MobileNav's contract already states the rule this follows: a surface covering the page is modal whether or not it is called one, because the content behind it must not be reachable by Tab, by a screen reader's own navigation, or by scrolling. A non-modal edge-anchored overlay would leave a reader tabbing into a page they cannot see. A panel that genuinely should not be modal belongs in the layout, which is what Panel is for.

decisions.decision: `edge` rather than separate BottomSheet and Drawer components
decisions.why: Everything that makes this hard — the top layer, the focus trap, the scroll lock with the scrollbar held open, the exit that must keep the layer alive — is identical on all four edges. What differs is which axis it slides along and which two corners are rounded, and that is geometry, not behaviour. Splitting by edge would be three copies of the difficult part to keep in step, which is the mistake Tabs and SegmentedControl were separated to avoid making in the other direction: they were split because their SEMANTICS differ, not their looks.

decisions.decision: `size` is one measure on whichever axis the sheet slides along
