decisions.why: A bottom sheet's size is its height; a drawer's is its width. They are the same question — how far does it come in — asked about different axes, so one prop answers it and the component knows which axis from `edge`. Two props would let a caller state the one that does not apply, which the type system cannot catch and which would silently do nothing.

decisions.decision: It reuses Dialog's scroll lock rather than its own
decisions.why: That lock counts holders instead of saving and restoring, because save-and-restore breaks the moment two things overlap — the second captures `hidden` as the value to put back, and closing it leaves the page locked with nothing open. A sheet over a dialog is an ordinary combination, so a second independent lock would reintroduce exactly that bug. It also holds the scrollbar's width open, measured at lock time because it is whatever the browser and the reader's settings make it.

decisions.decision: No drag to dismiss in this version
decisions.why: Close button, Escape and backdrop click are all supplied by the platform and all operable by keyboard and switch access. A drag gesture is a pointer state machine with a velocity threshold, a scroll-versus-drag conflict inside the sheet's own body, and no keyboard equivalent — so it needs its own pass through these gates rather than riding along with the geometry. No grab handle is drawn either: an affordance that does nothing is worse than none.

decisions.decision: Escape is prevented, then reported
decisions.why: Dialog's reasoning, unchanged: the platform would close the dialog itself and leave `open` still saying it is showing. Preventing the default and reporting through `onClose` keeps React the single source of truth.

decisions.decision: A native close is reported rather than ignored
decisions.why: `<form method="dialog">` is the documented HTML way to close a dialog and the platform can close one for its own reasons too. Neither goes through `onClose`, and the driving effect is keyed on `open`, so it never re-runs to notice — which in Dialog left the scroll lock on the body with nothing open and the page unable to scroll at all. The native `close` event reports `external`, and only while React still believes the sheet is open.

decisions.decision: Initial focus is a ref, because React's `autoFocus` cannot work here
decisions.why: React implements `autoFocus` by calling `.focus()` during commit rather than emitting the HTML attribute, so `showModal()` — which runs afterwards, in an effect — never sees an `[autofocus]` element and applies its own default, undoing it. `initialFocus` is applied after `showModal()` and therefore wins.

decisions.decision: The title is a real `<h2>`, as Dialog's is
decisions.why: Everything behind a modal is inert, so the outline inside it genuinely starts fresh and the title is the top of it. This is the difference from Panel, which sits inside the page's outline and has to be told its level.

decisions.decision: A bottom sheet stops short of a wide viewport's sides
decisions.why: Left open at gate 2 — the recipe said a sheet spans its edge with no cap, and that a sheet stopping short of both sides was a different shape needing its own entry. It does, and it now has one. Spanning the full width of a large monitor is the failure it prevents: the title sits at one corner and its close control at the other, with a line length in between that nothing else in this system permits. Capped and centred on the block edges only, because the equivalent on an inline edge would lift a drawer off the top and bottom and make it a floating panel instead.

base.summary: A modal surface held against one edge. Unlike Dialog it is flush with that edge, so only the corners that face the page are rounded.

tokens.border-radius on the two corners against: radius.none — a radius there would show the page through the gap

backdrop.summary: The wash over the inert page behind it. The same treatment as Dialog's, because it is the same statement about the page.

motion.summary: It slides in from the edge it is anchored to. The distance is the sheet's own measure, so it starts fully off-screen whatever its size.

tokens.enter transition: motion.modal.duration with motion.easing.enter, translating from off-screen to rest
tokens.translate axis: the axis the sheet's edge lies on — block for block-start and block-end, inline for inline-start and inline-end
tokens.reduced motion: the translate is dropped and only the backdrop's opacity transitions, at motion.modal.duration
tokens.exit pointer-events: none while closing — the top layer is held for the exit, so a click during it would land on a sheet that is leaving

size.summary: One measure across the sheet's own axis: block-size for a sheet on a horizontal edge, inline-size for one on a vertical edge. Derived from the control scale rather than stated in pixels, the same way Dialog's widths are.

tokens.cap across its own axis: 100% of the dialog's containing block less space.padding.lg — stated as a percentage rather than in viewport units on purpose: vh and vw are the LARGE viewport, so a bottom sheet measured in vh is taller than the screen whenever the mobile address bar is showing. Dialog's insets are percentages for the same reason.
tokens.measure across the other axis: the full containing block for an inline-edge sheet — a drawer spans the height it is anchored along. A BLOCK-edge sheet is capped at size.control.lg multiplied by 20 and centred with an auto inline margin: spanning a 2560px monitor puts the close control one corner away from the content it closes, and sets a line length nothing else in this system allows. That multiplier is the one Dialog's widest size uses, so a bottom sheet at its widest reads like the widest single surface here rather than like the page.
tokens.why the cap is block-edge only: The cross axis of an inline-edge sheet is its height, and capping that would lift a drawer off the top and bottom into a floating panel — a different shape, and not this component. A block-edge sheet stays flush to its own edge either way, so the two corners there stay square and the two facing the page keep radius.page.

footer.summary: The actions, reading after the body they act on.

dismiss.summary: The close control. Same construction as Dialog's, so a close button is the same control everywhere.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the sheet's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset
tokens.block alignment: centred on the title's first line, from type.heading.size and type.heading.line-height

name: side-nav
title: SideNav
description: A vertical navigation rail, grouped into named sections.

props.name: sections
props.description: The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav.
props.summary: The destinations, grouped. One unlabelled section is a flat nav.
use: A named section per group of related pages: "Billing", "Settings".
A single section with no `label` when there is nothing to group.
`items` on an entry for pages nested under it — it becomes a disclosure button rather than a link, and opens by default when one of its children is current.
`onClick` on an entry to intercept the navigation for a client-side router — the `href` stays real, so the row is still a link.
dont: A section per item. A group of one is a heading over nothing, and it reads as a mistake.
Actions. Everything here is announced as a destination and rendered as a link.
props.a11y: Each section is a list; a labelled one is pointed at its own label with `aria-labelledby`, so the group is announced with its name. The current item carries `aria-current="page"` — the only non-colour cue it has, since the visual distinction is a background tint and a text tone. An entry with `items` becomes a disclosure button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, and its parent-of-the-current-page state is `aria-current="true"` rather than `"page"`, because you are not on it. The nested list is unmounted while collapsed rather than hidden, so nothing in it can be reached by a find-in-page while the group claims to be shut.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Naming it for what it contains — "Invoices" for the rail inside that area — so it is distinguishable from the top nav in a landmark list.
dont: Leaving the default when a page also has a `TopNav`. Two navigation landmarks need distinct names, and that is the one place they matter most.
The word "navigation", which the role already says.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the nav, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Giving the rail its width, its inline padding, or making it stick — all layout decisions the component deliberately leaves to the page, so its rows line up with whatever else the page puts beside them.
dont: Changing the item treatment. The current-page marker is load-bearing, and a rail that marks it differently from the top nav reads as a different product.

usage.case: A grouped rail inside one area of the product
usage.when: The commonest case: enough pages that they need grouping.
usage.example:
<SideNav
  label="Invoices"
  sections={[
    {
      label: "Billing",
      items: [
        { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices", current: true },
        { label: "Credit notes", href: "/credit-notes" },
      ],
    },
    {
      label: "Setup",
      items: [
        { label: "Tax rates", href: "/tax" },
        { label: "Templates", href: "/templates" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: `label` names the landmark for what the rail contains, not for where it sits — "Invoices", not "Side". A page with a `TopNav` as well has two navigation landmarks, and that is exactly when the names earn their keep.

usage.case: A flat rail, with nothing to group
usage.when: Few enough destinations that a heading over them would be noise.
usage.example:
<SideNav
  label="Settings"
  sections={[
    {
      items: [
        { label: "Profile", href: "/profile", current: true },
        { label: "Notifications", href: "/notifications" },
        { label: "Security", href: "/security" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: One section with no `label`. The braces are the cost of there being a single shape rather than two props that cannot both be used — the contract's reasoning for that is in the behaviour notes.

usage.case: A group with pages nested under it
usage.when: A destination that is itself a section of several pages.
usage.example:
<SideNav
  label="Invoices"
  sections={[
    {
      items: [
        { label: "All invoices", href: "/invoices" },
        {
          label: "Reports",
          items: [
            { label: "Revenue", href: "/reports/revenue", current: true },
            { label: "Ageing", href: "/reports/ageing" },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: The group opens by itself because one of its children is current — a reader whose page is inside a collapsed group cannot see where they are. Note the two kinds of current again: the child is `aria-current="page"`, and its parent is `"true"` because you are only inside the area it leads to.

usage.case: Don't: a section for every item
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. A group of one is a heading over nothing: it doubles the reading length, and a screen reader announces a list of one item under a name that repeats it. Those are two flat items in one unlabelled section.

behavior.summary: A `<nav>` containing one list per section. No primitive and no keyboard handling: every link is its own tab stop, which is what navigation should be. Unlike TopNav this claims no page-level landmark beyond the nav itself — where the rail sits, and whether it is inside a `<main>` or beside it, is the caller's layout decision.

decisions.decision: Sections are the only shape, even for a flat list
decisions.why: A side nav exists because there are enough destinations to group; a flat one is the special case, not the default. Offering both `items` and `sections` would mean two mutually exclusive props and a rule about which wins — so a flat nav is one unlabelled section, which costs a pair of braces and removes the ambiguity entirely.

decisions.decision: A section's label names its list rather than being a heading
decisions.why: Same reasoning as Notice's title: a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under, and a wrong one breaks heading navigation for the whole page. The label is a plain element with an id, and the list points at it with `aria-labelledby` — so the group is announced with its name and the document outline is untouched.

decisions.decision: Collapsing to an icon-only rail is out of scope
decisions.why: A collapsed rail hides the labels, which is the point of collapsing and also the problem: a sighted reader then needs the name on hover, and this system has no Tooltip. Shipping the collapse without one would trade an accessible nav for a row of unexplained glyphs. It belongs with a Tooltip, not before one.

decisions.decision: The current page is stated per item, as in TopNav
decisions.why: Only the caller knows whether /invoices/123 counts as being on /invoices. Matching a path here would have to guess between exact and prefix and would be silently wrong for someone either way. It is shown as a tinted row rather than an edge marker: the marker was removed on request, which leaves the visual cue entirely colour and `aria-current` as the only cue that is not.

decisions.decision: A nested group is a disclosure expanded in place, not a popover
decisions.why: An item with `items` becomes a button that expands a list beneath it. Not a menu, for the reason getDisclosureProps documents: `role="menu"` announces a keyboard model a list of links does not have. And not a popover either, unlike TopNav's — a rail scrolls vertically, so a nested list pushes what follows it down and nothing has to escape an overflow. Keeping it inline also keeps the nesting visible, which is most of what a rail is for.

decisions.decision: A group holding the current page starts open
decisions.why: Not a convenience: a reader whose page sits inside a collapsed group cannot see where they are, which is the one question a nav exists to answer. `defaultExpanded` overrides it for the rare case where a group is long enough that opening it costs more than it explains.

decisions.decision: Rows carry an optional onClick, and still require a real href
decisions.why: Found by trying to build the playground's own rail out of this component: the rows navigate client-side, and with no way to intercept the click there was no way to use it without a full page load. The href stays required rather than becoming optional, because it is what makes the row a link — middle-click, copy-address and crawlers all depend on it, and a nav built from handlers with no addresses behind them loses all three without appearing to.

decisions.decision: The rows fill the rail; the page owns the inline padding
decisions.why: A rail is almost never alone — a search field, a button, a heading sit in it too — and inline padding on the nav doubles up with the page's own gutter, so the rows end up inset further than everything beside them. Filling the width also makes the whole row the target rather than just the words. Block padding stays, because vertical breathing room inside the rail affects nothing outside it.

base.summary: The rail. No background, no width and no inline padding of its own: it sits on whatever surface the page gives it, at whatever width, inset by the page's own gutter — so its rows fill the rail and line up with anything else the page puts there, such as a search field.

tokens.padding-inline: none — the rows fill the rail, and the page owns the gutter

section.summary: A named group. The label is the list's accessible name, not a heading — a nav cannot know what heading level it sits under.

item.summary: One destination, filling the rail's width so the whole row is the target.

tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — 14px. It was the sm step, 12px, which is the size this scale reserves for text inside a small control rather than for a row of running navigation: a rail and a bar are read, not squeezed into a 28px box. Every row takes it, because the disclosure trigger and the nested sublink both compose the link class.
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

item-current.summary: The page you are on: a tinted row, plus aria-current in the markup. The tint is the role's subtle step with fg.primary on it — a pairing the token contracts verify for text at any size — not the saturated fill, which is a non-text indicator tone.

name: skeleton
title: Skeleton
description: A placeholder in the shape of content that is about to load, so the layout does not jump when it arrives.

props.name: shape
props.description: What kind of content it stands in for.
props.summary: What kind of content it stands in for.
use: `text` for lines of running text — sized from the type scale.
`block` for an image, a chart or a media slot.
`circle` for an avatar.
dont: `block` for a paragraph. A grey rectangle where text will be does not tell the reader it is text, and it will not match the paragraph's height.
props.a11y: Visual only. Every shape is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: lines
props.description: How many lines a `text` skeleton stands in for.
props.summary: How many lines a `text` skeleton stands in for.
use: The usual line count of what replaces it — 3 for a summary, 1 for a title.
dont: Passing it with `block` or `circle`. Only text has lines.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes, for the size of a `block` or `circle` and its placement.
props.summary: Extra classes, for the size of a `block` or `circle` and its placement.
use: Taking the size of the thing it replaces, from the same layout rule that sizes that thing.
dont: A bare pixel width. Size it from the same token or layout rule as the content it replaces, or the content will jump.

usage.case: A list whose shape is known
usage.when: Rows of a known structure are loading, and the page should not jump when they arrive.
usage.example:
<section aria-busy={loading} aria-labelledby="activity-heading">
  <Heading level={2} id="activity-heading">Activity</Heading>
  {loading ? (
    <>
      <Spinner label="Loading activity" />
      <Skeleton lines={2} />
      <Skeleton lines={2} />
    </>
  ) : (
    <ActivityList items={items} />
  )}
</section>
usage.notes: The section carries `aria-busy` and the Spinner's `label` is the one announcement; the skeletons are `aria-hidden`, so the word is not read once per row.

usage.when: A Save button waiting on the server.
usage.example: <Skeleton shape="block" className="button-sized" />
usage.notes: Don't. The control already exists and its shape is not in question — that is `<Button loading>`, which keeps the button focusable and announced while it works.

behavior.summary: An `aria-hidden` block. The region that is loading — not the skeleton — carries `aria-busy` and says what is loading. No primitive: it holds no state and takes no input.

decisions.decision: Skeleton when the layout is known; Spinner when it is not
decisions.why: A skeleton promises a shape: a list of three rows, a card with a picture. When the shape is known it prevents the layout shift that makes a reader lose their place, and it lets them start reading the page's structure before the data arrives. When the shape is not known — an action in progress, a result of unknown size — a skeleton guesses, and the content that replaces it jumps anyway. That is Spinner's case. A button that is working is always a Spinner, via Button's `loading`.

decisions.decision: Every skeleton is `aria-hidden`, and the loading region owns the announcement
decisions.why: A page of twelve skeleton rows that each said "loading" would read the word twelve times. The container whose content is loading sets `aria-busy="true"` and holds one visually-hidden status — or a Spinner with a `label` — naming what is loading; when the content arrives, `aria-busy` comes off and the content is read normally. The skeleton itself is decoration with a layout job, and nothing more.

decisions.decision: A pulse between two background tokens, not a shimmer gradient
decisions.why: A gradient sweep needs a highlight colour that exists nowhere in the token set and would have to be invented and contrast-checked per brand; a pulse between `theme.bg.muted` and `theme.bg.subtle` uses two documented steps and changes with the theme for free. It runs at the slow band's slowest step because a skeleton is on screen for a while, and anything faster becomes a flicker in peripheral vision. Under reduced motion it stops entirely: a still block communicates "not yet" perfectly well.

decisions.decision: Sizing is the caller's, by design
decisions.why: A skeleton is only useful if it matches the content it stands in for, and only the caller knows that content. `text` sizes itself from the type scale, so a text skeleton is right by construction; `block` and `circle` take the size of whatever they replace — an Avatar's size, a media slot's aspect ratio — from the caller's layout. A `width` and `height` prop would invite exactly the bare pixel values this system has none of.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `span` (so it can sit inside text or inline layout) with `aria-hidden="true"`; the loading container carries `aria-busy`. React Native: a `View` with `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` and `accessibilityElementsHidden`, animated with the core `Animated` API and skipped when `AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled()` is true. The container's loading state is `accessibilityState={{ busy: true }}`. All props work on both. Rata-drawn (decision N5): there is no OS placeholder control. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A recessed block — the use `theme.bg.muted` documents for a skeleton — that pulses gently toward the next background step. No gradient sweep: a pulse needs only two existing tokens and degrades to a still block.

tokens.under prefers-reduced-motion: no animation — a still theme.bg.muted block

text.summary: One bar per line, sized from the type it stands in for so the paragraph that replaces it takes the same space.

tokens.block-size: type.body.size, centred in a line box of type.body.line-height
tokens.gap between lines: none — the line box already carries the leading
tokens.last line inline-size: a shorter fraction of the full width, so the block reads as a paragraph and not a wall

block.summary: A rectangle standing in for an image, a chart or a card's media.

circle.summary: A circle standing in for an avatar.

name: slider
title: Slider
description: Choose a value, or a range of two, along a bounded track.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: What the value measures. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: The quantity, with its unit when the output does not carry one: "Volume", "Max price (USD)".
dont: A sentence. It is read before every value change a screen reader announces.
props.a11y: Bound to the input by Field, so it is the slider's accessible name. For a range it names the group, and each thumb is named by `thumbLabels`.

props.name: value
props.summary: Controls the value from outside. A two-element tuple renders two thumbs.
use: A filter that other controls also write to, or a value persisted elsewhere.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`. One of them owns the state.
Switching between a number and a tuple across renders. The number of thumbs is decided once.

props.name: defaultValue
props.summary: The starting value when the component owns the state. Its shape decides one thumb or two.
use: `[min, max]` for a range filter that starts unconstrained.
dont: A value off the `step` grid. It is snapped on the first interaction, which looks like the control jumped by itself.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Fires continuously while the thumb moves.
use: Updating the visible output and anything cheap that should track the thumb.
dont: A network request. A drag fires this dozens of times a second — that is `onValueCommit`.

props.name: onValueCommit
props.summary: Fires once when an interaction ends: pointer release, a key press, or an assistive-technology adjustment.
use: Re-running a query or saving a preference — anything expensive enough that it should happen once per decision.
dont: Assuming it follows a drag only. Each arrow-key press is a complete interaction and commits.

props.name: min
props.summary: The lowest value.
use: The real floor of the quantity, not a guess at the usual one.

props.name: max
props.summary: The highest value.
use: The real ceiling. If there is none, this is the wrong control — a slider needs both ends to mean anything; use `NumberField`.

props.name: step
props.summary: The grid values snap to. Arrow keys move one step, PageUp and PageDown ten.
use: A step that makes every reachable value meaningful — a price filter in 5s, not in cents.
dont: So fine a step that the thumb cannot land on a chosen value by touch. A hundred steps across a phone-width track is about the limit; past it, add a `NumberField` beside the slider.

props.name: thumbLabels
props.summary: Names for the two thumbs of a range. Required when the value is a tuple.
use: "Minimum price" and "Maximum price" — each thumb is its own control and needs its own name.
dont: Setting it on a single-thumb slider. There is one control and `label` already names it.
props.a11y: Each becomes its thumb's `aria-label`, and the group keeps `label`. Without it a reader hears two identical sliders and cannot tell which end they are moving.

props.name: formatValue
props.summary: Turns a value into the text shown in the output and announced as `aria-valuetext`.
use: Units and currency: `(v) => `$${v}``, or `Intl.NumberFormat` for the page's locale.
Named stops on a discrete scale: `(v) => ["Off", "Low", "High"][v]`.
dont: Rounding away the step. The text announced has to be the value the reader will get.
props.a11y: Without it a screen reader announces the bare number, which is meaningless for a price, a percentage or a named level.

props.name: showValue
props.summary: Renders the current value as visible text beside the label.
use: Almost always. A slider without a number is a guess, and touch makes it a worse one — the finger covers the thumb.
dont: Turning it off because the value is shown elsewhere and then not tying the two together. If you hide it, the value has to be visible somewhere the reader is looking.
props.a11y: Rendered in an `<output>` tied to the input, but not a live region: the input's own `aria-valuetext` is already announced on every change, and a live output would say it twice.

props.name: name
props.summary: Form field name. A range submits two values under the same name, lower first.
use: A native form post or `FormData`.

props.name: labelHidden
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading or column header directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: the label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.summary: Stable id for the slider, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the field it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message, popup — is derived from this.

props.name: description
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: What the value affects, when the label alone does not say: "Applies to new uploads only."
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks adjustment while keeping the slider focusable, readable and announced.
use: A setting that depends on another being on.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. It still submits — the same consequence the text field documents.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` on each thumb. A range input has no `readOnly`, so the primitive blocks the change itself: keys and pointer down are refused, and an assistive-technology adjustment that slips past them is reverted to the current value.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the layout wants, not a restyle.
use: The inline size of the track, which is the layout's decision.
dont: Restyling the thumb or track. They are drawn from the recipe, and the thumb's hit area is sized for touch.

usage.when: A setting with a real floor and ceiling, where the approximate position matters more than the exact number.
usage.example:
<Slider
  label="Volume"
  defaultValue={40}
  formatValue={(v) => `${v}%`}
/>
usage.notes: `formatValue` is what makes the announcement "40%" rather than "40". The visible output uses the same text, so what is heard and what is seen cannot disagree.

usage.when: Two ends of one interval, adjusted independently.
usage.example:
<Slider
  label="Price"
  defaultValue={[0, 500]}
  max={500}
  step={10}
  thumbLabels={["Minimum price", "Maximum price"]}
  formatValue={(v) => `$${v}`}
  onValueCommit={applyFilter}
/>
usage.notes: `onValueCommit` re-runs the query once per decision rather than once per pixel. `thumbLabels` is required for a tuple: without it a screen reader hears two identical sliders.

usage.case: A discrete scale with named stops
usage.when: A handful of levels with names rather than numbers.
usage.example:
<Slider
  label="Image quality"
  max={2}
  defaultValue={1}
  formatValue={(v) => ["Low", "Medium", "High"][v]}
/>
usage.notes: Consider whether this wants to be a `SegmentedControl` instead. Three named options that are all visible at once are easier to choose between than a thumb whose stops are invisible.

usage.when: The reader knows the exact number they want.
usage.example: <Slider label="Quantity" max={1000} />
usage.notes: Don't. Landing a thumb on 347 out of 1000 by touch is a dexterity test. An exact number is a `NumberField`; if the approximate position also helps, put one beside the other bound to the same value.

behavior.summary: One or two native range inputs over a drawn track, composed with Field for the label and helper text. APG Slider and Multi-Thumb Slider, with the platform supplying the keyboard model and the touch-screen-reader gestures a scripted slider cannot receive.

decisions.decision: It is built on native `<input type="range">`, one per thumb, not a `div role="slider"`
decisions.why: The APG Slider and Multi-Thumb Slider patterns describe `role="slider"` on any element, and both are satisfied by a native range input, which brings things a div cannot: iOS VoiceOver's swipe-to-adjust, which fires no key events and so never reaches a scripted slider; form participation; and the platform's keyboard model including Home, End and PageUp/PageDown. A range is two inputs sharing a track, each its own tab stop with its own name — which is what the multi-thumb pattern asks for anyway.

decisions.decision: The native input is the hit surface; the track and thumb are drawn
decisions.why: A range input's thumb is a pseudo-element, styled differently in every engine and unable to carry a class. So the input is laid over the drawn track at full size and transparent, receiving every pointer, touch and key event, while the visible thumb is a real element positioned from the value. The hit area is the input's block-size, size.control.sm, independent of the drawn thumb's size — 2.5.8's target minimum met without a thumb that looks swollen.

decisions.decision: The thumb composes `.rata-state-layer`, which will also respond to `[data-hovered]` and `[data-pressed]`
decisions.why: The state layer reacts to `:hover` and `:active` on the element carrying the class, but here the element under the pointer is the transparent input and the element that shows the feedback is the drawn thumb. A `:has(input:hover)` rule would be the hand-rolled hover this system forbids. So `.rata-state-layer` is to be extended to respond to `[data-hovered]` and `[data-pressed]` as well, set by the slider primitive from pointer events on the input, and the thumb composes the class like any other control — identical feedback, with state.hover-opacity and state.press-opacity unchanged; only the trigger widens. That extension is a state-layer change in its own gated step, not part of this contract, and the slider cannot ship before it does (decision C9, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Track tone is split from Progress by role; track thickness is one shared token, still to be proposed
decisions.why: A slider's track belongs to an interactive control, so it takes theme.border.strong, which meets the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's boundary. Progress's track is a status mark, the recessed well theme.bg.muted is documented for, and keeps that tone. The two contracts had disagreed about thickness too; they now share one track-thickness token, proposed through the design-tokens interview (Purpose / Use when / Don't use for / Pairs with) rather than written ad hoc. Until it is approved the recipe holds space.1 as a placeholder, named as one so it is not shipped quietly (decision C8, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: A single pointer can always reach any value without dragging
decisions.why: WCAG 2.5.7 requires an alternative to dragging. Pressing anywhere on the track moves the nearest thumb there, which the native input already does, and is kept on purpose rather than suppressed for a drag-only feel.

decisions.decision: Horizontal only
decisions.why: A vertical slider on the web is a rotated input with a different keyboard direction, it fights vertical page scroll on touch, and every case seen so far — volume, zoom — is better served horizontally in the layouts this system builds. The track sets `touch-action: pan-y` so a horizontal drag adjusts while a vertical swipe still scrolls the page. Vertical can be added as an `orientation` prop when something needs it; it should not be paid for before.

decisions.decision: `onValueCommit` exists beside `onValueChange`
decisions.why: Change fires on every pointer move, and the commonest bug with sliders is a query per pixel. Commit fires once per interaction — release, keypress or AT adjustment — so the expensive work has a correct place to go that does not require the caller to build a debounce and guess its delay.

decisions.decision: No `status`, `message` or `required`
decisions.why: A slider always holds a value between `min` and `max` on the `step` grid, so there is no invalid state to show and no unanswered one to require. A constraint across two fields belongs to the form, which can report it in a Notice.

decisions.decision: No tick marks or labelled stops in this version
decisions.why: Marks look simple and carry three decisions: whether they snap, how their labels avoid colliding at narrow widths, and whether they are announced. A discrete scale is served meanwhile by `step` plus `formatValue` returning the stop's name, which gets the announcement right — the part that matters most.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getSliderProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet. The proposal returns the input, drawn-thumb, track and output prop bags for one or two thumbs, keeps two thumbs from crossing (each thumb's `min`/`max` is the other's value), snaps to `step`, implements the disabled guard described under `disabled`, and sets the `data-hovered` and `data-pressed` attributes the extended state layer responds to (decision C9).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: one `<input type="range">` per thumb, with `aria-valuetext` from `formatValue` and `aria-label` from `thumbLabels` on a range, inside a Field; a range is a `role="group"` labelled by `label`. Pointer, touch and keyboard all go through the native input. React Native: core no longer ships a Slider (it moved to a community package), and taking that dependency would make every native consumer install it, so the native component is a `View` driven by the responder system with `accessibilityRole="adjustable"`, `accessibilityValue={{ min, max, now, text }}` — `text` from `formatValue` — and `accessibilityActions` for increment and decrement, which is what VoiceOver's and TalkBack's swipe gestures call. A range is two adjustable views. `onValueCommit` maps to responder release and to each accessibility action. `name` is web-only. Rata-drawn (decision N5): React Native core has no slider any more and the community one cannot be styled to the recipe, so native draws the track and thumb itself rather than using an OS control. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: The track, the fill and the row they sit in. The drawn track is decoration over a transparent native input, so these measurements are what the reader sees, not what they touch.

tokens.hit area block-size: size.control.sm — the transparent input's height, and so the touch target, regardless of the drawn thumb
tokens.track background: theme.border.strong — the boundary tone tuned to the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control (decision C8). Progress's track is theme.bg.muted because a progress bar reports status; a slider's empty track is part of an interactive control and says how far the value can still go, so it has to be seen
tokens.fill background: theme.accent-role.bg — from min to the thumb, or between the two thumbs of a range
tokens.output font-variant: tabular-nums, so the number does not shift width as it changes

thumb.summary: The drawn handle. Surface-filled with an accent edge, so it reads against both the fill and the empty track it travels between.

tokens.inline-size / block-size: size.icon.md — the checkbox box's size, so a slider and a checkbox in one settings column carry the same visual weight
tokens.hover / press: compose the .rata-state-layer class, triggered by the data-hovered and data-pressed attributes the primitive sets (decision C9)
tokens.focus ring: focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset, drawn on the thumb when the input matches :focus-visible
tokens.movement: transform, not a layout property, with no transition while dragging — a thumb that lags the finger reads as broken

name: spinner
title: Loading: Spinner
description: Inline loading indicator that scales with font size.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label; omit when a parent already conveys the loading state.
props.summary: Accessible name for the loading state.
use: A standalone spinner, where nothing else announces that something is loading.
dont: A spinner inside a Button — the button already carries `aria-busy` and its own label, so a second announcement is noise.
props.a11y: Omitting this is correct only when a parent already conveys the loading state.

usage.when: A panel or list fetching its first page.
usage.example: <Spinner label="Loading results" />

usage.when: Composed automatically by Button's `loading` prop — you rarely write this yourself.
usage.example: <Spinner />
usage.notes: No label: Button's `aria-busy` already reports the state.

name: state-layer
title: State layer
description: Composable hover/press overlay that gives every interactive component identical state feedback.
note: No standalone React component — "State layer" is CSS-only (see registry description), composed onto other components' className.

usage.case: Giving a new interactive component hover and press feedback
usage.when: Always — this is the only supported way to express interaction feedback in this system.
usage.example: <button className="rata-thing rata-state-layer">…</button>
usage.notes: Add the class alongside the component's own; never write a competing `:hover` background rule. Feedback here is opacity-only by standing decision, which is why the role tokens carry no `bg-hover`/`bg-active` and why `ring.neutral` is deliberately unwired.

usage.when: The layer's default bleeds outward by border.default, so an unbordered host needs the opt-out or its tint sits a hairline proud of the element.
usage.example: <button className="rata-thing rata-state-layer rata-state-layer--flush">…</button>
usage.notes: The layer is an absolutely positioned pseudo-element, and `inset` on one resolves against the containing block's padding box — which excludes the border. At `inset: 0` the tint stopped a border-width short on every side, invisible under a filled background but plainly smaller on a host whose only fill is the layer itself. It now bleeds by border.default, since every bordered host in this system uses that width, and CSS gives no way to read a containing block's computed border-width. `--flush` restores `inset: 0` for hosts with none.

name: steps
title: Steps
description: Shows where the reader is in a linear multi-step flow, and lets them return to steps already reached.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: label
props.summary: Names the whole sequence: "Checkout progress".
use: The task the steps belong to, so a reader landing on the list knows what is being counted.
dont: "Steps". It is announced as a list already; the name says of what.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s or `<ol>`'s `aria-label`. Required, because a page can hold a step indicator and other lists, and an unnamed one is indistinguishable from them.

props.name: steps
props.summary: The steps in order, as `{ id, label, description?, invalid? }`.
use: Short noun labels — "Shipping", "Payment", "Review" — and `description` for the one-line detail under each.
`invalid` on an earlier step whose answer is now wrong, so the reader can see where to go back to.
dont: More than about seven. Past that the horizontal layout cannot fit labels and the sequence is better split into sections.
Changing the set mid-flow without saying so. A step that appears after the reader has started makes the count they were told untrue.
props.a11y: Each is an `<li>` whose accessible name includes its position and state — "Step 2 of 4, Payment, current" — through visually hidden text, so state is never carried by the marker's colour or glyph alone.

props.name: current
props.summary: The `id` of the step the reader is on. Steps before it are complete; steps after it are upcoming.
use: The step whose content is on screen.
dont: An id not in `steps`. There would be no current step and every step would read as upcoming.
props.a11y: That step gets `aria-current="step"`, which is the value WAI-ARIA defines for exactly this.

props.name: onStepSelect
props.summary: Makes completed steps navigable, and fires with the chosen step's id.
use: A flow where going back to change an earlier answer is allowed — the usual case.
dont: Expecting upcoming steps to become navigable. Only steps already reached can be returned to; jumping ahead would skip the validation each step does.
props.a11y: Without it every step is plain text. With it, completed and invalid steps become buttons, and the current and upcoming steps stay text, so the tab order holds only the places the reader can actually go.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Lays the steps out in a row or a column.
use: `vertical` beside a long form, where each step's description has room and the column doubles as a table of contents.
dont: `horizontal` with long labels in a narrow column. It collapses to the compact form anyway; choose `vertical` if you want the labels.
props.a11y: Visual only. The list order, and so the reading order, is the same either way.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the root — placement, not a restyle.
use: The margin the page wants above its first section.

usage.when: A short linear flow where each step is its own screen.
usage.example:
<Steps
  label="Checkout progress"
  current="payment"
  steps={[
    { id: "shipping", label: "Shipping" },
    { id: "payment", label: "Payment" },
    { id: "review", label: "Review" },
  ]}
  onStepSelect={goTo}
/>
usage.notes: Only Shipping is a button: it has been reached. Review stays plain text until the reader gets there.

usage.when: An earlier answer became invalid after a later one changed it.
usage.example:
<Steps
  label="Application progress"
  current="review"
  steps={[
    { id: "details", label: "Your details", invalid: true },
    { id: "documents", label: "Documents" },
    { id: "review", label: "Review" },
  ]}
  onStepSelect={goTo}
/>
usage.notes: The invalid step is marked in the danger role and named as needing attention. Put the reason on the Review screen too, in a Notice — the marker says where, not what.

usage.case: A long form with a table of contents
usage.when: One page in sections, where the steps double as navigation down the side.
usage.example:
<Steps
  label="Profile setup"
  orientation="vertical"
  current={section}
  steps={sections}
  onStepSelect={scrollTo}
/>
usage.notes: Vertical has room for each step's `description`, which the horizontal form hides when compact.

usage.when: Sections of a settings page the reader can visit in any order.
usage.example: <Steps label="Settings" current="profile" steps={settingsSections} />
usage.notes: Don't. Nothing here is a sequence, so "upcoming" is false about every section after the first. Sections visited in any order are `Tabs` or a `SideNav`.

behavior.summary: An ordered list of steps with `aria-current="step"` on the current one, each step's state stated in words as well as drawn. An indicator only: the caller owns which step is current and what each one renders.

decisions.decision: Named `steps`, not `stepper`
decisions.why: "Stepper" means two unrelated controls: Material and most web libraries use it for this progress indicator, and iOS, Android and most native toolkits use it for the plus-and-minus control that changes a number. Registering either under that name would hand half the people who type it the wrong component with total confidence. So neither owns it: this is `steps`, the increment control is `number-field`, and both list `stepper` as an alias — which the resolver reports as ambiguous and refuses to guess, the same treatment `drawer` gets for Sheet and MobileNav.

decisions.decision: An ordered list with `aria-current="step"`, not tabs
decisions.why: No APG pattern covers a step indicator. The tempting one is Tabs, and it is wrong: tabs are siblings that can be visited in any order and each owns a panel that is ready now, while steps are a sequence where the later ones are not available yet. So it is an `<ol>` — which announces "list, 4 items" and gives the count for free — with `aria-current="step"` on the current item, the value WAI-ARIA defines for this case. When steps are navigable the list is wrapped in a labelled `<nav>`.

decisions.decision: It shows progress; it does not own the flow
decisions.why: The caller holds which step is current and renders that step's content. A component that also owned the panels would have to own validation between steps, which differs in every flow. This is the indicator only, the same split Tabs would have been forced into if it had had to decide when a tab may be opened.

decisions.decision: Only reached steps can be navigated to
decisions.why: Going back to change an answer is a normal need; jumping forward past a step skips whatever that step checks. So with `onStepSelect` set, steps before `current` and any `invalid` step become buttons, and the current and upcoming steps stay plain text — not disabled buttons, since there is nothing they could ever do from here and each would be a dead stop in the tab order.

decisions.decision: State is in the accessible name, not only in the marker
decisions.why: Complete, current, upcoming and invalid are shown by the marker's fill, glyph and the label's weight — and each step's name also says it in words through visually hidden text: "Step 1 of 4, Shipping, completed". `aria-current` alone covers only one of the four states.

decisions.decision: Horizontal collapses to "Step 2 of 4" when it does not fit
decisions.why: A row of four labelled steps does not fit a phone. Below the width the full row needs — a container query, not a viewport breakpoint, because the indicator may sit in a narrow column on a wide screen — it renders the current step's marker, its label and "Step 2 of 4", with the list still in the accessibility tree whole. Truncating labels instead would leave a row of ellipses.

decisions.decision: Proposed primitive: `getStepsProps`
decisions.why: No primitive exists yet. It is small: derive each step's state from its position against `current` and its `invalid` flag, build each step's accessible name, and decide which are navigable. It still belongs in a primitive, because the native package needs exactly the same derivation.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: a `<nav aria-label>` (only when navigable) around an `<ol aria-label>` of `<li>`, with `aria-current="step"` on the current item and a system Button-styled `<button>` inside each navigable one; markers and connectors are `aria-hidden`. Pointer, touch and keyboard all reach the same buttons. React Native: a `View` with `accessibilityRole="list"`, each step a `View` — or a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="button"` when navigable — whose `accessibilityLabel` is the same derived name, and `accessibilityState={{ selected: true }}` on the current step, since native has no `aria-current`. The container query has no native equivalent, so the native package chooses the compact form from the window width instead. No prop is platform-specific. Rata-drawn (decision N5): neither platform has an OS step indicator, so it is drawn from the same recipe as the web. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: The row or column of steps and the connectors between them.

tokens.gap between label and description: space.0 — line-height leading already separates them, the reasoning the checkbox recipe gives

marker.summary: The circle holding the step's number or glyph. Sized from the icon scale, because it holds a glyph — the checkbox precedent.

tokens.upcoming: border.default solid theme.border.strong on theme.bg.surface, number in theme.fg.secondary
tokens.current: border.2 solid theme.accent-role.bg on theme.bg.surface, number in theme.accent-role.fg
tokens.complete: theme.accent-role.bg fill with a check glyph in theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on that fill
tokens.invalid: theme.danger-role.bg fill with an alert glyph in theme.danger-role.on — the role's own label token, never on-accent, which inverts in dark while the status fill does not

current.summary: The step the reader is on. Marked by the ring on its marker, the label's tone and weight, and aria-current — never by colour alone.

navigable.summary: A reached step that can be returned to. The whole row — marker and label — is one button.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

name: switch
title: Switch
description: An on/off setting that takes effect the moment it moves.

props.name: label
props.description: The setting's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The setting's label. Always required — `labelHidden` can take it off screen, but nothing removes it.
use: Always. Name the setting, not the action: "Notifications", not "Turn on notifications".
dont: A label that changes with the state. `aria-checked` says which way it is set, so a label that also says it produces "Turn off notifications, on".
Passing an empty string. An unnamed switch is a control nobody can describe; hide it with `labelHidden` instead.
props.a11y: A real `<label for>` bound to the input, so the text is part of the hit target.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A row in a settings table whose column already names the setting.
dont: A standalone switch. With nothing else naming it, the label is the only thing saying what is being turned on.
props.a11y: Clipped, not `display: none` — the label element is still rendered and still bound, so the accessible name is unchanged.

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the setting is on. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the setting is on. Makes the component controlled.
use: Whenever the setting lives outside the component, which for a setting is essentially always.
dont: Passing it without `onCheckedChange`; the switch would render its state and refuse to change it.
Flipping it optimistically when the change is a server round trip that can fail — the switch would be lying about the setting.
props.a11y: Drives `aria-checked`, which is announced as on/off rather than checked/unchecked.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled switch. Conflicts with `checked`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled switch.
use: A local view preference nothing else on the page reads.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.description: Called with the state the setting should move to.
props.summary: Called with the state the setting should move to.
use: Applying the change immediately — that is what makes this a switch rather than a checkbox.
dont: Deferring the effect to a Save button. If the change needs saving, the control is a Checkbox.

props.name: description
props.description: Helper text under the label.
props.summary: Helper text under the label, for a setting whose consequence is not obvious.
use: Saying what turning it on actually does, when the label alone cannot.
dont: Restating the label in more words.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks the change while keeping the switch focusable and readable.
props.summary: Blocks the change while keeping the switch focusable and readable.
use: A setting that cannot be changed yet but whose current state still matters to see.
dont: Expressing "off". Disabled and off are different facts, and a disabled switch can be either.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` and refuses activation. Never the native `disabled` attribute.

props.name: className
props.summary: Class for the switch's wrapper.
dont: Restyling the track or thumb — those are the approved token mapping.

usage.when: The canonical case, and the only one this component is for.
usage.example:
<Switch
  label="Notifications"
  checked={notifications}
  onCheckedChange={setNotifications}
/>
usage.notes: The label names the setting, not the action. `aria-checked` says which way it is set, so "Notifications" is announced as "Notifications, on" — which is what a setting sounds like.

usage.case: A setting whose consequence needs saying
usage.when: Where the label alone cannot explain what turning it on does.
usage.example:
<Switch
  label="Public profile"
  description="Anyone with the link can see your activity."
  checked={isPublic}
  onCheckedChange={setPublic}
/>

usage.case: A row in a settings table
usage.when: Where the column heading already names the setting.
usage.example: <Switch label="Email digest" labelHidden checked={row.digest} onCheckedChange={…} />
usage.notes: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, not the name — each row is still announced with what it controls.

usage.when: The change is not applied until a form is submitted.
usage.example:
<Switch label="Email me updates" checked={draft.email} onCheckedChange={setDraft} />
<Button>Save changes</Button>
usage.notes: Don't. A switch beside a Save button promises something it does not do: it says the setting took effect, and it did not. That is a Checkbox — a value you are about to submit. The distinction is the entire reason both components exist.

behavior.summary: A native input[type=checkbox] carrying role="switch". The platform supplies Space-to-toggle, the checked state and form participation; the role changes only how it is announced — "Notifications, on" rather than "Notifications, checked".

decisions.decision: A setting, not a value waiting to be submitted
decisions.why: This is the whole reason the component exists separately from Checkbox. A checkbox is a value you are about to submit with a form; a switch takes effect the moment it moves. Getting this wrong is worse than a styling mistake: a switch beside a Save button promises something the control does not do.

decisions.decision: role="switch" on a native checkbox, not a div
decisions.why: The role is the only thing that has to change. Rebuilding the keyboard handling, the checked state and the form participation on a div is how a switch ends up not announcing its state, and there is nothing to gain from it.

decisions.decision: No indeterminate state
decisions.why: A setting is on or off. "Partly on" is not a state a system can be in — a parent summarising children that disagree is a Checkbox, which has exactly that state for exactly that reason.

decisions.decision: The label does not change with the state
decisions.why: aria-checked already says which way it is set. Swapping the label to "Turn off notifications" means the name and the state contradict each other, and a screen reader announces "Turn off notifications, on" — a double negative the user has to unpick. The same rule toggle-button follows.

decisions.decision: Activation is guarded, not disabled
decisions.why: As everywhere in this system: aria-disabled plus a refused activation, so the switch stays focusable and keeps announcing which way it is set. readOnly is no help — it has no effect on a checkbox.

base.summary: A track the thumb slides along. The track's fill is the state, and the thumb's position says the same thing a second way, so the setting is never carried by colour alone.

tokens.track inline-size: size.control.lg — the track is twice the thumb's diameter plus its inset, which is what gives the thumb somewhere to travel; borrowing a control step keeps it on the scale
tokens.track block-size: size.icon.md — the same height as a checkbox's box, so a switch and a checkbox in one settings column line up
tokens.track background (off): theme.bg.muted — the most recessed surface, so an off switch reads as an empty channel rather than a filled control
tokens.track border: border.default solid theme.border.strong when off — an off track needs its own boundary at the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of a control's edge, because its fill is nearly its surroundings. On, the accent fill is the boundary and the border matches it
tokens.thumb size: space.gap.lg — a spacing step rather than the icon scale, because the thumb is a mark and not a glyph, the same reasoning the radio's dot follows. At 16px it fills 89% of the track's inner height, which is the proportion a switch reads as; smaller and it looks like a dot rattling in a channel
tokens.thumb background (on): theme.fg.on-accent — the only foreground permitted on the accent fill, and it inverts with the accent in the dark scheme
tokens.thumb inset: space.0-5 at both ends of the travel — tighter than the checkbox's inset on purpose, since a large thumb wants a couple of pixels of channel showing rather than a gutter
tokens.thumb travel: transform, not a layout property: the thumb slides rather than reflowing, so nothing around it moves
tokens.gap between label and description: none — the label and the description each carry line-height leading, which already reads as 7px of separation. A gap on top of that made 11px and read as two unrelated lines
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — drawn on the track, and the offset is kept: a pill this small has no room for a flush ring to read as separate from its own edge
tokens.transition: motion.interactive.duration with motion.interactive.easing, on the thumb's transform and the track's fill

name: table
title: Table
description: Rows of records compared column by column, with a caption, optional sorting and a horizontal scroll that keyboard users can reach.

props.name: caption
props.description: The table's name. Required.
props.summary: The table's name. Required.
use: A noun phrase naming the data: "Open invoices", "Deploys in the last 24 hours".
dont: Instructions or a summary of the data. Those belong in text above the table, where everyone reads them.
props.a11y: Rendered as `<caption>`, which names the table and its scroll region. Without it a reader who lands on the table hears only its dimensions.

props.name: hideCaption
props.description: Keeps the caption as the accessible name but hides it visually.
props.summary: Keeps the caption as the accessible name but hides it visually.
use: A table directly under a heading that already says the same thing.
dont: Hiding a caption nothing visible repeats. Sighted readers need the name too.
props.a11y: The caption is visually hidden, not removed, so the table is still named. Web only.

props.name: columns
props.description: The columns, in reading order.
props.summary: The columns, in reading order: each with a `key`, a `header`, and optionally a `cell` renderer, `align`, `sortable` and `rowHeader`.
use: `rowHeader: true` on the column that identifies each record — usually the first — so every cell in the row is announced with it.
`align: "end"` on numeric columns, so digits line up.
`cell` to render a Badge, a Link or a formatted number from the row.
dont: More than one `rowHeader` column. A row has one identity.
An empty `header` for an actions column. Name it — "Actions" — and hide it visually if it must be; an unnamed column is announced as nothing.
props.a11y: `header` becomes a `<th scope="col">`; the `rowHeader` column's cells become `<th scope="row">`, which is what lets a screen reader announce "INV-204, Amount, 120.00" instead of a bare number.

props.name: rows
props.description: The records, in the order they are shown.
props.summary: The records, in the order they are shown.
use: Already sorted to match `sort`. The table renders the order it is given.
dont: Thousands of rows at once. There is no virtualisation in this version — paginate with Pagination.

props.name: getRowKey
props.description: A stable identity for each row.
props.summary: A stable identity for each row.
use: The record's own id.
dont: The array index. Sorting reorders the rows, and an index key reuses the wrong row's DOM — and any focus inside it.

props.name: sort
props.description: Which column the rows are currently sorted by, if any.
props.summary: Which column the rows are currently sorted by, if any.
use: Reflecting the order the caller actually applied — from memory, from the server, from the URL.
dont: Setting it without sorting `rows`. The header would claim an order the data does not have.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-sort` on that column's header, and only that one.

props.name: onSortChange
props.description: Called when the reader asks to sort by a column.
props.summary: Called when the reader asks to sort by a column. Required for any column marked `sortable` to render a control.
use: Updating `sort` and re-ordering, or re-fetching, the rows.
dont: Marking columns `sortable` without it. With no handler, no sort buttons are rendered — the header would offer a control that does nothing.
props.a11y: The sort control is a `<button>` inside the header cell, named by the header text, so it is reachable by Tab and announced as a button.

props.name: density
props.description: How tall each row is.
props.summary: How tall each row is.
use: `compact` for a dense operational table read by people who live in it.
dont: `compact` to fit more columns. It changes row height, not width — fewer columns is the fix.
props.a11y: Visual only. Interactive content in a compact row still needs a target the size of a control.

props.name: empty
props.description: What to show in place of the rows when there are none.
props.summary: What to show in place of the rows when there are none.
use: An EmptyState saying why there is nothing here and what to do about it.
dont: Leaving it out on a table that can be empty. A header row over nothing reads as a rendering failure.
props.a11y: Rendered in a single row spanning every column, so the table's structure stays valid and the message is read as part of it.

props.name: className
props.description: Extra classes on the scroll region, for placement.
props.summary: Extra classes on the scroll region, for placement.
use: Placing the table in the page's layout.
dont: Striping rows or boxing the table. Rules separate rows in this system; zebra stripes and a card around the table are both declined.

usage.when: The commonest case: records with an identity column, a status and a number, sorted by the caller.
usage.example:
<Table
  caption="Open invoices"
  columns={[
    { key: "number", header: "Invoice", rowHeader: true, cell: (inv) => <Link href={inv.url}>{inv.number}</Link> },
    { key: "due", header: "Due", sortable: true },
    { key: "amount", header: "Amount", align: "end", sortable: true },
    { key: "status", header: "Status", cell: (inv) => <Badge variant={inv.overdue ? "danger" : "neutral"}>{inv.status}</Badge> },
  ]}
  rows={sortedInvoices}
  getRowKey={(inv) => inv.id}
  sort={sort}
  onSortChange={setSort}
/>
usage.notes: The row leads somewhere through a Link in its row-header cell, not through a clickable row. `sortedInvoices` is sorted by the caller to match `sort` — the table renders order, it does not create it.

usage.case: A table under a heading that already names it
usage.when: The section heading and the caption would say the same words.
usage.example:
<Heading level={2}>Deploys</Heading>
<Table caption="Deploys" hideCaption columns={columns} rows={deploys} getRowKey={(d) => d.id} empty={<EmptyState title="No deploys yet" />} />
usage.notes: The caption stays as the accessible name and only its visible copy goes. `empty` is passed because a deploy list can genuinely be empty, and a header over nothing reads as broken.

usage.when: A set of projects, each with a preview image and a description, chosen between rather than compared.
usage.example: <Table caption="Projects" columns={[{ key: "preview", header: "Preview" }, { key: "description", header: "Description" }]} rows={projects} getRowKey={(p) => p.id} />
usage.notes: Don't. Nobody compares descriptions down a column — each project is read on its own, which is a gallery of Cards. The table is for the question "which of these is larger, older, failing".

behavior.summary: A real `<table>` with a `<caption>`, `<thead>`, `<th scope>` headers and `aria-sort` on the sorted column, inside a focusable scroll region. Data-driven — `columns` and `rows` — like Breadcrumbs and SideNav, because hand-assembled `<tr>`/`<td>` markup is where scope, header association and sort state go missing. Proposed primitive: `getTableProps` in `packages/primitives/src/table.ts`, owning the sort cycle and the header and cell attributes; it is a proposal, not yet a commitment.

decisions.decision: A Table is for rows compared by column, and nothing else
decisions.why: The test from Card's contract, from the other side: if the reader's question is "which of these is larger, older, failing", the answer lives in a column, and only a table keeps the column. A list of things each read on its own is a list or a gallery of Cards. A layout grid is CSS grid. A `<table>` used for layout is announced as a data table, row and column counts included, which is noise at best.

decisions.decision: `caption` is required
decisions.why: A table's accessible name is how a reader who lands on it — or lists the page's tables — knows which one it is. A `<caption>` is the one naming mechanism every screen reader supports for tables. When the heading above the table already says the same thing, `hideCaption` keeps the name and drops the visible duplicate; the name itself is not optional.

decisions.decision: Sorting is controlled and the table never reorders data itself
decisions.why: The caller is the only one who knows whether sorting happens in memory, on the server, or across pages the table never sees. A table that sorted its own `rows` would be silently wrong the moment the data is paginated. So the table reports the request through `onSortChange` and renders whatever order it is given. The header carries `aria-sort` on the sorted column only — on every column it is noise — and the sort control is a real `<button>` inside the `<th>`, never a clickable header cell.

decisions.decision: The sort cycle is ascending, descending, then back to ascending
decisions.why: A three-state cycle through "unsorted" makes the third click on a header undo the reader's choice with no visible reason, and the original order is rarely meaningful — if it is, it deserves a column of its own. Two states, always predictable.

decisions.decision: Narrow viewports scroll the table; they do not reflow it into cards
decisions.why: Reflowing rows into stacked cards on a phone destroys exactly the comparison the table exists for, and WCAG 1.4.10 exempts data tables from reflow for that reason. The table scrolls horizontally inside its own region instead. That region is focusable — `tabindex="0"`, `role="region"`, named by the caption — because a keyboard user has no other way to scroll it. That costs one tab stop, and it is worth it.

decisions.decision: Rows are not clickable
decisions.why: A clickable `<tr>` is not focusable, has no role a screen reader announces as actionable, and steals text selection from a reader trying to copy a value. A row that leads somewhere puts a Link in its row-header cell; a row with actions puts Buttons in a cell of its own. Both are real controls that keyboard and assistive tech already understand.

decisions.decision: Out of this version: row selection, sticky headers, column resizing, virtualisation
decisions.why: Each one is a real need and each changes the table's semantics or its ARIA pattern — selection turns it toward `grid` with roving focus, which is a different keyboard contract entirely. Shipping the static, sortable table first means the common case does not pay for the machinery of the rare one. Each is its own gate 1.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: `<table>` with `<caption>`, `<th scope="col">` headers, `<th scope="row">` for the column marked `rowHeader`, and `aria-sort` on the sorted header; the scroll wrapper is `role="region"` labelled by the caption. React Native has no table: there is no core component and the platform screen readers have no table navigation to offer. On native the table renders as a `FlatList` with `accessibilityRole="list"`, one row per item, and each row is a single accessible element whose `accessibilityLabel` reads header and value pairs in column order ("Invoice, INV-204. Amount, 120.00. Status, Overdue.") — that is what makes a record usable without column navigation. Sorting is offered on native through a header row of `accessibilityRole="button"` controls carrying `accessibilityState` with `selected`. `hideCaption` and the scroll region are web-only. Rata-drawn (decision N5): neither platform has a table control in React Native, so the rows are drawn inside the core `FlatList`. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: Edge to edge and divided, with no box of its own: a table sits on whatever surface the page gives it, and its rows are separated by rules rather than by stripes or cards. This is the construction the playground's own `.pg-table` already uses, promoted.

tokens.background: transparent — the table takes the surface it sits on
tokens.row divider: border.default solid theme.border.default, on each row's block-end edge
tokens.numeric cell alignment: end, with tabular figures so digits line up down the column

header.summary: Column headers set as labels: smaller and quieter than the data, because the reader looks at them once and at the rows many times.

tokens.color: theme.fg.muted — verified at AA-text on canvas, surface and subtle
tokens.divider below the header: border.default solid theme.border.strong — heavier than a row rule, so the header reads as the boundary of the data

compact.summary: Tighter rows for a dense operational table. Only the block padding moves; type does not shrink, because a compact table is read just as closely.

sort-control.summary: The button inside a sortable column header. It fills the header cell so the whole label is the target.

tokens.color: currentColor — the header's own muted label colour
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

scroll-region.summary: The wrapper that scrolls horizontally when the columns do not fit. It is focusable, so it needs the ring like any other tab stop.

tokens.focus ring: focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible
tokens.border-radius: radius.inner — only so the ring has corners

name: tabs
title: Tabs
description: Several panels, one shown at a time, chosen from a row of tabs.

props.name: items
props.description: The tabs and their panels, in the order they are read.
props.summary: The tabs and their panels, in the order they are read.
use: Two to about six panels of one thing seen different ways: an invoice's details, its history, its notes.
dont: Steps in a sequence. Tabs are peers a reader moves between freely; a process with an order and a completion state is not this.
One tab. A tablist of one is a heading with extra keyboard behaviour.
Navigation between pages. These are regions of one page — a destination belongs in a nav, where it has an address.
props.a11y: Each entry becomes a `tab` pointing at its `tabpanel` with `aria-controls`, and the panel points back with `aria-labelledby`. The selected tab carries `aria-selected`; the rest are `hidden`, which keeps them out of both the accessibility tree and the tab order.

props.name: value
props.description: Which panel is showing. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Which panel is showing. Makes the component controlled.
use: Driving the selection from a URL, so a tab can be linked to and survives a reload.
dont: Passing it alongside `defaultValue`.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Starting panel for uncontrolled tabs. Defaults to the first.
props.summary: Starting panel for uncontrolled tabs. Defaults to the first.
use: Opening on something other than the first panel.

props.name: onValueChange
props.summary: Called with the panel that should be shown.
use: Controlled mode, to set `value`.
Loading a panel's data the first time it is opened.
dont: Assuming it fires once per tab. Under automatic activation it fires for every tab the arrow keys pass through — which is the reason `activation` exists.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the tablist. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element.
props.summary: Accessible name for the tablist.
use: Naming what the tabs divide: "Invoice" for a set covering one invoice's details, history and notes.
dont: The word "tabs", which the role already says.
props.a11y: Becomes the tablist's `aria-label`. Required unless `labelledBy` names an element — a tablist with no name is announced as a bare tablist.

props.name: labelledBy
props.summary: Names the tablist from an element the reader can see.
use: Pointing at the heading the tabs sit under, so the name changes with it.
dont: Passing it alongside `label` and expecting both. This one wins, and never renders the other.
props.a11y: Wins over `label`, because it points at text on screen.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Which axis the tabs run along.
use: `vertical` for a long set, or beside a wide panel.
dont: `vertical` for two or three short tabs, where a row is easier to scan.
props.a11y: Announced as `aria-orientation`, and it decides which arrow keys move: left/right on the horizontal axis, up/down on the vertical. Announcing it is a promise the component keeps.

props.name: activation
props.description: Whether the arrow keys select as they move.
props.summary: Whether the arrow keys select as they move.
use: `automatic` — the default, and what a reader expects — when the panels are already on the client.
`manual` when opening a panel costs something: a request, a render nobody asked for.
dont: `automatic` over panels that fetch. Arrowing across four tabs fires four requests, and the reader wanted the fifth.
props.a11y: Both are conforming. `manual` moves focus and waits for Enter or Space; `automatic` selects as focus moves. A disabled tab is reachable either way — this system's disabled controls stay focusable — and selection does not follow focus onto it.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the wrapper, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Constraining the width, or spacing the set from what surrounds it.
dont: Making it look like a segmented control. They are different patterns, and the appearance is the only cue a sighted reader gets — which is why this component stopped offering that appearance itself.

usage.when: The commonest case: panels of the same subject, all already loaded.
usage.example:
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  items={[
    { value: "details", label: "Details", content: <Details /> },
    { value: "history", label: "History", content: <History /> },
    { value: "notes", label: "Notes", content: <Notes /> },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: Automatic activation, which is the default: the panels are on the client, so selecting as the arrows move costs nothing and is what a reader expects.

usage.case: Panels that cost something to open
usage.when: A panel fetches, so arrowing past it must not.
usage.example:
<Tabs
  label="Invoice"
  activation="manual"
  value={tab}
  onValueChange={(next) => {
    setTab(next);
    load(next);
  }}
  items={items}
/>
usage.notes: `manual` is the whole point here: under automatic, arrowing from the first tab to the fourth fires three requests for panels nobody wanted to see. Controlled as well, so the tab can come from the URL and survive a reload.

usage.case: Don't: tabs standing in for a segmented control
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. Empty panels are the tell: nothing is being revealed, so this is a question being answered — `SegmentedControl`, which is what that component is for. Tabs tell a screen reader that regions are being shown and hidden, and the answer here would sit inside a region nobody submits.

behavior.summary: A `tablist` of `tab` buttons over a set of `tabpanel` regions, with roving tabindex and arrow-key movement along the declared axis. Every tab points at its panel and every panel back at its tab, which is the pairing that makes a tablist a tablist.
