decisions.decision: Which of three, when they all look like one bar of options
decisions.why: Three components here can look like one enclosed bar of options, so each one's contract says which is which. SegmentedControl is a question with a short fixed set of answers: single, always filled, cannot be cleared. ToggleButtonGroup is the same ARIA pattern with a wider API — multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants — so reach for it when you need any of those. Tabs is a different pattern entirely: tabs reveal a region, each naming a panel and each panel naming its tab, and if what is being chosen is which content is shown rather than what gets submitted, it is Tabs — which can be drawn to look exactly like the other two and is still announced as a tablist.

decisions.decision: It is not a segmented control, and no longer looks like one either
decisions.why:
`SegmentedControl` is the component for that, and the two are not the same control however they are painted. A segmented control picks a VALUE: it is a radiogroup, every option is announced as a choice, and the answer is submitted with the rest of the form. Tabs reveal a REGION: moving between them changes what is on screen rather than what will be sent. Using one for the other is not a style error — a radiogroup standing in for tabs tells a screen reader a form is being filled in, and tabs standing in for a form control hide the answer inside a region nobody submits.

Tabs carried a segmented appearance for a while, added when that look had nothing of its own. Once it did, two components able to draw the same bar made the pair harder to tell apart in precisely the place the difference matters — so the appearance went with it. Tabs look like tabs.

decisions.decision: Activation is the caller's choice, because it has a cost
decisions.why: Automatic — the arrow keys select as they move — is what APG recommends and what a reader expects, but arrowing past four tabs then renders four panels. Manual moves focus and waits for Enter or Space, which is right when a panel fetches something. The wrong one is not cosmetic: automatic over an expensive panel fires requests nobody asked for.

decisions.decision: An items array rather than children
decisions.why: The component owns the id wiring that makes a tablist a tablist — every tab pointing at its panel, every panel back at its tab — and that is the error-prone part. Handing it out to be assembled would mean cloning elements to inject ids, and a mis-wired pair looks perfectly fine on screen. The trade is that a tab is a label and some content rather than arbitrary structure; if that stops being enough the API should change rather than the caller working around it.

decisions.decision: Every panel stays mounted, all but one hidden
decisions.why: Unmounting would throw away whatever state each panel held — a half-filled form, a scroll position, an expanded row — every time the reader glanced at another tab. `hidden` keeps them out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order without destroying them.

decisions.decision: A panel is in the tab order even with nothing focusable inside it
decisions.why: Without `tabIndex={0}` on the panel, Tab from the tablist skips a panel of plain text entirely and the reader never reaches the content the tab just promised them.

decisions.decision: A horizontal strip scrolls; it never wraps
decisions.why:
A tab keeps its label on one line, so a strip with more tabs than its column is wide has to give somewhere. It scrolls sideways, the same bargain TopNav's list makes and for the same reason: a strip that grows to a second row moves everything below it, and a wrapped row of tabs reads as a mistake rather than as a choice. Before this it did neither and simply overflowed, which on a narrow viewport took the whole page into horizontal scroll — one strip of six families dragging every column of prose beside it.

Two details are load-bearing. The rule the markers sit on is drawn on the scrolling element itself, so it stays put while the tabs move under it. And the list carries bottom padding of exactly the rule's width, because the selected tab's marker hangs below its tab to cover that rule and a scroll container clips whatever hangs outside it — without the padding the marker loses its bottom half the moment a strip becomes scrollable. The cost is that the marker now sits flush on the rule rather than over it, which is one device pixel.

The scrollbar is hidden. This is a row of controls rather than a region to explore, every tab is reachable with the arrow keys regardless of what is on screen, and the marker under the selected tab already says there is more than one.

base.summary: The set. Tabs read as an edge with a marker on it, and only that — there was a segmented appearance for a while, added when that look had no component of its own. SegmentedControl is that component now, and two things able to draw the same bar made the pair hard to tell apart in exactly the place the difference matters.

tab.summary: One tab. The resting tone is the secondary text colour, so the selected one reads as emphasised rather than the rest reading as dimmed.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

tab-selected.summary: The panel you are looking at. Marked twice over: the bar is the visual cue and aria-selected is the announced one, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

tokens.indicator: theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, straddling the list's rule so the tab reads as joined to its panel

panel.summary: The region a tab reveals. Focusable even with nothing focusable inside, so Tab from the tablist reaches it.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

example:
<Tabs
        label="Invoice"
        items={[
          { value: "details", label: "Details", content: "Amount, dates, and the client." },
          { value: "history", label: "History", content: "Every change, most recent first." },
          { value: "notes", label: "Notes", content: "Anything the team wrote down." },
        ]}
      />

name: text
title: Text
description: Body and supporting text at a named role from the type scale.

props.name: children
props.description: The text.
props.summary: The text.
use: A paragraph, a sentence of help text, an eyebrow label.
dont: Block content inside `as="p"`. A paragraph cannot contain a list or another paragraph, and the browser will silently close it early.
props.a11y: Plain content. Nothing here is announced as anything but text, which is the point.

props.name: as
props.description: Whether this is a block of text or a run inside one.
props.summary: Whether this is a block of text or a run inside one.
use: `span` for text inside a sentence, a row or a control's label area.
dont: `span` for a paragraph. It is not a block, so the page's spacing rules will not apply to it.
props.a11y: Neither element carries a role, so this changes nothing that is announced — it changes what the text is, structurally, for spacing and for selection.

props.name: role
props.description: Which step of the scale this text is set at.
props.summary: Which step of the scale this text is set at.
use: `supporting` for help text under a field, a timestamp, secondary metadata in a row.
`large` for a standfirst — one paragraph introducing a page, set above body size.
`label` for an uppercase eyebrow over a section or a group of fields.
dont: `supporting` to mean disabled. It is smaller, not dimmer, and it is still meant to be read — `tone` is the prop that changes emphasis.
props.a11y: `label` renders uppercase through `text-transform`, so the text stays lowercase in the accessibility tree and a screen reader does not spell it out letter by letter. Typing it in capitals would.

props.name: tone
props.description: Which of the three documented foreground steps it takes.
props.summary: Which of the three documented foreground steps it takes.
use: `secondary` for text that supports the primary content and is still read in full.
`muted` for the least prominent text on a surface — a placeholder-like hint, a disabled row's caption.
dont: A status or accent colour. Those belong to a role, and running text carrying one reads as a link or an error; Notice is the component for a coloured message.
`muted` for anything load-bearing. It is the lowest of the three and the first to fail on an unusual background.
props.a11y: All three are contrast-verified against canvas, surface and subtle. None of them is below the text floor — this prop cannot make text fail contrast on a documented background, which is why it is a closed set of three rather than a colour.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The margin or measure the page wants, neither of which this component owns.
dont: Overriding size or colour. Those are `role` and `tone`, and a hand-written value drifts from the scale the moment the seed moves.

usage.case: A standfirst under a page title
usage.when: One paragraph introducing a page, set above body size so it reads as the way in rather than as the first paragraph of the content.
usage.example: <Text role="large" tone="secondary">Every value in this system comes from a token, and every token says what it is for.</Text>
usage.notes: `secondary` rather than `primary`: it supports the title above it and is still read in full. One of these per page — a second stops being an introduction.

usage.when: A line of guidance that belongs to the control above it.
usage.example: <Text role="supporting" tone="muted">Used for billing receipts only.</Text>
usage.notes: `supporting` is smaller, not dimmer — `tone` is what changes emphasis, and the two are separate so help text can be small and still fully legible. If the field is a TextField, its own `description` prop already does this and wires up the `aria-describedby`; reach for this only outside one.

usage.when: A short uppercase label naming a group of fields or a section of a settings page.
usage.example: <Text role="label" tone="secondary">Notifications</Text>
usage.notes: The capitals come from `text-transform`, so the text stays lowercase in the accessibility tree. Typed in capitals it may be spelled out letter by letter. This is also the right answer when a `<Heading>` was tempting but nothing navigates to the label.

usage.when: Part of a line needs a different step or tone from the rest of it.
usage.example: <Text>Last synced <Text as="span" tone="muted">four minutes ago</Text>.</Text>
usage.notes: `span` because it is not a block — a nested `p` would close the outer one early and the page's spacing rules would apply to something that is half a sentence.

usage.when: The message is a warning the reader has to act on.
usage.example: <Text tone="secondary">Your trial ends in three days.</Text>
usage.notes: Don't lean on this and then colour it — `tone` is deliberately closed to three neutral steps, because a status colour on running text reads as a link or an error. A message that needs a colour needs Notice, which has the role tokens, the icon and somewhere to put the action.

behavior.summary:
A `

` or a `` set to one named role of the type scale. No primitive and no state.

decisions.decision: Headings are a different component
decisions.why: A heading enters the document outline and is a navigation target; body text is neither. That is a difference in semantics rather than in looks, which is this system's test for splitting a component — the same test that separated Tabs from SegmentedControl. A single `as="h2"` prop here could not require a level only when the element happens to be a heading, and a heading without a level is the bug both components exist to prevent.

decisions.decision: `as` offers `p` and `span` and nothing else
decisions.why: Those are the two things running text is: a block of prose, or a run inside one. `div` is the one that would turn this into a layout wrapper — and a `<div>` holding text is how a component like this stops being about type and starts being about boxes. A text block that must contain block content is not one paragraph and should not pretend to be.

decisions.decision: `tone` is part of it, even though the type roles carry no colour
decisions.why: The type scale is size, weight and line-height only, so a caller styling text still has to pick a foreground — and picking wrongly is this system's most common token error, which `internal/vibe-tests` exists to measure. Three named steps that map onto the three documented and contrast-verified `theme.fg.*` values make the correct choice the shortest one. It is deliberately not open-ended: a role colour or a status colour on running text is a different decision, and Notice owns it.

decisions.decision: `code` is not a role here
decisions.why: `type.code` exists, but inline code is a `<code>` ELEMENT — a semantic claim about the content, not a size. Offering it as a role would mean either rendering the wrong element or accepting `as="code" role="code"`, which says the same thing twice. Inline code belongs to a base layer styling `code` directly, which `@rata/css` does not ship yet and which is a separate gap from this component.

decisions.decision: No line clamping in this version
decisions.why: `-webkit-line-clamp` is the only way to truncate at a line count and it needs three coupled declarations plus a fixed display mode, which changes how the element lays out — and truncated text needs its full value reachable some other way or the content is simply gone. It deserves its own pass rather than riding along with the scale.

base.summary: One type role and one foreground step. No box: text has no padding, no background and no margin of its own.

tokens.font-size: the chosen role's size — type.body.size, type.large.size, type.supporting.size or type.label.size
tokens.margin: space.0 — the page owns the space between blocks, for the reason Heading's contract gives

label.summary: The label role carries two things the others do not, and they come from the scale rather than from here.

tokens.letter-spacing: type.label.letter-spacing — uppercase text needs the extra tracking to stay readable, which is why that step exists

tone.summary: The three documented foreground steps for text, and the reason this prop exists at all: it is the shortest path to the right colour, so nobody reaches for a palette token.

tokens.all three: contrast-verified against theme.bg.canvas, theme.bg.surface and theme.bg.subtle — see the contrast page

name: text-field
title: Input: Text field
description: Single-line text input with label, helper text, and validation states.

props.name: label
props.description: The field's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The field's label. Always required — `labelHidden` can take it off screen, but nothing removes it.
use: Always. Every field has a label, whether or not it is visible.
dont: Placeholder-as-label — the placeholder disappears on first keystroke, taking the field's name with it. `labelHidden` exists so the visual choice never costs the name.
Passing an empty string. An empty label is an unnamed field, which is the one thing this component will not render; hide it with `labelHidden` instead.
props.a11y: Rendered as a real `<label for>` bound to the input's id, so clicking it focuses the field. Still a real label when hidden — only its pixels go away.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A field whose purpose is already unambiguous on screen — a search input beside a magnifier icon, a filter in a toolbar column with its own heading.
A dense row of fields under a table header that names each column, where repeating the name per row would be noise.
dont: Hiding a label because the form looks crowded. The label is the last thing to cut; if space is short the layout budget is wrong.
Hiding it and then relying on `placeholder` to say what the field is — the placeholder is gone the moment someone types, and this prop exists precisely so that trade is never necessary.
Hiding it when the field's only other context is its position. Position is not a name, and it is the first thing lost when a layout reflows.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so the accessible name is unchanged — it is clipped, not removed. It is not `display: none`, which would take the name with it. The required marker goes off screen with it; `aria-required` still carries that.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the input. Defaults to a generated one.
use: Linking an external `<label>` or an outside `aria-describedby` to this field.
Deep-linking or scroll-to-error, where the id has to be predictable across renders.
dont: Reusing one id across two fields — the derived description and message ids would collide too.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height and inline padding. Text size does not change with it.
props.summary: Control height and inline padding, from the `size.control.*` scale. Text size does not change with it.
use: `md` everywhere by default.
`sm` inside dense rows, table cells, and filter bars.
`lg` for a single prominent field on a sparse surface — a sign-in form, an empty-state search.
dont: Shrinking to `sm` to fit a cramped layout — fix the layout budget instead.

Expecting the text to grow with it. All three sizes set the same text size, so `size` buys a bigger target for the same field rather than a louder one — the same bargain `Button` makes, which is what lets a field and a button sit in one row and measure alike.
Mixing sizes down a single form. The fields are one set, so they measure as one set.
Setting height or padding yourself; the size prop is the only supported way to change either.

Reaching for the native HTML `size` attribute — it is deliberately shadowed by this prop. It measures a visible width in characters, a pre-CSS legacy, and width here belongs to the form via `className`.
props.a11y: Visual only. A larger control is a larger pointer target, which is a usability gain rather than an accessibility claim — none of the three sizes falls below the system's control heights.

props.name: status
props.description: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and the ring.
props.summary: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and which ring token the field wears.
use: `validating` for an in-flight async check, such as a uniqueness lookup.
`invalid` once a check has actually failed, paired with a `message` saying how to fix it.
`valid` only where confirmation carries information — a passing async check, not every filled field.
dont: Deriving it from whether `message` is non-empty — `idle` and `valid` are different states and must stay distinguishable.
`invalid` while the user is still typing their first attempt; validate on blur or submit.
props.a11y: `invalid` sets `aria-invalid`; `validating` sets `aria-busy`. Neither is conveyed by the ring colour alone, which is why the `message` is not optional in those states.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text under the input.
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the input — format hints, constraints, why the field is asked for.
use: Stating a constraint before it is violated, which is cheaper than an error after.
dont: Error text — that is `message`, which is announced and cleared with the status.
Text that only matters once, which belongs in the surrounding form copy.
props.a11y: Always in `aria-describedby`, in front of the message, so the constraint is heard before the failure.

props.name: message
props.description: Status-dependent message under the input: the error, confirmation, or in-flight note.
props.summary: Status-dependent message under the input: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.
use: Saying how to fix an `invalid` field, in the user's terms rather than the validator's.
dont: Leaving a stale message when the status returns to `idle` — it stays rendered but drops out of the description chain, which reads as a live region emptying.
Restating the label ('Email is invalid') where the fix ('Use the format name@example.com') would help.
props.a11y: Announced politely, and joins `aria-describedby` only while the status is not `idle`.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.
props.summary: Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable, and announced.
use: A field temporarily unavailable but still meaningful to read — awaiting a prior answer, say.
dont: Fields you need excluded from form submission: this emits `readOnly`, and a readOnly field still submits.
Permanently uneditable values, which should be text rather than a dead input.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native `disabled` attribute.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the field required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.summary: Marks the field as required to assistive technology and in the label.
use: Fields the form genuinely cannot be submitted without.
dont: Marking every field required, which makes the marker carry no information.
Relying on it for validation — it announces the requirement, it does not enforce it.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-required`. The visible required marker is the label's job, not the attribute's.

props.name: className
props.description: Class for the wrapper. The input itself is styled by the system.
props.summary: Class for the field's wrapper — the label, input and helper text are styled by the system.
use: Placing the field in a form's layout: a column span, a width, a margin token the parent cannot express.
dont: Restyling the input through a descendant selector. The border, ring and height are the approved token mapping, and overriding them here puts a second answer in a place the contract cannot see.
Setting a width on the wrapper to imply a maximum input length — that is a `maxLength` and, better, a `description` stating the constraint before it is violated.

usage.case: Plain labelled field with a format hint
usage.when: The default case. Helper text states the constraint before it can be violated.
usage.example: <TextField label="Email" description="We'll only use this for receipts." />

usage.when: A check has run and failed. The message says how to fix it, not merely that it is wrong.
usage.example:
<TextField
  label="Email"
  status="invalid"
  message="Use the format name@example.com"
/>
usage.notes: `aria-invalid` is set and the message joins the description chain; the danger ring is the visual half of the same signal, never the whole of it.

usage.when: A server-side check is running against what the user typed.
usage.example:
<TextField
  label="Workspace URL"
  status="validating"
  message="Checking availability…"
/>
usage.notes: `validating` is for a check on this field's own value — not for a pending form submit, which belongs to the submit button's `loading`.

usage.when: The one situation `valid` is for: a check ran, it passed, and saying so tells the user something they could not otherwise know.
usage.example:
<TextField
  label="Workspace URL"
  status="valid"
  message="acme.example.com is available"
/>
usage.notes: `valid` earns its place only where the confirmation carries information. A green ring on every correctly-filled field teaches people to ignore the ring, so it is worth nothing on the field where a check actually passed. Note this state sets no aria-invalid and no aria-busy — the ring and the message are the whole of it, which is why the message is not optional here either: a ring alone would be colour-only information.

usage.when: The field depends on an answer the user has not given yet.
usage.example:
<TextField
  label="State"
  disabled
  description="Choose a country first."
/>
usage.notes: Stays focusable and announced. Remember it still submits its value — clear it yourself if that matters.

usage.when: A search input beside a magnifier, or a column of fields under a header that names them — where a visible label per field would be noise.
usage.example: <TextField label="Search" labelHidden placeholder="Search…" />
usage.notes: `labelHidden` hides the pixels, not the name: the `<label for>` is still rendered and still bound, so the field is announced as "Search" exactly as it would be with the label visible. Note the `placeholder` is a convenience here, not the name — it disappears on the first keystroke, which is why the label still has to exist.

behavior.summary: The box of a single-line input, and its validation rings. Label/description/message association, the validation semantics and the disabled contract all come from Field, which this composes — the caller owns the `id` and every other id is derived from it, so association cannot be hand-wired wrong.

decisions.decision: `readOnly` is the disabled mechanism, not the native `disabled` attribute
decisions.why: Consistent with the system-wide rule that disabled controls stay focusable and screen-reader discoverable. A button blocks activation in its click guard; an input has no activation to guard, so `readOnly` is the analogue. Consequence to know: a readOnly field still submits its value, where a disabled one does not.

decisions.decision: One four-state `status` enum rather than separate booleans
decisions.why: `idle | validating | valid | invalid` maps one-to-one onto the four ring mappings in the token recipe, and drives `aria-invalid` and `aria-busy`. Separate `invalid`/`validating` booleans would make contradictory combinations expressible.

decisions.decision: The message is `aria-live="polite"`, not `role="alert"`
decisions.why: The message is already in `aria-describedby` whenever the status is not idle, so an assertive live region would announce it twice — once on change, once when focus lands. The tradeoff accepted: an error appearing while focus is elsewhere is announced at the next pause rather than immediately.

decisions.decision: The message joins `aria-describedby` only once the status leaves `idle`
decisions.why: An empty or stale message element in the description chain makes every field announce trailing silence, and `idle` is a real state distinct from `valid` — not merely 'no error yet'.

base.summary: The input's BOX, and nothing around it. The label, required marker, helper text, message and disabled dimming are Field's recipe — this component composes Field and overrides only inside the control, which is the split that lets Select and TextArea cost a stylesheet each.

tokens.input font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the text. The same constant the button family uses, so a field and a button in one row measure their text alike
tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes. Together with padding-inline this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.padding-inline: space.control.padding-inline.md — and the sm / lg steps at the other sizes
tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2, drawn as an inset shadow so the fill recedes 2px while the border stays border.1 and the outer edge does not move. Idle only — the validation rings occupy the same 2px and box-shadow does not accumulate
tokens.focus border-color: theme.fg.primary — the same tone as the outline, so the two read as one stroke instead of a dark ring around a lighter edge. The width is never touched
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary, offset space.0 — deliberately NOT theme.focus-ring, the only such departure in the library. It gives 16.75:1 against the field's fill where theme.focus-ring gives 4.31:1, so the indicator is stronger; the cost is that focus here does not match focus on a Button. An outline rather than a thicker border because outlines are out of flow: this control sets height but not width, so a wider border would widen the field

name: textarea
title: Textarea
description: A labelled multi-line text input.

props.name: label
props.description: The control's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
props.summary: The control's label. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.
use: A short noun phrase naming what goes in it: "Release notes", not "Type your release notes".
dont: Leaving it off because a placeholder says the same thing. The placeholder is gone on the first keystroke.
props.a11y: Bound to the control by Field, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

props.name: rows
props.description: How many lines of text the control shows before it scrolls.
props.summary: How many lines of text the control shows before it scrolls.
use: Three for a note, eight or more for something someone will draft in.
A number that matches what you expect, so the reader can see how much is wanted of them.
dont: One. A single-line control is a `TextField`, and a one-row textarea is that with worse keyboard behaviour — Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting.

props.name: resize
props.description: Whether the reader may drag the control taller.
props.summary: Whether the reader may drag the control taller.
use: `none` only where a taller control would break the layout around it — a fixed-height panel, a row in a dense table.
dont: `none` as a default because the handle looks untidy. It is the cheapest fix a reader has for a field that turned out too small, and taking it away costs them more than it saves you.

props.name: labelHidden
props.description: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
props.summary: Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
use: A control whose meaning is already carried by a heading directly above it.
dont: Pairing it with a placeholder standing in for the name.
props.a11y: The label element is still rendered and still bound. Only the pixels go.

props.name: id
props.description: Stable id for the control. Defaults to a generated one.
props.summary: Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.
use: A form library that addresses fields by id, or an error summary linking to the control it names.
dont: Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it is derived from this.

props.name: status
props.description: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and the ring.
props.summary: Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the ring.
use: `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.
dont: `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong; only the message says what.
props.a11y: Field's, unchanged: `invalid` sets `aria-invalid` and pulls the message into `aria-describedby`, and while idle the message stays on the page but leaves the chain.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text under the control.
props.summary: Persistent helper text under the control.
use: The length limit, stated before someone writes past it — this is where a counter's job mostly lives.
dont: Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name.
props.a11y: Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

props.name: message
props.description: Status-dependent message under the control.
props.summary: Status-dependent message under the control.
use: What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative: "Keep this under 500 characters."
dont: Putting the permanent limit here. It leaves the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.
props.a11y: Announced politely rather than as an alert, because it is already in `aria-describedby`.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the control required to assistive technology and in the label.
props.summary: Marks the control required, in the label and to assistive technology.
use: Controls that genuinely block submission.
dont: Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. Field renders one.
props.a11y: `aria-required` on the control; the rendered marker is `aria-hidden`.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks editing while keeping the control focusable, readable and announced.
props.summary: Blocks editing while keeping the control focusable, readable and announced.
use: A note whose content is decided elsewhere and should still be readable in full.
dont: Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits.
props.a11y: `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly` from Field, never the native attribute.

props.name: className
props.description: Class for the wrapper. The control itself is styled by the system.
props.summary: Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.
use: The measure or grid placement the form decides.
dont: Setting a height. That is `rows`, and a hand-written height stops matching the line count the reader sees.

usage.case: A note someone will actually draft in
usage.when: The commonest case: free text with a stated limit.
usage.example:
<Textarea
  label="Release notes"
  rows={8}
  description="Markdown is fine. Around 500 characters reads best."
/>
usage.notes: The limit goes in `description` rather than a counter, because it is the thing worth knowing BEFORE writing. Eight rows says how much is wanted more honestly than any sentence would.

usage.when: Reporting a limit the writer has passed.
usage.example:
<Textarea
  label="Release notes"
  status="invalid"
  message="Keep this under 500 characters."
/>
usage.notes: The message is the imperative, not the diagnosis — "too long" tells someone what happened, this tells them what to do. The ring and the colour say it twice more.

usage.case: A layout that cannot take a taller control
usage.when: A fixed-height panel, or a control inside a dense row.
usage.example: <Textarea label="Internal note" rows={2} resize="none" labelHidden />
usage.notes: `none` because the container genuinely cannot grow, which is the only reason for it. The label is hidden rather than absent — the row's own header is carrying the name visually, and nothing about the accessible name changes.

usage.when: The value is one line and Enter should submit the form.
usage.example: <Textarea label="Email" rows={1} />
usage.notes: Don't. That is `TextField`. A one-row textarea looks almost right and behaves wrong: Enter inserts a newline instead of submitting, and the value can arrive with line breaks in it that nothing upstream expects.

behavior.summary: A `<textarea>` inside a `Field`. No primitive of its own: `getFieldProps` already supplies every id and ARIA attribute, and a multi-line control needs nothing a single-line one does not.

decisions.decision: A separate component, not a `multiline` prop on TextField
decisions.why: `TextField` is typed to `HTMLInputElement` and forwards its ref as one, so a boolean that silently swapped the element would invalidate half its props at runtime while still compiling. The elements also differ in ways a caller has to know about: `rows` and `wrap` exist on one and not the other, and Enter inserts a newline here where it submits there. This system's test for splitting is a difference in semantics rather than in looks, and that is what this is — the same test that separated Text from Heading.

decisions.decision: `rows` sets the height, and there is no `size` prop
decisions.why: `TextField`'s `size` exists to choose a control height from the control scale. A multi-line control's height is how many lines it shows, which is what `rows` already says — offering both would be two props for one measurement, and a caller would have to guess which wins.

decisions.decision: It does not grow with its content in this version
decisions.why: The honest options are all costly: `field-sizing: content` is not supported widely enough to be the only mechanism, the replicated-content grid trick needs a wrapper element around the control that exists purely to be measured, and measuring in JS means a resize observer per field. Each is a real decision about the DOM this component puts on the page, and none of them should ride along with the box. `rows` plus a resize handle covers the case meanwhile, and the caller can see how much room they are giving.

decisions.decision: `resize` defaults to `vertical`, and horizontal is not offered
decisions.why: Letting a reader make the box taller is the cheapest possible fix for a field that turned out too small, and it costs the layout nothing — the control's inline size is the form's. Horizontal resize does cost the layout: a control dragged wider than its column overflows whatever contains it, and no form anticipates that. `none` is there for the layouts that cannot tolerate a height change either.

decisions.decision: No character counter
decisions.why: A counter is two things — a number that updates, and an announcement policy for when it should interrupt a typist — and both belong to the caller who knows the limit. `Field` already has the slot: `description` for the limit stated up front, `message` with `status="invalid"` for having passed it. Building it in would mean choosing a live-region policy on everyone's behalf.

decisions.decision: `disabled` is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, inherited from Field
decisions.why: Nothing new is decided here; it is named so the contract does not read as though the question were open. The same consequence applies — a readOnly control still submits its value.

base.summary: The box, and only the box — Field owns the label, helper text, message and disabled dimming. Every value below is the one `.rata-text-field-input` uses, deliberately: the two controls sit in the same form and a reader should not be able to tell they were built separately.

tokens.font-family: font.family.sans — a control inherits neither family nor size from the page, so both are stated
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — the same constant the button family and the text field use, so all three measure their text alike
tokens.line-height: type.control.line-height.md — and here it also decides the height, since `rows` multiplies it
tokens.padding-inline: space.control.padding-inline.md — matching the text field's md step, which is the only step this control has
tokens.padding-block: space.padding.xs — a single-line control centres its text with its height, and a multi-line one has no height to centre against, so the space has to be stated

states.summary: Selected from the primitive's data-status on the Field root, exactly as the text field's are. The rings are inset strokes, never the focus ring, so a control can be focused and invalid at once.

tokens.hover inner band: theme.bg.muted at border.2 as an inset shadow, idle only — the validation rings occupy the same 2px and box-shadow does not accumulate
tokens.focus outline: focus.ring-width solid theme.fg.primary at space.0 offset — the same deliberate departure the text field documents, so the two controls' focus looks identical
tokens.disabled cursor: not-allowed — the dimming itself is Field's, on the root

name: toast
title: Toast
description: A brief, polite confirmation of something the reader just did, shown away from the content and gone on its own.
note: No React implementation yet (status: future). There is nothing to look up — don't invent props for this one.

props.name: children
props.summary: The message — one short sentence about what just happened.
use: Past tense, naming the thing: "Invoice sent", "3 tokens copied".
dont: Anything the reader must act on, or an error about something on the page. That is a Notice, where the problem is.
More than one sentence. It is read while it is leaving.
props.a11y: Announced politely through the region's live region when the toast appears.

props.name: variant
props.summary: Whether the outcome says anything about health.
use: `neutral` for almost everything — a confirmation is not a celebration.
`success` when the outcome was in real doubt: a long export that finished.
`danger` for a failure that needs no action now: "Couldn't sync, will retry".
dont: `danger` for a failure the reader has to fix. That is a Notice beside the thing that failed.
props.a11y: Colour is not the only signal: the success and danger variants carry an icon, as Notice does, which is `aria-hidden` because the text already says it.

props.name: action
props.summary: One optional action — Undo, View — offered alongside the message.
use: Undo for a reversible action the reader may have done by mistake.
dont: An action that is reachable nowhere else, unless `duration` is `null`. The toast will leave, and the action with it.
Two actions. A choice between options is a Dialog.
props.a11y: Rendered as a real button. The timer pauses while focus is inside the toast, so a keyboard user reaching for it does not lose it.

props.name: duration
props.summary: Milliseconds before the toast leaves on its own, or `null` to stay until dismissed.
use: The default for almost everything.
`null` when the toast's action is the only path to something.
dont: Shortening it. The timer already pauses on hover and focus, but a short message read by a screen reader can take longer than it looks.
props.a11y: Paused while hovered, while focus is inside, and while the tab is hidden — the adjustment WCAG 2.2.1 requires for timed content.

props.name: onDismiss
props.summary: Called when the toast leaves — by timer, by the dismiss button, or by a swipe on native.
use: Cleaning up state that should not outlive the message.
dont: Treating it as "the reader saw it". A timed-out toast may have been read by nobody.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.summary: Accessible name for the dismiss button.
use: A translated label.
dont: Removing the button. Every toast is dismissible by hand, whatever its duration.
props.a11y: Becomes the icon-only button's `aria-label`.

usage.case: A confirmation that can safely be missed
usage.when: The reader did something whose result is not otherwise visible where they are.
usage.example:
const toast = useToast();

<Button onClick={() => { copy(path); toast.show(<Toast>Token path copied</Toast>); }}>
  Copy path
</Button>
usage.notes: Neutral, default duration, no action. `show` hands the toast to the `ToastRegion` mounted once at the app root. Focus stays on the button, and the message is announced politely after the button's own feedback.

usage.when: A destructive action that is cheap to reverse, where confirming in advance would be friction.
usage.notes: Archived rows must also be restorable from the archive itself — the toast will leave, and Undo with it. If they were not, this would need `duration={null}`.

usage.when: A save that failed because two fields are invalid.
usage.example: toast.show(<Toast variant="danger">Check the highlighted fields</Toast>);
usage.notes: Don't. The reader has to act, and the problem is in the form, not in the corner of the screen. That is a Notice at the top of the form with `live="assertive"`, and the fields' own invalid status.

behavior.summary: A message rendered into one app-level toast region, announced politely, never taking focus, and removed after `duration` unless the reader is hovering it, focused inside it, or away from the tab. The region is `ToastRegion`, mounted once near the app root, and a Toast is shown from an event handler with the `useToast()` hook — both approved at gate 1.

decisions.decision: Toast confirms; Notice informs; Dialog interrupts
decisions.why: A toast is for the result of something the reader just did, whose confirmation they can safely miss: "Saved", "Link copied", "Message sent". Anything the reader must see is not a toast, because a toast goes away on a timer and appears far from where they were looking. A problem with what is on the page — a validation summary, a failed save that left the form dirty — is a Notice in the page, beside the thing it is about. A decision that blocks the task is a Dialog. A toast that reports a form error is a message the reader has to hunt for, about a form it is not next to.

decisions.decision: Three variants, not Notice's four, and no warning
decisions.why: `neutral`, `success` and `danger`. There is no `info` because a neutral toast is already informational, and no `warning` because a warning is by definition something to act on — which is exactly what a self-dismissing message cannot carry. `danger` exists for failures that need no immediate action — "Couldn't sync, will retry" — and is the variant to question hardest at review.

decisions.decision: Always polite, never assertive, and focus never moves
decisions.why: The reader is mid-task, and a toast's content is by definition not urgent — urgent content is a Dialog or a Notice. So the region is a `role="status"` live region and every toast is announced politely, after whatever the screen reader is currently saying. Focus stays where the reader put it; stealing it to a corner of the screen for "Saved" would be a worse bug than missing the confirmation.

decisions.decision: The timer pauses, and an action means the toast is not the only way
decisions.why: WCAG 2.2.1 requires timed content to be adjustable. The countdown pauses while the pointer is over the toast, while focus is inside it, and while the tab is hidden, so a reader who is reading it, or reaching for its action, or who switched away, does not lose it. An action in a toast — Undo, View — must also be reachable somewhere else in the interface, because the toast will eventually leave; a toast whose action is the only path to something must pass `duration={null}` and stay until dismissed.

decisions.decision: `ToastRegion` and `useToast()` are part of the API
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C5, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). A toast is raised from an event handler — a save that finished, a path that was copied — far from where it is drawn, so rendering `<Toast>` in place would put it in whatever stacking context the handler's component happens to live in. `ToastRegion` is the one place every toast lands, mounted once near the app root; `useToast()` returns `show`, which hands a Toast to that region from anywhere below it. Toast itself stays a plain component with the props below, so the region owns the stack, the timers and the live region, and the message owns only what it says.

decisions.decision: One region per app, in the top layer, stacking at most three
decisions.why: Toasts from anywhere in the app have to land in one place, or two of them overlap and a screen reader hears neither cleanly. The region is a single `popover="manual"` element so it sits in the top layer without a z-index — there are no z-index tokens in this system and the top layer is why none are needed. More than three visible at once is a log, not a confirmation; the oldest leaves early to make room.

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: each toast is a `div` inside one `role="status"` region, named "Notifications" with `aria-label` so it can be found by landmark navigation; the region carries `popover="manual"`. Icons are `aria-hidden`, as in Notice. React Native has no top layer: the region is an absolutely positioned `View` mounted once at the root, above the navigation container. Each toast sets `accessibilityLiveRegion="polite"` on Android and is announced with `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility` on iOS, where live regions do not exist; the action is `accessibilityRole="button"`. Swipe-to-dismiss is native-only, and always backed by the dismiss button, because a gesture is not discoverable by a screen reader. The pause-on-hover half of the timer rule is web-only; on native the timer pauses while a screen reader is running. Rata-drawn on both platforms, not the OS's own toast (decision N5): Android's system Toast cannot carry an action or a dismiss button, and iOS has none, so one drawn component behaves the same everywhere. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: Open question for approval: toasts while a modal Dialog is open
decisions.why: `showModal()` makes everything outside the dialog inert, and whether a top-layer region opened earlier stays interactive and announced above it is something to verify in the browsers this system supports, not to assume. Until it is verified, the contract says: do not raise a toast from inside a modal; report the result inside the dialog, or after it closes.

base.summary: Notice's frame on a floating surface. The text, icon and dismiss are built exactly as Notice builds them, so a toast and a notice saying the same thing look like the same message; the difference is the shadow and where it sits.

tokens.inline-size: text bounded by size.measure.compact; the box is that plus its padding, never wider than the viewport less twice space.page.gutter

neutral.summary: The default, and the commonest: "Saved", "Link copied". A plain surface, because most confirmations say nothing about health.

success.summary: The role's subtle tint with its own foreground — the same pairing Notice uses.

danger.summary: A failure the reader should know about but does not have to act on now. The role's subtle tint with its own foreground; never the saturated fill.

region.summary: Where toasts stack. Fixed to the viewport's block-end edge, inset by the page's own gutter.

tokens.color: currentColor — inherited from the variant's own foreground
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

name: toggle-button
title: Toggle Button
description: A button that stays on: an on/off state the user sets directly, announced with aria-pressed.

props.name: pressed
props.description: Whether the toggle is currently on. Makes the component controlled.
props.summary: Whether the toggle is currently on. Makes the component controlled.
use: Whenever the state lives outside the component — which is nearly always, since a toggle usually reflects something a document or a preference already knows.
dont: Passing it without `onPressedChange`; the toggle would render its state and then refuse to ever change it.
Deriving it from the last click rather than from the thing being toggled — if the underlying change fails, the button is left lying about it.
props.a11y: Becomes `aria-pressed`, emitted in both states. This is the only thing that tells assistive technology the control is a toggle at all.

props.name: defaultPressed
props.description: Starting state for an uncontrolled toggle. Conflicts with `pressed`.
props.summary: Starting state for an uncontrolled toggle that owns its own value.
use: Genuinely local state nothing else reads — a disclosure of extra columns in one table, say.
dont: Anything the rest of the page reacts to. The moment two places need the value, uncontrolled means they disagree.
Resetting the toggle by changing this later — it is read once, at mount.
props.a11y: No difference in what is announced: `aria-pressed` is emitted either way.

props.name: onPressedChange
props.description: Called with the state the toggle should move to, not the one it is in.
props.summary: Called with the state the toggle should move to — not the one it is leaving.
use: Applying the change, then letting the new state flow back in through `pressed`.
dont: Reading the current value off the event target; the argument already says where it is going.
Treating it as a plain click handler — it does not fire when the toggle is disabled or loading.
props.a11y: Fires for keyboard activation too, since it hangs off the same click guard the button uses. Space and Enter behave as they do on any native button.

props.name: variant
props.description: How loud the toggle is in its off state.
props.summary: How loud the toggle is in its off state.
use: `tertiary` for a toolbar of many toggles, where a border each would be visual noise.
`secondary` for one or two toggles that need to read as controls on their own.
dont: Expecting a `primary` or `destructive` toggle. A filled accent control reads as "the action to take", which fights with "a state you are in", and a destructive thing you can leave switched on is a bug waiting to happen.
props.a11y: Visual only. The pressed state must never be carried by colour alone — the on state changes fill *and* is announced through `aria-pressed`.

props.name: size
props.summary: Control height and inline padding, from the `size.control.*` scale. Text size does not change with it.
use: Matching the density of the surrounding controls, exactly as `Button` does — including that the label stays one size across all three.
dont: Mixing sizes within one group of toggles — they read as a set, so they measure as a set.
Expecting an icon-only toggle's glyph to grow with it. The glyph follows the text size, which is constant, so only the box changes.

props.name: disabled
props.summary: Blocks activation while keeping the toggle focusable, announced, and readable in its current state.
use: A toggle that cannot change yet but whose current state still matters to see.
dont: Expressing "off". Disabled and unpressed are different facts, and a disabled toggle can be either.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled`, never the native `disabled` attribute: the control stays in the tab order and keeps announcing its pressed state.

props.name: loading
props.description: Shows a spinner and blocks activation while preserving focus.
props.summary: Shows a spinner and refuses activation while the change this toggle asked for is still in flight.
use: A toggle whose effect is a server round trip — starring, subscribing, publishing — where the state should not settle until the change lands.
dont: Flipping `pressed` optimistically *and* setting `loading`; pick one story about what the button currently means.
Pairing it with `disabled` — `loading` already blocks activation, and the two together say the same thing twice.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-busy` alongside `aria-disabled`, so the control is heard as busy rather than as broken. `aria-pressed` keeps reporting the state it is still in.

props.name: iconOnly
props.description: Square icon-only toggle; pass the icon as children and set aria-label.
props.summary: Square toggle carrying an icon and no visible text.
use: Toolbars where the icons are conventional and the row would otherwise be unreadably wide — bold, italic, alignment.
dont: Icons whose meaning is not already settled. An unlabelled toggle with an ambiguous glyph is a control nobody can describe to a colleague.
Relying on the icon alone to show the pressed state — the fill must change too.
props.a11y: You MUST pass `aria-label`. Nothing supplies an accessible name when there is no visible text, and the name must stay constant across states — the state is `aria-pressed`'s job, not the label's.

usage.case: A formatting toggle in a toolbar
usage.when: The canonical case: the state belongs to the document, so the toggle is controlled.
usage.example:
<ToggleButton
  variant="tertiary"
  iconOnly
  aria-label="Bold"
  pressed={isBold}
  onPressedChange={setBold}
>
  B
</ToggleButton>
usage.notes: The label stays "Bold" in both states. `aria-pressed` says which state it is in — renaming it to "Unbold" would make the announcement contradict itself.

usage.case: A toggle whose change has to reach a server
usage.when: Starring, subscribing, publishing — anything where the state should not settle until the write lands.
usage.example:
<ToggleButton pressed={starred} loading={saving} onPressedChange={star}>
  Star
</ToggleButton>
usage.notes: `loading` blocks repeat activation on its own — don't also pass `disabled`. If the write fails, leave `pressed` where it was rather than flipping it back, which reads as the user having done something.

usage.when: The rare uncontrolled case: one view's own disclosure of extra detail.
usage.example:
<ToggleButton defaultPressed onPressedChange={setShowDetail}>
  Show detail
</ToggleButton>
usage.notes: The moment a second place needs to know whether detail is showing, this becomes `pressed` — uncontrolled state that two components read is state that will disagree.

usage.when: The control is a setting in a form, applied immediately, and reads as a thing with a state.
usage.example:
<ToggleButton pressed={notifications} onPressedChange={setNotifications}>
  Notifications
</ToggleButton>
usage.notes: Don't. That is a switch, not a toggle button: it is a setting, not an action left engaged. Use Switch, which announces with aria-checked as "Notifications, on" — the sentence a setting should produce.

behavior.summary: Pressed-state semantics over the button's own activation contract. State is not held here: the caller owns `pressed` and is told what it should become, which is what lets a toggle inside a group and a toggle on its own be the same primitive.

decisions.decision: Composes `getButtonProps` instead of reimplementing activation
decisions.why: A toggle is a button that carries a state. Implementing the disabled and loading guards a second time is how the two drift apart — one gains a fix the other doesn't, and the difference only shows up in whichever one nobody tested.

decisions.decision: `aria-pressed` is emitted in both states, never omitted when false
decisions.why: Unlike `aria-disabled`, which is absent when it doesn't apply, a missing `aria-pressed` makes the control announce as an ordinary button — precisely when the user most needs to know it is a toggle that is currently off.

decisions.decision: `aria-pressed`, not `role="switch"`
decisions.why: A switch is an on/off setting that takes effect immediately and reads as a thing with a state ("Notifications, on"). A toggle button is an action you leave engaged — bold, mute, pin — and reads as a verb. When the control is a setting, the answer is Switch, and this component is the wrong one.

decisions.decision: The label does not change with the state
decisions.why: `aria-pressed` already says whether it is on. Swapping the label to "Unmute" as well means the name and the state contradict each other — a screen reader announces "Unmute, pressed", which is a double negative the user has to unpick. The visual treatment carries the state; the word stays put.

decisions.decision: No `data-pressed` attribute
decisions.why: `[aria-pressed="true"]` is already a CSS selector. A parallel data attribute would be a second copy of the same fact, free to go stale.

decisions.decision: Controlled by default, with an uncontrolled escape hatch
decisions.why: A toggle almost always reflects state that lives somewhere else — a document's formatting, a saved preference — so the controlled form is the honest default. `defaultPressed` exists for the genuinely local case, and passing both is a conflict rather than a precedence rule to memorize.

secondary.summary: The off state of a toggle that has to read as a control on its own — identical to the secondary button, because an unpressed toggle is one.

tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

secondary-pressed.summary: The on state: a tint, not a fill. A saturated accent background reads as "the action to take", which is the wrong sentence for "a state you are in" — the same reason this component has no primary variant.

tokens.border-color: theme.accent-role.fg — the border moves with the fill, so the pressed state is not carried by background alone
tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

tertiary.summary: The off state for a toolbar of many toggles, where a border each would be visual noise.

tokens.background: none — no fill in the off state, so a row of toggles reads as one surface
tokens.border-color: transparent — held so the box does not resize when the pressed state paints its border
tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

tertiary-pressed.summary: The on state of a borderless toggle: the tint alone separates it from its unpressed neighbours.

tokens.border-color: transparent — the tint is the cue; a border here would out-shout the secondary variant's pressed state
tokens.height: size.control.md — and size.control.sm / .lg at the other sizes; this is the only thing `size` changes
tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — constant across all three sizes, so `size` changes the box and not the label
tokens.hover/press: compose the .rata-state-layer class — do not swap the background

name: toggle-button-group
title: Toggle Button Group
description: A set of toggle buttons that holds a value: one choice out of several, or any number of independent states.

props.name: value
props.description: The current selection: a value in single mode, a list in multiple mode.
props.summary: The current selection: a value in single mode, a list in multiple mode, `null` or `[]` for none.
use: Whenever the selection is state the rest of the page reads — which is most of the time, since a toggle group usually is the setting rather than a view of it.
dont: Passing a bare string in multiple mode, or an array in single mode; the shape follows `selectionMode` and mixing them makes the selected state silently wrong.
Passing it without `onValueChange` — the group would render a selection and then refuse to change it.
props.a11y: Drives `aria-checked` in single mode and `aria-pressed` in multiple mode. It is also what places the group's single tab stop in single mode.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Starting selection for an uncontrolled group. Conflicts with `value`.
props.summary: Starting selection for an uncontrolled group that owns its own value.
use: A local view preference nothing else on the page reacts to.
dont: Anything persisted or shared. Two readers of an uncontrolled value are two readers that will disagree.
Changing it later to reset the group — it is read once, at mount.

props.name: onValueChange
props.description: Called with the selection the group should move to.
props.summary: Called with the selection the group should move to — a value, a list in DOM order, or `null`.
use: Applying the change and letting it flow back in through `value`.
dont: Assuming it only fires on click; in single mode the arrow keys select as they move, which is the radio pattern working correctly.
Re-sorting the array it hands you — it is already in the order the user sees.

props.name: selectionMode
props.description: Whether this group holds one answer or any number of independent states.
props.summary: Whether this group holds one answer or any number of independent states — which also decides its ARIA pattern.
use: `single` for a choice: alignment, a date range preset, a view mode.
`multiple` for independent states that happen to sit together: bold, italic, underline.
dont: `single` for navigation between views — that is a tab list, which announces itself as one and manages its own panels.
Switching it at runtime. The role, the focus model and the shape of `value` all change with it, so a mid-life switch is a different control appearing in place of the old one.
props.a11y: `single` renders a `radiogroup` of `radio`s with one tab stop and arrow-key navigation; `multiple` renders a `group` of `aria-pressed` toggles, each its own tab stop.

props.name: deselectable
props.description: Single mode only: whether clicking the selected option clears the selection.
props.summary: Single mode only: whether clicking the selected option clears the selection.
use: Filters, where "none of these" is a real answer the user should be able to get back to.
dont: Settings that must always have a value — a text alignment with nothing selected is a state the document cannot actually be in.
Multiple mode, where it means nothing: every item already deselects itself.
props.a11y: Only clicking clears the selection. Arrow keys always move to an option and select it, because an arrow key that could empty a radio group would make the group impossible to navigate through.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the group. Required unless `labelledBy` names an existing element.
props.summary: Accessible name for the group — the question these options answer.
use: Always, unless `labelledBy` points at a visible label that already asks it.
Naming the question, not the widget: "Text alignment", not "Alignment toggle group".
dont: Leaving it off. An unnamed radiogroup is announced as a group of options with nothing to say what they choose between.
props.a11y: Becomes the group's `aria-label`. In single mode this is the name a screen reader reads before "1 of 3", so without it the count is meaningless.

props.name: labelledBy
props.description: Id of a visible element that already names this group.
props.summary: Id of a visible element that already names this group.
use: A field label or heading sits above the group and says exactly what the name would.
dont: Pointing at an element that may not render — a dangling reference leaves the group unnamed with nothing on screen to show it.
props.a11y: Wins over `label` when both are passed: it names the group with text the user can see.

props.name: orientation
props.summary: Which way the options stack, and — in single mode — which arrows move between them.
use: `vertical` in a narrow rail where a row of options would wrap.
dont: Assuming it constrains the keys: both axes' arrow keys move in single mode regardless, because a user who reaches for Down in a horizontal group should not hit a dead end.
props.a11y: Announced as `aria-orientation` in single mode only, where arrow-key navigation actually exists to back the promise up.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height for every option. Set here, never per option.
props.summary: Control height and text size for every option, from the `size.control.*` scale.
use: Matching the density of the surrounding controls — set once here rather than on each option.
dont: Setting it per option. A set of options that measure differently is a ragged bar, which is why this prop lives on the group and not on the items.

props.name: attached
props.description: Joins the options into one continuous bar. Defaults to true.
props.summary: Joins the options into one continuous bar, with shared borders and only the outer corners rounded.
use: The default, and right whenever the options are one question: they close up so they read as one control rather than several buttons that happen to sit together.
dont: Keeping it attached when the options wrap onto a second line — a broken bar reads as two controls.

Reaching for this to build a segmented control. `SegmentedControl` is the component for that — narrower on purpose, and drawn as a well with the answer raised out of it. This one is the wider API: multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants.
props.a11y: Visual only. The role, the selection and the focus model are the same either way.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Blocks activation for every option while keeping them focusable.
props.summary: Blocks activation for every option while keeping them focusable, announced, and readable in their current state.
use: The whole question is unavailable — a filter over data that hasn't loaded, say.
dont: Disabling one option; that belongs on the option itself, which stays reachable and just refuses to become the answer.
Expressing "nothing selected" — an empty group and a disabled group are different facts.
props.a11y: Emits `aria-disabled` on each option, never the native `disabled` attribute. Arrow keys still move focus through the group so its options remain discoverable.

usage.case: Single choice — one question, several answers
usage.when: The default: one answer out of a few, all visible at once.
usage.example:
<ToggleButtonGroup
  label="Text alignment"
  value={align}
  onValueChange={setAlign}
>
  <ToggleButton value="left" iconOnly aria-label="Align left">⇤</ToggleButton>
  <ToggleButton value="center" iconOnly aria-label="Align center">↔</ToggleButton>
  <ToggleButton value="right" iconOnly aria-label="Align right">⇥</ToggleButton>
</ToggleButtonGroup>
usage.notes: A radiogroup: one tab stop, arrows move and select. Each icon-only option still needs its own `aria-label` — the group's name is the question, not the answers. For a plain segmented control reach for `SegmentedControl` instead; this shape is for when you need something it deliberately cannot do, such as icon-only options or a vertical bar.

usage.when: Several on/off states that are not alternatives to each other.
usage.example:
<ToggleButtonGroup
  label="Text style"
  selectionMode="multiple"
  value={styles}
  onValueChange={setStyles}
>
  <ToggleButton value="bold">Bold</ToggleButton>
  <ToggleButton value="italic">Italic</ToggleButton>
</ToggleButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Each option keeps its own tab stop here, and the value comes back in DOM order however the user clicked into it.

usage.case: A filter that can be cleared
usage.when: "None of these" is a real answer, so re-clicking the selected option should get back to it.
usage.example:
<ToggleButtonGroup
  label="Status filter"
  deselectable
  value={status}
  onValueChange={setStatus}
>
  <ToggleButton value="open">Open</ToggleButton>
  <ToggleButton value="closed">Closed</ToggleButton>
</ToggleButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Only clicking clears it. Arrow keys always land on an option and select it — an arrow that could empty the group would make it impossible to move through.

usage.when: The options switch between views rather than setting a value.
usage.example:
<ToggleButtonGroup label="Section" value={section} onValueChange={setSection}>
  <ToggleButton value="overview">Overview</ToggleButton>
  <ToggleButton value="activity">Activity</ToggleButton>
</ToggleButtonGroup>
usage.notes: Don't. Navigation between panels is a tab list: it announces itself as one, owns the relationship to the panels, and moves focus into them. This system has no Tabs yet — flag the gap rather than dressing a toggle group up as one.

behavior.summary: Selection state, the ARIA pattern that state implies, and — in single mode — roving focus with arrow-key navigation. Nothing here touches the DOM: where the radio pattern requires focus to move, the primitive reports which value should receive it and the wrapper does the focusing.

decisions.decision: Which of three, when they all look like one bar of options
decisions.why: Three components here can look like one enclosed bar of options, so each one's contract says which is which. SegmentedControl is a question with a short fixed set of answers: single, always filled, cannot be cleared. ToggleButtonGroup is the same ARIA pattern with a wider API — multiple selection, deselection, vertical orientation, the toggle-button variants — so reach for it when you need any of those. Tabs is a different pattern entirely: tabs reveal a region, each naming a panel and each panel naming its tab, and if what is being chosen is which content is shown rather than what gets submitted, it is Tabs — which can be drawn to look exactly like the other two and is still announced as a tablist.

decisions.decision: The selection mode picks the ARIA pattern: `single` is a radiogroup, `multiple` is a group of pressed toggles
decisions.why: They are different controls wearing the same clothes. "One of these" is a radio group, and announcing it as one is what tells a screen-reader user how many options there are and which is chosen. "Any of these" is a set of independent toggles, and forcing it into radio semantics would claim the options are mutually exclusive when they are not.

decisions.decision: Focus behaviour differs between the two modes, deliberately
decisions.why: Single mode is one tab stop with arrow keys between options, because that is the radio pattern and users of radio groups expect it. Multiple mode gives every item its own tab stop, consistent with `button-group` and with every other button in this system. The inconsistency is the ARIA patterns', not ours — matching them is what makes each mode behave the way its users already know.

decisions.decision: Roving tabindex is derived from the value, never stored
decisions.why: In a radio group the selected option is the tab stop, and an empty group is entered at its first option. Deriving it means focus position and value cannot disagree, because there is no second piece of state to fall out of step.

decisions.decision: Arrow keys select as they move, but a disabled option only takes focus
decisions.why: Selecting on arrow is the radio pattern. This system's disabled controls stay focusable and announced, so a disabled option must still be reachable — it just must not become the answer. Skipping it entirely would hide from a keyboard user that the option exists at all.

decisions.decision: The selection is always reported in DOM order
decisions.why: Multiple mode rebuilds the array from the item order rather than appending to it, so what the caller stores matches what the user sees. Click order is an implementation detail of how someone got there, and persisting it produces values that shuffle between sessions for no reason.

decisions.decision: Values are strings
decisions.why: They end up in `data-` attributes, form fields, query params and saved preferences, all of which are strings. A generic value type would push the stringification into every call site instead of settling it once here.

decisions.decision: `aria-orientation` is announced in single mode only
decisions.why: It is a promise that arrow keys move along that axis. Single mode keeps that promise; multiple mode deliberately does not implement arrow navigation, so announcing an orientation there would advertise a behaviour that isn't present.

decisions.decision: `size` belongs to the group; `variant` stays on the item
decisions.why: Mixed sizes break the shape — a segmented bar with items of two heights is ragged — so the group owns the decision that has to be uniform. Variant is a per-item emphasis choice that stays legible when it varies, and moving it to the group would mean two places could set it.

attached.summary: The default, and what a segmented control is: the options are one question, so they close up into one bar and only the outer corners round.

tokens.outer corner border-radius: radius.element, as logical corners so the bar flips in RTL
tokens.collapsed shared border: negative margin of border.1, so two adjacent borders read as one stroke
tokens.focused item stacking: raised above its neighbours so the focus ring is not clipped by the overlapping border — a stacking fix, not a token
tokens.item height: size.control.md — set once on the group and pushed to every option, because a bar of options at two heights is ragged
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — owned by the option, never drawn around the group

spaced.summary: Options that belong together but read as separate controls — the right shape when they can wrap, since a broken bar reads as two controls.

tokens.item border-radius: radius.element — each option keeps the corners it sets for itself
tokens.item height: size.control.md — set once on the group and pushed to every option, because a bar of options at two heights is ragged
tokens.outline (focus-visible): focus.ring-width solid theme.focus-ring, offset focus.ring-offset — owned by the option, never drawn around the group

example:
<ToggleButtonGroup
      label="Status filter"
      deselectable
      value={status}
      onValueChange={(next) => setStatus(next as string | null)}
    >
      <ToggleButton value="open">Open</ToggleButton>
      <ToggleButton value="closed">Closed</ToggleButton>
    </ToggleButtonGroup>

name: tooltip
title: Tooltip
description: A short, non-interactive text hint that names or describes the control it is attached to, shown on hover and keyboard focus.

props.name: content
props.description: The hint text. Plain text only — a string, so a link or a button cannot be passed.
props.summary: The hint text. Plain text only.
use: A few words: the name of an icon-only control, or one sentence of detail about a labelled one.
dont: Anything the reader needs to finish the task. It will not appear on touch — make it visible text instead.
A link, a button or formatting. Interactive content belongs in a Popover; the type is a string so it cannot be passed.
props.a11y: Becomes the trigger's accessible name or description, per `relationship`.

props.name: children
props.description: The one focusable element the tooltip is attached to.
props.summary: The one focusable element the tooltip is attached to.
use: A `Button`, usually an icon-only one, or a link.
dont: Plain text, an icon or a `div`. A tooltip on something unfocusable cannot be reached by keyboard at all — if the text needs explaining, explain it in visible text.
A trigger that already opens a Menu or Popover on hover. Two overlays from one control compete.
props.a11y: Cloned to receive the ARIA reference and the hover, focus and Escape handlers. It must be focusable, or the tooltip is pointer-only.

props.name: relationship
props.description: Whether the tooltip names the trigger or describes it.
props.summary: Whether the tooltip names the trigger or describes it.
use: `label` on an icon-only button, with the button's own `aria-label` set to the same words. Button requires it, and `aria-labelledby` wins over it, so the name is read once.
`description` on a control that already has a name, to add detail — including why an `aria-disabled` control is unavailable.
dont: `description` with the same text as the control's `aria-label`. It is read twice.
props.a11y: `label` wires `aria-labelledby`; `description` wires `aria-describedby`. On React Native these become `accessibilityLabel` and `accessibilityHint`.

props.name: placement
props.description: Which side of the trigger the tooltip prefers. Anchor positioning flips it near an edge.
props.summary: Which side of the trigger the tooltip prefers.
use: `block-end` for a trigger at the top of the viewport, where the default would always flip anyway.
dont: Using it to keep the tooltip on screen. Anchor positioning already flips it near an edge; this states a preference, not a guarantee.
props.a11y: Visual only. Logical, so `inline-start` is the left in a left-to-right document and the right in a right-to-left one. Web only.

usage.when: A toolbar of icon-only controls, where the tooltip text is the only name each one has.
usage.example:
<Tooltip content="Copy token path" relationship="label">
  <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="Copy token path">
    <Icon icon={Copy} />
  </Button>
</Tooltip>
usage.notes: `relationship="label"` makes the tooltip the button's name.
