The `aria-label` stays, with the same words, because Button requires it on every `iconOnly` button; `aria-labelledby` takes precedence, so it is announced once. On touch the tooltip never draws, but the name is still wired, so a screen-reader user hears "Copy token path, button" either way.

usage.case: Explaining why a control is unavailable
usage.when: A button that is `aria-disabled` until something else is done.
usage.example:
<Tooltip content="Add a payment method to publish">
  <Button disabled>Publish</Button>
</Tooltip>
usage.notes: This works only because disabled Buttons in this system are `aria-disabled` and stay focusable and hoverable — a native `disabled` button gets no events, so its tooltip could never show. The reason must also be somewhere visible on the page, because a touch user will never see this.

usage.when: A help icon beside a field, whose hint includes a "Learn more" link.
usage.example:
<Tooltip content="Used for invoices. Learn more">
  <Button variant="tertiary" iconOnly aria-label="About billing email">
    <Icon icon={CircleHelp} />
  </Button>
</Tooltip>
usage.notes: Don't. The link cannot live in a tooltip — it would be visible and unreachable — and the hint would never appear on touch. That is a Popover, opened on purpose by a tap or a press, with a real link inside. Better still, put a short version as the field's own description, where everyone reads it.

behavior.summary: A trigger and a short text in the top layer, positioned with CSS anchor positioning — the same machinery as Menu, with no measurement code and no dependency. It is never focusable and never contains anything interactive. Proposed primitive: `getTooltipProps` in `packages/primitives/src/tooltip.ts`, owning the open delay, the hover bridge and Escape; it is a proposal, not yet a commitment.

decisions.decision: A tooltip only ever repeats or supplements; it never holds the only copy of anything
decisions.why: It cannot be relied on to appear. There is no hover on a touchscreen, a reader zoomed to 400% may never see it, and a keyboard user only gets it when they happen to focus that exact control. So nothing a reader needs to complete a task can live only in a tooltip. If the content is essential, it is visible text. If it is supplementary and needs to be reachable on touch, it is a Popover the reader opens on purpose.

decisions.decision: Non-interactive content only, and that is the line between Tooltip and Popover
decisions.why: A tooltip disappears when the pointer leaves and is never in the tab order, so a link or a button inside it is something a keyboard user can see and can never reach. `content` is typed as a string rather than a node, so the type refuses it instead of the contract asking nicely. Anything with a control in it is a Popover.

decisions.decision: `relationship` says whether the tooltip is the control's name or a description of it
decisions.why: The two are wired differently and getting it wrong is audible. For an icon-only button the tooltip text IS the name, so it is wired with `aria-labelledby`. The button still carries an `aria-label` with the same words — Button's contract requires one on every `iconOnly` button, and it is the name that survives wherever the tooltip is not mounted — and because `aria-labelledby` takes precedence over `aria-label`, the name is read once, not twice. For a labelled control the tooltip adds detail, so it is wired with `aria-describedby` and announced after the name. A tooltip that repeats an `aria-label` as a description is read twice; one that names a control that already has a name is ignored. The caller knows which it is, so it is a prop rather than a guess.

decisions.decision: It meets WCAG 1.4.13: dismissible, hoverable, persistent
decisions.why: Escape closes it without moving focus, so a reader who summoned it by accident can get rid of it without losing their place. The pointer can travel from the trigger onto the tooltip without it closing, so a magnified reader can move over it to read it. It stays until the pointer leaves both, focus leaves the trigger, or Escape is pressed — never on a timer.

decisions.decision: Touch: it does not appear, by design
decisions.why: There is no hover on touch, and the two common substitutes are both worse. Showing on tap would hijack the tap that was meant to activate the control. Showing on long-press collides with the platform's own long-press — text selection, context menus, and on mobile web the browser's link preview. So on a touch pointer the tooltip stays hidden; the accessible name or description is still wired, so VoiceOver and TalkBack users still hear it, and the rule above — nothing essential in a tooltip — is what makes hiding it safe. A pen hover, where the platform reports one, does show it.

decisions.decision: It works on an `aria-disabled` control, which is one more reason this system does not use `disabled`
decisions.why: A natively disabled button receives no pointer or focus events, so the most useful tooltip there is — "why can't I press this?" — cannot be shown on it. Because disabled controls here stay focusable and hoverable, the tooltip appears on them like any other control, and `relationship="description"` is how the reason gets announced.

decisions.decision: An inverse surface, not Menu's
decisions.why: Approved at gate 1 (decision C3, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md). A tooltip is the one overlay that never holds a control and is never opened on purpose, and an inverse chip says so at a glance: it cannot be mistaken for a Menu or a Popover opened from the neighbouring control, both of which are surfaces the reader acts in. The cost is a new pairing — an inverse background and a foreground verified against it in both schemes and in every brand — which is why it goes through the design-tokens skill rather than into this recipe as a palette value.

decisions.decision: Surface: theme.bg.inverse with theme.fg.on-inverse
decisions.why: The tooltip inverts the scheme (decision C3): a small dark chip on a light page, a light one on a dark page, which reads as transient and needs no border. The pair is generated in the expander, documented as tooltip-only, and verified at 12.88:1 (light) and 13.3:1 (dark). Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Open delay: motion.delay.hint
decisions.why: A pointer resting on the trigger opens the tooltip after motion.delay.hint, which points at motion.duration.medium-max (280ms today) so it follows the motion seed. The user chose the shorter step over slow-min. Keyboard focus opens it immediately — focus is never a passing pointer. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Line length: size.measure.tight
decisions.why: A tooltip's text is bounded at size.measure.tight, 32ch. It is in ch, so it scales with the text rather than with a control size; a hint that needs more than that is a Popover. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: Web and native
decisions.why: Web: the trigger is the caller's element, cloned to receive `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby`; the tooltip is a `role="tooltip"` element carrying the `popover` attribute (`hint` where supported, `manual` otherwise) so it renders in the top layer without a portal. React Native has no hover and no tooltip core component, so nothing is drawn: with `relationship="label"` the text becomes the trigger's `accessibilityLabel`, and with `relationship="description"` it becomes its `accessibilityHint` — which is what both platform screen readers read after the name. `placement` is web-only. The native behaviour is the touch behaviour above, followed through: the information still reaches assistive tech, and nothing is drawn that a finger cannot dismiss. Neither OS control nor Rata-drawn (decision N5): nothing is drawn on native, and the platform screen reader is what delivers the text. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

base.summary: A small transient chip on an inverse surface, so it reads as a passing hint rather than as a menu or a popover. The inverse surface and its foreground do not exist yet, so the colour lines below are the closest existing tokens and are stand-ins; the measurements, shadow and motion are final.

tokens.border: none — the inverse surface separates itself from the page
tokens.open delay: motion.delay.hint on pointer hover; none on keyboard focus

example:
<Tooltip content="Add a payment method to publish">
        <Button disabled>Publish</Button>
      </Tooltip>

name: top-nav
title: TopNav
description: The page's banner: a brand, the primary navigation, and room for actions.

props.name: items
props.summary: The primary destinations, in the order they are read. Omitting them means no navigation landmark at all, not an empty one.
use: Between two and about seven top-level destinations. More than that is a side nav, or a nav plus an overflow menu.
Omitting it entirely for a banner whose navigation lives in a side rail — an ordinary layout, and the playground's own.
`items` on an entry for a group of sub-destinations — it becomes a disclosure button rather than a link, and its own `href` is then unnecessary.
`onClick` on an entry to intercept the navigation for a client-side router — the `href` stays real, so the row is still a link.
dont: Actions. A button that does something is not a destination — put it in `actions`, where it is outside the nav landmark.
Every page in the product. This is the top level; the rest belongs to a side nav within a section.
props.a11y: Rendered as a list inside the `<nav>`, so the count and the order are announced. The item marked `current` gets `aria-current="page"`. With no items there is no `<nav>` at all: an empty navigation landmark is worse than none, because it appears in a landmark list promising destinations and has none. An entry with `items` becomes a disclosure button with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` — deliberately not a menu, which would promise a keyboard model a list of links does not have; its panel is named by the trigger and its links stay ordinary tab stops. A parent of the current page is marked `aria-current="true"` rather than `"page"`, because you are not on it.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
props.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Changing it only when a page has more than one navigation landmark and they need telling apart — a top nav and a side nav on the same page do.
dont: The word "navigation". A screen reader already says the role; "Main navigation navigation" is what that produces.
Passing it when there are no `items`. There is no landmark to name, and a name for something that is not rendered is a claim the markup does not make.
props.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`. It names the nav, not the banner — the banner is unnamed, because a page has one.

props.name: brand
props.description: The product's mark, at the start of the bar.
props.summary: The product's mark, at the start of the bar.
use: A logo, a wordmark, or both — wrapped in a link to the root if it should be clickable.
dont: Relying on it for the accessible name of anything. If it is an image it needs its own alt text, and if it is a link it needs link text.
Putting navigation in it. It sits outside the nav landmark, so a destination here is not findable as one.
props.a11y: Outside the `<nav>` on purpose: a logo is not a destination in the list, even when it links home.

props.name: actions
props.description: Controls at the end of the bar — search, account, notifications.
props.summary: Controls at the end of the bar — search, account, notifications.
use: `Search`, a `Menu` for the account, a `Button` for the primary action.
dont: Destinations. Anything that navigates belongs in `items`, inside the landmark where it can be found.
props.a11y: Outside the `<nav>`, because none of it is navigation. Each control names itself as it would anywhere else — an icon-only button here still needs its `aria-label`.

props.name: className
props.summary: Extra classes on the banner, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Making it sticky, which is a layout decision the component deliberately leaves open.
dont: Changing its height or colours. Those come from the recipe, and a bar that differs per page reads as two different products.

usage.when: The commonest case: a mark, a few destinations, and an account menu.
usage.example: Ratā} items={[ { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices", current: true }, { label: "Clients", href: "/clients" }, { label: "Reports", href: "/reports" }, ]} actions={ } > Settings Sign out } />
usage.notes: `current` is stated rather than derived: only the caller knows whether the invoice they are looking at counts as being on Invoices. The account menu is an action, not a destination, so it sits outside the nav landmark where it cannot be mistaken for one.

usage.case: A banner beside a side nav, where both landmarks need names
usage.when: Any page with two navigation landmarks.
usage.example:
<TopNav label="Main" items={sections} brand={<Wordmark />} />
<SideNav label="Invoices" sections={pages} />
usage.notes: Two navigation landmarks with the same name are indistinguishable in a landmark list, which is the one place they are most useful. Naming them for what they contain — not "top" and "side", which describe where they happen to sit — survives a redesign that moves them.

usage.when: An area of the product with several pages under one name.
usage.example:
<TopNav
  items={[
    { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices" },
    {
      label: "Reports",
      current: true,
      items: [
        { label: "Revenue", href: "/reports/revenue", current: true },
        { label: "Ageing", href: "/reports/ageing" },
      ],
    },
  ]}
/>
usage.notes: The entry with `items` needs no `href` — it reveals rather than navigates, so it renders as a button. Note the two kinds of current: the child is `aria-current="page"` because you are on it, and the parent is `aria-current="true"` because you are merely inside the area it leads to. If the parent is itself a page worth reaching, put it in its own panel as the first child.

usage.case: Don't: an action in the items array
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. Everything in `items` is announced as part of a list of destinations and rendered as a link, so an action here is announced as a place and navigates nowhere. It belongs in `actions` as a `Button`.

behavior.summary: A `<header>` containing a `<nav>`: the bar is the page's banner landmark, and the links inside it are a navigation landmark of their own. No primitive — there is no keyboard interaction to own. Nav links are each a tab stop, which is correct for navigation; roving tabindex belongs to a menubar, and calling this one would promise arrow-key behaviour that navigation does not have.

decisions.decision: It renders the `<header>`, so it is the page's banner
decisions.why: A top nav IS the banner — brand, navigation and actions in one bar — and pretending otherwise would mean emitting a bare `<nav>` with a logo and an avatar menu inside it, neither of which is navigation. The consequence is a real constraint rather than a detail: one per page, and not nested inside a `<header>` you already have.

decisions.decision: Links are data; everything else is a slot
decisions.why: The component has to own what the list says — the ordered set of destinations, and which one you are on — so those come in as an array, the same bargain Breadcrumbs makes. A logo, a search box and an account menu are not destinations and do not belong in the nav landmark at all, so they are `brand` and `actions` slots outside it.

decisions.decision: The current page is stated per item, not matched from a path
decisions.why: Only the caller knows whether /invoices/123 counts as being on /invoices — that is their routing, not this component's. A `currentHref` prop would have to guess between exact and prefix matching and would be wrong for someone either way, silently. `current` on the item is one boolean the caller already has the answer to.

decisions.decision: A dropdown is a disclosure, never a menu
decisions.why: An item with `items` becomes a button that shows and hides a list of links. It is not given `role="menu"`, and that is the single most common mistake in a navigation bar: the menu role is for application commands and announces a keyboard model — one tab stop, arrow keys to move, typeahead — that a list of links does not have, so assistive technology describes the widget as something it is not. The W3C's own menubar-navigation examples are being withdrawn over exactly this. A disclosure promises only "this button reveals that", and everything inside stays in the tab order where it was.

decisions.decision: The panel is a popover, for a layout reason rather than a stylistic one
decisions.why: The destination list scrolls its overflow so a long nav does not wrap the bar onto two rows, and an overflow container clips its absolutely positioned descendants — a panel drawn inside the list would be cut off or scroll away with it. The top layer is the only place it can be and still be seen. It stays a child of its `<li>` in the DOM, which is what matters for assistive technology: the accessibility tree follows the document rather than the paint order, so those links are still inside the nav landmark. `popover="auto"` settles one-open-at-a-time and light dismiss for free.

decisions.decision: Rows carry an optional onClick, and still require a real href
decisions.why: Found by trying to build the playground's own rail out of this component: the rows navigate client-side, and with no way to intercept the click there was no way to use it without a full page load. The href stays required rather than becoming optional, because it is what makes the row a link — middle-click, copy-address and crawlers all depend on it, and a nav built from handlers with no addresses behind them loses all three without appearing to.

decisions.decision: No destinations means no navigation landmark
decisions.why: An empty `<nav>` is worse than none: it appears in a landmark list promising places to go and delivers none, which wastes the one tool that exists for skipping straight to the navigation. Found by using this component for the playground's own banner, whose navigation lives in the rail — the first version passed `items={[]}` and produced exactly that empty landmark, alongside a rail with the same name, which is the collision this contract already warned about two decisions above.

decisions.decision: The actions are pushed to the end by their own margin
decisions.why: The nav takes the slack when there is one, which was doing the job invisibly — and then `items` became optional, a banner with its navigation in a side rail rendered no nav at all, and the actions sat against the brand in the middle of the bar. An auto margin on the actions is correct either way: with a nav it adds nothing, without one it does the whole job.

base.summary: The bar. Its height comes from its padding and the controls inside it rather than a stated number, so a nav with a taller control in its actions slot grows instead of clipping.

tokens.actions alignment: pushed to the inline end by an auto margin, so they sit at the end of the bar whether or not there are destinations between them and the brand

item.summary: One destination. The resting colour is the secondary text tone, so the current page reads as the emphasised one rather than the others reading as dimmed.

tokens.font-size: type.control.size.md — 14px. It was the sm step, 12px, which is the size this scale reserves for text inside a small control rather than for a row of running navigation: a rail and a bar are read, not squeezed into a 28px box. Every row takes it, because the disclosure trigger and the nested sublink both compose the link class.
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

item-current.summary: The page you are on. Marked twice over: the accent bar is the visual cue and aria-current is the announced one, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

tokens.indicator: theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, along the block-end edge

name: visually-hidden
title: Visually hidden
description: Takes an element off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.
note: No standalone React component — "Visually hidden" is CSS-only (see registry description), composed onto other components' className.

usage.case: A label whose text is redundant on screen
usage.when: The component's own `labelHidden` prop composes this — a field in a toolbar, a checkbox under a column heading that already names it.
usage.example:
<label className="rata-field-label rata-visually-hidden" htmlFor={id}>
  Search
</label>
usage.notes: The point is what it is *not*: `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` both remove the element from the accessibility tree, so a label hidden that way takes the control's accessible name with it. This clips instead — the element is still rendered, still bound, still read.

usage.case: Naming a group with no visible heading
usage.when: A radiogroup whose question is obvious on screen but has no element to point `labelledBy` at.
usage.example: Billing period …
usage.notes: Better than leaving the group unnamed, and better than pointing `labelledBy` at an id that does not exist — a dangling reference leaves no accessible name at all.

usage.when: Content that should not be announced either.
usage.example: Decorative flourish
usage.notes: Don't. This keeps content in the accessibility tree — that is its entire purpose. Something a screen reader should skip wants `aria-hidden`, or simply not to be rendered.

base.summary: Geometry only. Nothing here is a colour or a type decision, because the element is off screen rather than restyled.

tokens.inline-size: border.1 — a 1px box rather than a zero-size one, because some assistive technology skips elements with no dimensions
tokens.margin: negative border.1, so the 1px box does not occupy a pixel of layout
tokens.clip-path: inset(50%) — clips to nothing, which is what keeps the element in the accessibility tree while display:none and visibility:hidden would not
tokens.overflow: hidden, so the clipped content cannot reappear as a scroll region
tokens.white-space: nowrap, so a long string does not lay out and affect scroll height before it is clipped
